C0001.name: extended reality
C0001.definition: Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

C0002.name: virtual reality
C0002.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

C0003.name: augmented reality
C0003.definition: Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.

C0004.name: mixed reality
C0004.definition: Mixed reality (MR) is an immersive technology that is the same as augmented reality, in which digital content is overlaid on the view of reality and can be interacted with.

C0005.name: head-mounted display
C0005.definition: A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.

C0006.name: virtual environment
C0006.definition: Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

C0007.name: virtual object
C0007.definition: A virtual object is an object that does not exist in the real world and can be seen in a virtual world or added to the real world so that it appears to coexist with real objects.

C0008.name: immersive technology
C0008.definition: Immersive technology is a technology that produces an experience in which a person perceives an environment through sensory organs as real, so that they cannot distinguish it from their real environment.

C0009.name: immersive experience
C0009.definition: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and perceives it as that real environment.

C0010.name: reality-virtuality continuum
C0010.definition: Reality-virtuality continuum is a scale whose extremes are a completely real environment with nothing virtual and a completely virtual environment with nothing real, with augmented reality and augmented virtuality as intermediate states between them.

C0011.name: augmented virtuality
C0011.definition: Augmented virtuality is the intermediate state on the reality-virtuality continuum, opposite augmented reality, in which a virtual environment is augmented with real-world images, videos, or live capture appearing in real time.

C0012.name: market size
C0012.definition: Market size is the monetary value of the extended reality market, split into hardware and software portions.

C0013.name: hardware
C0013.definition: Hardware is a part of an extended reality (XR) system, including input devices, output devices, processing devices, central processing units, graphics processing units, and memory.

C0014.name: software
C0014.definition: Software is a resource in extended reality that is used to process input data, generate output data, and create a relationship between the user and the virtual environment.

C0015.name: metaverse
C0015.definition: Metaverse is a broad view of an all-around three-dimensional environment in which people act as in the real world through natural interaction with digital content, reimagining human interaction with the digital world rather than being merely an application of virtual reality, mixed reality, or augmented reality technology.

C0016.name: three-dimensional environment
C0016.definition: A three-dimensional environment is an all-around environment in the metaverse in which people act as they do in the real world and use natural interaction with digital content.

C0017.name: natural interaction
C0017.definition: Natural interaction is a form of interacting with digital content in an all-around three-dimensional environment, in which people act as they do in the real world, unlike mostly flat two-dimensional screen interactions.

C0018.name: artificial intelligence
C0018.definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the major emerging areas identified by many national governments.

C0019.name: large language model
C0019.definition: A large language model is an emerging area that can be used for enhanced interactivity in extended reality applications.

C0020.name: generative artificial intelligence
C0020.definition: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is an emerging area that can be used for enhanced interactivity in extended reality applications.

C0021.name: drone
C0021.definition: Drone is one of the major emerging areas identified by many national governments.

C0022.name: nanomaterial
C0022.definition: Nanomaterial is one of the major emerging areas identified by many national governments.

C0023.name: mixed reality visual display
C0023.definition: A mixed reality visual display is the subject of an early influential paper in the field of mixed reality visual displays.

C0024.name: video games
C0024.definition: Video games are one of the application areas for extended reality.

C0025.name: healthcare
C0025.definition: Healthcare is a prominent application domain for virtual reality (VR) and mixed reality (MR), primarily for medical education and training.

C0026.name: engineering
C0026.definition: Engineering is one of the application areas in which extended reality is expected to have commercial potential.

C0027.name: live events
C0027.definition: Live events are one of the application areas in which extended reality has commercial potential.

C0028.name: video entertainment
C0028.definition: Video entertainment is one of the application areas in which extended reality has commercial potential.

C0029.name: real estate and architecture
C0029.definition: Real estate and architecture is a major virtual reality application area in which potential buyers can explore upcoming properties, including properties that do not yet exist, without visiting the place, so they can make informed purchase decisions.

C0030.name: retail
C0030.definition: Retail is one of the application areas in which extended reality has commercial potential.

C0031.name: defense
C0031.definition: Defense is one of the major current virtual reality (VR) application areas used for training, including simulation of vehicles, soldiers, and combat environments, virtual boot camp and combat training, medical personnel training, and maintenance and assembly technician training.

C0032.name: application domain
C0032.definition: An application domain is an area in which virtual reality or augmented reality applications are used.

C0033.name: gaming and entertainment
C0033.definition: Gaming and entertainment is an early and current virtual reality (VR) application domain in which immersive gaming products use immersive technologies and players wear headsets or other VR devices to experience immersion.

C0034.name: education
C0034.definition: Education is an emerging application domain for immersive technologies, from primary to tertiary levels, in which appropriate exposure can improve learners' engagement and learning outcomes, although excessive duration may create problems.

C0035.name: automobile industry
C0035.definition: The automobile industry is an evolving virtual reality application domain in which companies create immersive experiences of newly launched car models without showroom visits or actual driving to increase customer satisfaction and experience.

C0036.name: travel and tourism
C0036.definition: Travel and tourism is an emerging application domain for virtual reality, in which virtual tours and virtual tourism let users visit faraway places without physically going there and save money and physical effort.

C0037.name: virtual tourism
C0037.definition: Virtual tourism is a virtual reality application in travel and tourism that lets users visit faraway places without physically going there and save money and physical effort.

C0038.name: digital heritage preservation
C0038.definition: Digital heritage preservation is the process of using digital media to preserve cultural, educational, scientific, ecological, or other heritage by archiving, digitizing, and using immersive technologies such as virtual reality and augmented reality, allowing virtual exploration of heritage places that cannot be physically visited by large numbers of users or in all parts.

C0039.name: immersive gaming product
C0039.definition: Immersive gaming product is a virtual reality gaming product that uses immersive technologies, and players are expected to wear headsets or other VR devices to experience immersion.

C0040.name: virtual reality device
C0040.definition: A virtual reality device is a device worn by players in virtual reality gaming to experience immersion.

C0041.name: immersion
C0041.definition: Immersion is the objective, quantifiable degree to which a virtual reality system projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in an extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing way.

C0042.name: immersive simulation
C0042.definition: Immersive simulation is used in virtual or mixed reality healthcare applications to help medical education and training when obtaining cadavers is difficult.

C0043.name: virtual reality tour
C0043.definition: A virtual reality tour is a virtual reality experience for visiting a recreated place without physically going there, in which movement from one point to another is either user-controlled or system-controlled.

C0044.name: heritage tourism
C0044.definition: Heritage tourism is an emerging immersive-technology application for heritage places that cannot be physically visited by large numbers of users or in all parts for preservation reasons, letting users explore each part virtually.

C0045.name: training
C0045.definition: Training is a purpose of virtual reality applications, such as defense, and a part of agile development release and sprint processes with testing and documentation.

C0046.name: military training
C0046.definition: Military training is a specialized virtual reality training application for defense that simulates vehicles, soldiers, and combat environments with constraints.

C0047.name: simulation
C0047.definition: Simulation is used in defense virtual reality training to simulate vehicles, soldiers, and combat environments with constraints.

C0048.name: virtual boot camp
C0048.definition: Virtual boot camp is a virtual reality training application for specialized military training that uses head-mounted displays with motion trackers, full-body tracking systems, and wireless weapon controllers.

C0049.name: combat training
C0049.definition: Combat training is a virtual reality training application for defense that uses head-mounted displays with motion trackers, full-body tracking systems, and wireless weapon controllers.

C0050.name: motion tracker
C0050.definition: A motion tracker is used in virtual reality training with head-mounted displays.

C0051.name: full-body tracking system
C0051.definition: A full-body tracking system is used in virtual boot camp and combat training with head-mounted displays, motion trackers, and wireless weapon controllers.

C0052.name: wireless weapon controller
C0052.definition: A wireless weapon controller is used in virtual boot camp and combat training with head-mounted displays, motion trackers, and full-body tracking systems.

C0053.name: military medical personnel
C0053.definition: Military medical personnel are personnel for whom training is included in defense virtual reality applications.

C0054.name: maintenance and assembly technician training
C0054.definition: Maintenance and assembly technician training is one of the virtual reality training applications in defense.

C0055.name: virtual reality system
C0055.definition: A virtual reality system is a system that presents a computer-generated artificial environment, provides computer-generated sensory stimuli for an immersive experience, and lets the user's actions partially determine what happens in it.

C0056.name: non-immersive virtual reality system
C0056.definition: A non-immersive virtual reality system is a limited class of computer application that provides a computer-generated environment in which a user controls characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment. The user is psychologically engaged and remains physically attached to the real world, while the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user.

C0057.name: semi-immersive virtual reality system
C0057.definition: Semi-immersive virtual reality system is a type of virtual reality system, positioned between non-immersive and fully immersive systems, that gives the user a partial immersive experience by blocking some but not all senses while leaving the user free to sense the real world.

C0058.name: fully immersive virtual reality system
C0058.definition: Fully immersive virtual reality system is a virtual reality system that completely blocks the user's ability to sense the real world by blocking all senses, so the user senses only the virtual world and feels physically present in it.

C0059.name: computer application
C0059.definition: Computer application is the class of which a non-immersive virtual reality system is a specific, limited class.

C0060.name: computer system
C0060.definition: A computer system is a regular system that can be a non-immersive virtual reality application.

C0061.name: gaming application
C0061.definition: A gaming application is an application included in non-immersive virtual reality, and it relies on computer or video game console displays and input devices.

C0062.name: PlayStation
C0062.definition: PlayStation is a system whose games are examples of non-immersive virtual reality gaming applications.

C0063.name: Xbox
C0063.definition: Xbox is a system for games that are examples of non-immersive virtual reality.

C0064.name: World of Warcraft
C0064.definition: World of Warcraft is a gaming application that is an example of non-immersive virtual reality.

C0065.name: computer
C0065.definition: A computer is one of the major components of virtual reality (VR) hardware, a device that processes data from input sensors and activates output devices so that a user can perceive the world.

C0066.name: video game console
C0066.definition: A video game console is a system whose displays and input devices are used by non-immersive virtual reality gaming applications.

C0067.name: output device
C0067.definition: An output device is an XR hardware component that produces output to stimulate a user's sensory organs, not only a visual display; examples include visual displays, audio output, haptics, motion platforms, and treadmills.

C0068.name: input device
C0068.definition: Input device is XR hardware that captures or tracks a user's input, actions, or positions and sends that data to an XR system for processing.

C0069.name: keyboard
C0069.definition: A keyboard is an input device used in virtual reality to provide input and to control user locomotion.

C0070.name: mouse
C0070.definition: Mouse is an input device used with computer or console displays, and used in virtual reality to control an avatar's locomotion.

C0071.name: handheld controller
C0071.definition: A handheld controller is an input device held by the user, used in non-immersive VR, and an example of a self-grounded haptic device.

C0072.name: three-dimensional virtual environment
C0072.definition: Three-dimensional virtual environment is a virtual reality environment in which users can move by themselves through a computer screen, VR box, or VR headset, typically without real physical movement.

C0073.name: screen
C0073.definition: A screen is a display on which an image or content is shown so that a human can perceive it.

C0074.name: VR box
C0074.definition: A VR box is one of the ways users can move by themselves through a semi-immersive virtual reality environment.

C0075.name: virtual reality headset
C0075.definition: Virtual reality headset is a wearable display that places a screen close to the eyes and uses a lens to focus the screen's light on the retina, making the screen appear as a virtual image.

C0076.name: device-based virtual tour
C0076.definition: A device-based virtual tour is a kind of virtual tour that uses only a headset.

C0077.name: web-based virtual tour
C0077.definition: A web-based virtual tour is a virtual tour that uses only a headset and is an example of semi-immersive virtual reality.

C0078.name: helmet
C0078.definition: A helmet is a device used in fully immersive virtual reality systems through which users view the virtual environment.

C0079.name: glove
C0079.definition: A glove is one of the devices used in fully immersive virtual reality systems.

C0080.name: body connector
C0080.definition: A body connector is a device used in fully immersive virtual reality systems, with sense detectors, to detect a user's actual movements, reactions, and blinks and translate them into actions in the virtual environment.

C0081.name: sense detector
C0081.definition: A sense detector is part of body connectors in fully immersive virtual reality systems and is used to detect users' movements, reactions, and eye blinks.

C0082.name: body suit
C0082.definition: Body suit is a force feedback device, common in many extended reality (XR) systems, particularly virtual reality (VR) systems, that provides touch sensation, typically in the form of vibrations.

C0083.name: virtual shooting game zone
C0083.definition: A virtual shooting game zone is a dedicated fully immersive virtual reality system that detects and translates the user's actual movements, reactions, and even a blink of an eye into actions in a virtual environment while the user cannot sense the real world.

C0084.name: Pokemon Go
C0084.definition: Pokemon Go is an augmented reality (AR) gaming application.

C0085.name: Gatwick Airport passenger app
C0085.definition: The Gatwick Airport passenger app is a passenger app that used beacons placed at different points in a passenger terminal to tell a passenger their exact location and the direction to move to reach a desired terminal.

C0086.name: beacon
C0086.definition: A beacon is used by a passenger app at points in a terminal to tell a passenger their exact location and the direction to move to reach a desired terminal.

C0087.name: customer-experience application
C0087.definition: Customer-experience application is an augmented reality application that lets a customer preview or virtually try on a product before purchase.

C0088.name: IKEA Place app
C0088.definition: IKEA Place app is an augmented reality customer-experience application that lets a user scan a room and place IKEA objects in a digital image of the room to see how the room would look before purchase.

C0089.name: Dulux visualizer app
C0089.definition: The Dulux visualizer app is an augmented reality customer-experience application that lets a customer digitally paint walls on a screen and see the effect before deciding whether to buy paint.

C0090.name: virtual tape measure application
C0090.definition: Virtual tape measure application is an augmented reality application that can measure the heights and lengths of objects inside or outside a room using a mobile phone, so a physical tape is not needed.

C0091.name: mobile phone
C0091.definition: A mobile phone is used for augmented reality applications, and early mobile phones looked different from modern-day smartphones but were still used for mobile-based augmented reality applications.

C0092.name: try-on application
C0092.definition: A try-on application is an augmented reality customer-experience application used before purchase that lets a customer virtually try different products on a digital representation of themselves and decide whether to buy.

C0093.name: Sephora app
C0093.definition: The Sephora app is an augmented reality customer-experience try-on application before purchase that lets a customer virtually try different cosmetic looks on a digital face and choose the product color that satisfies the customer the most.

C0094.name: Rolex app
C0094.definition: The Rolex app is an augmented reality try-on application that lets a customer try different watch models on a digital representation of their hand before purchase.

C0095.name: augmented reality application
C0095.definition: An augmented reality application is an application that emphasizes augmenting digital content onto the real-world view rather than being immersive.

C0096.name: medical training
C0096.definition: Medical training is one of the augmented reality applications in healthcare.

C0097.name: telemedicine
C0097.definition: Telemedicine is an augmented reality application in healthcare that enables medical professionals to interact with patients.

C0098.name: diagnosis
C0098.definition: Diagnosis is a medical activity that real-time information in treatment areas of augmented reality applications supports.

C0099.name: surgery
C0099.definition: Surgery is one of the things in treatment areas that augmented reality applications can support with real-time information.

C0100.name: treatment plan
C0100.definition: A treatment plan is one of the things supported by real-time information in treatment areas in healthcare augmented reality applications.

C0101.name: AccuVein
C0101.definition: AccuVein is a handheld augmented reality device that, when pointed at a patient's skin surface, scans and visualizes the internal vein network and can indicate the patient's condition to help decide treatment.

C0102.name: vein network
C0102.definition: Vein network is a patient's internal vein network that can be scanned and visualized by an augmented reality device pointed at the skin surface to help decide the treatment course.

C0103.name: marker-based augmented reality application
C0103.definition: A marker-based augmented reality application is an augmented reality application that uses markers placed in the environment to trigger an augmented experience, with the desired digital content appearing at the detected marker's position in the real-world view.

C0104.name: markerless augmented reality application
C0104.definition: A markerless augmented reality application is an augmented reality application that does not require physical markers and lets users choose where to place virtual objects; it includes location-based, superimposition-based, projection-based, and outlining-based types.

C0105.name: location-based markerless augmented reality application
C0105.definition: A location-based markerless augmented reality application is a type of markerless augmented reality application that relies on a location sensor, such as a global positioning system (GPS) sensor, to detect the user's location with respect to a reference frame, with digital content augmented on the real-world view when the user is at a specific location.

C0106.name: superimposition-based markerless augmented reality application
C0106.definition: A superimposition-based markerless augmented reality application is a markerless augmented reality application that recognizes one or multiple physical objects using computer vision techniques and superimposes digital content on the real-world scene depending on the recognized objects.

C0107.name: projection-based markerless augmented reality application
C0107.definition: A projection-based markerless augmented reality application is a markerless augmented reality application that uses light projectors to project digital graphics, digital characters, or other digital content onto an object, a surface, or a space.

C0108.name: outlining-based markerless augmented reality application
C0108.definition: An outlining-based markerless augmented reality application is a markerless augmented reality application that uses object recognition to recreate the user's immediate surroundings and digitally enhance the view.

C0109.name: marker
C0109.definition: A marker is a real-world object or image placed in the environment that a system detects to identify its position or track a user's motion and to place digital content at that position.

C0110.name: quick response code
C0110.definition: A quick response code (QR) is a marker used in marker-based augmented reality applications.

C0111.name: simple color code
C0111.definition: A simple color code is a marker used in marker-based augmented reality applications.

C0112.name: color bar
C0112.definition: A color bar is one of the markers used in marker-based augmented reality applications.

C0113.name: fiducial marker
C0113.definition: A fiducial marker is a marker used in marker-based augmented reality applications and camera-based full-body tracking, and can aid registration.

C0114.name: computer vision
C0114.definition: Computer vision (CV) is an enabling technology for augmented reality and mixed reality applications that detects, recognizes, and tracks objects in real-world scenes.

C0115.name: location sensor
C0115.definition: A location sensor is a sensor that detects a user's location with respect to a reference frame in location-based markerless augmented reality applications.

C0116.name: global positioning system
C0116.definition: Global positioning system (GPS) is a positional tracking device, particularly useful outdoors, that generally offers low accuracy, particularly indoors, and allows only positional tracking. It is typically used when an approximate position is good enough or as part of a hybrid tracking system, and real time kinematic (RTK) technology can improve its basic accuracy.

C0117.name: reference frame
C0117.definition: A reference frame is a coordinate system in which locations or positions are defined.

C0118.name: light projector
C0118.definition: A light projector is a projector used in projection-based markerless augmented reality applications to project digital content onto an object, a surface, or a space.

C0119.name: holographic projection
C0119.definition: Holographic projection is a projection-based technique that can be used in augmented reality application development.

C0120.name: object recognition
C0120.definition: Object recognition is a computer vision operation used in outlining-based markerless augmented reality applications to recreate a user's immediate surroundings and digitally enhance the view.

C0121.name: virtual reality system category
C0121.definition: A virtual reality system category is a category of virtual reality systems based on the experience or psychological aspect, with non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems as the categories.

C0122.name: augmented reality system category
C0122.definition: An augmented reality system category is a category of augmented reality systems, broadly marker-based or markerless, based primarily on the technology used to develop and deploy them rather than on a psychological aspect.

C0123.name: marker-based augmented reality
C0123.definition: Marker-based augmented reality is a type of augmented reality system that recognizes a marker image by matching its color, shape, and size, and displays a three-dimensional model in the marker's place.

C0124.name: markerless augmented reality
C0124.definition: Markerless augmented reality is a type of augmented reality system and one of the main technologies relied on by handheld augmented reality devices.

C0125.name: markerless augmented reality technique
C0125.definition: Markerless augmented reality technique is an augmented reality technique that overcomes the difficulty of maintaining markers in marker-based systems and that relies primarily on computer vision and may rely on other sensors in location-based applications.

C0126.name: computer vision-based augmented reality application
C0126.definition: A computer vision-based augmented reality application is an augmented reality application that is superimposition-based or outline-based.

C0127.name: superimposition-based application
C0127.definition: A superimposition-based application is a kind of computer vision-based augmented reality application.

C0128.name: outline-based application
C0128.definition: An outline-based application is a kind of computer vision-based augmented reality (AR) application.

C0129.name: projection-based technique
C0129.definition: A projection-based technique is a technique that can be used in augmented reality application development.

C0130.name: virtual reality application
C0130.definition: A virtual reality application is an immersive application that involves creating a virtual environment, rendering a stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions.

C0131.name: virtual
C0131.definition: Virtual is a term that means being in essence or effect but not in fact, that is, something that is there but cannot be attributed to any factual things.

C0132.name: reality
C0132.definition: Reality is the state or quality of being real, as something that exists independently of ideas concerning it, or as something that constitutes a real or actual thing as distinguished from something merely apparent.

C0133.name: sensory experience
C0133.definition: Sensory experience is a characteristic of a virtual reality system in which the system provides computer-generated stimuli to the user's sensory organs, such as eyes and ears, so that the user immersively experiences an artificial or synthetic environment.

C0134.name: computer-generated stimuli
C0134.definition: Computer-generated stimuli are stimuli that a virtual reality system provides to a user's sensory organs for an immersive experience of an artificial or synthetic environment.

C0135.name: user action
C0135.definition: User action is an interaction by a user with elements in an environment, partially determining what happens in the environment.

C0136.name: real time
C0136.definition: Real time is a condition in which interactions are reflected immediately and content loading has minimal latency.

C0137.name: user interaction
C0137.definition: User interaction is a characteristic of a virtual reality system in which the user can act on or interact with elements in the environment, and user actions or inputs partially determine what happens, producing dynamic changes in the virtual environment.

C0138.name: interaction
C0138.definition: Interaction is the activity that takes place between a user and a system, often by manipulating an image or parts of it with input devices. In immersive environments it is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and system control.

C0139.name: computer-aided design system
C0139.definition: A computer-aided design system is a system that supports a virtual environment and interaction but does not support an immersive experience, because the user interacts with screen content through a mouse while still seeing the real world around the computer screen.

C0140.name: video conferencing system
C0140.definition: A video conferencing system is an interactive system that presents a real-world environment in real time through a screen, with the user remaining in the real world and the screen only aiding interaction, so it is not a virtual environment or an immersive experience.

C0141.name: three-dimensional movie experience
C0141.definition: A three-dimensional movie experience is a partly immersive, non-interactive experience that provides a virtual environment, but the viewer only watches and cannot change the displayed content.

C0142.name: augmented reality system
C0142.definition: An augmented reality system is a system with four required characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content registered in 3D, that content is experienced through the user's sensory organs, and it supports real-time interaction with that content in the enhanced environment.

C0143.name: three-dimensional
C0143.definition: Three-dimensional (3D) is used to describe registered augmented reality enhancements, selectable regions of virtual space, and games or interactive content.

C0144.name: sensory organ
C0144.definition: A sensory organ is hardware of sensing in the human body that contains receptors that receive stimuli and is designed to perceive the real world rather than a virtual world.

C0145.name: physical environment
C0145.definition: Physical environment is one extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, the other extreme being the virtual environment.

C0146.name: early era
C0146.definition: Early era is a phase in the historical evolution of virtual reality that existed before modern digital computers were developed and included a few key developments conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

C0147.name: digital computer
C0147.definition: A digital computer is a modern computer developed in the 1940s, and its advent ended the early era of virtual reality.

C0148.name: formative years
C0148.definition: Formative years are the second phase of the historical evolution of virtual reality, spanning roughly 1950 to 1990.

C0149.name: modern phase
C0149.definition: The modern phase is one of the phases in the historical evolution of virtual reality, spanning roughly from 1990 to 2015.

C0150.name: current growth phase
C0150.definition: The current growth phase is the last and continuing phase in the historical evolution of virtual reality, beginning roughly in 2016 when commercial virtual reality headsets made immersive experiences affordable to a large population and spurred growth in the field.

C0151.name: historical evolution
C0151.definition: Historical evolution is the development of virtual reality in eras or phases.

C0152.name: Sir Charles Wheatstone
C0152.definition: Sir Charles Wheatstone is a person whose demonstration of a stereoscopic device was roughly considered a first step toward immersive experience.

C0153.name: stereoscopic device
C0153.definition: A stereoscopic device is a device whose demonstration established that the human brain can process 2D images as 3D objects.

C0154.name: two-dimensional image
C0154.definition: A two-dimensional image is a representation of a scene that can be presented by a display device and that stereoscopic vision can make a user perceive as a three-dimensional object or space.

C0155.name: three-dimensional object
C0155.definition: A three-dimensional object is an object perceived through stereoscopic vision from two-dimensional images or rendered at a tracked position in augmented reality.

C0156.name: display device
C0156.definition: A display device is a device that uses a pixel grid to render two-dimensional images for an immersive experience, either in front of a user's eyes or in an environment surrounding the user.

C0157.name: stereoscopic vision
C0157.definition: Stereoscopic vision is the perception of three-dimensional objects and space from left and right two-dimensional images processed simultaneously, aided by binocular vision.

C0158.name: three-dimensional space
C0158.definition: Three-dimensional space is the space with x, y, and z axes in which an object can have three translational and three rotational degrees of freedom.

C0159.name: David Brewster
C0159.definition: David Brewster is a person whose compact-sized stereoscope was an early form of stereoscopic display.

C0160.name: stereoscope
C0160.definition: A stereoscope is a stereoscopic display that creates the illusion of depth in viewed images.

C0161.name: stereoscopic display
C0161.definition: Stereoscopic display is a display that creates the illusion of depth in viewed images.

C0162.name: illusion of depth
C0162.definition: Illusion of depth is an illusion created in viewed images by a stereoscopic display.

C0163.name: Edwin A. Link
C0163.definition: Edwin A. Link is the person who first introduced the flight simulator concept.

C0164.name: flight simulator
C0164.definition: A flight simulator is an early development considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality, evolving into sophisticated forms with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience.

C0165.name: sensor
C0165.definition: Sensor is a device that converts an energy source into electrical signals, or, in the human body, an organ that converts a stimulus into neural impulses; in XR hardware it is a tracking device that tracks a user's movements and extracts information from the real world.

C0166.name: computer monitor
C0166.definition: A computer monitor is a regular computer display.

C0167.name: Philco Corporation
C0167.definition: Philco Corporation is a corporation whose engineers developed an early head-mounted display (HMD).

C0168.name: Morton Heilig
C0168.definition: Morton Heilig is the person who introduced Sensorama, which can be considered the first immersive virtual reality system under the modern definition of virtual reality.

C0169.name: Sensorama
C0169.definition: Sensorama is an immersive virtual reality system that can be considered the first such system under the modern definition of virtual reality and that stimulated all sensory organs with 3D wide vision, stereo sound, smells, wind, and vibrations.

C0170.name: immersive virtual reality system
C0170.definition: Immersive virtual reality system is a virtual reality system under the modern definition of virtual reality.

C0171.name: stereo sound
C0171.definition: Stereo sound is one of the sensory features that Sensorama was publicized as having.

C0172.name: haptics
C0172.definition: Haptics is a virtual reality output device that lets a user feel vibrations.

C0173.name: Tom Furness
C0173.definition: Tom Furness is a person who, with colleagues at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, worked on visually coupled systems for pilots using head-mounted displays and began research on the US Air Force super cockpit program, which produced technologies relevant to augmented reality.

C0174.name: Wright-Patterson Air Force Base
C0174.definition: Wright-Patterson Air Force Base is an air force base where work on visually coupled systems for pilots that consisted of head-mounted displays was done.

C0175.name: visually coupled system
C0175.definition: A visually coupled system is a system that consists of a head-mounted display.

C0176.name: Sutherland
C0176.definition: Sutherland is a head-mounted display developer who was the first to demonstrate a head-mounted display with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

C0177.name: Sword of Damocles
C0177.definition: The Sword of Damocles is a head-mounted display (HMD) that was first demonstrated with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

C0178.name: head tracking
C0178.definition: Head tracking is a non-hand input technique in virtual reality that tracks the head, and it is commonly the most important thing to track and is sufficient for the visual and aural components related to the eyes and ears.

C0179.name: computer-generated imagery
C0179.definition: Computer-generated imagery is imagery that can be seen through a head-mounted display, either superimposed over a real-world view or replacing it.

C0180.name: Fred Brooks
C0180.definition: Fred Brooks is a person who developed a haptic feedback system.

C0181.name: University of North Carolina
C0181.definition: University of North Carolina is a university where a haptic feedback system was developed and augmented reality research projects were conducted.

C0182.name: haptic feedback system
C0182.definition: A haptic feedback system is a system that uses a force feedback device to let a user feel, through touch, objects shown on a screen while manipulating them.

C0183.name: force feedback device
C0183.definition: A force feedback device is an engineered device that provides touch sensation in extended reality, typically as vibrations, by letting users feel objects through touch while manipulating them.

C0184.name: Krueger
C0184.definition: Krueger is a person who used the term artificial reality, an early term that eventually evolved into virtual reality.

C0185.name: artificial reality
C0185.definition: Artificial reality is an early term that eventually evolved into the modern term virtual reality.

C0186.name: Scott Fisher
C0186.definition: Scott Fisher is a person at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration who, with colleagues, developed and launched a stereoscopic head-tracked head-mounted display.

C0187.name: National Aeronautics and Space Administration
C0187.definition: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is an organization that developed a head-tracked head-mounted display and whose HMDs are part of the evolution of head-mounted displays.

C0188.name: Virtual Visual Environment Display
C0188.definition: Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED) is the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic, head-tracked head-mounted display with a wide field of view.

C0189.name: stereoscopic
C0189.definition: Stereoscopic is used to describe a head-tracked head-mounted display.

C0190.name: field of view
C0190.definition: Field of view (FOV) is an angular measure of the region visible to the eye at a single point in time, and in virtual reality it is the amount of virtual environment visible.

C0191.name: data glove
C0191.definition: A data glove is a hand-worn input device with bend or fingertip sensors that detect hand postures, gestures, or pinch gestures.

C0192.name: Jaron Lanier
C0192.definition: Jaron Lanier is a person who proposed the term virtual reality.

C0193.name: CAVE system
C0193.definition: CAVE system is an immersive system that renders images in a surrounding setting, making a user feel surrounded by holograms.

C0194.name: University of Illinois at Chicago's Electronic Visualization Laboratory
C0194.definition: The University of Illinois at Chicago's Electronic Visualization Laboratory is the laboratory where the CAVE system was invented.

C0195.name: Silicon Graphics computer
C0195.definition: A Silicon Graphics computer is a computer used to render images in a surrounding immersive setting.

C0196.name: Sense8
C0196.definition: Sense8 is a company that developed the WTK software package for higher-level virtual reality application development.

C0197.name: world toolkit
C0197.definition: World toolkit (WTK) is a software package for higher-level application development in virtual reality.

C0198.name: virtual reality modeling language
C0198.definition: Virtual reality modeling language (VRML) is a modeling language for virtual reality.

C0199.name: modeling language
C0199.definition: A modeling language is a language for virtual reality.

C0200.name: extensible three-dimensional
C0200.definition: Extensible three-dimensional (X3D) is a modeling language for virtual reality.

C0201.name: Java 3D
C0201.definition: Java 3D is one of the modeling languages for virtual reality.

C0202.name: White 5
C0202.definition: White 5 is a head-mounted display (HMD) with a 150-degree field of view.

C0203.name: Mark Bolas
C0203.definition: Mark Bolas is one of the creators of the White 5 head-mounted display.

C0204.name: University of Southern California's MXR lab
C0204.definition: University of Southern California's MXR lab is a University of Southern California lab associated with the creation of the White 5 head-mounted display.

C0205.name: Ian McDowall
C0205.definition: Ian McDowall of Fakespace Labs is one of the creators of the White 5 head-mounted display.

C0206.name: Fakespace Labs
C0206.definition: Fakespace Labs is an organization linked to a creator of a head-mounted display.

C0207.name: Oculus Rift
C0207.definition: Oculus Rift is an inexpensive virtual reality headset that uses the Oculus SDK.

C0208.name: Palmer Luckey
C0208.definition: Palmer Luckey is the creator of the Oculus Rift, an inexpensive virtual reality (VR) headset.

C0209.name: Facebook
C0209.definition: Facebook is a well-known company that purchased and tried to popularize the Oculus Rift virtual reality headset.

C0210.name: HTC Vive
C0210.definition: The HTC Vive is one of the commercial virtual reality headsets.

C0211.name: High Tech Computer
C0211.definition: High Tech Computer (HTC) is a well-known company that released a commercial virtual reality headset.

C0212.name: PlayStation virtual reality headset
C0212.definition: The PlayStation virtual reality headset is a commercial virtual reality headset released by Sony.

C0213.name: Sony
C0213.definition: Sony is a company that released one of the commercial virtual reality headsets in 2016.

C0214.name: HoloLens
C0214.definition: HoloLens is a commercial virtual reality headset from Microsoft.

C0215.name: Microsoft
C0215.definition: Microsoft is a well-known company that released a commercial virtual reality headset.

C0216.name: Zuckerberg
C0216.definition: Zuckerberg is a person associated with Meta who popularized the term Metaverse.

C0217.name: Meta
C0217.definition: Meta is the name of the affiliation of the person who popularized the term Metaverse.

C0218.name: Apple Vision Pro
C0218.definition: Apple Vision Pro is a virtual reality headset.

C0219.name: Apple
C0219.definition: Apple is a company that released a virtual reality headset and launched an augmented reality software development kit.

C0220.name: immersive display
C0220.definition: An immersive display is one of the developments in virtual reality that is expected to improve as the VR growth phase continues.

C0221.name: experimental phase
C0221.definition: The experimental phase is a phase in the historical evolution of augmented reality (AR) that involved early experimentation defining AR concepts and showing the types of technology required for AR.

C0222.name: basic research phase
C0222.definition: Basic research phase is a phase in the historical evolution of augmented reality that followed the experimental phase and involved research into enabling technologies such as tracking, displays, and input devices.

C0223.name: tools or applications phase
C0223.definition: Tools or applications phase is the phase of the historical evolution of augmented reality from the mid-1990s to 2007 in which early applications were developed or explored, along with exploratory tasks related to interaction techniques, usability, and design theory for augmented reality.

C0224.name: commercial application phase
C0224.definition: Commercial application phase is the phase of the historical evolution of augmented reality from 2007 to the present, characterized by widespread augmented reality availability and newer applications in domains such as gaming, medicine, mobile, commerce, and marketing.

C0225.name: tracking
C0225.definition: Tracking is the integral XR hardware component that keeps track of physical-world motion, translating user pose, position, and orientation—or real objects—into virtual motion or 3D content registered to a real-world anchor.

C0226.name: interaction technique
C0226.definition: An interaction technique is a method used in virtual reality to select or manipulate virtual objects, navigate a virtual world, or issue system-control commands.

C0227.name: usability
C0227.definition: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user: the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

C0228.name: design theory
C0228.definition: Design theory is a topic of exploratory tasks in augmented reality, related to interaction techniques and the usability of early AR applications.

C0229.name: Ivan Sutherland
C0229.definition: Ivan Sutherland is one of the creators of the first truly computer-generated augmented reality prototype.

C0230.name: Bob Sproull
C0230.definition: Bob Sproull is one of the creators of the first truly computer-generated augmented reality prototype.

C0231.name: Sutherland-Sproull augmented reality prototype
C0231.definition: The Sutherland-Sproull augmented reality prototype is the first truly computer-generated augmented reality prototype, combining a cathode ray tube-based optical see-through head-mounted display with a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system that registered head movements in three dimensions.

C0232.name: cathode ray tube
C0232.definition: Cathode ray tube (CRT) is a display used in augmented reality and virtual reality systems.

C0233.name: optical see-through head-mounted display
C0233.definition: An optical see-through head-mounted display is a type of head-mounted display that is typically used in augmented reality.

C0234.name: mechanical tracking system
C0234.definition: A mechanical tracking system is a tracking system that registers head movements in three dimensions.

C0235.name: PDP-11 computer
C0235.definition: The PDP-11 computer is a computer connected to a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system and custom graphics hardware in an augmented reality prototype.

C0236.name: graphics hardware
C0236.definition: Graphics hardware is custom hardware used in an augmented reality prototype with a head-mounted display, a tracking system, and a computer.

C0237.name: ultrasonic tracker
C0237.definition: An ultrasonic tracker is a tracker that replaced a mechanical tracker used to register head movements in three dimensions in an augmented reality prototype.

C0238.name: super cockpit program
C0238.definition: The super cockpit program is a major US Air Force research program that produced technologies relevant to augmented reality, and in its super cockpit prototype a pilot wearing a head-mounted display saw computer-generated imagery superimposed over the real-world view in daylight and saw computer-generated imagery replace the real-world view at night or in bad weather.

C0239.name: super cockpit prototype
C0239.definition: The super cockpit prototype is an aircraft-cockpit prototype in which a pilot wearing a head-mounted display sees computer-generated imagery superimposed over the real-world view in daylight or replacing it at night or in bad weather.

C0240.name: head-mounted augmented reality display
C0240.definition: A head-mounted augmented reality display is a display used in modern aircraft.

C0241.name: virtual reality display
C0241.definition: A virtual reality display is a display, such as a head-mounted display.

C0242.name: input hardware
C0242.definition: Input hardware is hardware that early augmented reality experiments led to.

C0243.name: tracking hardware
C0243.definition: Tracking hardware is hardware involved in interactions in a virtual reality experience, and understanding how a camera works helps build it.

C0244.name: Tom Caudell
C0244.definition: Tom Caudell is a person often credited with coining the phrase augmented reality (AR).

C0245.name: registration tracking
C0245.definition: Registration tracking is a technique included in basic research projects for augmented reality.

C0246.name: see-through head-mounted display
C0246.definition: A see-through head-mounted display is a head-mounted display typically used in augmented reality.

C0247.name: Columbia University
C0247.definition: Columbia University is a university where augmented reality research was carried out.

C0248.name: KARMA system
C0248.definition: The KARMA system is an augmented reality system described in an early academic paper on augmented reality.

C0249.name: augmented reality interaction method
C0249.definition: An augmented reality interaction method is a method for interacting with augmented digital content.

C0250.name: mobile augmented reality system
C0250.definition: A mobile augmented reality system is an augmented reality system used with handheld or head-mounted displays to superimpose virtual content on real objects.

C0251.name: University of Toronto
C0251.definition: The University of Toronto is a university where augmented reality research was conducted.

C0252.name: stereoscopic video
C0252.definition: Stereoscopic video is video on which virtual cues were overlaid in augmented reality research.

C0253.name: Chameleon
C0253.definition: Chameleon is an early handheld or mobile augmented reality (AR) system that allowed a user to move a liquid-crystal display (LCD) over a piece of paper and see virtual content.

C0254.name: liquid-crystal display
C0254.definition: Liquid-crystal display (LCD) is a display that, in an augmented reality system, can be moved over a piece of paper to allow a user to see virtual content.

C0255.name: NaviCam
C0255.definition: NaviCam is a handheld or mobile augmented reality system that superimposed virtual tags on real objects using handheld and head-mounted displays.

C0256.name: shared augmented reality content
C0256.definition: Shared augmented reality content is augmented reality content that people in the same location can see and interact with.

C0257.name: medical application
C0257.definition: A medical application is an augmented reality application.

C0258.name: visualization of laparoscopic surgery
C0258.definition: Visualization of laparoscopic surgery is one of the medical applications of augmented reality developed during the mid-1990s tools or applications phase.

C0259.name: x-ray visualization
C0259.definition: X-ray visualization is a medical augmented reality application that is used to visualize a patient's body with X-ray.

C0260.name: image-guided surgery
C0260.definition: Image-guided surgery is a medical application of augmented reality.

C0261.name: wearable computing
C0261.definition: Wearable computing is a research area related to augmented reality that uses head-mounted displays.

C0262.name: real-world marker
C0262.definition: A real-world marker is a marker on which augmented reality content is overlaid.

C0263.name: three-dimensional registration
C0263.definition: Three-dimensional registration is the anchoring of virtual content in augmented reality at a suitable place in the real world so that it appears to be part of the physical environment and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects.

C0264.name: wearable computer
C0264.definition: A wearable computer is a carried computer that combines tracking sensors, batteries, display hardware, and input devices to show augmented-reality information in the real world.

C0265.name: outdoor augmented reality interface
C0265.definition: An outdoor augmented reality interface is an augmented reality interface that displays information in place in the real world, using tracking to register the augmented reality content in three dimensions.

C0266.name: outdoor wearable augmented reality application
C0266.definition: An outdoor wearable augmented reality application is a wearable augmented reality application used outdoors for terrestrial navigation, on-site viewing and creation of computer-aided design models, and game playing.

C0267.name: terrestrial navigation
C0267.definition: Terrestrial navigation is an outdoor wearable augmented reality application.

C0268.name: computer-aided design
C0268.definition: Computer-aided design (CAD) is used in outdoor wearable augmented reality applications for on-site viewing and creation of its models.

C0269.name: model
C0269.definition: A model is trained in machine-learning-based evaluation to automatically determine cybersickness, and a transparent model provides clear insight into its decision-making process.

C0270.name: game playing
C0270.definition: Game playing is an example of an outdoor wearable augmented reality application.

C0271.name: wearable augmented reality system
C0271.definition: A wearable augmented reality system is a wearable computer with a headset, a computer carried in a backpack, and different input devices.

C0272.name: custom computer hardware
C0272.definition: Custom computer hardware is computer hardware used in wearable augmented reality systems, such as a computer carried in a backpack, and its size can make those systems bulky and difficult to use.

C0273.name: battery
C0273.definition: A battery is a hardware part of wearable augmented reality systems and augmented reality smart glasses.

C0274.name: tracking sensor
C0274.definition: A tracking sensor is a part of wearable augmented reality systems or motion capture suits, with basic types typically including electromechanical, electromagnetic, inertial, three-dimensional structure sensing, and light-based sensing.

C0275.name: display hardware
C0275.definition: Display hardware is one of the parts of wearable augmented reality systems, and its size can make those systems bulky and difficult to use.

C0276.name: viewpoint tracking
C0276.definition: Viewpoint tracking is the tracking of a user's viewpoint in augmented reality so that three-dimensional registration of content can happen accurately.

C0277.name: computer-vision tracking system
C0277.definition: A computer-vision tracking system is a tracking system based on a printed matrix that can enable an augmented reality system to track a user's viewpoint.

C0278.name: printed matrix
C0278.definition: Printed matrix is a basis for a simple computer-vision tracking system that could enable an augmented reality system to track a user's viewpoint.

C0279.name: cyber code system
C0279.definition: Cyber code system is a computer-vision tracking system based on a printed matrix, used in software to enable an augmented reality system to track a user's viewpoint.

C0280.name: augmented reality toolkit
C0280.definition: An augmented reality toolkit (ARToolKit) is a low-level, open-source software library for developing augmented reality applications that primarily provides real-time, marker-based tracking of a user’s viewpoint, with only primitive rendering support and no built-in interaction support.

C0281.name: open-source software
C0281.definition: Open-source software is a type of software, such as the AR Toolkit tracking library.

C0282.name: real-time computer-vision tracking
C0282.definition: Real-time computer-vision tracking is the tracking of a square marker in real time that can enable an augmented reality system to track a user's viewpoint.

C0283.name: square marker
C0283.definition: A square marker is a marker tracked in real time by computer vision to help an augmented reality system track a user's viewpoint.

C0284.name: mobile-based augmented reality application
C0284.definition: A mobile-based augmented reality application is an augmented reality application based on a mobile phone.

C0285.name: smartphone
C0285.definition: A smartphone is a familiar handheld device used for augmented reality; when placed in a cardboard virtual reality headset, it displays stereoscopic views, and it can also serve as the processing element of a virtual reality system.

C0286.name: Sony PlayStation 3
C0286.definition: Sony PlayStation 3 is the basis for an augmented reality game.

C0287.name: The Eye of Judgment
C0287.definition: The Eye of Judgment is a PlayStation 3-based augmented reality (AR) game that was one of the first widely used consumer AR experiences.

C0288.name: Adobe Flash
C0288.definition: Adobe Flash is a popular authoring tool for creating prototypes with multimedia content for web and desktop platforms, and can be used through augmented reality plugins to prototype desktop and mobile augmented reality experiences.

C0289.name: augmented reality authoring tools
C0289.definition: Augmented reality authoring tools are tools that make experiencing augmented reality through web browsers possible.

C0290.name: web browser
C0290.definition: A web browser, when Flash-enabled, is used to run augmented reality experiences.

C0291.name: smartphone-based augmented reality
C0291.definition: Smartphone-based augmented reality is a factor in the move of augmented reality from research laboratories and specialist applications to widely available commercial technology.

C0292.name: software development kit
C0292.definition: Software development kit (SDK) is a platform-dependent installable package of software development tools for a specific hardware and operating system combination that provides fundamental tools to design, build, and test virtual or augmented reality experiences.

C0293.name: ARKit
C0293.definition: ARKit is Apple's augmented reality software development kit (SDK) for augmented reality system development.

C0294.name: Google
C0294.definition: Google is an augmented reality developer and researcher that has released ARCore for Android platforms and is exploring augmented reality contact lenses.

C0295.name: ARCore
C0295.definition: ARCore is used on Android operating system or Android platforms to enable many developers to create augmented reality applications.

C0296.name: Android operating system
C0296.definition: Android operating system is a mobile operating system used for creating augmented reality applications.

C0297.name: wearable device
C0297.definition: A wearable device is a type of hardware, exemplified by AR smart glasses and AR headsets.

C0298.name: mobile device
C0298.definition: Mobile device is one of the popular technological products that define the current stage referred to as ubiquitous computing or the Internet of Things, and it can run an augmented reality application primarily as a client or rendering device.

C0299.name: holographic projection-based device
C0299.definition: A holographic projection-based device is a type of augmented reality hardware device that is expected to see improvements as commercial augmented reality applications grow.

C0300.name: algorithm
C0300.definition: Algorithm is the minimum-time path computation that takes a graph, converts it to a complete time-weighted graph, solves a travelling salesman problem, and replaces hypothetical edges with shortest paths in the original graph.

C0301.name: three-dimensional tracking
C0301.definition: Three-dimensional tracking is part of augmented reality, and the development of algorithms, artificial intelligence, and computer vision technologies is making it more feasible on low-end devices.

C0302.name: registration
C0302.definition: Registration is the step in the tracking process that estimates the initial position and orientation of the sensor or user, so the starting point is known before movement is tracked, and sets the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds. It may be aided by fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags, or performed without them using computer vision.

C0303.name: sensory stimuli
C0303.definition: Sensory stimuli are computer-provided stimuli that let a user experience an artificial environment through all sensory organs, not only sight and sound.

C0304.name: technological issue
C0304.definition: The technological issue in virtual reality is one of the two major issues in experiencing virtual reality, concerning how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment.

C0305.name: psychological issue
C0305.definition: A psychological issue is the human-factor issue of perceiving sensory stimuli suitably in experiencing virtual reality, which technology does not address and which is likely to differ between users.

C0306.name: human factors
C0306.definition: Human factors is the system-design consideration that requires knowing users’ differing expectations, needs, skills, and how they perceive stimuli, so that suitable input and output can be designed.

C0307.name: presence
C0307.definition: Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.

C0308.name: extensive
C0308.definition: Extensive is a quality of immersion that refers to the range of sensory modalities presented to a user, increasing as more sensory organs are stimulated.

C0309.name: sensory modality
C0309.definition: Sensory modality is a kind of sense that computer-provided stimuli can present to a user, such as visual, auditory, physical force perception, smell, taste, and touch.

C0310.name: matching
C0310.definition: Matching is one of the qualities of immersion characterized by congruence between sensory modalities, especially a match between a user's physical movement and movement in the virtual world.

C0311.name: surrounding
C0311.definition: Surrounding is a quality of immersion in a virtual reality (VR) system that is the extent to which cues are panoramic, such as the extent of visual field of view or auditory source perception.

C0312.name: vivid
C0312.definition: Vivid is a quality of immersion that describes the amount of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality.

C0313.name: display resolution
C0313.definition: Display resolution is a hardware display quality, specified in pixels, that affects visual perception, immersion, and cybersickness, with higher values reducing cybersickness only up to a point.

C0314.name: lighting
C0314.definition: Lighting is a stage of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that assigns color to a constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible.

C0315.name: frame rate
C0315.definition: Frame rate is the speed, or temporal resolution, at which display pixels change, and in immersive environments higher frame rates are preferred so that motion is perceived smoothly without jitter.

C0316.name: audio bit rate
C0316.definition: Audio bit rate is a factor that affects the vividness of immersion, with a higher audio bit rate improving auditory perception and making immersion more vivid.

C0317.name: interactivity
C0317.definition: Interactivity is a quality of immersion that is the user's capability to make changes to the virtual world, receive responses from virtual entities to user actions, and influence future events, not merely one-way interaction.

C0318.name: virtual entity
C0318.definition: A virtual entity is something in a virtual world that responds to user actions.

C0319.name: plot-informing
C0319.definition: Plot-informing is a quality of immersion in virtual reality that is greater when the user can better understand, comprehend, or predict the consequences of actions and a scripted story's consistent portrayal, dynamic unfolding, and behavior of the world and its entities.

C0320.name: perfect presence
C0320.definition: Perfect presence is the inability to distinguish between the virtual world and the real world.

C0321.name: uncanny valley effect
C0321.definition: The uncanny valley effect is a phenomenon in human perception in which almost realistic, subtly imperfect artificial or digital human-like figures, objects, or environments evoke unease or eeriness rather than familiarity.

C0322.name: human perception
C0322.definition: Human perception is formed by the combination of physiology and experience stored in long-term memory; understanding it is needed to design better virtual reality systems or to identify and resolve their flaws.

C0323.name: familiarity
C0323.definition: Familiarity is a response that artificial or digital objects can evoke and that is plotted against human likeness in the uncanny valley effect.

C0324.name: human likeness
C0324.definition: Human likeness is the horizontal-axis value in the plot illustrating the uncanny valley effect, used to show how human-like an artificial or digital object in virtual reality is.

C0325.name: realism
C0325.definition: Realism is a user-rated quality of a virtual reality experience, enhanced by ambient sounds and instantaneous walking speed, but subject to uncanny-valley trade-offs over human-likeness.

C0326.name: photorealism
C0326.definition: Photorealism is a property of very good immersive film content that indicates the highest representational fidelity, although it is not required for presence in VR.

C0327.name: representational fidelity
C0327.definition: Representational fidelity is the degree to which a virtual reality experience conveys, matches, or exploits familiarity with a place that is or could be on Earth.

C0328.name: interaction fidelity
C0328.definition: Interaction fidelity is the degree to which physical actions for a virtual task correspond to physical actions for an equivalent real-world task, exploiting real-world experience, and it ranges from no physical motion to intense, realistic physical actions.

C0329.name: experiential fidelity
C0329.definition: Experiential fidelity is the degree to which a user's personal experience matches the virtual reality creator's intended experience, and it is higher when real-world constraints are placed on virtual navigation, movement, and interaction.

C0330.name: 360-degree video
C0330.definition: A 360-degree video is a form of immersive film content that can be used as a video in a virtual tour.

C0331.name: display technology
C0331.definition: Display technology is a technology that is used in augmented reality to overlay virtual content on the representation of the real world on a device.

C0332.name: input modality
C0332.definition: Input modality is a form of interaction used for real-time interaction in augmented reality, allowing a user to interact with digital content overlaid on a representation of the real world.

C0333.name: pose
C0333.definition: Pose is the position and orientation of a viewer or tracked object.

C0334.name: position
C0334.definition: Position is the component of pose that specifies the location of a three-dimensional point, represented by three coordinates in a vector.

C0335.name: orientation
C0335.definition: Orientation is a part of pose, together with position, that is tracked or estimated for a user, sensor, or head, and modified for an object.

C0336.name: anchor
C0336.definition: An anchor is a real-world reference relative to which a viewer's position and orientation are determined in augmented reality to register virtual content.

C0337.name: pose estimation
C0337.definition: Pose estimation is the process of determining a viewer's position and orientation relative to a real-world anchor so that virtual content can be registered in augmented reality. It includes a registration phase that determines the pose and a tracking phase that updates the pose as the viewer moves.

C0338.name: registration phase
C0338.definition: Registration phase is the part of pose determination in augmented reality that determines the viewer's pose relative to a real-world anchor when the user starts using the system.

C0339.name: tracking phase
C0339.definition: The tracking phase is one of two parts of pose determination in augmented reality that updates the viewer's pose relative to a previously known pose because the user is likely to move, so that virtual and real-world content appear properly mixed.

C0340.name: input mechanism
C0340.definition: An input mechanism is one of the major technological issues in augmented reality, alongside display technology and pose estimation, at the beginning and during system use.

C0341.name: cybersickness
C0341.definition: Cybersickness (CS) is a condition primarily relevant to virtual reality that may be caused by multiple internal and external factors and in which a user may experience symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, headache, or disorientation.

C0342.name: symptom
C0342.definition: Symptom is one of the possible signs whose occurrence during a virtual reality experience may indicate the onset of cybersickness or cybersickness itself.

C0343.name: nausea
C0343.definition: Nausea is a common symptom that may indicate cybersickness and is one of the scores considered from the simulator sickness questionnaire.

C0344.name: headache
C0344.definition: Headache is one of the common symptoms that may indicate the onset of cybersickness or cybersickness itself during a virtual reality experience.

C0345.name: excessive sweating
C0345.definition: Excessive sweating is one of the common symptoms that may indicate the onset of cybersickness or cybersickness itself during a virtual reality experience.

C0346.name: dryness of mouth
C0346.definition: Dryness of mouth is one of the common symptoms that may indicate the onset of cybersickness or cybersickness itself during a virtual reality experience.

C0347.name: fullness of stomach
C0347.definition: Fullness of stomach is one of the common symptoms that may indicate the onset of cybersickness or cybersickness itself.

C0348.name: vomiting
C0348.definition: Vomiting is one of the common symptoms that may indicate the onset of cybersickness or cybersickness itself during a virtual reality experience.

C0349.name: dizziness
C0349.definition: Dizziness is one of the common symptoms that may indicate the onset of cybersickness or cybersickness itself.

C0350.name: disorientation
C0350.definition: Disorientation is a common symptom of cybersickness and one of the scores considered in the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ).

C0351.name: fatigue
C0351.definition: Fatigue is one of the common symptoms that may indicate the onset of cybersickness during a virtual reality experience, and may occur when hands are held in front of a device's sensor or camera.

C0352.name: hand-eye coordination
C0352.definition: Hand-eye coordination is a form of coordination in VR that can be disrupted as a cybersickness symptom and may require tracking and matched motion of body parts.

C0353.name: acceptability
C0353.definition: Acceptability is an aspect of virtual reality systems for which reducing the impact of cybersickness is important, because it makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.

C0354.name: user experience
C0354.definition: User experience is a key concern in virtual reality system design that is enhanced by reducing cybersickness, affected by presence, and supported by wayfinding and environment design.

C0355.name: internal factors
C0355.definition: Internal factors are individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can increase the likelihood of experiencing cybersickness.

C0356.name: external factors
C0356.definition: External factors are the hardware factors and virtual reality content factors that can induce cybersickness.

C0357.name: virtual reality content
C0357.definition: Virtual reality content is a set of external content factors that can induce cybersickness, such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

C0358.name: age
C0358.definition: Age is an internal factor for cyber sickness, and its relationship to cyber sickness susceptibility is clearer for controllable content than for general virtual reality content.

C0359.name: gender
C0359.definition: Gender is one of the internal factors for cyber sickness, and the effect of gender on cyber sickness is not conclusive.

C0360.name: motion sickness
C0360.definition: Motion sickness (MS) is a condition in which the brain receives conflicting signals from various sensory organs, causing symptoms like nausea and dizziness.

C0361.name: motion sickness susceptibility
C0361.definition: Motion sickness susceptibility is one of the internal factors for cyber sickness, which are individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can increase the likelihood of experiencing cyber sickness.

C0362.name: physical condition
C0362.definition: Physical condition is one of the internal factors for cybersickness, which are individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can increase the likelihood of experiencing cybersickness.

C0363.name: emotional condition
C0363.definition: Emotional condition is an internal factor for cybersickness that can increase the likelihood of experiencing it, and negative emotions at the time of use, such as anxiety, stress, or frustration, are typically associated with cybersickness.

C0364.name: cyber sickness susceptibility
C0364.definition: Cyber sickness susceptibility is a user's susceptibility to cyber sickness that is related to age, motion sickness susceptibility, retinal eccentricity, and physical position, and can be measured with questionnaires.

C0365.name: controllable content
C0365.definition: Controllable content is content for which, unlike general virtual reality (VR) content, age may be a factor in cyber sickness, making the age relationship clearer.

C0366.name: inter-pupillary distance
C0366.definition: Inter-pupillary distance (IPD) is a factor in head-mounted display fit that determines stereoscopic vision.

C0367.name: inter-pupillary distance fit
C0367.definition: Inter-pupillary distance fit is a possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display users, because inter-pupillary distance determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit.

C0368.name: inter-pupillary distance adjustable range
C0368.definition: Inter-pupillary distance adjustable range is the range of inter-pupillary distance fit in virtual reality displays, and a wider range is suggested for female users.

C0369.name: cyber sickness risk
C0369.definition: Cyber sickness risk is a risk that is positively correlated with motion sickness susceptibility, so higher motion sickness susceptibility is associated with more severe cyber sickness symptoms.

C0370.name: cyber sickness symptoms
C0370.definition: Cyber sickness symptoms are symptoms that may be more severe in individuals with higher motion sickness susceptibility or neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis.

C0371.name: prior exposure to virtual reality systems
C0371.definition: Prior exposure to virtual reality systems is one of the conditions that can reduce the effect of motion sickness susceptibility on cybersickness and reduce cybersickness severity over time.

C0372.name: repeated exposure to virtual reality
C0372.definition: Repeated exposure to virtual reality is one of the conditions that can reduce the effect of motion sickness susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time.

C0373.name: cybersickness severity
C0373.definition: Cybersickness severity is the level of cybersickness that postural sway can indicate and that self-report scores or ratings, machine-learning classification labels, or sickness scores can assess or quantify.

C0374.name: body awareness
C0374.definition: Body awareness is the user's ability to attend to and perceive bodily sensations, a physical condition related to cyber sickness.

C0375.name: sleep quality
C0375.definition: Sleep quality is a condition that, when poor, can affect body awareness and may contribute to or increase the severity of cybersickness.

C0376.name: retinal eccentricity
C0376.definition: Retinal eccentricity is a property that, when greater, may make people more susceptible to cyber sickness.

C0377.name: neurological condition
C0377.definition: A neurological condition is a condition, such as multiple sclerosis, in which individuals may experience more severe cyber sickness symptoms.

C0378.name: multiple sclerosis
C0378.definition: Multiple sclerosis is a neurological condition that may be associated with more severe cyber sickness symptoms.

C0379.name: standing posture
