C0379.definition: Standing posture is a user's physical position while using a virtual reality system that is likely to induce more, or more severe, cyber sickness than sitting.

C0380.name: anxiety
C0380.definition: Anxiety is a negative emotion that is typically associated with an increased likelihood of cybersickness and can be reduced by consistent visual cues and smooth transitions in system design.

C0381.name: stress
C0381.definition: Stress is a negative emotion that is typically associated with cyber sickness and can increase the likelihood of cyber sickness.

C0382.name: frustration
C0382.definition: Frustration is a negative emotion that is typically associated with cyber sickness.

C0383.name: personality trait
C0383.definition: A personality trait is a trait, such as neuroticism, that may increase the likelihood of cyber sickness.

C0384.name: neuroticism
C0384.definition: Neuroticism is a personality trait that may increase the likelihood of cyber sickness.

C0385.name: latency
C0385.definition: Latency is the time delay, or time gap, in virtual reality between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world.

C0386.name: latency jitter
C0386.definition: Latency jitter is the variability in latency in which the time gap between a physical-world action and its virtual-world reflection changes from time to time.

C0387.name: display type
C0387.definition: Display type is an external hardware factor, the type of display used by the user, that significantly influences the severity of cybersickness.

C0388.name: conventional monitor
C0388.definition: A conventional monitor is a display type other than head-mounted displays or virtual reality headset displays.

C0389.name: stereoscopic three-dimensional video
C0389.definition: A stereoscopic three-dimensional video is a video used to compare cybersickness severity on flat screens, panoramic screens, and VR headsets.

C0390.name: flat screen
C0390.definition: A flat screen is a display type used for viewing stereoscopic three-dimensional videos, and it is one of the display conditions compared with panoramic screens and VR headsets in cybersickness studies.

C0391.name: panoramic screen
C0391.definition: A panoramic screen is a type of display on which stereoscopic 3D videos can be viewed.

C0392.name: brightness
C0392.definition: Brightness is a display quality of head-mounted displays associated with cybersickness.

C0393.name: clarity
C0393.definition: Clarity is a display quality of a head-mounted display (HMD).

C0394.name: contrast
C0394.definition: Contrast is one of the display qualities of head-mounted displays.

C0395.name: input method
C0395.definition: Input method is a type of input used in virtual reality, such as hand controllers, treadmills, and motion sensors, that can influence cybersickness.

C0396.name: hand controller
C0396.definition: A hand controller is one of the input methods used in virtual reality.

C0397.name: treadmill
C0397.definition: A treadmill is an output device for virtual reality that provides the sense of walking or running while staying in one place by providing different sorts of input to the feet or legs.

C0398.name: motion sensor
C0398.definition: A motion sensor is an input method used in virtual reality and a miniaturized component that can be placed on augmented reality contact lenses.

C0399.name: motion controller
C0399.definition: A motion controller is a VR controller, such as steering with handlebars.

C0400.name: joystick
C0400.definition: A joystick is a non-motion, world-grounded hand input device that is fixed in the real world, is commonly used to interact with grounded systems, and is used to navigate or teleport.

C0401.name: gamepad controller
C0401.definition: A gamepad controller is a controller that causes less cybersickness than a hand controller.

C0402.name: hardware factor
C0402.definition: A hardware factor is one of the external factors that can induce cybersickness, such as display type, latency, latency jitter, display resolution, and input technology.

C0403.name: input technology
C0403.definition: Input technology is a hardware factor among the external factors that cause cybersickness.

C0404.name: content factor
C0404.definition: A content factor is an external factor in the causes of cybersickness.

C0405.name: visual motion
C0405.definition: Visual motion is the movement experienced by a user in a virtual reality environment, and it is a virtual reality content factor that can increase the risk and severity of cybersickness.

C0406.name: locomotion
C0406.definition: Locomotion is the motor component of navigation in a virtual world, the actual movement between two locations, carried out by techniques that let a user move and perceive that the movement has taken place.

C0407.name: type of content
C0407.definition: Type of content is a VR content factor that affects cybersickness, and action content, fast movements, and abrupt alterations in a VR environment induce more cybersickness than neutral or static content.

C0408.name: duration
C0408.definition: Duration is a virtual reality content factor that can affect cybersickness.

C0409.name: visual complexity
C0409.definition: Visual complexity is an external virtual reality content factor that is positively correlated with cybersickness symptoms, so scenes with more objects of different shapes, sizes, and movements are more likely to induce cybersickness.

C0410.name: vection
C0410.definition: Vection is the illusion of self-motion in which a physically stationary person in a virtual environment receives visual input reporting movement or acceleration while balance or proprioception reports no motion, creating a sensory conflict; it is highest when sensed in peripheral stimuli.

C0411.name: self-motion
C0411.definition: Self-motion is the motion whose sensation is vection.

C0412.name: peripheral stimulus
C0412.definition: Peripheral stimulus is a stimulus that, when motion in it is sensed, makes the sensation of self-motion strongest.

C0413.name: visual motion stimulus
C0413.definition: Visual motion stimulus is a visual stimulus whose positive correlation with vection indicates that visual motion plays a crucial role in the onset and severity of cyber sickness.

C0414.name: height
C0414.definition: Height is the user's height in the natural walking-speed model.

C0415.name: speed
C0415.definition: Speed is a distance element divided by an instantaneous time, expressed as dx/dt.

C0416.name: viewpoint
C0416.definition: Viewpoint is the user's field of view in a virtual world, represented as an origin vector in the world coordinate system, and it changes as the user moves from one point to another.

C0417.name: turbulent visual motion
C0417.definition: Turbulent visual motion is visual motion that can induce cyber sickness with longer exposure, though brief exposure alone is not enough.

C0418.name: angular velocity
C0418.definition: Angular velocity is what a gyroscope captures in an inertial measurement unit, and sensor tracking relies mainly on its readings.

C0419.name: rotation
C0419.definition: Rotation is a basic modeling transformation specified by a clockwise or anticlockwise angle around an axis.

C0420.name: x axis
C0420.definition: X axis is one of the three axes in three-dimensional space along which translational degrees of freedom occur and around which rotation can take place.

C0421.name: y axis
C0421.definition: The y axis is one of the three axes in three-dimensional space, along which an object can have translational degrees of freedom.

C0422.name: z axis
C0422.definition: The z axis is one of the three axes in three-dimensional space along which an object can have translational degrees of freedom.

C0423.name: sensory mismatch
C0423.definition: Sensory mismatch is a conflict in a virtual environment between the sensory inputs a user receives and the physical movement or the brain's familiar processing, which can cause cybersickness.

C0424.name: control over motion
C0424.definition: Control over motion is an aspect of locomotion in a virtual world, meaning whether and how a user controls movement; greater control increases presence, and its type and extent determine the likelihood of cybersickness.

C0425.name: hand-based motion control
C0425.definition: Hand-based motion control is a control mechanism used in virtual reality that leads to significantly less cybersickness than whole-body motion control.

C0426.name: whole-body motion control
C0426.definition: Whole-body motion control is a type of control mechanism used in virtual reality (VR).

C0427.name: transition type
C0427.definition: Transition type is an aspect of locomotion that specifies how a scene changes from one field of view to another and can affect cybersickness.

C0428.name: teleportation
C0428.definition: Teleportation is a virtual reality locomotion operation in which a user selects a virtual target location and the virtual viewpoint instantly changes from the current location to that target, without physical movement.

C0429.name: naturalistic free movement
C0429.definition: Naturalistic free movement is a type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, such as walking, running, or jumping.

C0430.name: field of vision
C0430.definition: Field of vision is the user's or wearer's vision that a VR headset display captures and onto which AR contact lenses superimpose digital images or information.

C0431.name: head movement
C0431.definition: Head movement is input from a body part other than the hand, and head-tracking devices typically use it to detect yaw, roll, and pitch and change the view.

C0432.name: action content
C0432.definition: Action content is a type of virtual reality content that tends to induce more cybersickness than neutral or static content.

C0433.name: fast movement
C0433.definition: Fast movement is a type of virtual reality content that can induce more cybersickness than neutral or static content.

C0434.name: abrupt alteration
C0434.definition: Abrupt alteration is a virtual reality content type that is found to induce cybersickness more than neutral or static content.

C0435.name: neutral content
C0435.definition: Neutral content is a type of virtual reality content that, with static content, is found to induce less cybersickness than action content, fast movements, and abrupt alterations.

C0436.name: static content
C0436.definition: Static content is a kind of content in a virtual reality environment that is found to induce less cybersickness than action content.

C0437.name: genre
C0437.definition: Genre is an aspect of virtual environments and affects cybersickness.

C0438.name: geometry
C0438.definition: Geometry is part of a virtual environment, and, together with terrain, it affects cybersickness; in a mesh rendering workflow it is what a mesh renderer takes from a mesh filter and renders at a position defined by a transform component.

C0439.name: virtual terrain
C0439.definition: Virtual terrain is the terrain in a virtual environment over which users travel and that can be manipulated to reduce travel time.

C0440.name: weather conditions
C0440.definition: Weather conditions in a virtual environment are weather states, such as stormy or clear weather, that affect the induction of cybersickness.

C0441.name: exposure duration
C0441.definition: Exposure duration is the length of time a user spends in a virtual reality session, including travel and interaction time, and longer duration increases cybersickness.

C0442.name: locomotion controller
C0442.definition: A locomotion controller is a controller used by users to move from one point to another in a virtual environment during virtual reality navigation tasks.

C0443.name: navigation task
C0443.definition: A navigation task is a task in a virtual environment in which a user moves from one point to another using a locomotion controller.

C0444.name: locomotion technique
C0444.definition: Locomotion technique is a technique that lets a user travel in a virtual world from one place to another and perceive that travel has taken place.

C0445.name: live-action 180-degree video
C0445.definition: Live-action 180-degree video is a kind of video.

C0446.name: measurement technique
C0446.definition: A measurement technique for cybersickness is a process that relies on an input and generates an output, and it can be manual, automated, machine learning-based, or real-time during the experience.

C0447.name: questionnaire-based input
C0447.definition: Questionnaire-based input is a subjective input for measuring cybersickness that generally takes the form of ratings of users' discomfort or disorientation on a numerical scale.

C0448.name: physiological and biometric input
C0448.definition: Physiological and biometric input is an objective category of inputs for measuring cybersickness.

C0449.name: behavioral input
C0449.definition: Behavioral input is one of the four categories of inputs for measuring cybersickness, and it includes blink rate, head and body movement, the manner of those movements, and postural sway.

C0450.name: content-based input
C0450.definition: Content-based input is a category of inputs for measuring cybersickness that includes optical flow, depth cues, and exceptional motion velocity.

C0451.name: binary classes
C0451.definition: Binary classes are one possible output of cybersickness measurement.

C0452.name: multiple classes
C0452.definition: Multiple classes is one of the outputs of cybersickness (CS) measurement.

C0453.name: sickness score
C0453.definition: A sickness score is a numerical output of cybersickness measurement that quantifies the severity of the cybersickness experience and is generally produced by a regression model in machine learning-based evaluation.

C0454.name: simulator sickness questionnaire
C0454.definition: The simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) is a widely used questionnaire for measuring cybersickness in immersive experiences. It contains 16 items in oculomotor, disorientation, and nausea subscales, rated from 0 to 3, with subscale and total sickness scores.

C0455.name: oculomotor subscale
C0455.definition: Oculomotor subscale is a subscale of the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) in which participants rate the intensity of individual oculomotor symptoms from 0 to 3, with higher scores denoting more severe symptoms.

C0456.name: disorientation subscale
C0456.definition: The disorientation subscale is one of the three subscales of the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire, and participants rate the intensity of symptoms belonging to it on a scale from 0 to 3.

C0457.name: nausea subscale
C0457.definition: The nausea subscale is one of the three subscales of the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire.

C0458.name: Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire
C0458.definition: The Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire (VRSQ) is a questionnaire specifically designed for virtual reality that is relevant to cyber sickness in extended reality.

C0459.name: Cyber Sickness Questionnaire
C0459.definition: The Cyber Sickness Questionnaire (CSQ) is a questionnaire relevant to cyber sickness in extended reality that is good for evaluating virtual reality experiences with head-mounted displays.

C0460.name: Misery Scale
C0460.definition: The Misery Scale (MIS) is one of the shorter, more precise, and more concise questionnaires for extended reality (XR) that assess specific conditions.

C0461.name: Fast Motion Sickness Scale
C0461.definition: The Fast Motion Sickness Scale (FMS) is one of the shorter, more precise, and concise questionnaires for extended reality (XR) that assess specific conditions.

C0462.name: Motion History Questionnaire
C0462.definition: The Motion History Questionnaire (MHQ) is one of the questionnaires used to measure susceptibility to cybersickness in extended reality.

C0463.name: Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire
C0463.definition: Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (MS-SQ) is a questionnaire used to measure susceptibility to cybersickness.

C0464.name: Visually Induced Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire
C0464.definition: The Visually Induced Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (VIMS) is a questionnaire used to measure susceptibility to cybersickness in extended reality.

C0465.name: Nausea Scale
C0465.definition: The Nausea Scale is a questionnaire commonly used to assess overall discomfort in immersive extended reality (XR) experiences.

C0466.name: Motion Sickness Assessment Questionnaire
C0466.definition: The Motion Sickness Assessment Questionnaire (MSAQ) is one of the questionnaires commonly used to assess overall discomfort in immersive extended reality (XR) experiences.

C0467.name: physiological input
C0467.definition: Physiological input is an input used to detect cybersickness, because questionnaire-based inputs can be subjective, inaccurate, and not always reliable.

C0468.name: electroencephalogram
C0468.definition: An electroencephalogram (EEG) is one of the widely used physiological or biometric inputs for detecting cybersickness.

C0469.name: heart rate
C0469.definition: Heart rate is one of the physiological or biometric inputs for detecting cybersickness.

C0470.name: galvanic skin response
C0470.definition: Galvanic skin response (GSR) is one of the physiological or biometric inputs used for detecting cybersickness.

C0471.name: electrocardiogram
C0471.definition: An electrocardiogram (ECG) is one of the physiological or biometric inputs used for detecting cybersickness.

C0472.name: electrogastrogram
C0472.definition: An electrogastrogram (EGG) is a physiological or biometric input for detecting cybersickness.

C0473.name: electrooculography
C0473.definition: Electrooculography (EOG) is one of the physiological or biometric inputs for detecting cybersickness and a technique that eye-tracking systems can use.

C0474.name: respiration signal
C0474.definition: A respiration signal is a physiological or biometric input that is used for detecting cybersickness.

C0475.name: photoplethysmography
C0475.definition: Photoplethysmography (PPG) is one of the physiological or biometric inputs for detecting cybersickness.

C0476.name: electromyogram
C0476.definition: Electromyogram (EMG) is one of the physiological or biometric inputs used for detecting cybersickness.

C0477.name: blink rate
C0477.definition: Blink rate is one of the behavioral inputs used for measuring cybersickness.

C0478.name: head and body movement
C0478.definition: Head and body movement is one of the behavioral inputs for measuring cybersickness.

C0479.name: postural sway
C0479.definition: Postural sway is a behavioral input for measuring cybersickness during virtual reality exposure, monitored using axial movements or changes in the user's center of pressure, and can indicate cybersickness severity.

C0480.name: axial movement
C0480.definition: Axial movement is a means by which postural sway can be monitored for measuring cybersickness during virtual reality exposure.

C0481.name: center of pressure
C0481.definition: The center of pressure is a user-related measure whose changes are used to monitor postural sway for measuring cybersickness during virtual reality exposure.

C0482.name: postural instability
C0482.definition: Postural instability is positively correlated with the severity of cybersickness.

C0483.name: optical flow
C0483.definition: Optical flow is the apparent motion perceived by virtual reality users due to relative motion between the user and the environment.

C0484.name: depth cue
C0484.definition: A depth cue is a cue in human vision that is used as a content-based input for measuring cybersickness.

C0485.name: exceptional motion velocity
C0485.definition: Exceptional motion velocity is one of the content-based inputs for measuring cybersickness.

C0486.name: manual evaluation
C0486.definition: Manual evaluation is an input-based cybersickness measurement technique that relies entirely on human intervention, typically using a questionnaire distributed, collected, and reviewed by a person to decide the severity, onset, or possibility of cybersickness.

C0487.name: machine learning-based cybersickness evaluation
C0487.definition: Machine learning-based cybersickness evaluation is an input-based cybersickness measurement technique that uses automated algorithms trained on psychological, physiological, or biometric inputs to automatically determine cybersickness, producing classification labels or a numerical sickness score.

C0488.name: questionnaire-based assessment
C0488.definition: Questionnaire-based assessment is a manual evaluation for cybersickness in which a person distributes a questionnaire, collects feedback, and reviews the responses to decide the severity, onset, or possibility of cybersickness.

C0489.name: psychological input
C0489.definition: Psychological input is one of the inputs that machine learning-based evaluation of cybersickness can use to train models that automatically determine cybersickness.

C0490.name: transparent model
C0490.definition: A transparent model is a model used for machine learning-based evaluation of cybersickness that provides clear insight into its decision-making process and whose inner workings can be easily understood.

C0491.name: stepwise regression analysis
C0491.definition: Stepwise regression analysis is a transparent model that is used to measure cybersickness using a variety of physiological signals or physiological inputs.

C0492.name: interpretable model
C0492.definition: An interpretable model is a machine learning model used in cybersickness evaluation that reveals how or why its output is generated from its input and provides precise details about that relationship.

C0493.name: CN2 rule induction
C0493.definition: CN2 rule induction is one of the interpretable machine learning algorithms used to measure cybersickness.

C0494.name: bagged decision tree
C0494.definition: The bagged decision tree is one of the interpretable machine learning algorithms used to measure cybersickness.

C0495.name: Naive Bayes classifier
C0495.definition: A Naive Bayes classifier is an interpretable machine learning algorithm used to measure cybersickness.

C0496.name: K-nearest neighbors
C0496.definition: K-nearest neighbors (KNN) is an interpretable machine learning algorithm used to measure, predict, or classify cybersickness.

C0497.name: linear discriminant analysis
C0497.definition: Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) is an interpretable machine learning algorithm used to measure cybersickness.

C0498.name: long short-term memory
C0498.definition: Long short-term memory (LSTM) is a machine learning model used to measure or evaluate cybersickness.

C0499.name: explainable boosting machine
C0499.definition: Explainable boosting machine (EBM) is a machine learning technique that can be combined with other machine learning techniques to identify and provide insight into cybersickness.

C0500.name: decision tree
C0500.definition: A decision tree is a machine learning technique that has been used in combinations, with biophysiological and subjective measurements as input, to identify and provide insight into cybersickness.

C0501.name: logistic regression
C0501.definition: Logistic regression is a machine learning technique used in combinations or hybrid models to identify, predict, or classify cybersickness.

C0502.name: black-box model
C0502.definition: Black-box model is a model used in cybersickness evaluation that takes an input and produces an output without revealing how or why that output is generated; it generally provides higher prediction accuracy than transparent and interpretable models but requires large amounts of data and processing power.

C0503.name: convolutional neural network
C0503.definition: A convolutional neural network (CNN) is a black-box model studied for cybersickness evaluation, with a specialized form for electroencephalography prediction.

C0504.name: support vector machine
C0504.definition: Support vector machine (SVM) is a black-box model for cybersickness evaluation and measurement.

C0505.name: prediction accuracy
C0505.definition: Prediction accuracy is a property of cybersickness evaluation models.

C0506.name: hybrid model
C0506.definition: Hybrid model is a combination of different machine learning models used to predict or classify cybersickness, designed to provide high accuracy and some transparency.

C0507.name: deep embedded self-organizing map
C0507.definition: Deep embedded self-organizing map (DESOM) is part of hybrid models used to predict or classify cybersickness.

C0508.name: autoencoder
C0508.definition: An autoencoder is a component of hybrid models used to predict or classify cybersickness.

C0509.name: electroencephalogram network
C0509.definition: Electroencephalogram network (EEGNET) is a specialized convolutional neural network for electroencephalography prediction.

C0510.name: voting classifier
C0510.definition: A voting classifier is a classifier included in hybrid models for predicting or classifying cybersickness, combining random forest, K-nearest neighbors (KNN), logistic regression, and a multilayer perceptron neural network for binary and three-level classification.

C0511.name: random forest
C0511.definition: Random forest is one of the methods combined in a voting classifier used for binary or three-level classification of cybersickness.

C0512.name: multilayer perceptron
C0512.definition: A multilayer perceptron is a neural network used in a voting classifier for binary and three-level classification in hybrid models that predict or classify cybersickness.

C0513.name: classification based on the event of measurement
C0513.definition: Classification based on the event of measurement is a category of cybersickness evaluation technique that distinguishes detection, which uses input generated after the experience to determine whether cybersickness has occurred, from prediction, which occurs before the experience to determine whether cybersickness will occur.

C0514.name: cybersickness evaluation technique
C0514.definition: Cybersickness evaluation technique is a technique for evaluating cybersickness, and a classification based on the event of measurement distinguishes detection from prediction.

C0515.name: detection
C0515.definition: Detection is a cybersickness evaluation technique that uses input generated after the experience to determine whether cybersickness has occurred.

C0516.name: prediction
C0516.definition: Prediction is a cybersickness evaluation technique that occurs before an experience to determine whether cybersickness will occur, enabling mitigation measures before cybersickness occurs.

C0517.name: mitigation measures
C0517.definition: Mitigation measures are measures that can be enabled before cybersickness occurs.

C0518.name: video features
C0518.definition: Video features are used in limited machine-learning research to predict susceptibility to cybersickness or impending cybersickness episodes.

C0519.name: baseline measurements
C0519.definition: Baseline measurements are measurements taken before virtual reality immersion and used in limited research on predicting cybersickness.

C0520.name: cybersickness episode
C0520.definition: A cybersickness episode is an episode of cybersickness that can be impending and may be predicted by machine learning studies.

C0521.name: score
C0521.definition: A score is a rating-scale output of self-report questionnaires for cybersickness and can be used to assess the severity of cybersickness.

C0522.name: rating
C0522.definition: A rating is one of the outputs of self-report questionnaires for cybersickness that can be used to assess the severity of cybersickness.

C0523.name: rating scale
C0523.definition: A rating scale is a scale used to collect user feedback or self-report data as scores or ratings, such as a 1-to-10 scale where 1 is worst and 10 is best.

C0524.name: classification label
C0524.definition: A classification label is an output of machine learning-based cybersickness evaluation that indicates the likelihood or severity of cybersickness.

C0525.name: regression model
C0525.definition: A regression model is generally used in machine learning-based cybersickness evaluation to produce a sickness score that quantifies the severity of the cybersickness experience.

C0526.name: cybersickness mitigation
C0526.definition: Cybersickness mitigation is the use of measures that reduce or eliminate cybersickness or lessen its impact, while balancing that reduction against preserving presence and user experience.

C0527.name: developer perspective
C0527.definition: Developer perspective is one of the important perspectives from which cybersickness mitigation is considered, together with the user's perspective.

C0528.name: user perspective
C0528.definition: The user perspective is one of the two important perspectives from which cybersickness mitigation is considered.

C0529.name: field of view adjustment
C0529.definition: Field of view adjustment is a developer-side strategy that restricts parts of the field of view, reducing peripheral optical flow to mitigate cybersickness, though it can reduce presence and visual-task performance.

C0530.name: dynamic visual blur
C0530.definition: Dynamic visual blur is a developer-side technique for reducing the possibility of cybersickness that works by obscuring or reducing clarity and has two types: depth-of-field blur and peripheral blur.

C0531.name: rest frame
C0531.definition: A rest frame is a fixed element within a virtual environment that remains stationary relative to the real world regardless of the user's movements, and it is used to reduce cybersickness.

C0532.name: optical-flow manipulation
C0532.definition: Optical-flow manipulation is a developer-side cybersickness reduction technique that can visually mix optical-flow patterns in the reverse direction of virtual visual motion, use a restricted field of view aligned with optical flow, or reduce perceived optical flow by geometrical simplification of the virtual environment.

C0533.name: hardware-level alteration
C0533.definition: Hardware-level alteration is a developer-side strategy for reducing or eliminating cybersickness by modifying existing hardware to different degrees or by proposing completely new hardware.

C0534.name: locomotion modification
C0534.definition: Locomotion modification is a developer-side strategy for reducing cybersickness that changes locomotion methods, including teleportation, novel walking, dynamic steering speed, viewpoint snapping, and invisible ramps.

C0535.name: peripheral optical flow
C0535.definition: Peripheral optical flow is reduced by restricting the field of view, an adjustment that can, ideally, mitigate the onset or severity of cybersickness.

C0536.name: symmetric mask
C0536.definition: A symmetric mask is a classical field of view (FOV) adjustment technique that occludes the periphery in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity, but it can affect presence.

C0537.name: translational velocity
C0537.definition: Translational velocity is a velocity that, with or without angular velocity, can make a symmetric mask occlude the periphery in a field of view adjustment technique.

C0538.name: asymmetric mask
C0538.definition: An asymmetric mask is a field of view adjustment strategy, considered an adaptive restrictor, that obscures peripheral regions with higher optical flow during virtual locomotion and only one side of the periphery during virtual rotation, shifting the center of restriction in the direction of the turn.

C0539.name: adaptive restrictor
C0539.definition: An adaptive restrictor is a field of view adjustment strategy that adapts based on optical flow by obscuring peripheral regions with higher optical flow during virtual locomotion while leaving regions with lower optical flow visible.

C0540.name: side restrictor
C0540.definition: A side restrictor is a field of view adjustment strategy, described as an asymmetric mask, that obscures only one side of the periphery during virtual rotation and laterally shifts the center of restriction in the direction of the turn.

C0541.name: ground visible restrictor
C0541.definition: A ground visible restrictor is a field of view adjustment strategy that keeps the ground plane visible during movement.

C0542.name: ground plane
C0542.definition: Ground plane is a plane that remains visible during movement in a ground visible restrictor.

C0543.name: depth-of-field blur
C0543.definition: Depth-of-field blur is a type of dynamic visual blur, a technique for reducing the possibility of cybersickness, that uses well-known depth cues in human vision.

C0544.name: peripheral blur
C0544.definition: Peripheral blur is a type of dynamic visual blur, a technique for reducing the possibility of cybersickness.

C0545.name: head reference frame
C0545.definition: Head reference frame is a reference frame to which rest frames in a virtual environment can be attached.

C0546.name: independent visual background
C0546.definition: Independent visual background is a rest frame attached to the head reference frame that remains stationary relative to the real world regardless of the user's movements.

C0547.name: virtual nose
C0547.definition: Virtual nose is an example of an independent visual background, a rest frame attached to the head reference frame.

C0548.name: perceived optical flow
C0548.definition: Perceived optical flow is the virtual visual motion that optical-flow manipulation can reduce by geometrical simplification of the virtual environment.

C0549.name: geometrical simplification
C0549.definition: Geometrical simplification is used to reduce perceived optical flow in a virtual environment as part of a cybersickness reduction technique.

C0550.name: sparse peripheral display
C0550.definition: Sparse peripheral display is a hardware-level alteration for reducing cybersickness that expands the periphery of a head-mounted display with a colorful LED matrix.

C0551.name: light-emitting diode matrix
C0551.definition: Light-emitting diode matrix is used in a sparse peripheral display that expands the periphery of a head-mounted display as a hardware-level alteration for reducing cybersickness.

C0552.name: light-emitting diode screen
C0552.definition: A light-emitting diode screen is a miniature screen placed in a head-mounted display, used in hardware-level alterations for reducing cybersickness.

C0553.name: Noble camera setup twin cam
C0553.definition: A Noble camera setup twin cam is a hardware-level alteration used to reduce motion blur and cybersickness.

C0554.name: motion blur
C0554.definition: Motion blur is one of the things reduced by a hardware-level camera setup used to reduce cybersickness.

C0555.name: hybrid 360 panoramic video camera rig
C0555.definition: A hybrid 360 panoramic video camera rig is a hardware-level alteration that can be used to reduce cybersickness.

C0556.name: phantom legs
C0556.definition: Phantom legs is a hardware-level alteration that uses additional hardware to apply alternating haptic cues synchronized to users' footsteps and has been found to greatly reduce cybersickness.

C0557.name: haptic cue
C0557.definition: A haptic cue is an alternating cue synchronized to users' footsteps that is applied using additional hardware in a hardware-level alteration to reduce cybersickness.

C0558.name: floor vibration
C0558.definition: Floor vibration is a hardware-level alteration for reducing cybersickness that uses vibration-driven whole-body tactile feedback to match the vibrations of the virtual environment.

C0559.name: whole-body tactile feedback
C0559.definition: Whole-body tactile feedback is vibration-driven tactile feedback used in floor vibrations to match the vibrations of a virtual environment.

C0560.name: simultaneous presentation of sound and vibration
C0560.definition: Simultaneous presentation of sound and vibration is a hardware-level alteration that has been tried for reducing cybersickness.

C0561.name: walking vibe system
C0561.definition: A walking vibe system is a system that uses two small vibration motors behind the ears for vibrotactile feedback during a walking experience and has been tried for reducing cybersickness.

C0562.name: vibration motor
C0562.definition: A vibration motor is a small motor used for vibrotactile feedback during a walking experience.

C0563.name: vibrotactile feedback
C0563.definition: Vibrotactile feedback is feedback provided by vibration motors during a walking experience.

C0564.name: modified motion platform
C0564.definition: A modified motion platform is a hardware-level alteration that can be modified to produce short bursts of rotational acceleration matching visual forward acceleration to reduce cybersickness.

C0565.name: rotational acceleration
C0565.definition: Rotational acceleration is produced in short bursts by modified motion platforms to match visual forward acceleration and reduce cybersickness.

C0566.name: visual forward acceleration
C0566.definition: Visual forward acceleration is an acceleration that can be matched by short bursts of rotational acceleration in modified motion platforms to reduce cybersickness.

C0567.name: novel walking method
C0567.definition: A novel walking method is a locomotion modification for reducing cybersickness, used instead of natural walking.

C0568.name: natural walking
C0568.definition: Natural walking is a walking method that can be replaced by novel walking methods in locomotion modifications for reducing cybersickness.

C0569.name: steering-based locomotion
C0569.definition: Steering-based locomotion is a type of locomotion technique used to accomplish travel in navigation.

C0570.name: dynamic steering speed
C0570.definition: Dynamic steering speed is a locomotion modification for reducing cybersickness, and it skips certain locations when going over long distances to reduce the duration of virtual exposure.

C0571.name: viewpoint snapping
C0571.definition: Viewpoint snapping is a locomotion modification for reducing cybersickness that renders moving pictures in discrete chunks during rotation.

C0572.name: invisible ramp
C0572.definition: An invisible ramp is a locomotion modification placed on top of stairs for reducing cybersickness.

C0573.name: developer-side intervention
C0573.definition: A developer-side intervention is an intervention for reducing the effects of cybersickness that alone may not be sufficient.

C0574.name: countermeasure
C0574.definition: A countermeasure is a user-side measure used to reduce the effects of cybersickness.

C0575.name: virtual reality session
C0575.definition: A virtual reality session is an exposure to a virtual environment.

C0576.name: exposure
C0576.definition: Exposure is the amount of time users spend in a virtual environment, and longer exposure increases the risk of cybersickness.

C0577.name: maximum duration
C0577.definition: Maximum duration is the generally safe upper limit for a virtual reality session that is recommended to reduce cybersickness risk for the majority of users likely to suffer from cybersickness, and the limit may vary with device, content, and other factors.

C0578.name: habituation
C0578.definition: Habituation is the gradual decrease in the intensity of cybersickness after repeated experience in a virtual environment.

C0579.name: diaphragmatic breathing
C0579.definition: Diaphragmatic breathing is a slow, controlled breathing pattern that users can try to delay the onset, reduce the severity, and, to a large extent, reduce the possibility of cybersickness.

C0580.name: background music
C0580.definition: Background music is pleasant music used as a user-side strategy to calm or soothe the mind and reduce cybersickness.

C0581.name: air flow
C0581.definition: Air flow is a user-side strategy that can calm or soothe the mind and reduce cybersickness when adequate.

C0582.name: user-side strategy
C0582.definition: A user-side strategy is a strategy that can calm or soothe the mind and reduce cybersickness.

C0583.name: complete view
C0583.definition: A complete view is a view of a virtual reality system that includes the organism, typically the human user, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world, shows tracking from the organism to the VR hardware, stimulation from the VR hardware to the organism, and bidirectional data flows with the surrounding physical world, and the organism cannot be omitted.

C0584.name: organism
C0584.definition: Organism is the VR system component, alongside the hardware and surrounding physical world, that is typically the human user; it is always present, cannot be omitted, and is equally important as the hardware, sending tracking data to and receiving stimulation from it, while exchanging data with the world.

C0585.name: virtual reality hardware
C0585.definition: Virtual reality hardware is the component of a virtual reality system that receives user input, produces sensory output, and exchanges data with the surrounding physical environment. It consists of displays, sensors, and computers.

C0586.name: stimulation
C0586.definition: Stimulation is the data flow in a virtual reality system from VR hardware to the user (organism), carrying hardware-generated stimuli that override the user's senses.

C0587.name: data flow
C0587.definition: Data flow is the bidirectional exchange of data in a virtual reality system that occurs among the user, VR hardware, and surrounding physical world; between the user and hardware, tracking data from the user lets the hardware adjust the stimulation data sent to the user.

C0588.name: stimulus
C0588.definition: Stimulus is a particular input that activates the receptors of a sense organ and is converted into neural impulses. In virtual reality, output devices generate it to affect the user's sense organs. For human senses it can be electromagnetic energy, air pressure waves, tissue distortion, gravity or acceleration, or chemical composition.

C0589.name: tracking data flow
C0589.definition: Tracking data flow is a data flow in a virtual reality system that uses sensors to track user motions so the hardware can adjust hardware-generated stimuli based on those motions.

C0590.name: user motion
C0590.definition: User motion is a user's motion that a virtual reality system's sensors track so its hardware can adjust stimuli based on the motion.

C0591.name: button press
C0591.definition: Button press is one of the things that tracking may include in a virtual reality system, identifying which button is pressed in which context.

C0592.name: controller movement
C0592.definition: Controller movement is one of the things that may be tracked in a virtual reality system.

C0593.name: eye movement
C0593.definition: Eye movement is a tracked user motion, including where the user is looking and how the eyes move, that non-hand-based input devices may use to support interaction, compensation in rendering and display, or social interaction.

C0594.name: body part movement
C0594.definition: Body part movement is a movement of a body part other than the head that may be tracked in a virtual reality system.

C0595.name: surrounding physical environment
C0595.definition: Surrounding physical environment is the real-world surroundings of a VR user that is part of the VR system because it can affect user behavior through real-world stimuli.

C0596.name: immersive application
C0596.definition: An immersive application is an application that may use a robotic arm to change the position of objects in the surrounding physical environment.

C0597.name: robotic arm
C0597.definition: A robotic arm is an example of VR hardware that an immersive application can use to change the position of objects in the surrounding physical environment.

C0598.name: controller
C0598.definition: A controller is virtual reality hardware that a user operates to extend a ray for selection and to control navigation.

C0599.name: visual display
C0599.definition: Visual display is a display that is meant to stimulate the visual sense, that is, the eyes. Its three broad types are head-mounted displays (HMDs), world-fixed displays, and regular displays.

C0600.name: tracking device
C0600.definition: A tracking device is a sensor or input device used in virtual reality hardware to track a user's input and extract information from the real world.

C0601.name: virtual reality input device
C0601.definition: A virtual reality input device is an input device that is broadly either a hand input device, which requires hands to operate, or a non-hand input device, which does not require hands to operate.

C0602.name: hand input device
C0602.definition: Hand input device is a virtual reality input device that requires hands to operate.

C0603.name: non-hand input device
C0603.definition: A non-hand input device is a virtual reality input device that does not require hands to operate.

C0604.name: world-grounded device
C0604.definition: World-grounded device is a virtual reality hand input device that is fixed in the real world and does not move.

C0605.name: non-tracked handheld controller
C0605.definition: A non-tracked handheld controller is a virtual reality hand input device that is held in the hand but is not tracked in three-dimensional space, so the system does not know its exact position.

C0606.name: tracked handheld controller
C0606.definition: Tracked handheld controller is a virtual reality hand input device that has six degrees of freedom tracking, allowing the system to track its movements.

C0607.name: hand-worn device
C0607.definition: Hand-worn device is a type of virtual reality hand input device that is worn on the hands, arms, or fingers.

C0608.name: bare-hand input
C0608.definition: Bare-hand input is a virtual reality hand-input interaction that uses computer vision to track the user's bare hand, detect gestures, and translate them into commands in the virtual environment, without the user needing to wear anything or use any external device.

C0609.name: portability
C0609.definition: Portability is an issue for fixed, world-grounded hand input devices because the devices constrain the user to move within a specified area.

C0610.name: button
C0610.definition: A button is a physical controller and input device used for system control, including in non-tracked handheld controllers and navigation tools.

C0611.name: trigger
C0611.definition: A trigger is a Unity collider configured using the isTrigger property that does not behave as a solid object and allows other colliders to pass through.

C0612.name: traditional video game controller
C0612.definition: A traditional video game controller is an example of a non-tracked handheld controller.

C0613.name: break-in presence
C0613.definition: Break-in presence is discomfort about performing a task appropriately in a virtual world that is caused when untracked hand movements do not produce corresponding changes in virtual hand positions, affecting the perception of presence.

C0614.name: six degrees of freedom tracking
C0614.definition: Six degrees of freedom tracking is a tracking capability of hand input devices that allows a system to track their movements.

C0615.name: VIVE controller
C0615.definition: The VIVE controller is a tracked handheld controller that combines a joystick with six degrees of freedom tracking and is mainly used in virtual reality.

C0616.name: force feedback controller
C0616.definition: A force feedback controller is a controller that may sometimes resolve the issue that tracked handheld controllers prevent users from directly or fully touching and feeling passive virtual objects through tangible interaction.

C0617.name: tangible interaction
C0617.definition: Tangible interaction is a way of directly or fully touching and feeling passive virtual objects.

C0618.name: passive virtual object
C0618.definition: A passive virtual object is a virtual object that users cannot directly or fully touch and feel through tangible interaction while their hands are occupied with tracked handheld controllers.

C0619.name: electromyography band
C0619.definition: An electromyography band is an example of a hand-worn hand input device, a device worn on the hands, arms, or fingers.

C0620.name: ring
C0620.definition: A ring is a hand-worn hand input device worn on the hands, arms, or fingers.

C0621.name: bend-sensing data glove
C0621.definition: A bend-sensing data glove is a data glove with sensors at all bend positions or joints and other positions, whose processing unit receives continuous raw data from the bend sensors and processes the data to detect hand postures and gestures, providing a large degree of freedom for interaction.

C0622.name: bend sensor
C0622.definition: A bend sensor is a sensor in a data glove, placed at a bend position or joint, that provides continuous raw data for detecting hand postures and gestures.

C0623.name: processing unit
C0623.definition: A processing unit is the part of a bend-sensing data glove that receives continuous raw data from its bend sensors and processes it to detect hand postures and gestures.

C0624.name: hand posture
C0624.definition: Hand posture is one of the things that a bend-sensing data glove detects by processing continuous raw data from its bend sensors.

C0625.name: gesture
C0625.definition: A gesture is a hand movement or signal that a user provides to a system, and the system detects and translates the gesture into a command or object selection.

C0626.name: controller-based interaction
C0626.definition: Controller-based interaction is a method of implementing hand manipulation that uses a controller, such as a joystick-based controller.

C0627.name: pinch glove
C0627.definition: A pinch glove is a data glove in which sensors are placed only at fingertip positions, often including the thumb and index fingertips, and it detects a limited set of pinch gestures for discrete input such as object selection and mode switching.

C0628.name: pinch gesture
C0628.definition: Pinch gesture is one of a limited set of gestures detected by pinch gloves.

C0629.name: discrete input
C0629.definition: Discrete input is a type of input for which object selection and mode switching are examples.

C0630.name: object selection
C0630.definition: Object selection is an object interaction technique, typically used in immersive environments, that specifies one or more objects from a set of virtual objects in the virtual world.

C0631.name: mode switching
C0631.definition: Mode switching is a kind of discrete input for which pinch gloves are typically used.

C0632.name: line-of-sight issue
C0632.definition: Line-of-sight issue is a problem with some input devices in which the user's hand must be in the line of sight of a camera or sensor.

C0633.name: Leap Motion device
C0633.definition: The Leap Motion device is an infrared-based bare-hand input device: a hand-tracking sensor that typically contains three infrared LEDs and two wide-angle cameras. Its cameras pick up infrared light reflected from the hands, and software converts the signals into gestures; it can be attached to a head-mounted display to provide hand input.

C0634.name: infrared
C0634.definition: Infrared (IR) is light that, in a hand-tracking sensor, is generated by LEDs, reflected from hands, and picked up by cameras.

C0635.name: hand-tracking sensor
C0635.definition: Hand-tracking sensor is an infrared (IR)-based sensor that typically contains three IR light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and two wide-angle cameras; the LEDs generate IR light reflected from the hands, the cameras pick it up, and software converts the signals into gestures.

C0636.name: light-emitting diode
C0636.definition: A light-emitting diode (LED) is used to generate infrared light in hand-tracking sensors and can be a small colored fiducial in tracking.

C0637.name: wide-angle camera
C0637.definition: A wide-angle camera is a camera used in an infrared hand-tracking sensor to pick up light reflected from hands.

C0638.name: low-cost head-mounted display
C0638.definition: A low-cost head-mounted display is a head-mounted display that does not provide good-quality controllers or controller support.

C0639.name: cardboard-type device
C0639.definition: A cardboard-type device is a low-cost head-mounted display in which a smartphone provides a stereoscopic view and which does not support good-quality controllers or interaction.

C0640.name: stereoscopic view
C0640.definition: A stereoscopic view is a view displayed by a smartphone in a virtual reality headset to provide an immersive environment.

C0641.name: non-hand-based input devices
C0641.definition: Non-hand-based input devices are input devices that capture input from parts of the body other than the hand, including head movement, eye gaze, voice, and body movement.

C0642.name: eye gaze
C0642.definition: Eye gaze is input captured by non-hand-based input devices and can be used for pointing-based selection when hand tracking is unavailable.

C0643.name: head-tracking-based input devices
C0643.definition: Head-tracking-based input devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically use head motion for input, and a head-mounted display worn by the user can double as a head tracking device with sensors that detect yaw, roll, and pitch and infer the input to change the view.

C0644.name: head tracking device
C0644.definition: A head tracking device is a non-hand-based input device that typically uses head motion, using sensors that detect yaw, roll, and pitch to infer the input to change the view.

C0645.name: yaw
C0645.definition: Yaw is one of the three rotational degrees of freedom of an object in three-dimensional space, and head-mounted display sensors can detect it from head motion to change the view.

C0646.name: roll
C0646.definition: Roll is one of the three rotational degrees of freedom in three-dimensional space, along with yaw and pitch, and a head-mounted display can detect roll to infer input for changing the view.

C0647.name: pitch
C0647.definition: Pitch is the frequency of a sound wave, as referred to in pitch perception.

C0648.name: eye tracking devices
C0648.definition: Eye tracking devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically come integrated with headsets and track where the user is looking and how the eyes are moving, helping the system infer what action to take.

C0649.name: Midas touch problem
C0649.definition: The Midas touch problem is an eye tracking-based input problem in which a system cannot differentiate an intentional gaze meant to select an object from a habitual blank gaze, so the system may select an object or perform an action even though the user did not intend to.

C0650.name: eye tracking
C0650.definition: Eye tracking is a non-hand-based input technique that tracks a user's gaze point or area, using optical, camera-based or other tracking techniques in systems that may be head-mounted or externally attached, to help a system infer what action to take.

C0651.name: multimodal input
C0651.definition: Multimodal input is a form of input that uses other forms of input in addition to eye tracking for interacting with a system.

C0652.name: input
C0652.definition: Input is one of the three major hardware components of a virtual reality (VR) system and, in XR systems, the data that the user provides to interact with the system.

C0653.name: output
C0653.definition: Output is the stimuli that an XR system generates so that the user can sense, understand, and perceive them, in order to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality.

C0654.name: processor
C0654.definition: Processor is one of the three major hardware components of any virtual reality (VR) system.

C0655.name: non-hand input technique
C0655.definition: Non-hand input technique is a virtual reality input technique that includes head tracking, eye tracking, full-body tracking, and sound-based tracking.

C0656.name: full-body tracking
C0656.definition: Full-body tracking is a non-hand input method in virtual reality that tracks a user's full-body movement, beyond the head, hands, and eyes. It can add to the illusion of self-embodiment and social presence by showing a fuller representation of the user. Its two broad approaches are motion capture suits and camera-based tracking.

C0657.name: sound-based tracking
C0657.definition: Sound-based tracking is a non-hand input technique in virtual reality (VR) that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound for interaction using simple microphones or microphone arrays.

C0658.name: self-embodiment
C0658.definition: Self-embodiment is a virtual-world illusion that full-body tracking can add to by showing the user a fuller representation of themselves.

C0659.name: social presence
C0659.definition: Social presence is an illusion in a virtual world that full-body tracking can add to by showing the user a fuller representation of themselves.

C0660.name: motion capture suit
C0660.definition: A motion capture suit (MOCAP) is a suit for full-body tracking that records the wearer's movements through sensors that capture and transmit raw movement data, which are combined and converted into full-body position and movement.

C0661.name: camera-based tracking
C0661.definition: Camera-based tracking is a full-body tracking approach in which multiple surrounding cameras observe an actor wearing a suit with fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, and infer the actor's overall body movement from the markers' movement.

C0662.name: raw movement data
C0662.definition: Raw movement data is the data captured and transmitted by sensors in a motion capture suit for full-body tracking, and it is combined and converted into full-body position and movement.

C0663.name: Perception Neuron suit
C0663.definition: The Perception Neuron suit is a motion capture suit that uses straps with inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors on the legs, hands, arms, and head.

C0664.name: inertial measurement unit
C0664.definition: An inertial measurement unit (IMU) is a self-contained composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, accelerometer, and magnetometer to measure changes in orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration rather than absolute values.

C0665.name: camera
C0665.definition: A camera is a sensor or component that captures or renders a view and can provide data for tracking.

C0666.name: reflective marker
C0666.definition: Reflective marker is a fiducial marker used on an actor's suit in camera-based full-body tracking, where surrounding cameras infer the actor's body movement from the markers' movement.

C0667.name: OptiTrack
C0667.definition: OptiTrack is an example of a camera-based full-body tracking system.

C0668.name: Microsoft Kinect
C0668.definition: Microsoft Kinect is a three-dimensional camera device that is used as a sensor in spatial augmented reality systems and is an example of a camera-based full-body tracking system.

C0669.name: voice
C0669.definition: Voice is a sound captured by sound-based tracking in virtual reality for interaction.

C0670.name: speech
C0670.definition: Speech is a sound that sound-based tracking captures in virtual reality for interaction.

C0671.name: non-speech sound
C0671.definition: Non-speech sound is a type of sound captured by sound-based tracking for interaction in virtual reality.

C0672.name: microphone
C0672.definition: A microphone is a sound-capturing component in virtual and augmented reality hardware and sound-based tracking that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound for interaction.

C0673.name: microphone array
C0673.definition: A microphone array is a set of microphones that captures sound in a 360-degree environment.

C0674.name: input sensor
C0674.definition: Input sensor is a sensor that provides data to the processing part of a VR system or is used to capture real world scene information as points in point sample rendering.

C0675.name: personal computer
C0675.definition: A personal computer (PC) is a standard computer that may serve as the processing element in a virtual reality system.

C0676.name: workstation
C0676.definition: A workstation is a high-end processing element with a high-quality graphics processing unit that may be used as the computer in a virtual reality system.

C0677.name: graphics processing unit
C0677.definition: Graphics processing unit (GPU) is a parallel hardware component of a graphics card, with its own memory, that speeds up the rendering process by exploiting the inherent parallelism of graphics operations.

C0678.name: distributed computer system
C0678.definition: A distributed computer system is one possible processing element or computer in a virtual reality (VR) system, interconnected through a high-speed communication network.

C0679.name: communication network
C0679.definition: A communication network is a high-speed network that interconnects a distributed computer system used as the processing element of a VR system.

C0680.name: central processing unit
C0680.definition: Central processing unit (CPU) is a major component of a computer used as the processing element in a VR system that handles many tasks and passes graphics rendering tasks to a GPU.

C0681.name: random access memory
C0681.definition: Random access memory (RAM) is one of the major components of a computer used as the processing element in a virtual reality system.

C0682.name: rendering
C0682.definition: Rendering is the multi-stage computational process that creates a scene's visual output as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed, and, in a broad sense, output for other senses.

C0683.name: parallel processing
C0683.definition: Parallel processing is an inherent ability of a graphics processing unit (GPU) that speeds up the rendering process for complex graphics and complex scenes that are part of realistic virtual reality (VR) experiences.

C0684.name: parallelism
C0684.definition: Parallelism is an inherent feature of graphics operations and rendering that a GPU exploits to speed up rendering.

C0685.name: graphics
C0685.definition: Graphics are rendered by graphics processing units (GPUs) in realistic virtual reality (VR) experiences.

C0686.name: Unity scene
C0686.definition: A Unity scene is a specific type of Unity asset that contains all or part of a game or application and is composed of game objects. Unity provides a scene interface to create, edit, or modify it.

C0687.name: virtual reality experience
C0687.definition: Virtual reality experience is an experience that utilizes human senses, created by virtual reality software driving hardware to generate appropriate stimuli that are appropriately received to stimulate human sense organs.

C0688.name: multi-GPU system
C0688.definition: A multi-GPU system is typically used for building virtual reality applications.

C0689.name: display controller
C0689.definition: Display controller is the rendering component in a generic graphics system that is responsible for image generation, receives display commands from the CPU, uses a GPU for rendering, and sends the generated two-dimensional digital image to video memory.

C0690.name: multicore processor
C0690.definition: A multicore processor is a processor, nowadays the default, that greatly increases computational capacity in virtual reality processing compared with non-multicore or unicore processors.

C0691.name: computational capacity
C0691.definition: Computational capacity is a processing capability in virtual reality processing that multicore processors greatly increase compared with non-multicore or unicore processors.

C0692.name: unicore processor
C0692.definition: A unicore processor is a non-multicore processor in virtual reality (VR) processing.

C0693.name: extended reality engine
C0693.definition: An extended reality engine is the middleware in an extended reality system that is required to support, develop, and render virtual reality experiences by using hardware resources to generate output data.

C0694.name: middleware
C0694.definition: Middleware is software that sits between hardware and higher-level application software, abstracts hardware functionalities for developers, and supports the development and rendering of extended reality (XR) experiences.

C0695.name: audio output
C0695.definition: Audio output is an output device typically used in a virtual reality setup that provides specialized 3D audio to give a sense of where sounds are coming from, using speakers fixed in space or moving with the head. Headphones are preferred for a fully immersive system because the sound source can change with head movement.

C0696.name: motion platform
C0696.definition: A motion platform is a virtual reality hardware output device that moves the entire body to produce a sense of physical motion and gravity, conveying a sense of orientation, vibration, acceleration, and jerks; it may be active (controlled by a computer simulation) or passive (controlled by the user).

C0697.name: sensory output system
C0697.definition: A sensory output system is a virtual reality output system that stimulates the taste and smell sensory organs, namely the tongue and nose.

C0698.name: world-fixed display
C0698.definition: World-fixed display is a non-wearable, stationary visual display that renders graphics onto a fixed surface or screen that does not move with the user's head, while the user can move within a physical space.

C0699.name: regular display
C0699.definition: A regular display is a non-specialized visual display that can be mobile or stationary, is typically relevant for non-immersive virtual reality, and is mostly used for augmented reality.

C0700.name: monoscopic viewing
C0700.definition: Monoscopic viewing is the use of one small screen in a head-mounted display to place images directly in front of a user's eyes.

C0701.name: stereoscopy
C0701.definition: Stereoscopy is the process in which two eyes view two images simultaneously, the left eye processing the left image and the right eye processing the right image, with a common part seen by both eyes and some parts seen by only one eye.

C0702.name: non-see-through head-mounted display
C0702.definition: A non-see-through head-mounted display is a type of head-mounted display that is typically used in virtual reality.

C0703.name: video see-through head-mounted display
C0703.definition: A video see-through head-mounted display is a type of head-mounted display typically used in augmented virtuality.

C0704.name: surround screen
C0704.definition: A surround screen is a world-fixed display that completely surrounds the user, typically with three to six large screens for visual immersion, is usually driven by one or several powerful graphics engines, and requires elaborate tracking of the user's movements.

C0705.name: fish tank display
C0705.definition: A fish tank display is an early world-fixed virtual reality display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube monitor as output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user’s head moves.

C0706.name: monitor
C0706.definition: A monitor is a world-fixed display.

C0707.name: optical head tracker
C0707.definition: Optical head tracker is an input used in a virtual reality display so that the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user's head moves.

C0708.name: haptic device
C0708.definition: A haptic device is a physical object or computer-controlled physical feedback output that activates touch sensation when a user interacts with virtual objects.

C0709.name: stereo perspective view
C0709.definition: Stereo perspective view is a view of a 3D scene in a virtual reality display that changes as the user's head moves.

C0710.name: three-dimensional scene
C0710.definition: A three-dimensional scene is a scene in a three-dimensional world coordinate system from which a portion is selected and projected onto a two-dimensional display.

C0711.name: graphics engine
C0711.definition: A graphics engine is a powerful engine that can drive a surround screen or cave system.

C0712.name: tablet
C0712.definition: A tablet is a common, non-specialized handheld regular display that is mostly used for augmented reality (AR) and is typically relevant for non-immersive virtual reality (VR).

C0713.name: non-immersive virtual reality
C0713.definition: Non-immersive virtual reality is a kind of virtual reality for which regular displays that are not specialized are typically relevant.

C0714.name: three-dimensional audio
C0714.definition: Three-dimensional audio is specialized audio that gives a sense of where sounds are coming from, with speakers fixed in space or moving with the head.

C0715.name: speaker
C0715.definition: A speaker is a part of audio output in a virtual reality setup, fixed in space or moving with the head.

C0716.name: headphone
C0716.definition: A headphone is an audio output device that is preferred for a fully immersive virtual reality system because the sound source can change with head movement.

C0717.name: haptic rendering system
C0717.definition: A haptic rendering system is an output that activates touch sensation and explores touch perception.

C0718.name: haptic output
C0718.definition: Haptic output is a device that activates touch sensation and explores touch perception, categorized as passive or active, tactile or proprioceptive, and self-grounded or world-grounded.

C0719.name: touch perception
C0719.definition: Touch perception is a perception formed when the brain processes neural impulses from somatosensory receptors activated by a hand touching an object.

C0720.name: passive haptic device
C0720.definition: A passive haptic device is a static real-world physical object that matches the shape of virtual objects and is not controlled by a computer.

C0721.name: active haptic device
C0721.definition: An active haptic device is a physical object or physical feedback that is controlled by a computer and provides a sense of touch when interacting with virtual objects.

C0722.name: tactile haptics
C0722.definition: Tactile haptics are haptic devices that provide touch sensations through the skin, including vibrotactile stimulation using mechanical vibration and electrotactile stimulation using electrodes that pass current through the skin.

C0723.name: vibrotactile stimulation
C0723.definition: Vibrotactile stimulation is a type of tactile haptic that provides touch sensations through the skin using mechanical vibration.

C0724.name: electrotactile stimulation
C0724.definition: Electrotactile stimulation is a tactile haptic that provides touch sensations through the skin using electrodes that pass current through the skin.

C0725.name: electrode
C0725.definition: An electrode is used in electrotactile stimulation and taste interfaces to pass current through the skin or provide stimulation over and under the tongue.

C0726.name: proprioceptive force-based haptics
C0726.definition: Proprioceptive force-based haptics are haptic outputs that use forces to activate joints or muscles and provide a sense of limb movement and muscular resistance by providing corresponding signals to muscles and joints.

C0727.name: self-grounded haptic device
C0727.definition: A self-grounded haptic device is a haptic output device that is worn or held by the user and moves with the user.

C0728.name: world-grounded haptic device
C0728.definition: A world-grounded haptic device is a haptic output that activates touch sensation, is physically attached to the real world, cannot be moved, and can provide the sense of fully solid objects that do not move.

C0729.name: active motion platform
C0729.definition: An active motion platform is a motion platform that is controlled by computer simulation.

C0730.name: passive motion platform
C0730.definition: A passive motion platform is a motion platform that is controlled by the user with no direct computer control.

C0731.name: omnidirectional treadmill
C0731.definition: Omnidirectional treadmill is a treadmill that is common in virtual reality systems and can be active, with computer-controlled mechanically moving parts that create the sensation of walking or moving, or passive, containing no computer-controlled mechanically moving parts and controlled by the user.

C0732.name: active omnidirectional treadmill
C0732.definition: An active omnidirectional treadmill is an omnidirectional treadmill, common in virtual reality systems, that has computer-controlled mechanically moving parts that create the sensation of walking or moving.

C0733.name: passive omnidirectional treadmill
C0733.definition: A passive omnidirectional treadmill is a kind of omnidirectional treadmill that contains no computer-controlled mechanically moving parts and is controlled by the user.

C0734.name: augmented reality device
C0734.definition: An augmented reality device is a device that can be categorised into headsets and glasses, handheld devices, projection-based systems, spatial augmented reality, head-up displays, and contact lenses.

C0735.name: augmented reality headset
C0735.definition: An augmented reality headset is a powerful wearable augmented reality device that presents real-world content with full 3D holograms, is generally larger, more immersive, and has a wider field of view than smart glasses, and typically includes built-in cameras and depth sensors.

C0736.name: smart glasses
C0736.definition: Smart glasses are lightweight augmented reality wearable devices that resemble standard eyeglasses and provide heads-up display-type digital content overlays rather than full 3D holograms.

C0737.name: handheld device
C0737.definition: Handheld device is an augmented reality device category whose display element is held by the user.

C0738.name: projection-based system
C0738.definition: A projection-based system is one of the categories of augmented reality devices.

C0739.name: spatial augmented reality system
C0739.definition: Spatial augmented reality system is an augmented reality system that typically projects digital content onto physical objects in the surrounding environment, so virtual content appears to coexist with real objects and multiple users can interact with it without a display held by the user.

C0740.name: head-up display
C0740.definition: A head-up display (HUD) is an augmented reality display category that projects images onto a transparent surface, usually a screen or visor; ideally the surface is invisible and only the content is visible, although borders or shades may be visible.

C0741.name: augmented reality contact lens
C0741.definition: An augmented reality contact lens is a very small, emerging wearable display technology, still in the future, that can be placed directly on the eye, is not visible to outsiders, and superimposes digital images or information on the wearer's field of vision.

C0742.name: Microsoft HoloLens
C0742.definition: The Microsoft HoloLens is an augmented reality headset and a see-through display that integrates high-definition holograms or digital content with the real-world view obtained through special glasses. Interaction takes place through eye movements, voice commands, and hand gestures.

C0743.name: Google Glass
C0743.definition: Google Glass is an augmented reality smart glasses device that presents data in a smartphone-like format, operates hands-free, and supports natural-language voice-command interaction with built-in command detection.

C0744.name: Vuzix Blade Glasses
C0744.definition: Vuzix Blade Glasses are smart glasses, one of the examples of augmented reality (AR) headsets, smart glasses, and handheld devices.

C0745.name: Nintendo device
C0745.definition: A Nintendo device is a handheld device in augmented reality.

C0746.name: projection keyboard
C0746.definition: A projection keyboard is a spatial augmented reality system that projects a virtual keyboard onto a flat surface, converting the surface into an interactive keyboard, and it may use infrared sensors to detect finger positions, a more common way to handle key-press interaction.

C0747.name: interactive projector
C0747.definition: An interactive projector is a spatial augmented reality system that projects images or interfaces onto any surface, turning that surface into an interactive display.

C0748.name: augmented reality sandbox
C0748.definition: An augmented reality sandbox is a spatial augmented reality system that uses a projector and a sensor to project a topographic map onto a physical box of sand and update it in real time as users move the sand or gesture.

C0749.name: industrial augmented reality system
C0749.definition: An industrial augmented reality system is an augmented reality projection-based system.

C0750.name: medical system
C0750.definition: A medical system is an example of an augmented reality projection-based system.

C0751.name: projection mapping software
C0751.definition: Projection mapping software is one example of spatial augmented reality.

C0752.name: laser projector
C0752.definition: A laser projector is an example of spatial augmented reality.

C0753.name: Innovega
C0753.definition: Innovega is an entity involved in ongoing research on augmented reality contact lenses.

C0754.name: Mojo Vision
C0754.definition: Mojo Vision is associated with ongoing research into augmented reality contact lenses, through its Mojo Lens.

C0755.name: Mojo Lens
C0755.definition: Mojo Lens is one of the current activities developing augmented reality (AR) contact lenses.

C0756.name: eye optic system
C0756.definition: Eye optic system is an example of a current activity for developing augmented reality contact lenses.

C0757.name: depth sensor
C0757.definition: A depth sensor is a built-in sensor often included in augmented reality headsets, used to understand the geometry and lighting conditions of a physical environment for spatial augmented reality.

C0758.name: depth camera
C0758.definition: A depth camera is a camera included in the Microsoft HoloLens.

C0759.name: port
C0759.definition: A port is a part of a Microsoft HoloLens for attaching headphones.

C0760.name: tilt mechanism
C0760.definition: A tilt mechanism is one of the components included in the Microsoft HoloLens.

C0761.name: nose pad
C0761.definition: A nose pad is a part of the Microsoft HoloLens.

C0762.name: projector
C0762.definition: A projector is a part of some augmented reality devices that is used to project images or graphical information onto physical objects or three-dimensional space.

C0763.name: hologram
C0763.definition: A hologram is a form of digital content that is integrated with a real-world view in augmented reality.

C0764.name: voice command
C0764.definition: Voice command is one of the interactive methods for system control.

C0765.name: hand gesture
C0765.definition: Hand gesture is a user hand motion used for interaction or to indicate that manipulation is done.

C0766.name: natural-language voice command
C0766.definition: Natural-language voice command is an interaction method for augmented reality smart glasses, in which the user gives natural-language commands that the glasses detect.

C0767.name: gyroscope
C0767.definition: A gyroscope is an inertial sensor that captures angular velocity. In an inertial measurement unit, it is a main component, and sensor tracking relies mainly on its readings.

C0768.name: accelerometer
C0768.definition: An accelerometer is an inertial sensor that captures linear acceleration along the x, y, and z axes, and in an inertial measurement unit its readings can be used to detect drift errors.

C0769.name: magnetometer
