C0769.definition: A magnetometer is a sensor that captures magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes and can be used to detect drift errors in tracking.

C0770.name: ambient light sensor
C0770.definition: An ambient light sensor is one of the sensors included in Google Glass.

C0771.name: proximity sensor
C0771.definition: A proximity sensor is a component of Google Glass.

C0772.name: Wi-Fi
C0772.definition: Wi-Fi is a component of Google Glass.

C0773.name: Bluetooth
C0773.definition: Bluetooth is one of the components included in Google Glass.

C0774.name: touchpad
C0774.definition: Touchpad is a component included in augmented reality (AR) smart glasses.

C0775.name: Vuzix's Blade
C0775.definition: Vuzix's Blade is an example of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses.

C0776.name: output actuator
C0776.definition: An output actuator is a component included in augmented reality (AR) smart glasses.

C0777.name: haptic feedback component
C0777.definition: A haptic feedback component is an output actuator found in augmented reality smart glasses.

C0778.name: display engine
C0778.definition: A display engine is a component included in augmented reality smart glasses.

C0779.name: see-through display
C0779.definition: A see-through display is a display, typically good for mixed reality or augmented reality, that enables users to see and interact with the physical world while adding virtual objects to the real world or visually enhancing real objects, as a computer uses wearable device sensors to detect which real object the user is dealing with.

C0780.name: noise-cancelling microphone
C0780.definition: A noise-cancelling microphone is a microphone that is included as a component of certain augmented reality smart glasses.

C0781.name: memory storage
C0781.definition: Memory storage is one of the components of augmented reality smart glasses.

C0782.name: universal serial bus connectivity
C0782.definition: Universal serial bus connectivity is a component included in augmented reality smart glasses.

C0783.name: Epson glasses
C0783.definition: Epson glasses are an example of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses.

C0784.name: Magic Leap glasses
C0784.definition: Magic Leap glasses are one example of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses.

C0785.name: handheld augmented reality device
C0785.definition: Handheld augmented reality device is a familiar, accessible device, such as a smartphone or tablet, that uses its own camera to capture a live real-world image, displays it on its screen, overlays digital content on that image, and typically relies on marker-based or markerless augmented reality.

C0786.name: projection-based augmented reality system
C0786.definition: A projection-based augmented reality system is an augmented reality system generally similar in idea to spatial augmented reality systems.

C0787.name: projection mapping
C0787.definition: Projection mapping is a software-based application of spatial augmented reality that uses software solutions and standard projectors to create complex projections in three-dimensional space without a surface.

C0788.name: interactive display
C0788.definition: An interactive display is a surface that a spatial augmented reality system can turn into an augmented reality experience by projecting images or interfaces onto it.

C0789.name: Sony Xperia Touch
C0789.definition: Sony Xperia Touch is an example of a spatial augmented reality system.

C0790.name: three-dimensional camera
C0790.definition: A three-dimensional camera is a sensor used in a spatial augmented reality system to support real-time updates when users move or gesture.

C0791.name: infrared sensor
C0791.definition: An infrared sensor is an optical sensor that can be deployed to detect or track a pose.

C0792.name: virtual keyboard
C0792.definition: A virtual keyboard is a keyboard that a projection keyboard projects onto a flat surface, converting that surface into an interactive keyboard.

C0793.name: TouchDesigner
C0793.definition: TouchDesigner is a software solution used in projection mapping technology with standard projectors to create complex projections onto three-dimensional space without a surface.

C0794.name: MadMapper
C0794.definition: MadMapper is a software solution used in projection mapping technology with standard projectors to create complex projections onto three-dimensional space without a surface.

C0795.name: HeavyM
C0795.definition: HeavyM is a software solution used with standard projectors in projection mapping to create complex projections onto three-dimensional space without a surface.

C0796.name: projection mapping display
C0796.definition: A projection mapping display is a display that can be interacted with by rotating, pinching, zooming in, or zooming out.

C0797.name: wearable technology
C0797.definition: Wearable technology is a category of technology that includes future examples such as augmented reality contact lenses.

C0798.name: imager
C0798.definition: An imager is a miniaturized component that can be placed on augmented reality contact lenses and can be made using complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technology.

C0799.name: complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technology
C0799.definition: Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technology (CMOS) is a technology used to make imagers.

C0800.name: wireless component
C0800.definition: A wireless component is a miniaturized component that can be placed on an augmented reality contact lens.

C0801.name: smart contact lens project
C0801.definition: The smart contact lens project is one of the current activities developing augmented reality contact lenses.

C0802.name: sense-organ tracking
C0802.definition: Sense-organ tracking is a tracking category that tracks the position and orientation of the user's sense organs so that a display attached to them is perceived as attached to the surrounding world and the virtual world or user experience is updated. In VR it mostly focuses on head tracking, which is sufficient for the visual and aural components.

C0803.name: body-part tracking
C0803.definition: Body-part tracking is a category of tracking in which the user's other body parts are tracked to represent the body in a virtual world, where perfect matching is not required.

C0804.name: environment tracking
C0804.definition: Environment tracking is a category of tracking that tracks the surrounding environment not related to the user, and may involve tracking physical objects in the real world. In virtual reality, it can alert users to physical objects not represented in the virtual world; augmenting a virtual world with live capture of the real world is a form of environment tracking.

C0805.name: sense organ
C0805.definition: Sense organ is a bodily organ whose receptors target particular stimuli and are activated only when a particular type of stimulus arrives, converting the stimulus into neural impulses for perception.

C0806.name: human eye
C0806.definition: The human eye is the sense organ for vision that contains a cornea, iris, pupil, and natural lens and focuses visible light on the retina, where photoreceptors convert it into neural pulses sent to the brain.

C0807.name: ear
C0807.definition: The ear is the sense organ for the auditory sense.

C0808.name: body-controlled degree of freedom
C0808.definition: Body-controlled degree of freedom is one of the degrees of freedom of the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, whose position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience.

C0809.name: avatar
C0809.definition: An avatar is a representation of a user's body in a virtual world.

C0810.name: virtual hand technique
C0810.definition: Virtual hand technique is the simplest and most intuitive hand selection technique for virtual objects, in which a visible virtual hand acts as an avatar of the user's physical hand and is tied to it by a one-to-one mapping of the physical hand's motion and orientation.

C0811.name: facial expression
C0811.definition: Facial expression is a kind of user motion that may be tracked or supported in a virtual world for interaction or social interaction.

C0812.name: matched zone
C0812.definition: A matched zone is the safe real-world region in a virtual reality application where the real and virtual worlds perfectly align, so the user's restricted physical movement within it is translated into movement in other parts of the virtual world.

C0813.name: movement
C0813.definition: Movement is a body-part movement in a virtual world whose approximate representation can provide a good experience when tracking a user's other body parts.

C0814.name: input signal
C0814.definition: Input signal is a simple explicit signal sent to change a user's body to a predetermined configuration without elaborate or further tracking.

C0815.name: body configuration
C0815.definition: Body configuration is a predetermined configuration of body parts that a simple explicit input signal can cause without further tracking.

C0816.name: physical object
C0816.definition: A physical object is a real-world object around the user that can be tracked in augmented reality or virtual reality.

C0817.name: real-world view
C0817.definition: Real-world view is an augmented reality context in which moved physical objects are tracked and 3D structures are modeled so that digital content can be registered in three-dimensional space.

C0818.name: digital content
C0818.definition: Digital content is the content that, in augmented reality, is appropriately registered in three-dimensional space after a moved physical object is tracked.

C0819.name: user tracking
C0819.definition: User tracking is tracking in virtual reality that is not useful for alerting users to physical objects not represented in the virtual world.

C0820.name: touch feedback
C0820.definition: Touch feedback is used in virtual reality to give a user the feeling of touching a real object surface.

C0821.name: telepresence
C0821.definition: Telepresence is used in applications that can bring a large part of the physical world into a virtual world through live capture, which is generally classified as augmented virtuality and as a form of tracking the surrounding environment.

C0822.name: live capture
C0822.definition: Live capture is a form of tracking the surrounding environment, generally classified as augmented virtuality, that in telepresence applications brings a large part of the physical world into a virtual world, augmenting it.

C0823.name: tracking method
C0823.definition: A tracking method is a technique for tracking, and choosing it depends on tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types.

C0824.name: tracker position
C0824.definition: Tracker position is the position of the tracker or sensor that provides input for tracking; the choice of tracking method or technique depends on it, and tracking is categorized into outside-in tracking and inside-out tracking based on it.

C0825.name: tracker types
C0825.definition: Tracker types are one of the factors on which the choice of how to track, and which tracking method or technique to apply, depends.

C0826.name: outside-in tracking
C0826.definition: Outside-in tracking is a tracking category, based on sensor position, in which the user's experience device does not contain the tracking sensors; instead, external sensors in the real world provide data to identify and track the user's motion, pose, and orientation. It is restricted to the specific area where its external sensors are placed.

C0827.name: inside-out tracking
C0827.definition: Inside-out tracking is a tracking type in which the cameras or other sensors needed for tracking are located within the device used for the experience or attached to the user, so no external sensors are required.

C0828.name: external sensor
C0828.definition: An external sensor is a tracking sensor or tracker in the real world, not contained in the user's experience device, that provides data to help a system attached to the user identify and track the user's motion, pose, and orientation.

C0829.name: motion
C0829.definition: Motion is perceived in a virtual world with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported.

C0830.name: sensor range
C0830.definition: Sensor range is the area within which outside-in tracking can track a user.

C0831.name: Intel Project Alloy
C0831.definition: Intel Project Alloy is an example of inside-out tracking.

C0832.name: Qualcomm VR820
C0832.definition: Qualcomm VR820 is an example of inside-out tracking.

C0833.name: inside-out
C0833.definition: Inside-out is a way to obtain input for tracking in which a camera mounted with the user detects external targets and estimates poses from them.

C0834.name: outside-in
C0834.definition: Outside-in is an infrared tracking input method that uses cameras placed in the environment rather than on the tracked object to detect targets attached to the object and determine its pose and position.

C0835.name: calibration
C0835.definition: Calibration is the step in the tracking process that transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value, reducing sensor error.

C0836.name: integration
C0836.definition: Integration is a stage of the tracking process that aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or input data sources at discrete time points to combine the values and track sense organs, body parts, or the environment, and computes the current sensor orientation from the initial orientation estimated during registration and calibrated angular velocity samples.

C0837.name: drift correction
C0837.definition: Drift correction is a step in the tracking process that compensates for the difference between estimated and actual position and orientation of the user, sense organs, body parts, or objects in the environment, reducing estimation error. It is usually done by blending values from at least two sensors, such as a gyroscope and camera, to estimate and correct drift.

C0838.name: sensor error
C0838.definition: Sensor error is reduced by calibration in the tracking process.

C0839.name: sensory measurement
C0839.definition: Sensory measurement is a measurement from sensors or input data sources that is aggregated in the tracking process at discrete time points to combine values and track sense organs, body parts, or the environment.

C0840.name: estimation error
C0840.definition: Estimation error is the difference between the estimated and actual position and orientation of a user, their sense organs, body parts, or objects in an environment during tracking.

C0841.name: linear acceleration
C0841.definition: Linear acceleration is a quantity captured by an accelerometer along the x, y, and z axes in an inertial measurement unit (IMU).

C0842.name: magnetic field strength
C0842.definition: Magnetic field strength is what a magnetometer captures along the x, y, and z axes in an inertial measurement unit (IMU).

C0843.name: drift error
C0843.definition: Drift error is an error in inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor tracking that can be detected using accelerometer and magnetometer readings.

C0844.name: measured angular velocity
C0844.definition: Measured angular velocity is the angular velocity value produced by an inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor, which can differ from the actual angular velocity because the measurement is imperfect and is transformed by calibration into a value that is the closest possible match to it.

C0845.name: actual angular velocity
C0845.definition: Actual angular velocity is the angular velocity value closely approximated by a highly accurate benchmark sensor in the calibration of inertial measurement unit sensors, and the value that measured and calibrated readings are made to match as closely as possible.

C0846.name: measurement error
C0846.definition: Measurement error is the difference between measured angular velocity and actual angular velocity in the calibration of inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, caused by imperfect devices and measurement technique.

C0847.name: calibration model
C0847.definition: A calibration model is a model that assumes a relationship between measured angular velocity and actual angular velocity; one simple model assumes a linear relationship, though other relationships are possible.

C0848.name: linear relationship
C0848.definition: A linear relationship is a relationship that a simple calibration model can assume between measured angular velocity and actual angular velocity, but it is not the only possible relationship.

C0849.name: paired samples
C0849.definition: Paired samples are pairs of measurements, one from an inertial measurement unit and one from a benchmark sensor, used in calibration to compare measured values with actual values.

C0850.name: benchmark sensor
C0850.definition: A benchmark sensor is an expensive, highly accurate sensor that produces the actual values, very close rather than exact or ideal, used in calibration with measured values from a less accurate sensor.

C0851.name: linear least squares regression
C0851.definition: Linear least squares regression is a classical optimization technique that finds constants for a linear expression by minimizing the sum of the squared differences between the expression and actual values.

C0852.name: calibrated value
C0852.definition: Calibrated value is a value that calibration transforms from an inexpensive measured angular velocity into the closest possible match with the actual value, using omega_cal = C1 + C2 omega_g.

C0853.name: initial orientation
C0853.definition: Initial orientation is the starting orientation of a sensor or user, found during registration to set the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds. In a simplifying assumption, it is taken as the headset's facing direction when tracking starts, with the initial alignment set to the forward direction.

C0854.name: initial alignment
C0854.definition: Initial alignment is the alignment between the real and virtual worlds set by registration from the initial pose or orientation of the sensor or user; as a simplifying assumption, it is set to the forward direction when the tracking system is turned on.

C0855.name: tracking system
C0855.definition: A tracking system is a basic tracking approach in which the headset's facing direction when the system is turned on is taken as the initial orientation.

C0856.name: reflector
C0856.definition: Reflector is an aid that can be used for registration.

C0857.name: tag
C0857.definition: A tag is an aid that can be used to make registration simpler.

C0858.name: current sensor orientation
C0858.definition: Current sensor orientation is the sensor orientation at the current time, computed by adding the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples multiplied by the sampling interval over the elapsed samples to the initial orientation estimated during registration.

C0859.name: calibrated angular velocity sample
C0859.definition: A calibrated angular velocity sample is an angular velocity sample from a gyroscopic sensor at an instant that indicates a change in orientation equal to the sample multiplied by the sampling interval, and is used to compute the sensor orientation.

C0860.name: sampling interval
C0860.definition: Sampling interval is the usually regular, discrete time interval between samples in the sensor data stream, used to multiply angular velocity samples to compute orientation changes.

C0861.name: sensor data stream
C0861.definition: A sensor data stream is sensor data that usually arrives at regular discrete intervals.

C0862.name: angular velocity sample
C0862.definition: An angular velocity sample is a sample from a gyroscopic sensor at an instant that indicates a change in orientation equal to its value multiplied by the sampling interval.

C0863.name: gyroscopic sensor
C0863.definition: A gyroscopic sensor is a sensor that provides angular velocity samples, which indicate a change in orientation.

C0864.name: drift
C0864.definition: Drift is what drift correction estimates and corrects, usually by blending the values of at least two extra sensors.

C0865.name: drift-corrected orientation
C0865.definition: Drift-corrected orientation is an orientation resulting from a drift-correction approach that combines, at the same time instant, an orientation obtained by integrating gyroscope values and an orientation obtained with a camera, using a gain parameter alpha between 0 and 1 so that the gyroscope orientation is weighted by alpha and the camera orientation by 1 minus alpha.

C0866.name: gain parameter
C0866.definition: Gain parameter is a normalized value between 0 and 1 used in a classic drift-correction approach to combine a gyroscope-derived orientation with a camera-derived orientation.

C0867.name: tracking technology
C0867.definition: Tracking technology is used in virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) and is categorized into electromechanical, electromagnetic, acoustic or ultrasonic, vision-based, inertial, and other tracking technologies, including location-based and hybrid technologies.

C0868.name: electromechanical tracking
C0868.definition: Electromechanical tracking is one of the tracking technologies used in virtual reality and augmented reality.

C0869.name: electromagnetic tracking
C0869.definition: Electromagnetic tracking is a tracking technology used in virtual reality and augmented reality that uses stationary transmitters and receivers that move with the head or the user's body and does not require line of sight between transmitter and receiver.

C0870.name: acoustic tracking
C0870.definition: Acoustic tracking is a VR and AR tracking technology that uses ultrasonic signals from stationary transmitters to determine the real-time position of receivers attached to a head-mounted display, requiring line of sight between transmitter and receiver.

C0871.name: vision-based tracking
C0871.definition: Vision-based tracking is a category of tracking technologies used in virtual reality and augmented reality.

C0872.name: inertial tracking
C0872.definition: Inertial tracking is one of the categories of tracking technologies used in virtual reality and augmented reality.

C0873.name: location-based tracking
C0873.definition: Location-based tracking is one of the tracking technologies used in virtual reality and augmented reality, grouped in the others category with hybrid tracking.

C0874.name: hybrid tracking
C0874.definition: Hybrid tracking is one of the tracking technologies included in the others category of tracking technologies used in virtual reality and augmented reality.

C0875.name: electromechanical tracker
C0875.definition: An electromechanical tracker is a serial or parallel kinematic structure composed of links interconnected by joints with sensors, in world-fixed or wearable forms, with wearable forms translating body movement into animated avatar movement in a virtual world.

C0876.name: kinematic structure
C0876.definition: A kinematic structure is a serial or parallel structure composed of links that are interconnected using joints with sensors.

C0877.name: link
C0877.definition: A link is a component of a serial or parallel kinematic structure in an electromechanical tracker or of a node-based scene graph.

C0878.name: joint
C0878.definition: A joint is a component of a physics engine that connects a rigid body to another rigid body or to a fixed point in space. It can apply forces that move the rigid bodies, has limits that restrict that movement, and is used to model realistic movement of objects or characters.

C0879.name: world-fixed tracker
C0879.definition: A world-fixed tracker is a cumbersome type of electromechanical tracker with a display attached to a mechanically pivoting, tracked setup that has tracking sensors and a counterbalance for stability.

C0880.name: wearable tracker
C0880.definition: A wearable tracker is an electromechanical tracker that is worn on a person's body and tracks and translates that person's movements into animated avatar movement in a virtual world.

C0881.name: counterbalance
C0881.definition: Counterbalance is a part of a world-fixed electromechanical tracker, and it is used to make the setup stable.

C0882.name: IGS 190
C0882.definition: IGS 190 is a wearable electromechanical tracker.

C0883.name: Gypsy 6
C0883.definition: Gypsy 6 is a wearable electromechanical tracker product.

C0884.name: Gypsy Gyro
C0884.definition: Gypsy Gyro is a product included among wearable electromechanical trackers.

C0885.name: exoskeleton tracker
C0885.definition: An exoskeleton tracker is a wearable electromechanical tracker.

C0886.name: electromagnetic tracker
C0886.definition: An electromagnetic tracker is a non-contact position measurement device in which a stationary transmitter in the environment generally has three antennas producing three orthogonal magnetic fields, and a receiver attached to a headset derives the head's real-time position relative to a fixed position from the magnetic field direction and resulting AC or DC currents.

C0887.name: transmitter
C0887.definition: A transmitter is a stationary part of a position measurement device that produces a magnetic field or ultrasonic signals for a moving receiver to determine position.

C0888.name: magnetic field
C0888.definition: A magnetic field is produced by a transmitter in an electromagnetic tracker, and its direction or the currents it generates in a receiver are used to determine the receiver's real-time position.

C0889.name: receiver
C0889.definition: A receiver is a part of electromagnetic or acoustic tracking that is attached to a headset, moves with the head or user's body, and whose real-time position is determined from magnetic fields or ultrasonic signals produced by stationary transmitters.

C0890.name: antenna
C0890.definition: An antenna is a part of an electromagnetic tracker transmitter that produces magnetic fields used to track a head's position.

C0891.name: alternating current
C0891.definition: Alternating current (AC) is a current generated in the receiver of an electromagnetic tracker by its magnetic fields, and it helps track a head's position relative to a fixed position in the environment.

C0892.name: direct current
C0892.definition: Direct current (DC) is a current that can be generated in the receiver of an electromagnetic tracker by magnetic fields, helping track the head's position.

C0893.name: ultrasonic signal
C0893.definition: An ultrasonic signal is a signal from stationary transmitters that acoustic tracking uses to determine the real-time position of receivers attached to a head-mounted display.

C0894.name: line of sight
C0894.definition: Line of sight is a line between a transmitter and a receiver, with no obstacle in between.

C0895.name: vision-based tracker
C0895.definition: A vision-based tracker is a tracker that determines poses, such as position and orientation, using optical sensors or cameras.

C0896.name: optical sensor
C0896.definition: An optical sensor is a sensor that vision-based trackers use to determine poses, such as position and orientation; its main categories are infrared, visible light, and 3D structure sensors.

C0897.name: visible light sensor
C0897.definition: A visible light sensor is an optical sensor that can be deployed to detect or track a pose and is used in visible light tracking.

C0898.name: three-dimensional structure sensor
C0898.definition: Three-dimensional structure sensor is one of the main categories of optical sensors that can be deployed to detect or track a pose.

C0899.name: infrared tracking
C0899.definition: Infrared tracking is a vision-based technique used in virtual reality or augmented reality that detects bright light-emitting or reflecting targets using infrared sensing, is robust to poor ambient lighting, and estimates pose and position either outside looking in or inside looking out.

C0900.name: target
C0900.definition: A target is a light-emitting or light-reflecting part in infrared tracking, bright against its surroundings, attached to a tracked object or placed externally, that cameras detect to estimate pose and position.

C0901.name: infrared sensing
C0901.definition: Infrared sensing is a form of sensing used by infrared tracking instead of visible light sensing.

C0902.name: visible light sensing
C0902.definition: Visible light sensing is a form of sensing that is contrasted with infrared sensing in the context of tracking.

C0903.name: visible light tracking
C0903.definition: Visible light tracking is a tracking technique that uses visible light sensors or optical cameras and is classified into fiducial tracking, natural feature tracking, and model-based tracking.

C0904.name: optical camera
C0904.definition: An optical camera is the most common type of optical sensor used in visible light tracking.

C0905.name: fiducial tracking
C0905.definition: Fiducial tracking is a visible light tracking technique that adds fiducials, artificial landmarks in the environment, to aid registration and tracking of an object.

C0906.name: natural feature tracking
C0906.definition: Natural feature tracking is a visible light tracking technique that registers camera pose in real time by detecting features already present in the natural environment, calculating unique descriptors, and matching scene features with features of the tracked object, using advanced image processing or computer vision.

C0907.name: model-based tracking
C0907.definition: Model-based tracking is a tracking technique of visible light tracking and is the third category of visible light-based sensing.

C0908.name: fiducial
C0908.definition: A fiducial is an artificial landmark in the environment that is added to aid the registration and tracking of an object.

C0909.name: multi-ring fiducial
C0909.definition: A multi-ring fiducial is a kind of fiducial used for detection at greater distances.

C0910.name: proportional width ring fiducial
C0910.definition: A proportional width ring fiducial is a kind of fiducial used in fiducial tracking, whose appearance changes with distance.

C0911.name: constant width ring fiducial
C0911.definition: A constant width ring fiducial is a fiducial whose ring width remains constant.

C0912.name: visual light-based sensing
C0912.definition: Visual light-based sensing is a category that includes natural feature tracking as its second category.

C0913.name: camera pose
C0913.definition: Camera pose is what natural feature tracking registers in real time and estimates by using calculated feature descriptors to match features detected in the scene with features detected in the object to be tracked.

C0914.name: image processing
C0914.definition: Image processing is an advanced technique used in natural feature tracking to detect features that are unique to the surroundings.

C0915.name: feature
C0915.definition: A feature is a unique, already present part of a natural environment, such as a point, corner, or line intersection, that is detected and distinguished by descriptors to estimate camera pose.

C0916.name: point
C0916.definition: A point is a position in a coordinate system, represented by coordinates or a vector, that can be transformed between coordinate systems and mapped to integer pixel-grid coordinates for display.

C0917.name: corner
C0917.definition: A corner is a kind of feature that natural feature tracking detects in the surroundings of an object to be tracked.

C0918.name: line intersection
C0918.definition: Line intersection is one of the features that are unique to the surroundings with respect to the object to be tracked and that image processing or computer vision techniques detect in natural feature tracking.

C0919.name: feature descriptor
C0919.definition: A feature descriptor is a unique descriptor calculated for each detected feature in natural feature tracking, used to identify and differentiate it from other features and to match features detected in the scene with features detected in the object to be tracked for camera pose estimation.

C0920.name: scale invariant feature transform
C0920.definition: Scale invariant feature transform (SIFT) is one of the popular natural feature detection and description algorithms used for natural feature tracking.

C0921.name: speeded up robust features
C0921.definition: Speeded up robust features (SURF) is one of the popular natural feature detection and description algorithms used for natural feature tracking.

C0922.name: binary robust independent elementary features
C0922.definition: Binary robust independent elementary features (BRIEF) is a popular natural feature detection and description algorithm used for natural feature tracking.

C0923.name: binary robust invariant scalable key points
C0923.definition: Binary robust invariant scalable key points (BRISK) is one of the popular natural feature detection and description algorithms used for natural feature tracking.

C0924.name: simultaneous localization and mapping
C0924.definition: Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is a technique that simultaneously creates and updates a map of a real environment while localizing positions within it, enabling real-time, drift-free tracking of unknown environments.

C0925.name: map
C0925.definition: A map is a way of showing a real or virtual space or place, including objects or points, the user's current position, and routes, and can be updated to support wayfinding, movement, real-time tracking, or forming mental models.

C0926.name: localization
C0926.definition: Localization is the determination of an object’s position within a real environment.

C0927.name: robot navigation
C0927.definition: Robot navigation is a use for which Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) was originally developed.

C0928.name: parallel tracking and mapping
C0928.definition: Parallel tracking and mapping (PTAM) is a further optimization of simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). It was specifically designed for augmented reality and allows tracking of the camera and mapping of the environment as separate activities.

C0929.name: mapping
C0929.definition: Mapping is an activity in Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) that is performed separately from camera tracking.

C0930.name: tracking accuracy
C0930.definition: Tracking accuracy is one of the things that Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) improved, along with overall performance.

C0931.name: performance
C0931.definition: Performance is a characteristic that can be improved and that developers can optimize by choosing and implementing physics-support algorithms.

C0932.name: computational requirement
C0932.definition: Computational requirement is the amount of computation needed for tracking or rendering, and it is higher for larger environments or rich interactive multimodal content.

C0933.name: three-dimensional structure tracking
C0933.definition: Three-dimensional structure tracking is a tracking technique that uses commercial sensors to obtain 3D positions of points in a scene and creates 3D models of structures in the environment to augment the real-world view.

C0934.name: commercial sensor
C0934.definition: A commercial sensor is a sensor used in 3D structure tracking to detect 3D structure information from an environment and obtain 3D positions of points in a scene for creating 3D models.

C0935.name: three-dimensional position
C0935.definition: Three-dimensional position is a position of a point in a scene that a tracking technique obtains to create models of structures for augmenting the real-world view.

C0936.name: three-dimensional model
C0936.definition: A three-dimensional model is a model of objects, structures, or environments used in virtual reality tours and augmented reality applications.

C0937.name: structure
C0937.definition: Structure is part of the environment that 3D structure tracking creates 3D models of for augmentation of the real-world view.

C0938.name: augmentation
C0938.definition: Augmentation is the real-world view's being augmented by 3D models of structures in the environment that 3D structure tracking creates.

C0939.name: three-dimensional structure information
C0939.definition: Three-dimensional structure information is information that can be detected from the environment by commercial sensors.

C0940.name: Kinect Fusion
C0940.definition: Kinect Fusion is an augmented reality system and an example of 3D structure tracking that uses data from the Kinect's structured light depth sensor to create high-quality 3D models of real objects and environments and uses those models to track the Kinect's pose.

C0941.name: structured light depth sensor
C0941.definition: A structured light depth sensor is a sensor whose data are used to create high-quality 3D models of real objects and environments for pose tracking.

C0942.name: microelectromechanical system
C0942.definition: A microelectromechanical system (MEMS) is a system that inertial trackers are typically based on.

C0943.name: hybrid software-level sensor
C0943.definition: A hybrid software-level sensor is a sensor that can be designed using primary inertial sensors and can be part of a device.

C0944.name: electromechanical tracking sensor
C0944.definition: An electromechanical tracking sensor is one of the basic types of tracking sensors typically used.

C0945.name: electromagnetic tracking sensor
C0945.definition: Electromagnetic tracking sensor is one of the basic types of tracking sensors typically used.

C0946.name: light-based sensing
C0946.definition: Light-based sensing is one of the basic types of tracking sensors typically used.

C0947.name: acoustic sensing
C0947.definition: Acoustic sensing is a sensing approach that does not directly fit into the basic tracking sensor categories.

C0948.name: positional tracking
C0948.definition: Positional tracking is what a positional tracking device, such as a global positioning system (GPS), allows.

C0949.name: real time kinematic
C0949.definition: Real time kinematic (RTK) is a technology that can be used with a basic global positioning system sensor to improve detection accuracy by using global positioning system signal carrier waves for measurement.

C0950.name: hybrid tracking system
C0950.definition: A hybrid tracking system is a tracking system that may include the global positioning system (GPS) along with other tracking systems.

C0951.name: motion capture
C0951.definition: Motion capture is a technique for digitally recording movements of real things, usually humans, that can be based on any tracking method. It is packaged as wearable suits with tracking sensors that record users' movements, and it can be real-time or non-real-time.

C0952.name: facial tracker
C0952.definition: A facial tracker is a tracking sensor included in motion capture wearable suits, typically one or two of them, in a system that records the movements of users who wear the suits.

C0953.name: full body tracking device
C0953.definition: A full body tracking device is a tracking device that can be a camera and is used in a wearable motion-capture suit in which the movements of users are recorded.

C0954.name: real-time tracking
C0954.definition: Real-time tracking is a form of tracking, in contrast to non-real-time tracking, that motion capture need not be.

C0955.name: non-real-time tracking
C0955.definition: Non-real-time tracking is a possible kind of motion capture, distinct from real-time tracking.

C0956.name: external display
C0956.definition: An external display is a display to which an eye-tracking system can be remotely attached.

C0957.name: optical tracking
C0957.definition: Optical tracking is used in eye-tracking systems with a high-resolution camera-based tracking device.

C0958.name: camera-based tracking device
C0958.definition: A camera-based tracking device is a high-resolution device used by eye-tracking systems for optical tracking.

C0959.name: infrared lighting-based eye tracking
C0959.definition: Infrared lighting-based eye tracking is a technique that eye-tracking systems can use.

C0960.name: video-oculography
C0960.definition: Video-oculography (VOG) is a technique that eye-tracking systems can use.

C0961.name: gaze point
C0961.definition: A gaze point is a point of the user's gaze that eye-tracking systems typically track.

C0962.name: gaze area
C0962.definition: A gaze area is the area of a user's gaze that eye-tracking systems typically track, as an alternative to the gaze point.

C0963.name: hybrid tracker
C0963.definition: A hybrid tracker is a tracking method that combines two or more basic tracking systems or approaches, typically performing better than single-technology-based tracking.

C0964.name: emotion capture
C0964.definition: Emotion capture is an example of a hybrid tracker, a tracking method that uses two or more basic tracking systems or approaches.

C0965.name: single-technology-based tracking
C0965.definition: Single-technology-based tracking is a tracking approach that relies on a single technology, and hybrid trackers are typically found to perform better than it.

C0966.name: virtual reality software
C0966.definition: Virtual reality software is software that drives virtual reality or augmented reality hardware so that it generates appropriate stimuli that stimulate human sense organs, creating a virtual reality experience that utilizes human senses, and supports developers in creating virtual environments, rendering stereoscopic output views, and incorporating interactions.

C0967.name: augmented reality hardware
C0967.definition: Augmented reality hardware is hardware that virtual reality software drives to generate stimuli that stimulate human sense organs.

C0968.name: human sense organs
C0968.definition: Human sense organs are the organs that are stimulated by appropriate stimuli generated by virtual reality or augmented reality hardware to create a virtual reality experience that utilizes human senses.

C0969.name: sense
C0969.definition: Sense is one of six human senses—vision, auditory, touch, balance, taste, or smell—each classified by a stimulus, receptors, and a sense organ in which the receptors receive the stimulus.

C0970.name: interaction design
C0970.definition: Interaction design is the activity of designing user input in an XR system from the user's point of view to make the user's interaction easy, effective, and seamless.

C0971.name: perceptual design
C0971.definition: Perceptual design is the user-centered design and modeling of output stimuli in an extended reality system so that generated stimuli match the user's perception and are appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived.

C0972.name: modeling
C0972.definition: Modeling is required in the data flow between a user and virtual reality hardware for the user's interaction with input devices and for stimuli generated by output devices to suitably stimulate the user's sense organs.

C0973.name: game engine
C0973.definition: A game engine is a software development environment and middleware that sits between hardware and higher-level application software, abstracting hardware for developers to build games or extended reality (XR) experiences. It typically provides rendering, physics, audio, scripting, and low-level platform-specific support.

C0974.name: software-and-database component
C0974.definition: A software-and-database component is one of two components that represent the software part of a virtual reality data-flow diagram.

C0975.name: environment modeling
C0975.definition: Environment modeling is the activity of creating the virtual environment in a virtual reality experience.

C0976.name: high-level description
C0976.definition: A high-level description is a description that a virtual reality developer provides to virtual reality software so that the software automatically determines all the low-level details.

C0977.name: low-level detail
C0977.definition: Low-level detail is a detail in virtual reality (VR) software that is ideally automatically determined from high-level descriptions, although in practice a developer may implement functionality from scratch instead of providing high-level descriptions.

C0978.name: software library
C0978.definition: A software library is a low-level software development tool that software calls for a function, such as tracking or rendering, so developers can avoid micro-level activities.

C0979.name: platform
C0979.definition: A platform is the combination of hardware and an operating system.

C0980.name: operating system
C0980.definition: Operating system (OS) is a part of a platform, which is the combination of hardware and an operating system.

C0981.name: device driver
C0981.definition: A device driver is one of the lowest-level, platform-specific operations that a software development kit may handle in practical virtual reality development.

C0982.name: display output
C0982.definition: Display output is a lowest-level, platform-specific operation in practical virtual reality development that an SDK for a headset or platform may handle, along with device drivers and head tracking.

C0983.name: virtual world generator
C0983.definition: Virtual world generator (VWG) is a black-box abstraction of a virtual reality software system that maintains an internal reality that appears real and can use renderers to produce visual, aural, and haptic output synchronized with input.

C0984.name: black box
C0984.definition: A black box is an abstraction of a system whose internal operation is not considered.

C0985.name: head tracker
C0985.definition: A head tracker is a low-level input system that estimates a user's head position and orientation.

C0986.name: head position
C0986.definition: Head position is the position of a user's head that a head tracker estimates and from which a virtual ray is extended for head pointing when hand tracking is unavailable.

C0987.name: head orientation
C0987.definition: Head orientation is the orientation of a user's head estimated by a head tracker and received as input by a virtual world generator.

C0988.name: game controller
C0988.definition: A game controller is an input device used in virtual reality to control a user's avatar for locomotion and to operate a vehicle's controls.

C0989.name: input event
C0989.definition: Input event is an input arranged in a queue so that simultaneous input can be processed systematically.

C0990.name: queue
C0990.definition: A queue is used to arrange simultaneous input events so that they can be processed systematically.

C0991.name: renderer
C0991.definition: A renderer is a part of a virtual world generator that extracts information and calculates outputs for a display. It can be visual, aural, or haptic, generating a visual, aural, or haptic display.

C0992.name: synchronization
C0992.definition: Synchronization is used by a virtual world generator to keep output devices synchronized with the input data to maintain an input-output match.

C0993.name: input-output match
C0993.definition: Input-output match is maintained by a virtual world generator that keeps output devices synchronized with input data.

C0994.name: visual renderer
C0994.definition: Visual renderer is an output renderer that generates a visual display.

C0995.name: aural renderer
C0995.definition: Aural renderer is an output renderer that a virtual world generator can use to generate an aural display sensed by the ears.

C0996.name: aural display
C0996.definition: An aural display is a display generated by an aural renderer and sensed by the ears.

C0997.name: haptic renderer
C0997.definition: A haptic renderer is an output renderer in a virtual world generator that generates a haptic display sensed by the skin.

C0998.name: haptic display
C0998.definition: Haptic display is a display that is sensed by the skin and generated by a haptic renderer.

C0999.name: triangular mesh
C0999.definition: A triangular mesh is a three-dimensional surface made of triangles, into which graphics systems convert surfaces for a scene to be rendered regardless of how a developer defines an object, and whose vertices a GPU receives as input, one at a time, to assemble into triangles.

C1000.name: material surface property
C1000.definition: Material surface property is a property of a surface in a completely synthetic virtual world that indicates how the surface interacts with light, sound, and forces.

C1001.name: light
C1001.definition: Light is energy that can be described as photons, waves, or rays, can propagate through a vacuum, and the intensity of light reflected from a surface to the eye determines perceived color.

C1002.name: sound
C1002.definition: Sound is a vibration that requires a medium, usually air, to propagate as pressure variations from compression to rarefaction, and it is perceived at the human eardrum as an auditory experience. It is represented as a sound wave characterized by frequency, amplitude, and phase.

C1003.name: force
C1003.definition: Force is a parameter associated with moving body parts that joints can apply to move rigid bodies and with which surfaces in synthetic virtual worlds interact.

C1004.name: computer graphics
C1004.definition: Computer graphics (CG) is the area that addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models. It creates or represents objects, synthesizes them into a scene, allows users to manipulate images on a screen, creates the perception of motion, and renders the scene on a display so humans can perceive it.

C1005.name: computer-generated image
C1005.definition: A computer-generated image is an image from synthetic models addressed by computer graphics.

C1006.name: synthetic model
C1006.definition: A synthetic model is a model from which computer-generated images are created in computer graphics.

C1007.name: texture mapping
C1007.definition: Texture mapping is a common computer-graphics operation that maps camera images of a real object onto a synthetic object to create a virtual world.

C1008.name: synthetic object
C1008.definition: A synthetic object is an object onto which, in texture mapping, camera images of a real object are mapped to create a virtual world.

C1009.name: matched motion
C1009.definition: Matched motion is the maintenance, in virtual reality, of correspondence between a user's motions in the real world and the virtual world.

C1010.name: obstacle mismatch
C1010.definition: Obstacle mismatch is a situation, in an immersive virtual reality application that is not carefully implemented, that can occur when a virtual obstacle blocks the user without a corresponding physical obstacle in the matched zone, or when a physical obstacle exists in the matched zone without a corresponding virtual obstacle.

C1011.name: virtual obstacle
C1011.definition: A virtual obstacle is an obstacle in an immersive virtual reality application that can block a user.

C1012.name: physical obstacle
C1012.definition: A physical obstacle is an obstacle in the matched zone of an immersive virtual reality application that can exist without a corresponding virtual obstacle.

C1013.name: user locomotion
C1013.definition: User locomotion is moving oneself in virtual reality (VR) while one's physical motion in the real world is not matched.

C1014.name: locomotion operation
C1014.definition: A locomotion operation is a virtual reality operation, such as teleportation, in which a user can be sent to a desired virtual location without making any physical movement.

C1015.name: vehicle metaphor
C1015.definition: Vehicle metaphor is a virtual reality user locomotion technique in which a user's avatar boards a vehicle and operates its controls while the user remains seated.

C1016.name: physics support
C1016.definition: Physics support is a required key support in a virtual world generator that makes the virtual world appear to behave like the real world, for example by making a dropped ball accelerate due to gravity and replicating how light, sound, or smell propagate.

C1017.name: locomotion support
C1017.definition: Locomotion support is a support in a virtual world generator, listed with physics support, computer graphics and computer vision support for rendering, and matched motion support.

C1018.name: matched motion support
C1018.definition: Matched motion support is one of the required key supports in a virtual world generator.

C1019.name: object motion
C1019.definition: Object motion is motion in a virtual world generator that, in most cases, should be governed by basic laws of mechanics.

C1020.name: basic laws of mechanics
C1020.definition: Basic laws of mechanics are the laws by which object motion in a virtual world generator should be governed in most cases.

C1021.name: gravity
C1021.definition: Gravity is one stimulus for the balance sense and what makes dropped objects accelerate toward the ground in virtual-world physics.

C1022.name: collision support
C1022.definition: Collision support is a virtual world generator component that ideally includes collision detection, which determines whether two or more bodies intersect, and collision response, which determines how they should behave after a collision occurs.

C1023.name: collision detection
C1023.definition: Collision detection is a part of collision support in a virtual world generator that determines whether two or more bodies intersect.

C1024.name: collision response
C1024.definition: Collision response is the part of collision support in a virtual world generator that determines how bodies should behave after a collision occurs.

C1025.name: collision
C1025.definition: Collision is the intersection of two or more bodies in a virtual world, and a collision response determines how the bodies should behave after it occurs.

C1026.name: body
C1026.definition: Body is one of the things checked for intersection by collision detection in a virtual world generator.

C1027.name: surface
C1027.definition: Surface is a boundary of an object that can be polygonal or curved.

C1028.name: light source
C1028.definition: A light source is an element that emits light that falls on a surface point directly or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces.

C1029.name: smell
C1029.definition: Smell is a human chemical sense in which chemoreceptors in the nasal passage work by chemical reaction with specific molecules or chemical stimuli at appropriate concentrations.

C1030.name: networked collaborative virtual reality experience
C1030.definition: A networked collaborative virtual reality experience is a collaborative virtual reality experience created over a network, in which a system or server maintains a shared virtual world and must manage user interactions, including collisions, whether users are close or spread around the world.

C1031.name: collaborative virtual reality experience
C1031.definition: A collaborative virtual reality experience is a virtual reality experience that may be created over a network in which a shared virtual world is maintained by a system or a server, although such a network experience may not be required everywhere.

C1032.name: shared virtual world
C1032.definition: A shared virtual world is part of a networked collaborative virtual reality experience; it is maintained by a system or server, and user interactions within it must be managed by the virtual reality system.

C1033.name: physical collision
C1033.definition: Physical collision is an unwanted event that must be avoided when users are close in a networked collaborative virtual reality setting.

C1034.name: body language
C1034.definition: Body language is one of the things a virtual world generator should support, along with eye movements and facial expressions, in networked collaborative virtual reality when social interaction is important.

C1035.name: social interaction
C1035.definition: Social interaction is a consideration in networked collaborative virtual reality settings, and when it is important, virtual world generators should support eye movements, facial expressions, and body language, with the burden of matched motion possibly increasing as users meet each other.

C1036.name: driver
C1036.definition: A driver is one of the things that a basic software development kit for a headset, device, or platform is typically expected to provide to drive the hardware.

C1037.name: application programming interface
C1037.definition: Application programming interface (API) is a predefined set of functions provided by a library that, when invoked with appropriate arguments or parameters, perform specific tasks, allowing a programmer to deal with lower-level tasks without needing to know every detail of the underlying system or platform.

C1038.name: tracking data
C1038.definition: Tracking data is data that is accessed through interfaces or application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by a basic software development kit (SDK) for a headset, device, or platform.

C1039.name: native rendering library
C1039.definition: A native rendering library is a software library that sits above an operating system and provides graphics APIs that a virtual reality or game engine calls to perform rendering, rather than the developer accessing it directly.

C1040.name: physics
C1040.definition: Physics is a support in a virtual world that handles an avatar's movement, collision detection, the occurrence of a collision, and the response to it.

C1041.name: collaborative virtual reality
C1041.definition: Collaborative virtual reality is a networked virtual reality experience whose support may be required in a virtual world generator.

C1042.name: lighting model
C1042.definition: A lighting model is a computer graphics model used in color computation that simulates the reflection of incident light from a surface point to the viewer's eye, computing the intensity of that reflected light, which is the point's color, as a continuous value, typically between 0 and 1, mapped to discrete display values.

C1043.name: audio support
C1043.definition: Audio support is a core functionality of game engines and a support that must be built when building a virtual world generator from a basic software development kit.

C1044.name: OpenSimulator
C1044.definition: OpenSimulator is an open-source system that provides ready-made virtual world generator support for developers building a virtual society of avatars.

C1045.name: Second Life
C1045.definition: Second Life is a virtual world for building a virtual society of avatars.

C1046.name: Unity3D
C1046.definition: Unity3D is a popular game engine that has been adapted to work for virtual reality.

C1047.name: application software
C1047.definition: Application software is interactive software that is intended for laypersons and, in a typical VR system, is the highest layer above a game engine.

C1048.name: hardware abstraction
C1048.definition: Hardware abstraction is an abstraction of hardware functionalities for developers of extended reality (XR) applications, supported by a virtual reality (VR) engine.

C1049.name: software development environment
C1049.definition: A software development environment is, for example, a game engine used for building extended reality (XR) experiences, on which a developer can build their own application.

C1050.name: physics engine
C1050.definition: Physics engine is a component of a game engine that emulates the laws of physics realistically by providing functions to simulate physical forces and collisions acting on various objects within the scene at runtime.

C1051.name: rendering engine
C1051.definition: A rendering engine is a component of a game engine that helps generate animated three-dimensional graphics by rendering methods and is typically built on rendering application programming interfaces that provide software abstractions of a graphics processing unit.

C1052.name: audio engine
C1052.definition: An audio engine is a component of a game engine that consists of algorithms related to loading, modifying, and generating sound through a speaker system.

C1053.name: user interface
C1053.definition: A user interface is an interface whose design and qualities make it usable, and where usability issues arise.

C1054.name: authoring tool
C1054.definition: An authoring tool is a tool that lets a developer create software or content by accessing underlying system functionalities, with options for loading, feature-setting, and logic-setting; for augmented reality, it can be standalone or an existing tool extended by a plugin.

C1055.name: scripting
C1055.definition: Scripting is programming used in game-engine development and in building virtual and augmented reality systems, and it can set logic, customize features, and handle user input; customized experiences require it, while basic systems can be built with menu-based IDE support without it.

C1056.name: game engine development environment
C1056.definition: A game engine development environment is a development environment that comprises a game engine plus other components, and it may include the entire authoring tool, which may provide loading options, feature-setting options, and logic-setting options, sometimes through scripting.

C1057.name: Unity Hub
C1057.definition: Unity Hub is a standalone application whose installation is not mandatory. It is the primary way to install the Unity Editor and Unity Game Engine and streamlines finding, downloading, and managing Unity projects, installations, and multiple Unity versions.

C1058.name: rendering support
C1058.definition: Rendering support is one of the core functionalities typically included in game engines.

C1059.name: networking support
C1059.definition: Networking support is a core functionality of game engines, primarily for multiplayer collaborative virtual reality experiences.

C1060.name: low-level support
C1060.definition: Low-level support is a core functionality of game engines that supports platform-specific tasks, including memory management.

C1061.name: platform-specific task
C1061.definition: A platform-specific task is a low-level task supported by game engines, such as memory management, which includes threading and localization support.

C1062.name: memory management
C1062.definition: Memory management is a platform-specific task for which game engines provide low-level support.

C1063.name: threading
C1063.definition: Threading is a low-level, platform-specific support in game engines that is part of memory management.

C1064.name: localization support
C1064.definition: Localization support is part of memory management in game engines.

C1065.name: three-dimensional graphics
C1065.definition: Three-dimensional graphics is animated graphics that a rendering engine in a game engine can generate using rendering methods such as rasterization or ray tracing.

C1066.name: rendering method
C1066.definition: A rendering method is a method that a rendering engine uses to generate animated three-dimensional graphics.

C1067.name: rasterization
C1067.definition: Rasterization is the fifth stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that transforms continuous device coordinate descriptions into discrete pixel-grid screen descriptions by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels.

C1068.name: ray tracing
C1068.definition: Ray tracing is one of the rendering methods used to generate animated three-dimensional graphics.

C1069.name: Direct3D
C1069.definition: Direct3D is a graphics library and rendering application programming interface that provides software abstractions of the graphics processing unit and is part of the native rendering library layer in layered virtual reality software architectures.

C1070.name: open graphics library
C1070.definition: Open Graphics Library (OpenGL) is a native graphics library and rendering API that provides software abstractions of a graphics processing unit (GPU) for performing rendering.

C1071.name: vulkan
C1071.definition: Vulkan is one of the rendering application programming interfaces that provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit.

C1072.name: memory
C1072.definition: Memory is part of the hardware in typical virtual reality systems and standalone computing devices.

C1073.name: speaker system
C1073.definition: A speaker system is a system through which an audio engine generates sound.

C1074.name: application-specific integrated circuit
C1074.definition: An application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) is a dedicated integrated circuit on which an audio engine can perform its calculations.

C1075.name: open audio library
C1075.definition: Open audio library (OpenAL) is an abstraction application programming interface (API) on top of which an audio engine can be built.

C1076.name: simple directmedia layer audio
C1076.definition: Simple directmedia layer audio is one of the abstraction application programming interfaces (APIs) on top of which an audio engine can be built.

C1077.name: x audio 2
C1077.definition: X audio 2 is an abstraction application programming interface (API) on top of which an audio engine can be built.

C1078.name: wave audio
C1078.definition: Wave audio is one of the abstraction application programming interfaces (APIs) on top of which an audio engine can be built.

C1079.name: physical force
C1079.definition: A physical force is one of the things that a physics engine simulates as acting on objects within a scene at runtime.

C1080.name: runtime
C1080.definition: Runtime is the time when a physics engine simulates physical forces and collisions in a scene and a script instantiates a prefab within an application.

C1081.name: unreal engine
C1081.definition: Unreal Engine is a game engine whose major features are freely available.

C1082.name: cryengine
C1082.definition: CryEngine is an example of a game engine.

C1083.name: godot
C1083.definition: Godot is an example of a game engine.

C1084.name: lumberyard
C1084.definition: Lumberyard is an example of a game engine.

C1085.name: amazon sumerian
C1085.definition: Amazon Sumerian is an example of a game engine and one of the complete development and deployment tools for applications on the web.

C1086.name: deployment
C1086.definition: Deployment is the development stage in which a built system is made available, either as a native application requiring tailored software development kits or as a web application that allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device.

C1087.name: native application deployment
C1087.definition: Native application deployment is a way of deploying a virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR) application that requires software development kits (SDKs) tailored to the platform and hardware, which can be proprietary or open source.

C1088.name: web application deployment
C1088.definition: Web application deployment is a type of virtual reality application deployment that allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device.

C1089.name: view plane
C1089.definition: A view plane is the two-dimensional plane in a three-dimensional view coordinate system onto which a selected portion of a three-dimensional scene is projected; it is usually a rectangular area and an abstract intermediate representation that has nothing to do with the display.

C1090.name: Mac OS
C1090.definition: Mac OS is a desktop operating system, an example of a desktop platform.

C1091.name: desktop platform
C1091.definition: A desktop platform is a platform that, in deployment, typically consists of an operating system and hardware.

C1092.name: iPhone operating system
C1092.definition: iPhone operating system (iOS) is one of the mobile platforms in deployment.

C1093.name: mobile platform
C1093.definition: Mobile platform is a deployment platform, typically meaning the operating system plus hardware, such as Android or iOS.

C1094.name: software development tool
C1094.definition: A software development tool is a tool in a software development kit, used to design, build, and test virtual reality experiences for specific platforms.

C1095.name: proprietary
C1095.definition: Proprietary is an availability category used to classify native deployment software development kits.

C1096.name: open source
C1096.definition: Open source is an availability category for native deployment software development kits, as distinct from proprietary.

C1097.name: virtual reality software development kit
C1097.definition: Virtual reality software development kit (VR SDK) is a software development kit used by head-mounted displays.

C1098.name: OpenVR software development kit
C1098.definition: An OpenVR software development kit (OpenVR SDK) is a virtual reality software development kit by Valve that can be used with the HTC Vive system.

C1099.name: SteamVR software development kit
C1099.definition: SteamVR software development kit (SteamVR SDK) is a virtual reality software development kit that can be used with the HTC Vive system.

C1100.name: VRTK software development kit
C1100.definition: VRTK software development kit is one of the virtual reality software development kits that can be used with the HTC Vive system.

C1101.name: Oculus software development kit
C1101.definition: The Oculus software development kit (Oculus SDK) is a virtual reality software development kit used by the Oculus Rift.

C1102.name: Samsung Gear VR
C1102.definition: Samsung Gear VR is a head-mounted display that uses the Oculus Mobile SDK.

C1103.name: Oculus Mobile software development kit
C1103.definition: The Oculus Mobile software development kit is a virtual reality software development kit used by the Samsung Gear VR head-mounted display.

C1104.name: Sony PlayStation
C1104.definition: Sony PlayStation is a head-mounted display that uses the PSVR SDK.

C1105.name: PSVR software development kit
C1105.definition: The PSVR software development kit is a virtual reality software development kit used by Sony PlayStation.

C1106.name: Google Daydream View
C1106.definition: Google Daydream View is a head-mounted display that uses the Google VR SDK.

C1107.name: Google Cardboard
C1107.definition: Google Cardboard is a head-mounted display in which a smartphone is inserted to provide a 360-degree virtual reality experience.

C1108.name: Google virtual reality software development kit
C1108.definition: The Google virtual reality software development kit (Google VR SDK) is an open source virtual reality software development kit used by Google Daydream View or Google Cardboard, although it is no longer very much supported.

C1109.name: web deployment tool
C1109.definition: A web deployment tool is a tool for web-based deployment, broadly including cloud hosting and rendering, development libraries, complete development and deployment tools, generic development editors, and software development kit support.

C1110.name: cloud hosting and rendering tool
C1110.definition: A cloud hosting and rendering tool is a web deployment tool that provides only hosting and rendering over a network.

C1111.name: library for development support for deployment over the web
C1111.definition: A library for development support for deployment over the web is one of the broad categories of Web deployment tools.

C1112.name: complete development and deployment tool for applications on the web
C1112.definition: A complete development and deployment tool for applications on the web is a broad category of web deployment tools.

C1113.name: generic development editor for writing code for web-based deployment
C1113.definition: A generic development editor for writing code for web-based deployment is a kind of web deployment tool.

C1114.name: hosting
C1114.definition: Hosting is provided over a network by cloud hosting and rendering support tools for web deployment.

C1115.name: azure remote rendering
C1115.definition: Azure remote rendering is one of the cloud hosting and rendering support tools for three-dimensional (3D) rendering.

C1116.name: three-dimensional rendering
C1116.definition: Three-dimensional rendering is a purpose of cloud hosting and rendering support tools.

C1117.name: nvidia cloudxr
C1117.definition: Nvidia CloudXR is a cloud hosting and rendering support tool.

C1118.name: immersive stream
C1118.definition: Immersive Stream is a cloud hosting and rendering support tool for extended reality (XR) that works on Google Cloud.

C1119.name: google cloud
C1119.definition: Google Cloud is a cloud on which the extended reality tool Immersive Stream works.

C1120.name: eco3d
C1120.definition: Eco3D is a cloud hosting and rendering support tool.

C1121.name: arbor xr
C1121.definition: Arbor XR is one of the cloud hosting and rendering support tools.

C1122.name: webxr
C1122.definition: Webxr is a popular library for development support for deployment over the web that uses WebGL.

C1123.name: three.js
C1123.definition: Three.js is a popular library for development support for deployment over the web that is used for rendering and makes WebGL easier.

C1124.name: augmented reality.js
C1124.definition: Augmented reality.js is one of the popular libraries for development support for deployment over the web.

C1125.name: three.xr.js
C1125.definition: Three.xr.js is one of the popular libraries for development support for deployment over the web.

C1126.name: wavexr
C1126.definition: Wavexr is a popular library for development support for deployment over the web that is built on three.js.

C1127.name: aframe
C1127.definition: Aframe is a popular library for development support for deployment over the web.

C1128.name: babylon.js
C1128.definition: Babylon.js is a popular library for development support for deployment over the web.

C1129.name: reactxr.js
C1129.definition: ReactXR.js is a popular library for development support for deployment over the web.

C1130.name: web graphics library
C1130.definition: Web graphics library (WebGL) is a web component technology used by WebXR and by developers who write code for fast, non-flash, browser-based augmented reality prototypes.

C1131.name: zappair
C1131.definition: Zappair is one of the complete development and deployment tools for applications on the web.

C1132.name: 8thwall
C1132.definition: 8thwall is a complete development and deployment tool for applications on the web.

C1133.name: mywebar
C1133.definition: Mywebar is one of the complete development and deployment tools for applications on the web.

C1134.name: vrdirect
C1134.definition: Vrdirect is one of the complete development and deployment tools for applications on the web.

C1135.name: gmetrixr
C1135.definition: Gmetrixr is one of the complete development and deployment tools for applications on the web.

C1136.name: instavr
C1136.definition: InstaVR is a complete development and deployment tool for applications on the web.

C1137.name: plugxr
C1137.definition: PlugXR is a complete development and deployment tool for applications on the web.

C1138.name: augmented reality software tool
C1138.definition: An augmented reality software tool is a software tool for augmented reality that can be categorized by developer skill, target application platform, or tracking technology.

C1139.name: programming skill
C1139.definition: Programming skill is one way to categorize augmented reality software tools according to the level of skill required to use them.

C1140.name: application platform
C1140.definition: Application platform is one of the ways augmented reality software tools can be categorized, with desktop or mobile augmented reality applications as examples.

C1141.name: desktop augmented reality application
C1141.definition: A desktop augmented reality application is one of the target application platform categories used to categorize augmented reality software tools.

C1142.name: mobile augmented reality application
C1142.definition: A mobile augmented reality application is an augmented reality application that targets mobile platforms, such as iOS or Android.

C1143.name: computer vision-based tracking
C1143.definition: Computer vision-based tracking is a tracking technology for augmented reality software tools.

C1144.name: skill-based hierarchy
C1144.definition: A skill-based hierarchy is an arrangement of augmented reality software tools into four categories ordered by decreasing programming skill.

C1145.name: low-level software library or framework
C1145.definition: Low-level software library or framework is an AR software tool that requires strong programming or coding ability and an understanding of how to call the library functions, with the highest programming-skill requirement among AR software tools.

C1146.name: rapid prototyping tool
C1146.definition: Rapid prototyping tool is an augmented reality software tool that requires some programming ability and may require design prototyping skills, and is used to visualize an augmented reality idea with simple means before major development and show it to end users or clients, so an unsuitable idea does not require further coding.

C1147.name: plugin to existing tools
C1147.definition: A plugin to existing tools is a category of augmented reality (AR) software in which a plugin is added to an existing interactive 2D or 3D content authoring tool that may not support AR content, adding AR-specific functions such as tracking, visualization, and 3D registration, while relying on that tool for content authoring.

C1148.name: developer tool
C1148.definition: A developer tool is an existing tool used with AR plugins.

C1149.name: standalone augmented reality authoring tool
C1149.definition: A standalone augmented reality authoring tool is an application that lets users create augmented reality experiences without programming experience, and it is a complete package that includes content authoring and augmented reality support without depending on any other tool.

C1150.name: library function
C1150.definition: A library function is a function that must be called when using low-level software libraries or frameworks for augmented reality software.

C1151.name: design prototyping skill
C1151.definition: Design prototyping skill is a skill that may be required for rapid prototyping tools.

C1152.name: OSG Art
C1152.definition: OSG Art is an augmented reality software tool in the low-level software libraries or frameworks category.

C1153.name: StudiersTube
C1153.definition: StudiersTube is an example of a low-level augmented reality software library or framework.

C1154.name: MXR Toolkit
C1154.definition: MXR Toolkit is an example of an Augmented Reality software tool in the low-level software libraries or frameworks category.

C1155.name: flash augmented reality manager
C1155.definition: Flash augmented reality manager is an Adobe Flash framework that combines augmented reality tracking libraries with three-dimensional graphics libraries, primarily for prototyping desktop and mobile augmented reality experiences rather than full-fledged development.

C1156.name: OpenFrameworks
C1156.definition: OpenFrameworks is an open-source C++ middleware framework and library that is a non-web-based authoring and rapid prototyping tool for desktop and mobile augmented reality applications, combining multiple libraries to support tracking, rendering, and interaction.

C1157.name: augmented reality media plugin
C1157.definition: An augmented reality media plugin is an AR software tool in the category of plugins for existing developer tools.

C1158.name: Vuforia
C1158.definition: Vuforia is a cross-platform augmented reality (AR) software development kit (SDK) that uses computer vision to recognize and track images and objects in the real world for creating AR applications.

C1159.name: MetaIO Unity plugin
