C1159.definition: MetaIO Unity plugin is an example of an augmented reality software tool, listed as a plugin for existing developer tools.

C1160.name: Dart
C1160.definition: Dart is an augmented reality software tool that is a plugin for existing developer tools.

C1161.name: BuildAR
C1161.definition: BuildAR is an example of a standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tool.

C1162.name: MetaIO Creator
C1162.definition: MetaIO Creator is an example of a standalone augmented reality authoring tool.

C1163.name: Wikitude augmented reality browser app
C1163.definition: Wikitude augmented reality browser app is a free augmented reality browser application for mobile prototyping that treats the device mainly as a rendering device and retrieves content and user-interface specifications from backend servers.

C1164.name: low-level library and framework
C1164.definition: Low-level library and framework is the augmented reality (AR) software category that requires the maximum skill from the developer because it provides access to the core tracking and display functionality used to build an AR application.

C1165.name: C
C1165.definition: C is used to write a software library for developing augmented reality applications.

C1166.name: Linux
C1166.definition: Linux is a platform that ARToolKit supports.

C1167.name: marker-based tracking
C1167.definition: Marker-based tracking is a form of augmented reality tracking that recognizes a marker and its position.

C1168.name: ARToolWorks
C1168.definition: ARToolWorks is a source from which a commercial version of ARToolKit and an AR Toolkit for Unity are available.

C1169.name: natural feature
C1169.definition: A natural feature is a feature that can be tracked on an arbitrary image using computer vision techniques.

C1170.name: framework
C1170.definition: A framework is a kind of low-level augmented reality software that provides access to core tracking and display functionality for building an application, and that can be created by combining multiple libraries, especially libraries that provide interaction and realistic graphics support.

C1171.name: scene graph
C1171.definition: A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene and supports 3D graphics pipeline operations such as sorting objects by visibility, clipping, and state management, allowing selective manipulation of its nodes to manipulate the scene, create realistic effects, and support interaction.

C1172.name: point of interest
C1172.definition: Point of interest (POI) is a significant spot in a virtual tour, modeled as a graph node or vertex with importance and a maximum waiting time, that need not be a physical object and is visited to inspect or interact with objects.

C1173.name: computer graphics scene
C1173.definition: A computer graphics scene is a scene represented by a scene graph.

C1174.name: three-dimensional graphics pipeline
C1174.definition: The three-dimensional graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process of computation that starts from object representation and ends by computing pixel intensities for a pixel-grid display, with five stages: object representation, modeling transformation, lighting, a viewing pipeline, and scan conversion.

C1175.name: visible surface detection
C1175.definition: Visible surface detection is an operation in a 3D graphics pipeline that sorts objects according to visibility.

C1176.name: clipping
C1176.definition: Clipping is the process in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that discards objects or portions of objects that are part of the scene but outside the view volume before projection.

C1177.name: state management
C1177.definition: State management is an operation supported by scene graph-based representations that is part of a three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline.

C1178.name: Open Scene Graph
C1178.definition: Open Scene Graph (OSG) is an open-source scene graph library that is written in C++, built on top of OpenGL, and supports many plugins for additional functionality.

C1179.name: Vulkan Scene Graph
C1179.definition: Vulkan Scene Graph (VSG) is an open-source scene graph library that is a successor to Open Scene Graph.

C1180.name: C++
C1180.definition: C++ is used to write scene-graph libraries and in a middleware framework and library.

C1181.name: model loading
C1181.definition: Model loading is an example of additional functionality supported by plugins, primarily in virtual reality and partly in augmented reality.

C1182.name: shadow rendering
C1182.definition: Shadow rendering is an example of additional functionality supported by plugins.

C1183.name: virtual camera
C1183.definition: A virtual camera is a node in a scene-graph representation whose parameters can be manipulated.

C1184.name: projection
C1184.definition: Projection is a graphics-rendering node in an augmented reality scene graph, and clipping is performed before projection so projection is applied to fewer vertices and computational complexity is reduced.

C1185.name: orthographic projection
C1185.definition: Orthographic projection is one of the graphics-rendering nodes in a scene-graph representation.

C1186.name: transformation
C1186.definition: Transformation is a coordinate change that takes a point in an object's local coordinate system to a new point that should ideally be in the world coordinate system, typically by multiplying the point by a matrix in a homogeneous coordinate system.

C1187.name: ART 3 library
C1187.definition: ART 3 library is a framework that combines tracking and rendering libraries, linking ARToolKit for tracking support with Open Scene Graph for real-time rendering.

C1188.name: Goblin XNA
C1188.definition: Goblin XNA is a framework that combines tracking and rendering libraries, using the ART tag tracking library with the Microsoft XNA game platform.

C1189.name: ART tag tracking library
C1189.definition: The ART tag tracking library is a tracking library that is combined with the Microsoft XNA game platform in the Goblin XNA framework.

C1190.name: Microsoft XNA game platform
C1190.definition: The Microsoft XNA game platform is a game platform that Goblin XNA combines with the ART tag tracking library.

C1191.name: Metaio SDK
C1191.definition: Metaio SDK is an augmented reality (AR) tracking technology that provides AR tracking in frameworks that combine tracking and rendering libraries.

C1192.name: DroidAR
C1192.definition: DroidAR is a mobile-specific augmented reality framework that uses sensors for tracking support, rather than computer vision.

C1193.name: ARToolKit for mobile
C1193.definition: ARToolKit for mobile is a mobile-specific augmented reality framework that is a version of ARToolKit available for mobile platforms and that is integrated with Open Scene Graph (OSG) but developed for mobile.

C1194.name: prototype
C1194.definition: A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that can be built quickly to model or demonstrate a design idea and to test whether it will work in practice. It can be discarded after testing or refined into the final product.

C1195.name: flar toolkit
C1195.definition: Flar toolkit is a version of the augmented reality (AR) Toolkit ported to Adobe Flash that lets a user run an AR experience in a web browser by activating a camera, tracking AR markers, and overlaying virtual content onto the tracked image for 3D registering with a few lines of code.

C1196.name: augmented reality experience
C1196.definition: An augmented reality experience is an experience that can be prototyped for desktop or mobile, run from within a web browser, and developed with minimal effort using tracking and overlay code.

C1197.name: augmented reality marker
C1197.definition: An augmented reality marker is something tracked in a camera view in order to overlay virtual content onto the tracked image for 3D registering.

C1198.name: three-dimensional registering
C1198.definition: Three-dimensional registering is the purpose for which an augmented reality toolkit activates a camera, tracks AR markers, and overlays virtual content onto a tracked image.

C1199.name: overlay
C1199.definition: Overlay is an augmented reality activity that is required, together with tracking, to develop an augmented reality experience.

C1200.name: flar tracker
C1200.definition: Flar tracker is an augmented reality tracking library.

C1201.name: augmented reality tracking library
C1201.definition: An augmented reality tracking library is a library that can be combined with a three-dimensional graphics library, primarily for prototyping rather than full-fledged development.

C1202.name: three-dimensional graphics library
C1202.definition: A three-dimensional graphics library is a graphics library that can be combined with an augmented reality tracking library primarily for prototyping rather than full-fledged development.

C1203.name: alternative 3d
C1203.definition: Alternative 3d is a three-dimensional (3D) graphics library that can be combined with an augmented reality tracking library, primarily for prototyping.

C1204.name: away 3d
C1204.definition: Away 3d is one of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics libraries that can be combined with an augmented reality tracking library, primarily for prototyping rather than full-fledged development.

C1205.name: away 3d lite
C1205.definition: Away 3d lite is a three-dimensional graphics library that can be combined with an augmented reality tracking library, primarily for prototyping rather than full-fledged development.

C1206.name: paper vision 3d
C1206.definition: Paper vision 3d is one of the three-dimensional graphics libraries that can be combined with an augmented reality tracking library, primarily for prototyping rather than full-fledged development.

C1207.name: sandy 3d
C1207.definition: Sandy 3D is a three-dimensional (3D) graphics library.

C1208.name: non-flash-based authoring tool
C1208.definition: A non-flash-based authoring tool is an authoring tool for augmented reality prototyping.

C1209.name: flash-based tool
C1209.definition: A flash-based tool is an authoring tool for augmented reality prototyping that has greater market penetration than non-Flash-based authoring tools.

C1210.name: rapid prototyping
C1210.definition: Rapid prototyping is used in augmented reality to create a fast prototype.

C1211.name: non-flash-based browser tool
C1211.definition: A non-flash-based browser tool is an augmented reality rapid prototyping browser tool that can avoid third-party browser plugins by letting a developer with mastery of HyperText Markup Language, Web Graphics Library, or similar web component technologies write their own code to create a fast prototype.

C1212.name: browser plugin
C1212.definition: A browser plugin is something that non-flash-based browser tools for augmented reality rapid prototyping can avoid by letting a developer write their own code using HTML, WebGL, or similar web component technologies.

C1213.name: hyper text markup language
C1213.definition: Hyper text markup language (HTML) is a web component technology that developers can use to write code for non-flash-based browser augmented reality rapid prototyping.

C1214.name: web component technology
C1214.definition: Web component technology is a technology similar to HTML and WebGL that developers can use to write code to create fast augmented reality prototypes.

C1215.name: tracking library
C1215.definition: A tracking library is a library that can be used to create augmented reality applications, for example for hand tracking.

C1216.name: hand tracking
C1216.definition: Hand tracking is a form of tracking, for example in augmented reality application development, that allows a virtual ray in pointing-based selection to be attached to a virtual hand.

C1217.name: three-dimensional scene graph
C1217.definition: A three-dimensional scene graph is a library used for rendering in augmented reality application development.

C1218.name: audio playback library
C1218.definition: An audio playback library is a library that can be combined in augmented reality (AR) application development to generate different effects.

C1219.name: browser application
C1219.definition: A browser application is an application that can be a free augmented reality mobile prototyping tool on mobile devices.

C1220.name: mobile prototyping tool
C1220.definition: A mobile prototyping tool is a useful application that runs on mobile devices and is used for prototyping augmented reality.

C1221.name: client
C1221.definition: Client is usually separate from end users and is a source of functional and non-functional requirements in interactive system development, and may not accept the system being developed.

C1222.name: rendering device
C1222.definition: A rendering device is a device, such as a mobile device, used as a client while an application connects to backend servers for content and user interface elements, with computation not on the device but possibly on the backend server.

C1223.name: backend server
C1223.definition: A backend server is a server to which an application connects for content and user interface element specifications, and on which computation may occur instead of on the mobile device.

C1224.name: user interface element
C1224.definition: A user interface element is part of a user interface whose content and specification an application can obtain from backend servers.

C1225.name: prototyping
C1225.definition: Prototyping is a stage in the design, prototyping, and evaluation cycle of interactive system development, a cycle repeated with quick evaluation to find problems and refine the design.

C1226.name: augmented reality software
C1226.definition: Augmented reality software is software for AR content or system development, available in four categories based on required programming skill: low-level libraries and frameworks, standalone authoring tools, rapid prototyping tools, and plugins to existing content authoring tools.

C1227.name: content authoring
C1227.definition: Content authoring is the function of an existing interactive 2D or 3D main authoring tool that a plugin relies on while adding AR-specific functions.

C1228.name: visualization
C1228.definition: Visualization is one of the AR-specific functions that a plugin can add to an existing 2D or 3D content authoring tool.

C1229.name: interactive three-dimensional graphics authoring tool
C1229.definition: An interactive three-dimensional graphics authoring tool is a tool used to create interactive 3D applications.

C1230.name: Unity
C1230.definition: Unity is a popular cross-platform game engine and developer environment that provides an editor interface and implementation support for the computer graphics pipeline, enabling developers to create, build, and deploy 2D and 3D interactive content, including XR experiences.

C1231.name: Vizard
C1231.definition: Vizard is an interactive three-dimensional (3D) graphics authoring tool used to create interactive 3D applications.

C1232.name: Lumion
C1232.definition: Lumion is an interactive 3D graphics authoring tool used to create interactive 3D applications.

C1233.name: augmented reality visualization
C1233.definition: Augmented reality visualization is support provided by AR plugins for interactive three-dimensional graphics authoring tools.

C1234.name: AR Toolkit for Unity
C1234.definition: The AR Toolkit for Unity is an AR plugin for Unity that provides marker-based tracking, image-based or computer-vision-based tracking, and AR visualization support.

C1235.name: image-based tracking
C1235.definition: Image-based tracking is a computer-vision-based tracking method that an augmented reality plugin can provide.

C1236.name: software configuration
C1236.definition: Software configuration is the configuration of software that, when plugins are used to add augmented reality support to existing content authoring tools, depends on the underlying authoring tool.

C1237.name: hardware configuration
C1237.definition: Hardware configuration is a configuration that, together with software configuration, depends on the underlying authoring tool when plugins are used to add augmented reality support to existing content authoring tools.

C1238.name: proprietary player software
C1238.definition: Proprietary player software is software on which content produced with an authoring tool usually becomes dependent.

C1239.name: low-level software development tool
C1239.definition: A low-level software development tool is a software development tool that is used to build a system from scratch rather than depending on a third-party tool.

C1240.name: higher-level tool
C1240.definition: A higher-level tool is a tool or plugin, such as an augmented reality tool, that may have limitations which can be resolved by using low-level software development tools to build a system from scratch.

C1241.name: third-party tool
C1241.definition: Third-party tool is a higher-level tool that a system may depend on instead of using low-level software development tools and building from scratch.

C1242.name: scene construction
C1242.definition: Scene construction is a capability of standalone augmented reality authoring tools and a part of the computer graphics pipeline.

C1243.name: animation
C1243.definition: Animation is computer graphics content or an asset used for creating the perception of motion and in representing objects or complex characters.

C1244.name: interactive behavior
C1244.definition: Interactive behavior is a kind of realistic behavior that can be added by augmented reality authoring tools and imposed by graphical user interface event functions.

C1245.name: graphical user interface
C1245.definition: Graphical user interface (GUI) is a drag-and-drop interface that most standalone augmented reality authoring tools provide to allow users with basic personal computer skills to create applications without coding.

C1246.name: scripting language
C1246.definition: Scripting language is a programming language, such as C#, that authoring tools can provide or systems can use to support more flexible applications.

C1247.name: Wikitude Studio
C1247.definition: Wikitude Studio is a standalone, web-based augmented reality authoring tool that allowed users to create rich mobile augmented reality content and deploy it either to an augmented reality browser app or as a custom mobile app, including 3D models and animations registered to the real world.

C1248.name: low-level library
C1248.definition: A low-level library is a category of augmented reality software tools and packages that requires the highest programming skill.

C1249.name: low-level framework
C1249.definition: A low-level framework is an augmented reality software tool or package in the low-level libraries and frameworks category, which requires the highest programming skill.

C1250.name: extended reality system
C1250.definition: An extended reality system is an interactive system that comprises hardware, an XR engine as middleware, and the application layer, in which input devices track the user's actions and positions, send them as input data, the data is processed to render an environment, and output devices stimulate the user's senses.

C1251.name: interactive system
C1251.definition: Interactive system is a system in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user, a lay person who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how it works.

C1252.name: disappearing technology
C1252.definition: Disappearing technology is the statement that the most profound technologies are those that disappear from the user's perception, so that the user feels they are dealing with any other item rather than a specialized technological item.

C1253.name: earliest computer
C1253.definition: The earliest computer is a computer that occupied a huge room with many wires, whose programming involved reconnecting the wires, and that was accessible only to a very few select people.

C1254.name: programming
C1254.definition: Programming is the software development task used to create prototypes and to build and deploy virtual and augmented reality systems, with customized experiences requiring scripting and more programming.

C1255.name: flexible device
C1255.definition: A flexible device is one of the popular technological products associated with the current stage referred to as Internet of Things (IoT) or ubiquitous computing.

C1256.name: connected device
C1256.definition: Connected device is a popular technological product in the current Internet of Things (IoT) or ubiquitous computing stage.

C1257.name: internet of things
C1257.definition: Internet of Things (IoT) is a current stage in the development of computer systems in which users are surrounded by multiple connected computers that can communicate with each other without the user separately operating them, moving toward making technology disappear from the user's point of view.

C1258.name: connected computer
C1258.definition: A connected computer is a computer in ubiquitous computing or the Internet of Things that can communicate with other connected computers without a user separately operating it.

C1259.name: lay person
C1259.definition: A lay person is a user of an interactive system who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how the system works.

C1260.name: error message
C1260.definition: An error message is a message used in error handling when an error occurs, and it should be simple and easy to understand rather than using technical jargon or status codes.

C1261.name: event log
C1261.definition: Event log is one of the technical terms in a system error message that should not be expected to be understood or acted upon by a lay end user.

C1262.name: security accounts manager
C1262.definition: Security accounts manager is an example of a technical term in a system error message that should not be expected to be understood or acted upon by a lay end user.

C1263.name: safe mode
C1263.definition: Safe mode is a technical term in a system error message that should not be expected to be understood or acted upon by a lay end user.

C1264.name: hexadecimal status code
C1264.definition: A hexadecimal status code is a technical term in a system error message that is generally incomprehensible to a layperson.

C1265.name: user-centric approach
C1265.definition: A user-centric approach is the process of designing computer systems in which users' needs and expectations are taken care of by considering user characteristics, starting with understanding those characteristics, needs, and expectations, then designing the system on that basis.

C1266.name: user characteristic
C1266.definition: User characteristic is an attribute of a user, such as needs, expectations, skills, or typing behavior, that designers consider when designing systems to match users' needs and expectations.

C1267.name: interface element
C1267.definition: Interface element is an element on a screen or interface that a user-centric approach designs to be acceptable to users.

C1268.name: layout
C1268.definition: Layout is a design that organizes interface elements on a screen or interface to meet user expectations.

C1269.name: interface
C1269.definition: An interface is the way a system interfaces with users, its environment, and other systems, letting users provide input, see outcomes, and act on outcomes; on a computer screen it is the whole content seen there.

C1270.name: system state
C1270.definition: System state is the state of a system that users perceive and that user interactions or commands can change to reach a goal state.

C1271.name: goal state
C1271.definition: A goal state is a desired system state that users transition to in order to get work done.

C1272.name: human-computer interaction
C1272.definition: Human-computer interaction (HCI) is the discipline concerned with the design, evaluation, and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use and with studying the major phenomena surrounding interactive computing systems; its core concern is incorporating humans into the design by first understanding users and then incorporating user characteristics into the design.

C1273.name: ACM SIGCHI
C1273.definition: ACM SIGCHI is the official body that deals with human-computer interaction (HCI) and provides the definition of HCI.

C1274.name: system design
C1274.definition: System design is the part of interactive system development in which user characteristics, usability requirements, and observed user activities are used to plan system features.

C1275.name: field study
C1275.definition: A field study is a kind of contextual inquiry in which user behavior is observed and recorded, and users are interviewed to understand who they are and how they behave.

C1276.name: novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization
C1276.definition: Novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization is a broad three-class classification of interactive-system users that distinguishes first-time, occasional, and regular long-term users, with expert users meaning efficient system users rather than technology experts, and provides a starting point for understanding likely user behavior and making design decisions instead of always starting with empirical or field studies.

C1277.name: novice user
C1277.definition: A novice user is an interactive-system user who uses the system for the first time.

C1278.name: intermittent user
C1278.definition: An intermittent user is an interactive-system user who uses the system occasionally.

C1279.name: expert user
C1279.definition: Expert user is an interactive-system user who uses the system regularly over a long period and can use it efficiently, rather than being a technology expert.

C1280.name: interactive-system design
C1280.definition: Interactive-system design is a kind of design in which user classes provide a starting point for making decisions and users must be taken into account in every stage and involved as active or passive participants.

C1281.name: word processing application
C1281.definition: A word processing application is a processing application that can provide multiple options for the same task to cater to different user groups.

C1282.name: hotkey combination
C1282.definition: A hotkey combination is one of the options an application can provide for a task, and it can be faster than a menu option but is generally harder to remember.

C1283.name: menu option
C1283.definition: A menu option is an application option for a task that relies on recognition rather than recall and is suitable for novice first-time users who may not remember hotkey combinations.

C1284.name: task
C1284.definition: A task is an activity that users perform, involving a sequence of user actions and corresponding interface changes, and whose performance data can be used to evaluate an interface.

C1285.name: file
C1285.definition: A file is something that can be saved.

C1286.name: user-centered design
C1286.definition: User-centered design (UCD) is a design approach in which users are actively or passively involved in the overall design lifecycle, and the design is based on the user's abilities, context, goals, needs, and expectations, ideally from the users' point of view rather than the programmer's convenience, to build a usable application.

C1287.name: chip
C1287.definition: A chip is a hardware-level feature that can be made smaller to reduce product size.

C1288.name: development lifecycle
C1288.definition: A development lifecycle is a lifecycle used to build a usable software application and to account for users' characteristics, needs, and expectations.

C1289.name: International Standards Organization 9241-210-2009 standard
C1289.definition: The International Standards Organization 9241-210-2009 standard is a standard that defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

C1290.name: effectiveness
C1290.definition: Effectiveness is a measure of usability that indicates whether a user can do what they want to do.

C1291.name: efficiency
C1291.definition: Efficiency is one of the measures of usability that shows how fast a user can do what they want to do.

C1292.name: satisfaction
C1292.definition: Satisfaction is a usability measure that indicates how satisfied a user is when using a system.

C1293.name: context of use
C1293.definition: Context of use is the specific usage scenario or work setting in which users perform tasks with a product, with respect to which its usability is defined.

C1294.name: cooperative design
C1294.definition: Cooperative design is a term that refers to taking users into the design process.

C1295.name: participatory design
C1295.definition: Participatory design is a design term that refers to taking users into the design process.

C1296.name: contextual design
C1296.definition: Contextual design is a term that is more or less similar in concept to user-centered design and refers to taking users into the design process.

C1297.name: human-centered design
C1297.definition: Human-centered design is a term that refers to taking users into the design process.

C1298.name: international organization for standardization
C1298.definition: International organization for standardization (ISO) is an organization that prefers human-centered design as the standard term rather than user-centered design.

C1299.name: user-centric software design
C1299.definition: User-centric software design is the design of usable systems that meet the needs and expectations of laypersons.

C1300.name: software development
C1300.definition: Software development is the use of programming to create a prototype, which high-fidelity prototyping can do on a reduced scale.

C1301.name: software development lifecycle
C1301.definition: Software development lifecycle (SDLC) is a systematic, structured set of connected stages for developing and deploying software, ideally followed in sequence but highly iterative for usable interactive systems, that captures design and development activities and helps identify the best valid design choice for usability.

C1302.name: extended reality software
C1302.definition: Extended reality software is software that creates a relationship between a user and a virtual environment.

C1303.name: application layer
C1303.definition: Application layer is the topmost layer of a layered virtual reality software architecture that calls the software development kit layer and is part of an Extended Reality system.

C1304.name: input data
C1304.definition: Input data is the data of a user's tracked actions and positions that input devices send in an XR system.

C1305.name: output data
C1305.definition: Output data is data that the XR engine generates in an XR system and that output devices use to stimulate the user's senses.

C1306.name: user input modeling
C1306.definition: User input modeling is used in XR systems and should follow a user-centered design approach so that users can provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily.

C1307.name: output modeling
C1307.definition: Output modeling is used in an Extended Reality (XR) system to ensure, through a user-centered design approach, that generated output stimuli match the user's perception so the user can perceive and understand the output easily.

C1308.name: output stimulus
C1308.definition: An output stimulus is an output generated in an XR system that should match the user's perception so that the user can perceive and understand it easily.

C1309.name: perception
C1309.definition: Perception is the abstract level of the perceptual process that follows sensing, in which the brain interprets a stimulus by combining sensory signals with long-term memory and learned experience, not by sensory input alone.

C1310.name: illusion of reality
C1310.definition: Illusion of reality is the best possible sense of reality, not actual reality, created by an XR system's interaction and perceptual stimuli to enhance presence, and creating it is especially crucial in virtual reality.

C1311.name: perceptual system
C1311.definition: The perceptual system is the user's system that a VR system can fool into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.

C1312.name: artificial stimulation
C1312.definition: Artificial stimulation is the sensory signals that virtual reality generally provides to the brain, inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

C1313.name: biological mechanism
C1313.definition: A biological mechanism is a mechanism in human bodies and sensory organs that evolved over a long period in a natural environment and is affected by artificial stimulation in virtual reality.

C1314.name: physiology
C1314.definition: Physiology is one part of human perception, along with experience stored in long-term memory, and, for perceptual psychology, a basic human-body topic involving sense organs, neural pathways, and their connections to the brain.

C1315.name: long-term memory
C1315.definition: Long-term memory is a part of human memory that stores experience or knowledge used to interpret sensory input.

C1316.name: sensory input
C1316.definition: Sensory input is the real-time input in perceptual processing that is combined with long-term memory to produce an interpretation of a stimulus.

C1317.name: adaptation
C1317.definition: Adaptation is a possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation, in which the body adapts to the new stimuli.

C1318.name: non-adaptation
C1318.definition: Non-adaptation is the body's inability to adapt to generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation, which can cause increased fatigue or headaches and may lead to cyber sickness, such as dizziness, nausea, or other symptoms.

C1319.name: perceptual psychology
C1319.definition: Perceptual psychology is the science that explains how the brain converts sensory stimulation received by sensors from the real world into perceived phenomena.

C1320.name: video resolution
C1320.definition: Video resolution is the amount needed to avoid seeing pixels in a virtual world or virtual object.

C1321.name: pixel
C1321.definition: A pixel is an element in the grid of a graphic display screen that, when activated, emits light with a specific intensity, helping to form a colored image perceived on the screen.

C1322.name: point of view
C1322.definition: Point of view is the view in a virtual world for which the user's head should appear at the proper height.

C1323.name: virtual sound
C1323.definition: Virtual sound is a sound in a virtual world that perceptual psychology considers when asking where it appears to come from.

C1324.name: neural pathway
C1324.definition: A neural pathway is part of the basic physiology of the human body that perceptual psychology requires knowledge of.

C1325.name: brain
C1325.definition: The brain is the part of the human body that receives neural impulses from sense organs and neural pathways, processes them into touch perception, and can send messages back for corrective motor actions.

C1326.name: perceptual process
C1326.definition: Perceptual process is a process that proceeds from sensing, the lowest level, to perception, a very abstract level, and perception can occur only after sense organs are stimulated by a particular type of stimulus and convert that input stimulus into neural impulses.

C1327.name: energy source
C1327.definition: An energy source is what a sensor in a device or system converts into electrical signals in a circuit.

C1328.name: electrical signal
C1328.definition: Electrical signal is a signal that can be produced in a circuit when a sensor in a device or system converts an energy source, and that can be passed across a synapse between neurons.

C1329.name: circuit
C1329.definition: A circuit is a part of a device or system in which electrical signals are present.

C1330.name: neural impulse
C1330.definition: A neural impulse is what a sense organ transmits through a neural network to the brain after converting a stimulus.

C1331.name: receptor
C1331.definition: A receptor is a bodily sensor that is part of a sense organ, targets particular stimuli, and is activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives. Types include photoreceptors, chemoreceptors, mechanoreceptors, and thermoreceptors.

C1332.name: visual sense
C1332.definition: Visual sense is a human sense that has electromagnetic energy as its stimulus, photoreceptors as its receptors, and the eye as its sense organ.

C1333.name: electromagnetic energy
C1333.definition: Electromagnetic energy is the stimulus for vision that activates the eyes' photoreceptors in the frequency range of visible light.

C1334.name: photoreceptor
C1334.definition: Photoreceptor is a bodily sensor in the eye's retina that is activated only by visible light and converts visible light into neural pulses for visual perception.

C1335.name: auditory sense
C1335.definition: Auditory sense is a human sense that responds to air pressure waves via mechanoreceptors in the ear.

C1336.name: air pressure wave
C1336.definition: An air pressure wave is the stimulus for the auditory sense.

C1337.name: mechanoreceptor
C1337.definition: Mechanoreceptor is a type of receptor that senses motion, vibration, or gravitational force and is involved in the auditory, touch, and balance senses.

C1338.name: touch
C1338.definition: Touch is a human sense that detects tissue distortion with mechanoreceptors and temperature changes with thermoreceptors in the skin and muscles.

C1339.name: tissue distortion
C1339.definition: Tissue distortion is the stimulus for the sense of touch.

C1340.name: thermoreceptor
C1340.definition: A thermoreceptor is a receptor involved in the sense of touch that detects changes in temperature.

C1341.name: skin
C1341.definition: Skin is a sense organ for touch that has epidermis, dermis, and hypodermis layers, with touch receptors embedded in the epidermis and dermis.

C1342.name: muscle
C1342.definition: Muscle is a sense organ for touch that contains muscle spindles and is connected to bones by tendons.

C1343.name: balance sense
C1343.definition: Balance sense is one of the six human senses that involves mechanoreceptors for gravity or acceleration and helps a person know which way the head is oriented, including the upward direction.

C1344.name: acceleration
C1344.definition: Acceleration is a stimulus for the balance sense and is reported by visual input, with kinesthesis providing information on it during movement.

C1345.name: vestibular organ
C1345.definition: A vestibular organ is a sense organ for the balance sense.

C1346.name: taste
C1346.definition: Taste is a human chemical sense that uses chemoreceptors in the mouth, particularly on the tongue, to provide signals based on the chemical composition of matter.

C1347.name: chemical composition
C1347.definition: Chemical composition is the stimulus for taste and smell, the senses whose chemoreceptors provide signals based on it.

C1348.name: chemoreceptor
C1348.definition: A chemoreceptor is a type of receptor that provides signals based on the chemical composition of matter through chemical reaction with specific molecules or chemical stimuli at appropriate concentrations; not all chemoreceptors respond to all chemical stimuli.

C1349.name: mouth
C1349.definition: Mouth is the sense organ for taste.

C1350.name: nose
C1350.definition: The nose is the sense organ for smell.

C1351.name: sensory system selectivity
C1351.definition: Sensory system selectivity is the phenomenon in which the receptors in a sense organ, as bodily sensors, target particular stimuli and are activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives.

C1352.name: visible light
C1352.definition: Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves, ranging from red light to violet light, that can excite the cones in the eye and produce color perception.

C1353.name: vibration
C1353.definition: Vibration is used as a typical form of force feedback to provide touch sensation in XR systems.

C1354.name: gravitational force
C1354.definition: Gravitational force is a force sensed by mechanoreceptors in the auditory, touch, and balance senses.

C1355.name: temperature
C1355.definition: Temperature is what thermoreceptors detect as changes in the sense of touch.

C1356.name: tongue
C1356.definition: Tongue is where chemoreceptors for taste are located.

C1357.name: nasal passage
C1357.definition: A nasal passage is the location in which smell relies on chemoreceptors that provide signals based on the chemical composition of matter.

C1358.name: physiology of the senses
C1358.definition: Physiology of the senses is a part of perceptual psychology.

C1359.name: sensing
C1359.definition: Sensing is the lowest level of the perceptual process, in which sense organs are stimulated by a particular type of stimulus and convert that input stimulus into neural impulses.

C1360.name: neuron
C1360.definition: Neuron is a part of the brain that aggregates information from other neurons through dendrites, processes it in its cell body, and transmits it to other neurons through axons across synapses.

C1361.name: cerebral cortex
C1361.definition: The cerebral cortex is a large, heavily folded sheet of neurons, the part of the brain responsible for perception and other functions such as attention, memory, language, and consciousness.

C1362.name: attention
C1362.definition: Attention is one of the functions of the cerebral cortex.

C1363.name: language
C1363.definition: Language is a function of the cerebral cortex.

C1364.name: consciousness
C1364.definition: Consciousness is one of the functions of the cerebral cortex, the part of the brain responsible for perception.

C1365.name: cognitive ability
C1365.definition: Cognitive ability is an ability that, along with perception, depends on the interconnection of neurons.

C1366.name: cell body
C1366.definition: A cell body is the part of a neuron that processes input carried toward it by dendrites and transmits that processing to other neurons through axons.

C1367.name: dendrite
C1367.definition: Dendrite is a part of a neuron that carries neural impulses toward the cell body, through which the neuron aggregates information from other neurons. It receives signals from a paired axon across a gap called a synapse, without physical connection.

C1368.name: axon
C1368.definition: An axon is a part of a neuron that carries neural impulses away from the cell body to other neurons, with electrical or chemical signals crossing a synapse to a dendrite of the next neuron.

C1369.name: axon branch
C1369.definition: An axon branch is a part of a neuron.

C1370.name: axon terminal
C1370.definition: An axon terminal is a part of a neuron.

C1371.name: neural interconnection
C1371.definition: Neural interconnection is the network of connections among neurons, which can be thought of as a directed graph in which cell bodies are nodes that process input, dendrites are input edges, and axons are output edges.

C1372.name: directed graph
C1372.definition: A directed graph is a network of nodes connected by input edges toward the nodes and output edges away from the nodes.

C1373.name: network
C1373.definition: A network is a directed graph that can be used to represent the interconnection of neurons.

C1374.name: neural network
C1374.definition: A neural network is an interconnection of neurons, thought of as a directed graph, that carries neural impulses from sense organs to the brain.

C1375.name: deep learning
C1375.definition: Deep learning is used to build better experiences and more intelligent systems in extended reality.

C1376.name: input edge
C1376.definition: Input edge is a dendrite in a directed graph of neurons that carries neural impulses toward a cell body.

C1377.name: output edge
C1377.definition: An output edge is an edge in a directed graph of neuron interconnection that carries neural impulses away from a cell body, corresponding to an axon.

C1378.name: synapse
C1378.definition: A synapse is the gap between an axon of one neuron and a dendrite of the next neuron, across which electrical or chemical signals are passed for communication between neurons.

C1379.name: chemical signal
C1379.definition: A chemical signal is one kind of signal passed across a synapse between neurons.

C1380.name: synaptic connection
C1380.definition: A synaptic connection is a connection from one neuron to another neuron in the human brain.

C1381.name: edge
C1381.definition: An edge is a connection between two nodes or vertices in a graph, which can be weighted by a distance or by a shortest path length.

C1382.name: hierarchical processing
C1382.definition: Hierarchical processing is the neural processing performed as signals from sense organ receptors propagate through the neural network to the cerebral cortex, where signals are combined at successive levels into higher-level information that enables increasingly complex patterns to be detected.

C1383.name: neural processing
C1383.definition: Neural processing is the processing performed as signals from sense organ receptors propagate through the neural network to the cerebral cortex.

C1384.name: signal
C1384.definition: Signal is what propagates from numerous sense organ receptors of different types through the neural network to the cerebral cortex and is combined at successive levels by neurons.

C1385.name: staged aggregation
C1385.definition: Staged aggregation is a process in hierarchical processing in which signals from numerous receptors of different types are combined at successive levels by neurons until the cerebral cortex is reached, with each level producing higher-level information rather than lower-level information.

C1386.name: interpretation of a stimulus
C1386.definition: Interpretation of a stimulus is the result produced, once sensory signals reach the cerebral cortex, by combining real-time sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory, not by sensory input alone, and it depends on the interpreter's long-term experience.

C1387.name: perceptual phenomena
C1387.definition: Perceptual phenomena are produced in perception when real-time sensory input is combined with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory, not by sensory input alone.

C1388.name: face recognition
C1388.definition: Face recognition is one of the perceptual phenomena produced when sensory signals in the cerebral cortex combine real-time sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory.

C1389.name: song identification
C1389.definition: Song identification is an example of a perceptual phenomenon produced by combining real-time sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory.

C1390.name: perceptual processing
C1390.definition: Perceptual processing is the outcome of hierarchical processing and the combination of real-time sensory input with long-term knowledge or experience.

C1391.name: proprioception
C1391.definition: Proprioception is a sense of the human somatosensory system that gives conscious awareness of the pose and movement of each movable body part relative to other body parts, and of the muscular effort involved in moving them.

C1392.name: muscular effort
C1392.definition: Muscular effort is the amount of effort involved in, or required to, moving body parts.

C1393.name: motor cortex
C1393.definition: The motor cortex is a part of the brain that controls body motion and sends efference copies to other parts of the brain to communicate what motions have been executed.

C1394.name: body motion
C1394.definition: Body motion is motion that the motor cortex controls.

C1395.name: efference copy
C1395.definition: Efference copy is a signal that the motor cortex sends to other parts of the brain, including the cerebral cortex, to communicate executed motions so relative positions of body parts and muscular effort required to move them can be understood.

C1396.name: sensory processing
C1396.definition: Sensory processing is a long-term learned process in the brain.

C1397.name: visual input
C1397.definition: Visual input is information that reports movement or acceleration to a person moving in a virtual environment while physically stationary.

C1398.name: retina
C1398.definition: Retina is the non-planar image surface at the back of the eye where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain by optic nerve fibers.

C1399.name: lens
C1399.definition: A lens is an engineered part of a virtual reality headset or a natural part of the human eye that guides and refracts light so that images are focused on the retina.

C1400.name: light propagation
C1400.definition: Light propagation is used to understand VR headsets and visual perception, to model and render virtual worlds, and to choose camera setups and positions for panoramic videos.

C1401.name: visual perception
C1401.definition: Visual perception is a kind of perception that can be led to by light propagating through lenses and the human eye, and that requires photoreceptors in the retina as bodily sensors.

C1402.name: camera setup
C1402.definition: Camera setup is what knowledge of how light propagates, how lenses and the eye work, and how cameras work is used to understand.

C1403.name: panoramic video
C1403.definition: Panoramic video is used to present virtual worlds.

C1404.name: tracking software
C1404.definition: Tracking software is software that is built with the help of understanding how a camera works.

C1405.name: photon view
C1405.definition: Photon view is one of the views of light that describes light as a large number of photons, tiny energy particles moving through space at a very high speed, often called the speed of light, and is helpful for understanding or calculating the amount of light received by a sensor or receptor.

C1406.name: wave view
C1406.definition: Wave view is one of three views of light that describes light as waves, ripples through space, and is helpful for explaining the spectrum of color.

C1407.name: ray view
C1407.definition: The ray view is a view of light that describes it as rays, which are trajectories or paths assumed to be traces of the motion of a single hypothetical photon.

C1408.name: photon
C1408.definition: A photon is a tiny energy particle that moves through space at a very high speed, often called the speed of light, and is helpful for understanding or calculating the amount of light received by a sensor or receptor.

C1409.name: speed of light
C1409.definition: The speed of light is the very high speed at which photons, tiny energy particles, move through space.

C1410.name: wave
C1410.definition: Wave is a ripple through space that helps explain the spectrum of color rather than explaining color in terms of light as particles.

C1411.name: color spectrum
C1411.definition: Color spectrum is explained by the wave view of light rather than in terms of light as particles.

C1412.name: color
C1412.definition: Color is an observed combination of different amounts of red, green, and blue light emitted by the pixel elements of a color display and mixed in the eye.

C1413.name: ray
C1413.definition: A ray is a trajectory or path in the ray view of light that is assumed to be the trace of the motion of a single hypothetical photon.

C1414.name: visibility
C1414.definition: Visibility is a concept that the ray view of light helps explain.

C1415.name: light ray
C1415.definition: A light ray is a ray that may strike a material surface and then pass through the material, be absorbed and terminate inside the material, or be reflected from the surface.

C1416.name: material surface
C1416.definition: A material surface is a surface that light rays can strike, where light can be transmitted, absorbed, or reflected.

C1417.name: transmission
C1417.definition: Transmission is a possible interaction when light rays strike a material surface, in which some of the rays pass through the material and come out of it.

C1418.name: absorption
C1418.definition: Absorption is one of the possible interactions of light rays with a material surface in which some of the light rays that strike the surface are absorbed by the material and terminate inside it, so they do not propagate further outside it.

C1419.name: reflection
C1419.definition: Reflection is one of the possible interactions between a light ray and a material surface, in which the light ray is reflected from the surface without entering or penetrating it.

C1420.name: color perception
C1420.definition: Color perception is photopic vision, which visible light waves produce by exciting the cones in the eye and which gives a sense of color.

C1421.name: perceived color
C1421.definition: Perceived color is the color of a surface point in color perception that is determined by the intensity of the light reaching the viewer's eye.

C1422.name: light intensity
C1422.definition: Light intensity is the strength of light reaching a point or the viewer’s eye, which determines the perceived color of a surface point; in the simple lighting model it is the sum of ambient, diffuse, and specular intensities and typically diminishes with distance from the light source.

C1423.name: ambient light
C1423.definition: Ambient light is light that falls on a surface after being reflected from surrounding surfaces.

C1424.name: cornea
C1424.definition: The cornea is a refracting medium in the human eye that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, helping focus incoming light onto the retina.

C1425.name: pupil
C1425.definition: The pupil is the part of the human eye between the cornea and the lens through which incident light passes, and it is dilated or constricted by the iris to control the amount of light entering the eye.

C1426.name: aqueous humor
C1426.definition: Aqueous humor is an internal semi-liquid medium of the human eye that lies between the cornea and the pupil and through which light passes before reaching the retina.

C1427.name: vitreous humor
C1427.definition: Vitreous humor is an internal semi-liquid medium in the human eye, between the lens and the retina, through which light passes before reaching the retina.

C1428.name: iris
C1428.definition: Iris is a part of the human eye that controls the amount of light entering it by dilating or constricting the pupil, typically dilating it in dark surroundings and constricting it in bright light.

C1429.name: optic nerve fiber
C1429.definition: An optic nerve fiber is a neuron in the retina that carries the visual signal to the brain.

C1430.name: rod
C1430.definition: A rod is a type of photoreceptor in the human eye, more numerous in the peripheral retina, that is used for peripheral scotopic vision, and multiple such photoreceptors can share one optic nerve fiber, which aids sensitivity to lower levels of light.

C1431.name: cone
C1431.definition: Cone is a photoreceptor in the human eye, mainly located in the fovea, the central region of the retina, that is used for photopic vision, in which color is perceived, and is served by approximately one optic nerve fiber, which aids image acuity.

C1432.name: fovea
C1432.definition: Fovea is the small central region of the retina that has the greatest concentration of photoreceptors, particularly cones.

C1433.name: image acuity
C1433.definition: Image acuity is a visual ability that is aided by approximately one optic nerve fiber serving each cone.

C1434.name: photopic vision
C1434.definition: Photopic vision is a form of vision accomplished only with cones, in which visible light can excite those cones and color is perceived; it is more related to direct or central vision.

C1435.name: central vision
C1435.definition: Central vision is one of the two types of human vision that requires the eyes to be focused and pointed straight at an object to perceive a sharp color image.

C1436.name: scotopic vision
C1436.definition: Scotopic vision is a type of vision, accomplished only with rods, that is more related to peripheral vision and perceives weak lights as grays, with poor color perception.

C1437.name: peripheral vision
C1437.definition: Peripheral vision is a type of human vision supported by the peripheral region of the retina, where photoreceptor density is lower, with lower rod density and very low cone density, and it detects movement better than central vision but does not provide effective color perception.

C1438.name: spectrum
C1438.definition: A spectrum is a range of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves, such as visible light.

C1439.name: frequency
C1439.definition: Frequency is a property of a sound wave, measured in hertz (Hz), that is the number of changes from one maximum to another maximum per second.

C1440.name: electromagnetic light wave
C1440.definition: Electromagnetic light wave is a wave that has a spectrum of frequencies including visible light, which can excite cones in the eye.

C1441.name: red light
C1441.definition: Red light is one end of the visible light spectrum, at a frequency of 4.3 × 10^14 hertz and a wavelength of 700 nanometers.

C1442.name: hertz
C1442.definition: Hertz (Hz) is the unit used to measure frequency and represent refresh rate.

C1443.name: wavelength
C1443.definition: Wavelength is a value in nanometers used to describe visible light waves.

C1444.name: nanometer
C1444.definition: Nanometer is used to express the wavelength of visible light.

C1445.name: violet light
C1445.definition: Violet light is visible light that has a frequency of 7.5 × 10^14 hertz and a wavelength of 400 nanometers.

C1446.name: photoreceptor density
C1446.definition: Photoreceptor density is a basic physiological property that varies greatly across the retina, is lower in the peripheral region of the retina, and can directly impact engineering requirements for visual display hardware.

C1447.name: angular range
C1447.definition: Angular range is used to describe the size of the innermost part of the fovea.

C1448.name: rod density
C1448.definition: Rod density is lower in the peripheral region of the retina.

C1449.name: cone density
C1449.definition: Cone density is a density of cones in the retina, and in the peripheral region of the retina it is very low.

C1450.name: blind spot
C1450.definition: Blind spot is a region of the retina with no photoreceptors, so light or visual stimuli falling there produce no perception.

C1451.name: optic nerve
C1451.definition: The optic nerve is a nerve that transmits neural pulses from the retina to the brain.

C1452.name: neural signal
C1452.definition: A neural signal is a signal from the retina that is transmitted to the brain through optical nerves.

C1453.name: visual stimulus
C1453.definition: A visual stimulus is one of the things that can fall on the retina's blind spot and produce no perception.

C1454.name: natural lens
C1454.definition: The natural lens is the convex lens inside the human eye with variable focal depth that works with the cornea to focus light on the retina.

C1455.name: focal depth
C1455.definition: Focal depth is a property of a lens in the human eye, fixed in the cornea and variable in the natural lens.

C1456.name: lens setup
C1456.definition: A lens setup is an artificially created setup in which light passes through air after the lens and which has a focal plane.

C1457.name: focal plane
C1457.definition: Focal plane is a plane in an artificially created lens setup.

C1458.name: medium
C1458.definition: A medium is something that sound requires to propagate and that light passes through.

C1459.name: refractive index
C1459.definition: Refractive index is a value that a medium in the human eye has as a ray of light passes through it.

C1460.name: diopter
C1460.definition: A diopter is a unit used to express the optical power of lenses.

C1461.name: convex lens
C1461.definition: A convex lens is a lens used in the human eye and in a VR headset to focus light onto the retina.

C1462.name: optical power
C1462.definition: Optical power is a focusing property of the human eye's convex lenses, measured in diopters, whose combined value is sufficient to focus images of faraway objects onto the retina.

C1463.name: engineered lens
C1463.definition: An engineered lens is a lens in a virtual reality headset at whose focal length the screen is placed, so that the screen appears to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance.

C1464.name: focal length
C1464.definition: Focal length is the position at which the screen of a virtual reality headset is placed relative to the headset's engineered lens for the best experience, so that the screen appears to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance.

C1465.name: virtual image
C1465.definition: A virtual image is an image that appears to a user, as the screen of a virtual reality headset appears at an infinite distance, although a real image is formed on the retina.

C1466.name: real image
C1466.definition: A real image is, in a virtual reality headset, an image that is formed on the retina, and a person cannot perceive the world unless real images are formed on the retina.

C1467.name: view frustum
C1467.definition: A view frustum is the region visible to the human eye.

C1468.name: horizontal field of view
C1468.definition: Horizontal field of view (FOV) is the horizontal range in which the human eye sees things.

C1469.name: vertical field of view
C1469.definition: The vertical field of view is a field of view of the human eye.

C1470.name: binocular vision
C1470.definition: Binocular vision is a form of vision in which both eyes see the same image over a common region, and their left and right two-dimensional images are processed to enhance depth perception and produce a three-dimensional view.

C1471.name: left eye
C1471.definition: The left eye is one of the two eyes in stereoscopy, the eye that processes the left image.

C1472.name: right eye
C1472.definition: The right eye is one of the two eyes used in binocular vision and stereoscopy, and it may see areas not seen by the left eye and, in stereoscopy, it processes the right image.

C1473.name: depth perception
C1473.definition: Depth perception is enhanced by binocular vision.

C1474.name: three-dimensional view
C1474.definition: A three-dimensional view is a view of objects that is generated by the simultaneous processing of left and right two-dimensional images.

C1475.name: translational movement
C1475.definition: Translational movement is a type of three-dimensional movement in a virtual world that is used for navigating in that world.

C1476.name: rotational movement
C1476.definition: Rotational movement is a type of movement in a 3D virtual world that is primarily used for moving at different angles along the translational axis.

C1477.name: degree of freedom
C1477.definition: Degree of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space; in 3D space, an object can have six degrees of freedom: three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes, and three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch.

C1478.name: six degrees of freedom
C1478.definition: Six degrees of freedom is the total of six freedoms an object can have in three-dimensional space, consisting of three rotational freedoms called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational freedoms along the x, y, and z axes.

C1479.name: rotational degree of freedom
C1479.definition: Rotational degree of freedom is a degree of freedom of an object in three-dimensional space that is rotational rather than translational, and is one of yaw, roll, or pitch.

C1480.name: translational degree of freedom
C1480.definition: Translational degree of freedom is a degree of freedom of an object in three-dimensional space, along one of the x, y, or z axes.

C1481.name: visual display hardware
C1481.definition: Visual display hardware is display hardware whose engineering requirements can be directly impacted by basic physiological properties such as photoreceptor density.

C1482.name: spatial resolution
C1482.definition: Spatial resolution is the needed number of pixels per square area that a display must have to match the performance of the human visual sense.

C1483.name: intensity resolution
C1483.definition: Intensity resolution is the number of producible intensity values in a display, determined by how many can be processed without compromising perceptual quality.

C1484.name: intensity range
C1484.definition: Intensity range is the minimum and maximum of the producible intensity values that a display can process to match human visual sense without compromising perceptual quality.

C1485.name: temporal resolution
C1485.definition: Temporal resolution is the frame rate, or speed at which display pixels change, that in a VR headset must be much higher than ordinary television or movie standards to allow motion to be perceived smoothly without jitter.

C1486.name: jitter
C1486.definition: Jitter is a lack of smoothness in perceived display motion that temporal resolution must avoid.

C1487.name: aliasing
C1487.definition: Aliasing is distortion that may occur when scan conversion renders pixels close to, rather than exactly on, points of an original shape, making lines, especially diagonals, appear jagged or staircase-shaped.

C1488.name: screen door effect
C1488.definition: The screen door effect is an effect in which an image appears to have a screen on top of it, commonly noticed in images produced by liquid crystal display projectors and can occur in virtual reality headsets.

C1489.name: retina display
C1489.definition: A retina display is a display with a minimum resolution of 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi), although for head-mounted or other wearable displays close to the eye the traditional 326 ppi criterion is not very suitable and the required ppi is probably seven to eight times higher.

C1490.name: pixels per linear inch
C1490.definition: Pixels per linear inch (ppi) is a display-resolution measure used to state a minimum resolution criterion, with a traditional value suitable for distant displays but not for close displays.

C1491.name: retina display criterion
C1491.definition: A retina display criterion is a display-resolution criterion requiring a minimum of 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi), suitable for displays at a distance from the eye but not very suitable for close-to-eye head-mounted or wearable displays, which may need seven to eight times higher resolution.

C1492.name: wearable display
C1492.definition: A wearable display is a virtual reality headset or augmented reality head-mounted display in which a magnifying lens brings the display close to the eye.

C1493.name: magnifying lens
C1493.definition: A magnifying lens is a lens used in augmented reality (AR) head-mounted displays, virtual reality (VR) headsets, or other wearable displays to bring a display close to the eye.

C1494.name: corrective mechanism
C1494.definition: A corrective mechanism is used in virtual reality headsets to avoid or reduce aliasing or the screen door effect, including adjusting field of view, foveated rendering techniques, and other ways of rendering content, in addition to increasing spatial resolution.

C1495.name: foveated rendering
C1495.definition: Foveated rendering is a corrective rendering technique that is used to avoid or reduce aliasing or the screen door effect in virtual reality headsets.

C1496.name: motion perception
C1496.definition: Motion perception is an immersive-environment case for which temporal resolution in a virtual reality headset requires frame rates much higher than ordinary television or movie standards, with higher frame rates preferred.

C1497.name: immersive environment
C1497.definition: An immersive environment is an environment that, in the ideal case, blocks the user's senses and cuts the user off from the real world.

C1498.name: audio component
C1498.definition: An audio component is a component of a virtual reality system that combines sound with vision to enhance the immersive experience, make the virtual environment believable, and increase presence.

C1499.name: high-fidelity audio
C1499.definition: High-fidelity audio is audio that technologies can bring into virtual reality to improve the immersive experience.

C1500.name: audio recording
C1500.definition: Audio recording is the recording of sound, speech, or non-speech sound.

C1501.name: audio reproduction
C1501.definition: Audio reproduction is output generation that can itself be considered a virtual reality (VR) experience even if other senses are missing.

C1502.name: surround sound effect
C1502.definition: Surround sound effect is a sound effect that audio reproduction can provide in cave-like virtual reality versions.

C1503.name: cave-like virtual reality version
C1503.definition: Cave-like virtual reality version is a virtual reality version that is a surround environment surrounded by display devices.

C1504.name: headset virtual reality version
C1504.definition: Headset virtual reality version is a wearable display version of virtual reality.

C1505.name: size
C1505.definition: Size is a property of virtual objects or a measure of virtual reality applications, appearing in perception, object selection, modeling, and storage optimization.

C1506.name: volume
C1506.definition: Volume is a property of a virtual environment that is perceived, and its perception is reinforced when vision is augmented with auditory effects.

C1507.name: material
C1507.definition: Material is a part of a model file that describes the appearance of an object's surface by specifying how it should be rendered, including references to textures, tiling information, color tints, and other information.

C1508.name: distance
C1508.definition: Distance is a variable in XR that gives how far an object is from a viewpoint or camera position, how far directly connected nodes are apart, or how far a light source is from a surface point.

C1509.name: virtual experience
C1509.definition: A virtual experience is an experience in a virtual environment that has a virtual world part represented as a weighted graph of points of interest.

C1510.name: believable
C1510.definition: Believable is the degree to which a virtual experience is closer to reality and everyday experience.

C1511.name: emotional connection
C1511.definition: Emotional connection is a connection with a virtual environment that can be created or increased when vision is coupled with audio, and vision alone may not be able to achieve it.

C1512.name: attachment
C1512.definition: Attachment is something required for presence in a virtual environment, developed to a virtual experience along with reinforcing that experience as believable.

C1513.name: propagation
C1513.definition: Propagation is the passage of sound or light, where sound requires a medium to propagate, sound propagation is caused by pressure variations, and light can propagate without a medium or through a vacuum.

C1514.name: vacuum
C1514.definition: A vacuum is a condition in which there is no sound, while light can propagate through it.

C1515.name: pressure variation
C1515.definition: Pressure variation is a change in pressure over time that causes sound propagation through a medium, created when sound is generated and molecules in the medium are displaced, ranges from compression to rarefaction extremes, and is converted into an auditory experience at the human eardrum.

C1516.name: compression extreme
C1516.definition: Compression extreme is the end of the pressure variations in sound propagation through a medium where pressure is extremely high.

C1517.name: decompression extreme
C1517.definition: Decompression extreme is the very low pressure extreme of the pressure variations that cause sound to propagate through a medium.

C1518.name: eardrum
C1518.definition: The eardrum is the location at which pressure variation is converted into a perceptual auditory experience.

C1519.name: sound wave
C1519.definition: A sound wave is a plot of air pressure variation against time, in which pressure varies from one extreme to another like a sinusoidal wave.

C1520.name: human audible frequency range
C1520.definition: Human audible frequency range is the range of frequencies, from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, that are audible to the human ear, and is a limitation of human physiology.

C1521.name: human ear
C1521.definition: The human ear is the part of human physiology to which only frequencies from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz are audible.

C1522.name: amplitude
C1522.definition: Amplitude is a property of a sound wave that is the maximum displacement from the wave's mean or rest position, measured in decibels relative to the minimum sound detectable by humans at 1000 Hz.

C1523.name: decibel
C1523.definition: Decibel (dB) is used to measure the amplitude of a sound wave relative to the minimum sound detectable by humans at 1000 Hz.

C1524.name: phase
C1524.definition: Phase is a property of a sound wave that is the start position of a cycle of the wave, which can begin from 0 to 360 degrees and is measured in degrees.

C1525.name: human hearing system
C1525.definition: The human hearing system is a three-part system that contains the outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear.

C1526.name: outer ear
C1526.definition: The outer ear is the part of the human hearing system that receives a sound wave in its receiver part and forces it to propagate through the outer-ear canal, which boosts sound pressure for a range of frequencies, while its complex folds attenuate high-frequency sound waves.

C1527.name: middle ear
C1527.definition: Middle ear is a part of the human hearing system that is an air-filled chamber in which sound vibrations from the tympanic membrane are transferred to the malleus, incus, and stapes.

C1528.name: inner ear
C1528.definition: The inner ear is one of the three parts of the human hearing system, and it houses the cochlea, the sense organ for hearing.

C1529.name: receiver part
C1529.definition: The receiver part is a part of the outer ear that receives a sound wave and forces it to propagate through the outer-ear canal; its complex folds, together with those in the canal, attenuate high-frequency sound waves.

C1530.name: outer-ear canal
C1530.definition: The outer-ear canal is a canal in the outer ear through which sound waves pass, working as an amplifier that boosts sound pressure for a range of frequencies, while its complex folds attenuate high-frequency waves.

C1531.name: amplifier
C1531.definition: An amplifier is a part that boosts the sound pressure of a sound wave for a range of frequencies.

C1532.name: sound pressure
C1532.definition: Sound pressure is what the outer-ear canal boosts for a range of frequencies as a sound wave propagates through the outer-ear canal.

C1533.name: tympanic membrane
C1533.definition: The tympanic membrane is in the middle ear, where a sound wave passing through the outer-ear canal strikes it, causing it to vibrate and transfer the vibration to the ossicles.

C1534.name: ossicle
C1534.definition: An ossicle is one of the three parts in an air-filled chamber of the middle ear, the malleus, incus, and stapes, to which vibration from the tympanic membrane is transferred.

C1535.name: malleus
C1535.definition: Malleus is one of the three ossicles in the middle ear to which vibration from the tympanic membrane is transferred.

C1536.name: incus
C1536.definition: The incus is one of three ossicles in the air-filled chamber of the middle ear to which vibration from the tympanic membrane is transferred.

C1537.name: stapes
C1537.definition: Stapes is one of the three ossicles in the middle ear.

C1538.name: cochlea
C1538.definition: The cochlea is the sense organ for hearing in the inner ear that is connected to nerves and converts sound energy into neural impulses transmitted to the brain through the neural network.

C1539.name: nerve
C1539.definition: A nerve is a structure connected to the cochlea.

C1540.name: sound energy
C1540.definition: Sound energy is converted by the cochlea into neural impulses that are transmitted to the brain through the neural network.

C1541.name: sound perception
C1541.definition: Sound perception is the perception of sounds at three levels—social, warning, and primitive—where social helps individuals carry out social interactions, warning provides an alert or warning, and primitive is the intuitive perception of mostly ignored background noises that may not lead to meaningful action, and these levels together give a person an overall idea of the surroundings.

C1542.name: social-level sound perception
C1542.definition: Social-level sound perception is a level of sound perception, one of three, that helps an individual carry out social interactions with other individuals.

C1543.name: warning-level sound perception
C1543.definition: Warning-level sound perception is the level of sound perception that provides an alert or warning about something.

C1544.name: primitive-level sound perception
C1544.definition: Primitive-level sound perception is a level of sound perception involving the intuitive perception of naive sounds, such as background noises, that people mostly ignore and that may not lead to any meaningful action.

C1545.name: sound effects
C1545.definition: Sound effects are auditory effects generated for a virtual reality system to support the desired level of sound perception.

C1546.name: psychophysics
C1546.definition: Psychophysics is the scientific study that examines perceptual phenomena produced by physical stimuli.

C1547.name: physical stimulus
C1547.definition: A physical stimulus is a stimulus that produces perceptual phenomena studied in psychophysics.

C1548.name: psychoacoustics
C1548.definition: Psychoacoustics is a more specific area of psychophysics that scientifically studies the perceptual phenomena produced by acoustic stimuli or sound.

C1549.name: acoustic stimulus
C1549.definition: Acoustic stimulus is a stimulus in auditory perception that produces the perceptual phenomena studied in psychoacoustics.

C1550.name: Stevens' power law
C1550.definition: Stevens' power law is a result from psychophysics that relates perceived magnitude P to physical stimulus magnitude M by P = C M^x, where x is an exponent and C a constant depending on units.

C1551.name: perceived magnitude
C1551.definition: Perceived magnitude is the magnitude of a physical stimulus as perceived, represented by P in Stevens' power law.

C1552.name: exponent
C1552.definition: Exponent is the value in Stevens' power law that relates the actual magnitude of a physical stimulus to its perceived magnitude.

C1553.name: just noticeable difference
C1553.definition: Just noticeable difference (JND) is the amount of change in a stimulus required for subjects to perceive it as changed in at least 50 percent of trials.

C1554.name: Weber's law
C1554.definition: Weber's law is a law from psychophysics that states the just noticeable difference, the noticeable change in a stimulus's magnitude or intensity, is a constant fraction of the stimulus's magnitude or intensity.

C1555.name: perceived loudness
