C1555.definition: Perceived loudness is the perceived loudness of a pure tone, where a much higher pressure level is perceived as only a bit louder when the Stevens' power law exponent is less than 1.

C1556.name: pure tone
C1556.definition: A pure tone is a tone used when describing perceived loudness.

C1557.name: pressure level
C1557.definition: Pressure level is a level related to the perceived loudness of a 3000 Hz pure tone, where a much higher pressure level is perceived as only a bit louder.

C1558.name: pitch perception
C1558.definition: Pitch perception is the context in which the frequency of a sound wave is referred to as pitch.

C1559.name: sound localization
C1559.definition: Sound localization is a main area of psychoacoustics that estimates the location of a sound source by hearing it.

C1560.name: sound source
C1560.definition: A sound source is a thing whose location is estimated by sound localization and represented relative to a listener's head.

C1561.name: minimum audible angle
C1561.definition: Minimum audible angle (MAA) is the minimum angular variation in the direction of a sound source that a human listener can detect, depending on the sound's frequency and direction.

C1562.name: spherical coordinate system
C1562.definition: Spherical coordinate system is a coordinate system with the listener's head as the origin, used to represent a sound source location using azimuth, elevation, and radius.

C1563.name: azimuth
C1563.definition: Azimuth is the angle in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the projection of the sound source direction in a spherical coordinate system used to represent a sound source location, ranging from -180 to 180 degrees.

C1564.name: elevation
C1564.definition: Elevation is a parameter in the spherical coordinate system used to represent a sound source location, and it is the angle between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane, ranging from -90 degrees to 90 degrees.

C1565.name: radius
C1565.definition: Radius is a parameter in a spherical coordinate system used to represent a sound source location that specifies the distance from the listener's head origin to the source.

C1566.name: direction
C1566.definition: Direction is the orientation of a sound source, an object to be selected, or user movement in two- or three-dimensional space, used to describe sound-source location, support object selection, and support wayfinding.

C1567.name: sound localization cue
C1567.definition: A sound localization cue is a cue that is either monaural, involving a single ear, or binaural, involving both ears, and can indicate the direction from which a sound is coming or be used to locate the source.

C1568.name: monaural sound localization cue
C1568.definition: A monaural sound localization cue is a sound localization cue involving a single ear.

C1569.name: binaural sound localization cue
C1569.definition: A binaural sound localization cue is a sound localization cue that involves both ears.

C1570.name: interaural level difference
C1570.definition: Interaural level difference (ILD) is a binaural sound localization cue that is the difference in sound magnitude heard by each ear, where the ear without obstruction receives a stronger sound and the difference can indicate the direction from which the sound is coming.

C1571.name: acoustic shadow
C1571.definition: An acoustic shadow is the occurrence in which a sound wave does not reach one ear, caused by an object in front of the sound source or by the position of the head.

C1572.name: interaural time difference
C1572.definition: Interaural time difference is a binaural sound localization cue from different sound arrival times at the ears, which can be used to locate the source.

C1573.name: auditory component
C1573.definition: The auditory component is a component of an extended reality (XR) system, one that should ideally be non-stationary, moving with the user, and interactive, dependent on the listener's actions.

C1574.name: head-related transfer function
C1574.definition: Head-related transfer function (HRTF) is a model that describes how a listener receives sound from a location in space. It depends on the size and shape of the head, ears, and ear canal, so each person's is unique; an average listener's is used, and a pair for both ears can synthesize binaural sound and support localization in XR.

C1575.name: binaural sound
C1575.definition: Binaural sound is a kind of sound that can be synthesized using a pair of head-related transfer functions for both ears.

C1576.name: human somatosensory system
C1576.definition: Human somatosensory system is a sensory system that handles touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis.

C1577.name: sensory system
C1577.definition: A sensory system is a perceptual system, such as the human somatosensory system, which handles touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis.

C1578.name: visual perceptual system
C1578.definition: The visual perceptual system is a human sensory system.

C1579.name: auditory perceptual system
C1579.definition: An auditory perceptual system is a human sensory system.

C1580.name: kinesthesis
C1580.definition: Kinesthesis is the awareness of the parameters associated with moving body parts, providing information on velocities, accelerations, and forces during movement.

C1581.name: body part
C1581.definition: A body part is a movable part of the human body, such as legs, arms, fingers, tongue, mouth, and lips.

C1582.name: velocity
C1582.definition: Velocity is one of the parameters associated with moving body parts for which kinesthesis provides information during movement.

C1583.name: touch receptor
C1583.definition: Touch receptor is a human somatosensory receptor devoted to the sense of touch, embedded in the epidermis or dermis, that transforms touch into neural impulses for the brain.

C1584.name: epidermis
C1584.definition: The epidermis is the first layer of the skin, in which touch receptors are embedded.

C1585.name: dermis
C1585.definition: The dermis is the second layer of the skin.

C1586.name: hypodermis
C1586.definition: The hypodermis is a layer of the skin.

C1587.name: Merkel's disc
C1587.definition: Merkel's disc is one of the touch receptors of the human somatosensory system.

C1588.name: hair follicle receptor
C1588.definition: Hair follicle receptor is a touch receptor of the human somatosensory system.

C1589.name: free nerve ending
C1589.definition: A free nerve ending is one of the touch receptors of the human somatosensory system.

C1590.name: Ruffini's ending
C1590.definition: Ruffini's ending is one of the touch receptors of the human somatosensory system.

C1591.name: Meissner's corpuscle
C1591.definition: Meissner's corpuscle is one of the touch receptors of the human somatosensory system.

C1592.name: Pacinian corpuscle
C1592.definition: A Pacinian corpuscle is a touch receptor of the human somatosensory system.

C1593.name: muscle spindle
C1593.definition: A muscle spindle is a receptor in the human somatosensory system that is embedded in muscles and reports changes in muscle length to the brain, supporting proprioception and kinesthesis.

C1594.name: muscle length
C1594.definition: Muscle length is the length of a muscle, whose changes are reported to the brain by muscle spindles used for proprioception and kinesthesis.

C1595.name: Golgi tendon organ
C1595.definition: A Golgi tendon organ is a receptor, used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system, that is embedded in tendons connecting muscles to bones and reports changes in muscle tension associated with movement.

C1596.name: tendon
C1596.definition: A tendon is a body part that connects muscles to bones.

C1597.name: bone
C1597.definition: Bone is a body part to which muscles are connected by tendons and which forms joints.

C1598.name: muscle tension
C1598.definition: Muscle tension is associated with movement, and changes in it are reported by Golgi tendon organs.

C1599.name: joint receptor
C1599.definition: A joint receptor is a receptor used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system that is located at joints between bones, coordinates muscle movement, and provides information on relative bone positions.

C1600.name: muscle movement
C1600.definition: Muscle movement is movement that joint receptors at joints between bones coordinate.

C1601.name: relative bone position
C1601.definition: Relative bone position is information provided by joint receptors at joints between bones.

C1602.name: hand
C1602.definition: A hand is a thing that can touch an object and activate somatosensory receptors.

C1603.name: object
C1603.definition: An object is a part of a computer graphics image or scene that may be a three-dimensional model or interface object and is created, represented, synthesized, and rendered.

C1604.name: corrective motor action
C1604.definition: A corrective motor action is a motor action, such as removing a hand from a hot object, that the brain can cause by sending messages back through a neural network.

C1605.name: haptic perception
C1605.definition: Haptic perception is a major part of somatosensory perception that involves perceiving the overall geometric shape of objects through touch, at levels from input received by skin receptors to object manipulations called haptic explorations, and helps create mental models and improve the immersive experience in virtual environments.

C1606.name: somatosensory perception
C1606.definition: Somatosensory perception is a perception that has haptic perception as a major part.

C1607.name: shape
C1607.definition: Shape is a geometric property of an object that haptic exploration can infer and shearing can change.

C1608.name: haptic exploration
C1608.definition: Haptic exploration is the manipulation of geometric objects through touch that is used to form a mental model of their overall shape, size, weight, and hardness.

C1609.name: lateral motion
C1609.definition: Lateral motion is a type of haptic exploration needed for texture perception.

C1610.name: texture perception
C1610.definition: Texture perception is an object property perception that lateral motion haptic exploration is needed for.

C1611.name: pressure
C1611.definition: Pressure is one of the types of haptic exploration used for hardness perception.

C1612.name: hardness perception
C1612.definition: Hardness perception is an object property perception that is perceived through pressure during haptic exploration.

C1613.name: enclosure
C1613.definition: Enclosure is a type of haptic exploration needed for global shape or volume perception.

C1614.name: global shape perception
C1614.definition: Global shape perception is an object property perception for which the haptic exploration of enclosure is needed.

C1615.name: static contact
C1615.definition: Static contact is a type of haptic exploration used for temperature perception.

C1616.name: temperature perception
C1616.definition: Temperature perception is one of the object property perceptions in haptic exploration, specifically the one associated with static contact.

C1617.name: unsupported holding
C1617.definition: Unsupported holding is one of the six types of haptic exploration, used for weight perception.

C1618.name: weight perception
C1618.definition: Weight perception is an object property perception for which unsupported holding is the corresponding type of haptic exploration.

C1619.name: contour following
C1619.definition: Contour following is a type of haptic exploration used for local shape perception.

C1620.name: local shape perception
C1620.definition: Local shape perception is a type of object property perception that contour following, a type of haptic exploration, is used for.

C1621.name: spatial information
C1621.definition: Spatial information is information that is combined with temporal information in haptic exploration used to perceive different properties of objects.

C1622.name: temporal information
C1622.definition: Temporal information is information used in haptic exploration, together with spatial information, to perceive different properties of objects.

C1623.name: somatosensory signals
C1623.definition: Somatosensory signals are signals from in-hand manipulation of an object that are integrated in haptic exploration to help form a geometric mental model of the object.

C1624.name: geometric mental model
C1624.definition: A geometric mental model is a learned model of an object in terms of properties such as shape, size, weight, and hardness.

C1625.name: weight
C1625.definition: Weight is used as the Euclidean distance or computed travel time that weights graph edges between points of interest in the minimum-time approach.

C1626.name: hardness
C1626.definition: Hardness is a property of an object that can be learned through haptic exploration involving in-hand manipulation.

C1627.name: mental model
C1627.definition: Mental model is a spatial knowledge base of the surroundings and overall environment that consists of landmark, procedural, and topological knowledge to make locating oneself and identifying a suitable path easier.

C1628.name: touch sensation
C1628.definition: Touch sensation is an extended reality sensation that can be provided by engineered devices, most popularly through force feedback, typically in the form of vibrations.

C1629.name: force feedback
C1629.definition: Force feedback is the most popular form of touch sensation in extended reality, typically provided as vibrations by force feedback devices, particularly in virtual reality.

C1630.name: force feedback mouse
C1630.definition: A force feedback mouse is a force feedback device that provides touch sensation in extended reality, typically through vibrations.

C1631.name: smart glove
C1631.definition: A smart glove is a force feedback device used in XR to provide touch sensation and to implement hand manipulation.

C1632.name: KGS dot view model DV-2
C1632.definition: The KGS dot view model DV-2 is a haptic pin array with a matrix of pins that a computer controls, forcing them upward according to signals generated for objects in the virtual world to simulate the texture of an object surface when the user's fingertip scans across it.

C1633.name: haptic pin array
C1633.definition: A haptic pin array is a computer-controlled matrix of pins that are forced upward, according to signals generated for objects in the virtual world, to simulate the texture of an object surface when a user's fingertip scans across it.

C1634.name: virtual avatar
C1634.definition: A virtual avatar is a virtual object that appears in a virtual world and is associated with a real-world object.

C1635.name: tangible user interface
C1635.definition: Tangible user interface is a real-world object whose virtual avatar appears in a virtual world and that, by aligning the real world and the virtual world, provides feedback to the user's somatosensory system in place of computer-controlled haptic devices.

C1636.name: wearable device sensor
C1636.definition: A wearable device sensor is used in a see-through display to detect which real object a user is dealing with, allowing the computer to change the view of that object or add virtual objects to the real world.

C1637.name: chemical sense
C1637.definition: A chemical sense is a sense, such as taste or smell, whose chemoreceptors work by chemical reaction with specific molecules or chemical stimuli at appropriate concentrations, and not all chemoreceptors respond to all chemical stimuli.

C1638.name: chemical stimuli
C1638.definition: Chemical stimuli are specific molecules at appropriate concentrations with which taste and smell chemoreceptors chemically react, and not all chemoreceptors respond to all of them.

C1639.name: touch sense
C1639.definition: Touch sense is a sense in extended reality systems for which there is more research than for smell and taste.

C1640.name: Smell-O-Vision
C1640.definition: Smell-O-Vision is a system for adding smell to films in which odors were injected into movie theater seats at different points during a film according to the scenery.

C1641.name: smell interface
C1641.definition: A smell interface is an interface that provides odor stimuli to the nose, usually by using air pumps or micropumps to spray chemical compounds near the nose, with other components that help create the odor.

C1642.name: air pump
C1642.definition: Air pump is a pump used in a smell interface to spray chemical compounds near the nose.

C1643.name: micropump
C1643.definition: A micropump is a pump used in a smell interface to spray chemical compounds near the nose.

C1644.name: chemical compound
C1644.definition: A chemical compound is usually sprayed near the nose by air pumps or micropumps in a smell interface to help create odor stimuli.

C1645.name: room-scale delivery
C1645.definition: Room-scale delivery is the delivery of odor on a room scale for social or larger experiences.

C1646.name: odor intensity
C1646.definition: Odor intensity is a factor in smell interfaces that room-scale delivery generally makes hard to control.

C1647.name: uniformity
C1647.definition: Uniformity is an aspect of odor delivery in smell interfaces that room-scale delivery generally makes hard to control.

C1648.name: odor concentration
C1648.definition: Odor concentration is varied over a large area for localization in room-scale smell interfaces.

C1649.name: taste interface
C1649.definition: A taste interface is an interface that can place electrodes over and under the tongue to provide stimulation that simulates the main taste types.

C1650.name: main taste types
C1650.definition: Main taste types are taste types that a taste interface can simulate by placing electrodes over and under the tongue to provide stimulation.

C1651.name: interactive software
C1651.definition: Interactive software is a kind of software, such as extended reality (XR) application software intended for laypersons, that is developed through the interactive system development lifecycle.

C1652.name: design space
C1652.definition: Design space is a set of all possible designs.

C1653.name: calendar application
C1653.definition: A calendar application is an application that displays a fixed and large number of elements, such as month names, dates, and possibly the year.

C1654.name: stage
C1654.definition: A stage is a step in an interactive system development lifecycle, a set of stages that should ideally be followed in a particular sequence, with iterations that may return to a previous stage.

C1655.name: participant
C1655.definition: A participant is a user selected for an experiment on the basis of a user profile so that the selected users form a representative sample of the whole user group.

C1656.name: user-centric design approach
C1656.definition: A user-centric design approach is an approach to usable interactive systems and extended reality software that includes users' needs and expectations, requiring a highly iterative software development lifecycle with loops between stages.

C1657.name: iteration
C1657.definition: Iteration is a cycle that returns to a previous stage of interactive system development to account for user feedback, in which a design is prototyped, evaluated, and refined until it is stabilized.

C1658.name: user feedback
C1658.definition: User feedback is the involvement of users in different ways, not only through feedback, that iterations between stages in an interactive system development lifecycle account for.

C1659.name: feasibility study
C1659.definition: A feasibility study is a stage in the interactive system development lifecycle.

C1660.name: requirement gathering
C1660.definition: Requirement gathering is a stage of the interactive system development lifecycle that collects functional and non-functional requirements from clients and end users, focuses on end-user usability requirements, and specifies them for design, implementation, and deployment.

C1661.name: analysis
C1661.definition: Analysis is part of the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development and a step in developing a model from empirical data.

C1662.name: specification
C1662.definition: Specification is a stage in the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development.

C1663.name: design-prototype-evaluate cycle
C1663.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle is a cycle in the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development that quickly prototypes, evaluates, and refines interface and interaction design, not code design, until the design stabilizes.

C1664.name: design
C1664.definition: Design is the interface and interaction design part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle in interactive system development, not code design, that may be based on intuition, design guidelines, or team brainstorming, and is refined through prototyping and quick evaluation until stable.

C1665.name: early evaluation
C1665.definition: Early evaluation is an evaluation point in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle of the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development that quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time.

C1666.name: code design
C1666.definition: Code design is one of two design stages in interactive system development, separate from interface and interaction design, and, like code design in other non-interactive software, it produces the design of the code using notations such as DFD, ER, object-oriented approaches, or UML before coding and testing.

C1667.name: implementation
C1667.definition: Implementation is a stage in interactive system development that involves coding followed by code testing.

C1668.name: code testing
C1668.definition: Code testing is a standard software development stage in interactive system development that evaluates code as part of coding and implementation by ensuring it is bug-free and executes properly, but does not establish whether the system is usable.

C1669.name: empirical study
C1669.definition: Empirical study is a usability-testing stage in interactive system development, performed after code testing, that systematically tests a fully implemented system with end users through a controlled experiment to collect and analyze data for assessing overall usability.

C1670.name: maintenance
C1670.definition: Maintenance is part of the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development.

C1671.name: end user
C1671.definition: End user is involved in interactive system development from the requirement-gathering stage onward, usually distinct from the client, and usability requirements primarily come from the end user.

C1672.name: requirement analysis
C1672.definition: Requirement analysis is an analysis in the development of interactive systems that typically refers to the requirements of the client.

C1673.name: requirement
C1673.definition: A requirement is an end-user requirement that states what must be done to make a system usable, without specifying how to implement it; it can be functional or non-functional.

C1674.name: contextual inquiry
C1674.definition: Contextual inquiry (CI) is a usability requirement-gathering method, often described as a semi-structured interview process, that observes users performing tasks in their natural work setting and asks users questions to clarify behavior.

C1675.name: ethnographic study
C1675.definition: Ethnographic study is one of the methods for gathering end user requirements in the requirement-gathering stage.

C1676.name: cultural probe
C1676.definition: A cultural probe is a method for gathering end user requirements in the requirement-gathering stage.

C1677.name: design-prototype-evaluate loop
C1677.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate loop is an iterative design loop for interactive systems in which an early design is prototyped, evaluated with user feedback, and refined through many quick iterations until few significantly different problems are identified. It includes interface and interaction design from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later activity.

C1678.name: turnaround time
C1678.definition: Turnaround time is the overall project time that increases significantly when repeated design, prototype, evaluation, coding, and testing cycles are not completed quickly, potentially causing cost overruns.

C1679.name: interface design
C1679.definition: Interface design is an activity in interactive system development that involves designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, uses a design-prototype-evaluate cycle, repeated with prototyping and quick evaluation until stable, and is separate from code design.

C1680.name: coding
C1680.definition: Coding is a stage in interactive system development, carried out after code design and before code testing.

C1681.name: interactive system development lifecycle
C1681.definition: Interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC) is a staged development method that is similar to regular software development but distinctive in its end-user requirement gathering, iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle, and empirical usability evaluation.

C1682.name: iterative software development life cycle
C1682.definition: Iterative software development life cycle is a software development life cycle that has three evaluation points: early evaluation, code testing, and empirical study.

C1683.name: executability
C1683.definition: Executability is a quality of code in which the code is bug-free and executes properly.

C1684.name: usability testing
C1684.definition: Usability testing is a systematic empirical study that involves users to estimate whether an interactive system is usable, distinct from code testing, which only shows that a system is executable.

C1685.name: iterative design
C1685.definition: Iterative design is the design of usable extended reality systems in which the design-prototype-evaluate cycle is the only loop designed to be performed quickly, and other loops should not be frequent.

C1686.name: development cost
C1686.definition: Development cost is the cost of a project in manpower, time, and resources.

C1687.name: development stage
C1687.definition: A development stage is one of the stages in building a usable extended reality system that should be completed carefully to avoid the need to return to previous stages.

C1688.name: design-prototype-evaluate
C1688.definition: Design-prototype-evaluate is one of the stages of the interactive system development lifecycle in which building interactive software differs from building regular software.

C1689.name: system development lifecycle
C1689.definition: System development lifecycle is a lifecycle used for interactive systems that can be followed to build extended reality systems.

C1690.name: Majuli case study
C1690.definition: The Majuli case study is a virtual reality case study focused on designing, implementing, and evaluating an immersive interactive tour that digitally preserves the ecological heritage and tangible and intangible cultural heritage of the Majuli River Island.

C1691.name: digital preservation
C1691.definition: Digital preservation is the use of digital media to preserve educational, scientific, and other resources.

C1692.name: evaluation
C1692.definition: Evaluation is a study of an extended reality system that measures usability aspects, such as user engagement, presence, and comfort, and identifies potential improvements by collecting end-user data through a controlled experiment and a structured questionnaire.

C1693.name: Majuli
C1693.definition: Majuli is a river island on the Brahmaputra River in Assam that is surrounded on all sides by the river and its tributaries and is considered the world's largest inhabited river island.

C1694.name: river island
C1694.definition: A river island is a kind of island, for example Majuli River Island, a river island on the Brahmaputra River in eastern Assam, Northeast India.

C1695.name: Brahmaputra River
C1695.definition: The Brahmaputra River is a river on which Majuli River Island lies.

C1696.name: United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization World Heritage Site
C1696.definition: A United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization World Heritage Site is a site for which Majuli River Island is a potential contender.

C1697.name: monsoon season
C1697.definition: Monsoon season is the season in Majuli that typically runs from May to September.

C1698.name: non-monsoon season
C1698.definition: The non-monsoon season is the season on Majuli that lasts from October to April.

C1699.name: precipitation
C1699.definition: Precipitation is an average annual amount, with Majuli's value given as 1704 millimeters.

C1700.name: maximum temperature
C1700.definition: Maximum temperature is a temperature value for Majuli.

C1701.name: minimum temperature
C1701.definition: Minimum temperature is a temperature of Majuli.

C1702.name: area
C1702.definition: Area is a measurement of the size of a place, given in square kilometers.

C1703.name: flood
C1703.definition: Flood is a severe annual event affecting Majuli.

C1704.name: river erosion
C1704.definition: River erosion is the reduction of an island's habitable area, causing formerly habitable areas to become sandbars, river banks, underwater areas, or barren areas.

C1705.name: habitable area
C1705.definition: Habitable area is an area that remains habitable rather than becoming a sandbar, river bank, underwater area, or barren area.

C1706.name: sandbar
C1706.definition: A sandbar is an area that a formerly habitable area can become when severe floods and river erosion make it no longer habitable.

C1707.name: river bank
C1707.definition: River bank is one of the kinds of areas that formerly habitable areas can become when river erosion makes them no longer habitable.

C1708.name: cultural resource
C1708.definition: A cultural resource is a resource that severe annual floods and erosion can endanger.

C1709.name: satra
C1709.definition: A satra is a monastery on Majuli, Assam, that is an authoritative center of the Vaishnavite faith and a living workshop for visual and performing arts.

C1710.name: Vaishnavite faith
C1710.definition: Vaishnavite faith is a faith whose authoritative centers in Assam are the satras, Vaishnavite monasteries on Majuli.

C1711.name: visual arts
C1711.definition: Visual arts are one of the kinds of arts for which satras on Majuli are living workshops.

C1712.name: performing arts
C1712.definition: Performing arts are one of the heritage aspects included in the intangible heritage of Majuli.

C1713.name: tribal community
C1713.definition: A tribal community is a community on Majuli with distinctive ways of living, rituals, heritage, and culture.

C1714.name: Mishing
C1714.definition: Mishing is one of the three major tribal communities of Majuli island.

C1715.name: Deori
C1715.definition: Deori is one of three distinctive tribal communities of Majuli island, each of which is supposed to have a distinct tangible and intangible cultural identity.

C1716.name: Sonowal Kachari
C1716.definition: Sonowal Kachari is one of the major tribal communities of Majuli island.

C1717.name: tangible heritage
C1717.definition: Tangible heritage is a form of heritage that someone can touch and feel.

C1718.name: cultural artifact
C1718.definition: Cultural artifact is a tangible heritage aspect that someone can touch and feel.

C1719.name: mask
C1719.definition: A mask is a cultural artifact and a tangible heritage aspect of Majuli that someone can touch and feel.

C1720.name: musical instrument
C1720.definition: A musical instrument is a cultural artifact that can be part of tangible heritage.

C1721.name: architecture
C1721.definition: Architecture is one of the tangible heritage aspects of Majuli that someone can touch and feel.

C1722.name: traditional tribal home
C1722.definition: A traditional tribal home is one of the architectural aspects of the tangible heritage of Majuli.

C1723.name: intangible heritage
C1723.definition: Intangible heritage is heritage that cannot be touched and felt but can be sensed, including traditional skills, knowledge, and aesthetic norms embedded in the daily and occasional activities of social life.

C1724.name: music
C1724.definition: Music is one of the intangible heritage aspects of Majuli that can be sensed rather than touched or felt.

C1725.name: dance
C1725.definition: Dance is one of the intangible heritage aspects of Majuli.

C1726.name: drama
C1726.definition: Drama is an intangible heritage aspect of Majuli, included among traditional skills, knowledge, and aesthetic norms embedded in social life.

C1727.name: mask making
C1727.definition: Mask making is a traditional craft of Majuli island residents and part of the intangible heritage of Majuli.

C1728.name: vernacular architecture
C1728.definition: Vernacular architecture is an intangible heritage aspect of Majuli that cannot be touched and felt but can be sensed.

C1729.name: weaving
C1729.definition: Weaving is one aspect of the intangible heritage of Majuli, a heritage aspect that cannot be touched and felt but can be sensed.

C1730.name: food
C1730.definition: Food is one of the intangible heritage aspects of Majuli.

C1731.name: agricultural practices
C1731.definition: Agricultural practices are part of the intangible heritage of Majuli, which consists of heritage aspects that cannot be touched and felt but can be sensed and are typically embedded in daily and occasional activities of social life.

C1732.name: ecological heritage
C1732.definition: Ecological heritage is the flora and fauna that exist because of a natural formation's unique geology, geography, and topography.

C1733.name: flora
C1733.definition: Flora is one part of ecological heritage, alongside fauna, that exists because of unique geology, geography, and topography from natural formation.

C1734.name: fauna
C1734.definition: Fauna is part of Majuli's ecological heritage, existing because of the island's unique geology, geography, and topography from natural formation.

C1735.name: geology
C1735.definition: Geology is one of the unique natural characteristics of an island, along with geography and topography, that helps determine its flora and fauna.

C1736.name: geography
C1736.definition: Geography is one of the unique aspects of Majuli, along with geology and topography, that contribute to its ecological heritage.

C1737.name: topography
C1737.definition: Topography is one of the natural aspects of an island, along with geology and geography, that causes its flora and fauna to exist.

C1738.name: traditional preservation methods
C1738.definition: Traditional preservation methods are methods for preserving cultural heritage, including oral traditions, museums, maintenance of historical sites, and documentation.

C1739.name: cultural heritage
C1739.definition: Cultural heritage is a form of heritage that has tangible and intangible aspects and can be preserved by traditional methods, captured in a multimodal heritage archive, or explored in virtual reality.

C1740.name: oral traditions
C1740.definition: Oral traditions are one of the traditional methods for preserving cultural heritage.

C1741.name: documentation
C1741.definition: Documentation is a part of the standard interactive system development lifecycle that is prepared for each stage and included in agile release and sprint testing.

C1742.name: digital media
C1742.definition: Digital media is used to preserve educational, scientific, and other resources and heritage.

C1743.name: archiving
C1743.definition: Archiving is storing visual and audio files that capture the heritage information of a particular entity, object, space, or place in digital heritage preservation.

C1744.name: digitizing
C1744.definition: Digitizing is part of the process of digital heritage preservation.

C1745.name: digital avatar
C1745.definition: A digital avatar is a digital version of the elements and objects of a physical space, and it can preserve fragile artifacts and be close to reality.

C1746.name: artifact
C1746.definition: An artifact is a physical object that can be preserved through digital avatars and explored with immersive technologies.

C1747.name: heritage site
C1747.definition: A heritage site is a site that virtual reality and other immersive technologies allow a global audience to explore remotely from home without visiting the physical site.

C1748.name: heritage preservation
C1748.definition: Heritage preservation is creating an archive of heritage information using virtual reality (VR) and other immersive technologies, ideally a multimedia archive comprising images, videos, audio, and text, with images and videos in 2D and 360-degree forms, to preserve heritage for future generations.

C1749.name: multimedia archive
C1749.definition: A multimedia archive is an archive comprising images, videos, audio, and text, with images and videos in 2D and 360-degree forms, used for an immersive virtual tour or exploration of heritage.

C1750.name: image
C1750.definition: An image is the whole interface displayed on a computer screen, not only the main object, comprising geometric shapes or objects, including interface objects such as menus and icons, with colors assigned to them.

C1751.name: video
C1751.definition: Video is one of the items in a virtual reality multimedia archive, where it may be 360-degree, drone, or regular two-dimensional content and is used to provide location-relevant cultural or ecological information.

C1752.name: audio
C1752.definition: Audio is a component of a multimedia archive of heritage information.

C1753.name: text
C1753.definition: Text is one of the content types in a multimedia heritage information archive for a virtual reality heritage preservation system.

C1754.name: two-dimensional form
C1754.definition: Two-dimensional form (2D) is a form of images and videos in a multimedia archive.

C1755.name: 360-degree form
C1755.definition: 360-degree form is a form for images and videos included in a multimedia archive for a VR heritage-preservation system, alongside two-dimensional form.

C1756.name: Majuli Island virtual reality tour
C1756.definition: The Majuli Island virtual reality tour is a heritage preservation tour focused mainly on the island's tangible and intangible cultural heritage, in which preservation produces tour content and immersive virtual tours let users explore the island, aiming to make them feel present and reduce cyber sickness.

C1757.name: preservation
C1757.definition: Preservation is a component of a digital heritage preservation system that produces the content of a virtual tour.

C1758.name: tribal village
C1758.definition: A tribal village is a village on Majuli island where distinct tribal cultures are present and whose unique traditions and customs are reproduced in a virtual tour.

C1759.name: festival
C1759.definition: A festival is part of the intangible cultural heritage of Majuli island, is celebrated throughout the year, and has forms and timings that can be reproduced in a virtual world.

C1760.name: ritual
C1760.definition: A ritual is a form of intangible cultural heritage, alongside festivals, that celebrates cultural diversity and whose timing and form can be reproduced in a virtual world.

C1761.name: Bihu
C1761.definition: Bihu is a traditional harvest festival of Assam.

C1762.name: Kati Bihu
C1762.definition: Kati Bihu is one of the festivals included in the intangible cultural heritage of Majuli island.

C1763.name: Raas Leela
C1763.definition: Raas Leela is one of the festivals included in the intangible cultural heritage of Majuli island.

C1764.name: Ali Ai Ligang
C1764.definition: Ali Ai Ligang is a festival in the intangible cultural heritage of Majuli island.

C1765.name: Bhogali Bihu
C1765.definition: Bhogali Bihu is one of the festivals included in the intangible cultural heritage of Majuli island.

C1766.name: Mati Akhara dance
C1766.definition: The Mati Akhara dance is part of the intangible cultural heritage of Majuli island, performed while the Khol musical instrument is played.

C1767.name: Khol
C1767.definition: Khol is a musical instrument that is part of the intangible cultural heritage of Majuli island and is played while the Mati Akhara dance takes place.

C1768.name: pottery
C1768.definition: Pottery is one of the traditional crafts of Majuli island residents.

C1769.name: silk production
C1769.definition: Silk production is one of the traditional crafts of Majuli island residents.

C1770.name: boat building
C1770.definition: Boat building is one of the traditional crafts of Majuli island residents.

C1771.name: cultural landscape
C1771.definition: Cultural landscape is the tangible and intangible cultural heritage of the Majuli island, represented by a map with hotspots.

C1772.name: hotspot
C1772.definition: A hotspot is a numbered place on a map of Majuli that represents a satra, village, town, or other place used to capture tangible and intangible cultural heritage.

C1773.name: village
C1773.definition: A village is one of the Majuli hotspots used to capture the tangible and intangible heritage aspects of tribal culture.

C1774.name: town
C1774.definition: Town is a place among the Majuli hotspots that is used to capture the tangible and intangible heritage aspects of mixed culture.

C1775.name: tribal culture
C1775.definition: Tribal culture is a culture whose tangible and intangible heritage aspects are captured in villages among the Majuli hotspots.

C1776.name: mixed culture
C1776.definition: Mixed culture is the culture whose tangible and intangible heritage aspects are captured in towns and other places among the Majuli hotspots.

C1777.name: multimodal heritage archive
C1777.definition: A multimodal heritage archive is a collection of 2D and 360-degree images and videos, drone shots and videos, 3D models, and text that captures tangible and intangible heritage and is used to recreate a virtual landscape and virtual tour.

C1778.name: 360-degree image
C1778.definition: A 360-degree image is a captured image of a place used to model places and to move from one point to another in a virtual reality tour.

C1779.name: two-dimensional video
C1779.definition: Two-dimensional video is a regular video used to capture intangible cultural aspects and is one of the videos users can access in a virtual tour.

C1780.name: two-dimensional drone shot
C1780.definition: A two-dimensional drone shot is a part of a multimodal heritage archive used to showcase the landscape, top view, flora, and fauna of locations and to preserve cultural and ecological heritage.

C1781.name: drone video
C1781.definition: A drone video is a video in the multimodal heritage archive used to showcase the landscape and top view of locations and to digitally recreate and preserve cultural and ecological heritage.

C1782.name: textual description
C1782.definition: A textual description is descriptive text that provides additional context about locations, significant spots, artifacts, objects, or elements in a virtual tour or multimodal archive.

C1783.name: architectural heritage
C1783.definition: Architectural heritage is tangible heritage that is captured in a heritage archive and recreated from captured images as three-dimensional models.

C1784.name: virtual landscape
C1784.definition: A virtual landscape is a recreated virtual setting used in a virtual tour of an island.

C1785.name: file size
C1785.definition: File size is an average megabyte measure of image and video files.

C1786.name: user requirement
C1786.definition: User requirement is an end-user requirement that ensures usability and is specified so it can be converted into plans for system design, implementation, and deployment.

C1787.name: testing
C1787.definition: Testing is checking whether a design meets user requirements; it means usability testing rather than only code testing, although code testing is part of it.

C1788.name: client requirement
C1788.definition: Client requirement is a requirement other than an end-user requirement, which the requirement gathering stage in an interactive system development life cycle concerns.

C1789.name: requirement specification
C1789.definition: Requirement specification is required for system implementation.

C1790.name: system implementation
C1790.definition: System implementation is a process for which a requirement specification is required.

C1791.name: system-centered design
C1791.definition: System-centered design (SCD) is a design approach that makes the system, rather than the user, its main concern, with development driven by the developer's skill and interest, by what can be easily built on the platform, and by available tools rather than user needs and expectations.

C1792.name: programming language
C1792.definition: Programming language is used to develop an application, with Java or JavaScript as examples.

C1793.name: Java
C1793.definition: Java is a programming language that can be used to develop an application for a mobile platform.

C1794.name: JavaScript
C1794.definition: JavaScript is a programming language that can be used to develop an application for a mobile platform.

C1795.name: feasibility stage
C1795.definition: The feasibility stage is the stage related to decisions in requirement gathering about a mobile platform and programming language, rather than to end-user usability requirements.

C1796.name: relational database management system
C1796.definition: A relational database management system (RDBMS) is a tool that can be used for storing information.

C1797.name: my structured query language
C1797.definition: My structured query language is a relational database management system (RDBMS) tool.

C1798.name: design stage
C1798.definition: Design stage is a stage in the interactive system development lifecycle that may involve interface design or code design.

C1799.name: functional requirement
C1799.definition: Functional requirement (FR) is a formally specifiable requirement that specifies a system feature as a black-box function with a well-defined input and output, optionally its purpose, making it easy to convert into code.

C1800.name: non-functional requirement
C1800.definition: Non-functional requirement (NFR) is a system characteristic that cannot be expressed as a function and is typically related to quality attributes of software.

C1801.name: quality attribute
C1801.definition: A quality attribute is an attribute of software that non-functional requirements are typically related to.

C1802.name: usability requirement
C1802.definition: A usability requirement is a type of non-functional requirement that concerns the design and qualities of the user interface that make the interface usable.

C1803.name: performance-related requirement
C1803.definition: Performance-related requirement is a category of non-functional requirements.

C1804.name: operating constraint
C1804.definition: An operating constraint is one of the categories of non-functional requirements.

C1805.name: economic consideration
C1805.definition: Economic consideration is one of the categories of non-functional requirements.

C1806.name: lifecycle requirement
C1806.definition: Lifecycle requirement is one of the categories of non-functional requirements.

C1807.name: interface issue
C1807.definition: Interface issue is a category of non-functional requirements that concerns interface design or usability, covering how a system interfaces with its environment, users, and other systems, including external hardware-software interfaces and user interfaces.

C1808.name: external system interface
C1808.definition: An external system interface is an interface between hardware and software.

C1809.name: phenomenological research method
C1809.definition: Phenomenological research method is the term used to highlight the importance of contextual inquiry in user-centered design.

C1810.name: semi-structured interview
C1810.definition: A semi-structured interview is a process that consists of both interviews and observations.

C1811.name: interview
C1811.definition: Interview is the part of contextual inquiry that may involve asking users questions during observations to clarify behaviors or activities, and it is used to gather usability requirements and identify user groups.

C1812.name: observation
C1812.definition: Observation is a part of contextual inquiry in which people in their natural work settings are observed and data are recorded, enabling designers to learn about the task domain, work culture, and physical and social constraints.

C1813.name: user behavior
C1813.definition: User behavior is the way users perform tasks in a specific work context, and knowing it is essential to ensure usability and gather insight about end-user requirements.

C1814.name: task domain
C1814.definition: Task domain is something about which designers gather knowledge by observing and interacting with users in contextual inquiry to support design decisions.

C1815.name: work culture
C1815.definition: Work culture is one of the things that contextual inquiry enables designers to learn about.

C1816.name: physical constraint
C1816.definition: Physical constraint is one kind of constraint at the workplace.

C1817.name: social constraint
C1817.definition: A social constraint is one of the workplace constraints that designers can learn about through contextual inquiry, which supports design decisions.

C1818.name: design decision
C1818.definition: A design decision is a decision in design that is supported by contextual inquiry, in which observations and interaction with users help designers learn about the task domain, work culture, and physical and social constraints at the workplace.

C1819.name: system development
C1819.definition: System development is an area in which contextual inquiry is important for studying users and enabling design refinement.

C1820.name: design refinement
C1820.definition: Design refinement is something that contextual inquiry enables in system development.

C1821.name: user activities
C1821.definition: User activities are the activities of users that contextual inquiry observes and that a system design must support as features to be usable.

C1822.name: calendar app
C1822.definition: A calendar app is a scheduling application for managerial staff that supports setting meeting dates and reminders and checking day-wise or overall schedules.

C1823.name: user group
C1823.definition: A user group is a category of potential users for which a virtual tour's content and features are tailored.

C1824.name: active mode
C1824.definition: Active mode is a mode of contextual inquiry in which the observer is physically present in the environment where users are doing their tasks.

C1825.name: passive mode
C1825.definition: Passive mode is a mode of contextual inquiry in which no observer is present while users perform tasks, and their activities are recorded or videotaped for later observation, with issues clarified through interaction with the users.

C1826.name: master-apprentice model
C1826.definition: The master-apprentice model is a model for genuine contextual inquiry in which the observer acts as an apprentice or learner, treats users as masters or teachers, and learns how users behave instead of advising or teaching them how to behave, with advice prohibited.

C1827.name: plan stage
C1827.definition: Plan stage is the first stage of contextual inquiry that involves identifying observation goals, gathering task-domain knowledge, planning recording arrangements, identifying the users and date, time, and place of the observation, and scripting and rehearsing the procedure as a helpful practice.

C1828.name: initiate stage
C1828.definition: Initiate stage is a stage of contextual inquiry that involves obtaining all necessary permissions from relevant authorities before observing employees in their workplace and opening communication with end users to remove anxieties that the observation may lead to something bad for them, so that they behave naturally.

C1829.name: execute stage
C1829.definition: The execute stage is a stage of contextual inquiry in which the actual inquiry takes place through performing observations and recording data.

C1830.name: close stage
C1830.definition: Close stage is the fourth stage of contextual inquiry, in which the inquiry is formally closed, ideally by sending thank-you notes or a message of gratitude to users and, possibly, to authorities.

C1831.name: reflect stage
C1831.definition: Reflect stage is the final stage of contextual inquiry in which the observer or experimental team analyzes data collected during the execute stage and identifies design goals.

C1832.name: design goal
C1832.definition: A design goal is a goal that is identified in the reflect stage of contextual inquiry.

C1833.name: affinity diagram method
C1833.definition: Affinity diagram method is a technique used in the reflect stage of contextual inquiry to analyze collected data by generating, displaying, sorting similar ideas into named groups, and drawing the finished diagram to reveal patterns for design recommendations.

C1834.name: design specification
C1834.definition: Design specification is a specification of design goals that follows from finding patterns in collected data from contextual inquiry.

C1835.name: group header
C1835.definition: A group header is a name or identifier assigned to a group in an affinity diagram after the ideas have been sorted, referring to the pattern that binds the ideas within the group.

C1836.name: class note-taking application
C1836.definition: A class note-taking application is an example application in which a design recommendation, such as an erase-content facility for correcting mistakes, states what must be done to make the system usable without specifying implementation.

C1837.name: design guideline
C1837.definition: Design guideline is a statement about an interactive system that says what should or should not be done to make it usable, without saying how to implement it; it can be generic or particular to a system, and is only a starting point to be implemented and tested.

C1838.name: informed design choice
C1838.definition: An informed design choice is a design recommendation or guideline that is produced by analyzing data collected during a contextual inquiry, ensuring that users' needs and expectations are taken into account.

C1839.name: uninformed design choice
C1839.definition: An uninformed design choice is a guideline created without contextual inquiry that does not ensure that users' needs and expectations are taken into account.

C1840.name: reminder setting
C1840.definition: Reminder setting is a header in an affinity diagram that groups observations about users setting reminders.

C1841.name: work scheduling
C1841.definition: Work scheduling is a header in an affinity diagram for grouping contextual inquiry observations about checking deadlines, dates, timetables, and meeting or lecture schedules, later refined into overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling.

C1842.name: overall scheduling
C1842.definition: Overall scheduling is a group header in the finished affinity diagram for a calendar app, created from contextual inquiry observations not related to reminder setting.

C1843.name: day-wise scheduling
C1843.definition: Day-wise scheduling is one of the final group headings in an affinity diagram, produced by refining work scheduling observations.

C1844.name: design principle
C1844.definition: A design principle is a form in which the outcome of contextual inquiry, a usability requirement gathering method, can be utilized.

C1845.name: function
C1845.definition: A function is a well-defined input-output unit that, when invoked with appropriate arguments or parameters, performs a specific task.

C1846.name: functional specification
C1846.definition: Functional specification is a specification of requirements in terms of functions that have well-defined inputs and outputs, making such requirements easier to convert to code.

C1847.name: code
C1847.definition: Code is what functional requirements can be converted into, and implementing a vertical prototype does not necessarily involve writing code.

C1848.name: note-taking application
C1848.definition: The note-taking application is an example in which generic guidelines framed from observations specify what the application should or should not do and observed user behaviors are included in system design.

C1849.name: feedback
C1849.definition: Feedback is information that is provided to users about actions and results or gathered from customers and stakeholders, and used to involve users in design, guide requirements, and guide development changes.

C1850.name: software requirements specification
C1850.definition: Software requirements specification (SRS) is a textual document that specifies all of a system's requirements, both functional and non-functional, including the formal specification of its functional requirements.

C1851.name: requirement hierarchy
C1851.definition: A requirement hierarchy is a hierarchy in which requirements are generally organized in a software requirements specification, with identifiers distinguishing top-level requirements from sub-requirements, each representing a function with a clearly defined input and a clearly defined output.

C1852.name: requirement identifier
C1852.definition: A requirement identifier is an identifier in a software requirements specification hierarchy that represents a function with a clearly defined input, a clearly defined output, and an optional description of what it does.

C1853.name: top-level requirement
C1853.definition: A top-level requirement is a requirement in the hierarchy generally used by a software requirements specification, identified by an identifier such as R1.

C1854.name: sub-requirement
C1854.definition: A sub-requirement is a requirement in a software requirements specification hierarchy that is generally identified by an identifier such as R1.1 under a top-level requirement.

C1855.name: Majuli virtual reality tour
C1855.definition: The Majuli virtual reality tour is an immersive virtual reality case study tour for non-resident students, tourists, and pilgrims, intended to capture and digitally preserve the tangible and intangible heritage of Majuli river island.

C1856.name: field trips
C1856.definition: Field trips are used to gather usability requirements and identify potential user groups for a virtual reality (VR) tour.

C1857.name: students or learners
C1857.definition: Students or learners are one of the potential user groups of the Majuli VR Tour case study, interested in knowing about the island.

C1858.name: tourists
C1858.definition: Tourists are one of the user groups for the Majuli VR Tour, consisting of people interested in exploring tourist spots or other interesting places on the island.

C1859.name: pilgrims
C1859.definition: Pilgrims are one of the potential user groups in the Majuli VR Tour case study and are interested in religious places and practices.

C1860.name: system features
C1860.definition: System features are the features identified in contextual inquiry as needing to be supported for each user group.

C1861.name: design challenge
C1861.definition: A design challenge is one of the key design problems in the Majuli VR Tour case study.

C1862.name: large geographical area
C1862.definition: A large geographical area is a geographical space in a virtual tour for which comprehensive coverage, navigation support, and accurate location information are important to avoid cybersickness and disorientation.

C1863.name: multimodal data
C1863.definition: Multimodal data is collected data used in a virtual reality tour to present a large geographical area, where using all of it may be time consuming and may cause cyber sickness.

C1864.name: data subset restriction
C1864.definition: Data subset restriction is a restriction that allows each user group to access only a subset of the collected data, based on what that group typically does, reducing the expanse of information and the possibility of cyber sickness.

C1865.name: data set
C1865.definition: A data set is the entire data that can be made accessible to all users.

C1866.name: location information
C1866.definition: Location information is information in a virtual reality tour that tells users where they are in the geographical space.

C1867.name: geographical space
C1867.definition: Geographical space is the area in a virtual reality tour in which accurate location information tells users where they are.

C1868.name: location awareness
C1868.definition: Location awareness is a wayfinding feature for ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.

C1869.name: tangible heritage experiences
C1869.definition: Tangible heritage experiences are heritage experiences to be provided along with intangible heritage experiences and combined for a seamless user experience.

C1870.name: intangible heritage experiences
C1870.definition: Intangible heritage experiences are heritage experiences intended to be provided and combined with tangible heritage experiences for a seamless user experience.

C1871.name: interaction aid
C1871.definition: An interaction aid is a virtual reality design aid that enhances user experience by providing navigation support, user-friendly interfaces, and natural interactions that increase presence.

C1872.name: navigation support
C1872.definition: Navigation support is an interaction aid for enhanced user experience, used to cover a large geography.

C1873.name: user-friendly interfaces
C1873.definition: User-friendly interfaces are included in interaction aid for enhanced user experience.

C1874.name: non-interactive software development
C1874.definition: Non-interactive software development is a kind of software development in which code design is the same as code design in the interactive system development lifecycle.

C1875.name: design-prototype-evaluation cycle
C1875.definition: The design-prototype-evaluation cycle is a cycle involved in designing an immersive experience to incorporate user requirements.

C1876.name: interface and interaction design
C1876.definition: Interface and interaction design is the design activity that addresses where or how to start the design process and how to express a design, which means having a design language, so it can be brainstormed and refined.

C1877.name: design process
C1877.definition: Design process is a process in interface and interaction design that can be started from creativity or from guidelines.

C1878.name: design language
C1878.definition: A design language is a specification of a design that expresses it so that it can be brainstormed and refined; there can be different languages for specifying a design.

C1879.name: Ben Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules
C1879.definition: Ben Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules are a set of eight generic design rules, primarily intended for graphical user interfaces, that can be partly or fully applied to other interactive systems, including extended reality (XR) systems.

C1880.name: Donald Norman's seven principles
C1880.definition: Donald Norman's seven principles are generic design guidelines covering broad, high-level aspects of interactive systems, primarily intended for graphical user interfaces but applicable to other domains.

C1881.name: Apple's human interface guidelines
C1881.definition: Apple's human interface guidelines are design guidelines originally developed for Apple's user interfaces.

C1882.name: specific design guideline
C1882.definition: A specific design guideline is a virtual reality-specific guideline for avoiding or minimizing cyber sickness that is typically applicable to virtual reality or immersive systems where immersion is very important, but may not apply to augmented reality systems.

C1883.name: immersive system
C1883.definition: An immersive system is a system in which immersion is very important.

C1884.name: generic design guideline
C1884.definition: Generic design guideline is a guideline applicable to any interactive system, including extended reality systems, although it is mostly, not fully, applicable to such systems.

C1885.name: generic design rule
C1885.definition: A generic design rule is a design rule developed primarily for graphical user interfaces that can be partly or fully applicable to other types of interfaces, including extended reality systems.

C1886.name: consistency
C1886.definition: Consistency is a rule of system and interface design that calls for internal consistency and external or environmental consistency.

C1887.name: internal consistency
C1887.definition: Internal consistency is a type of consistency in system design in which the same elements and interactions are used for the same task across different parts of a design and different usage instances, rather than separate objects, elements, or interactions.

C1888.name: external consistency
C1888.definition: External consistency is a type of consistency in system design in which the elements and interactions in a virtual world closely match the user's real-world experience and knowledge, so that real-world knowledge transfers to the virtual world.

C1889.name: Shneiderman's second golden rule
C1889.definition: Shneiderman's second golden rule is the rule that a system should be designed for universal usability by providing facilities for all user categories and supporting different user categories rather than only specific user categories.

C1890.name: universal usability
C1890.definition: Universal usability is a design rule requiring a system to provide facilities for all user categories and to support different user categories rather than only specific user categories.

C1891.name: Control plus S
C1891.definition: Control plus S is a hotkey that is faster than menu-based options.

C1892.name: recognition
C1892.definition: Recognition is a computer vision operation, alongside object detection and tracking.

C1893.name: recall
C1893.definition: Recall is a skilled task, as opposed to recognition, in which users may need to remember options rather than recognize them.

C1894.name: usable design
C1894.definition: Usable design is a set of design rules whose third rule is to provide informative feedback to users for whatever action they perform.

C1895.name: informative feedback
C1895.definition: Informative feedback is feedback that, for user actions, tells the user what the system is doing, how much of a task is complete, or whether the action was completed successfully.

C1896.name: progress bar
C1896.definition: A progress bar is informative feedback that sometimes appears during a task, shows the percentage of the task completed, and gives the user a sense of how much longer to wait.

C1897.name: save icon
C1897.definition: A save icon is used to indicate, by changing color after a save operation, that the save operation is done successfully.

C1898.name: dialogue
C1898.definition: Dialogue is used to yield closure by organizing task execution into beginning, middle, and end parts and providing feedback at the end of each group.

C1899.name: closure
C1899.definition: Closure is a result that is yielded by designing dialogues to organize task execution into beginning, middle, and end parts and providing feedback at the end of each group, so the user feels the task is started, executed, and completed.

C1900.name: error prevention
C1900.definition: Error prevention is a system design rule in which the design helps users prevent errors by aiming to keep error rates low, because user errors cannot be completely eliminated.

C1901.name: error handling
C1901.definition: Error handling is a system design practice that, when an error occurs, gives simple, easy-to-understand information rather than complicated error messages.

C1902.name: user error
C1902.definition: User error is a wrong action that a user may accidentally choose.

C1903.name: error rate
C1903.definition: Error rate is the rate of user errors that a system design should aim to keep low.

C1904.name: reversal of actions
C1904.definition: Reversal of actions is a system design rule that permits users to return from an erroneous situation, ideally by keeping a reversal option available, with undo and redo facilities primarily meant to permit it.

C1905.name: reversal option
C1905.definition: A reversal option is a design option kept available so that users can return from an erroneous situation.

C1906.name: undo
C1906.definition: Undo is a facility primarily meant to permit easy reversal of actions.

C1907.name: redo
C1907.definition: Redo is a facility that is primarily meant to permit easy reversal of actions.

C1908.name: keeping users in control
C1908.definition: Keeping users in control is a usability rule that requires lay users to feel in control, perceive that their interaction changes the system state, and receive feedback on their actions and results.

C1909.name: human memory
C1909.definition: Human memory is, in a broad sense, the combination of short-term and long-term memory, where short-term memory is a note-like non-permanent store used to bring information from long-term memory to aid day-to-day activities.

C1910.name: short-term memory
C1910.definition: Short-term memory is a note-like non-permanent store that holds five to nine chunks of information at a time and is used to bring information from long-term memory to aid day-to-day activities.

C1911.name: seven plus or minus two rule
C1911.definition: Seven plus or minus two rule is a psychological finding that states the short-term memory limit is five to nine chunks of information at a time.

C1912.name: short-term memory limit
C1912.definition: Short-term memory limit is the limit on the number of chunks of information that short-term memory can hold at a time, five to nine chunks.

C1913.name: chunk of information
C1913.definition: A chunk of information is a unit of information that can be a letter, a word, a whole sentence, or a whole concept, depending on the application.

C1914.name: reducing short-term memory load
C1914.definition: Reducing short-term memory load is a usability rule that requires keeping the information needed to operate an interface or perform an interaction between five and nine chunks, and not forcing users to remember more than nine.

C1915.name: short-term memory load
C1915.definition: Short-term memory load is a usability rule that requires keeping the information needed to operate an interface or perform an interaction between five and nine chunks.

C1916.name: object interaction
C1916.definition: Object interaction is a kind of interaction in immersive virtual environments that involves selecting one or more virtual objects in the environment and manipulating a selected object to change its properties.

C1917.name: navigation
C1917.definition: Navigation is an interaction in an immersive virtual world that moves the user from one point to another by changing the user's viewpoint, mostly without object interaction, and has two components: locomotion and wayfinding.

C1918.name: interaction for system control
C1918.definition: Interaction for system control is an interaction technique in immersive environments that issues commands to change system state, mode, or system-related settings.

C1919.name: object manipulation
C1919.definition: Object manipulation is an interaction technique in immersive environments that, typically after selection, modifies a virtual object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, or behavior.

C1920.name: navigation technique
C1920.definition: A navigation technique is an interaction technique for moving from one point to another in a virtual world with a change in viewpoint, mostly without object interaction; it is broadly categorized as walking-based, steering-based, selection-based, or manipulation-based.

C1921.name: system control
C1921.definition: System control is a mostly regular type of interaction in immersive experiences that uses familiar computer-system techniques to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus.

C1922.name: object selection technique
C1922.definition: An object selection technique is a technique in a virtual world for selecting objects, and its kinds include hand, pointing-based, image plane, volume-based, and bimanual selection.

C1923.name: selection performance
C1923.definition: Selection performance is the performance of a user while accomplishing an object selection task in a virtual experience, and a suitable object selection technique is chosen so that it is maximized.

C1924.name: selection task
C1924.definition: A selection task is a task in a virtual experience, and user performance while accomplishing the selection task is influenced by variables such as the distance, direction, and size of the object to be selected, object density, and number of targets.

C1925.name: density
C1925.definition: Density is one of the parameters that influence user performance in a virtual object selection task, including the density of objects around the target object.

C1926.name: target object
C1926.definition: A target object is an object to be selected in an object selection task in a virtual experience.

C1927.name: number of targets
C1927.definition: The number of targets is a variable used to determine the kind of object selection technique that is suitable in a virtual experience, so that selection performance is maximized.

C1928.name: target occlusion
C1928.definition: Target occlusion is the partial or full occlusion of a target by other surrounding objects, which can make locating and selecting the target challenging and may require specialized techniques.

C1929.name: selection with the hand
C1929.definition: Selection with the hand is one of the object selection techniques in a virtual world.

C1930.name: pointing-based selection
C1930.definition: Pointing-based selection is an object selection technique in a virtual world in which a user points a visible virtual ray from a hand, head, or eye to select the first object intersected by that ray.

C1931.name: image plane selection
C1931.definition: Image plane selection is a two-dimensional selection technique in which the user selects on a view plane that contains the object as viewed from a distance and holds one or two hands or fingers between the eye and the object and provides a signal such as a gesture or hand movement when the object lines up.

C1932.name: volumetric selection
C1932.definition: Volumetric selection is an object selection technique in a virtual world that extends image plane selection by letting the user select a three-dimensional region, such as a box, sphere, or cone, and select the objects within it.

C1933.name: bimanual selection
C1933.definition: Bimanual selection is one of the object selection techniques in a virtual world.

C1934.name: hand selection technique
C1934.definition: Hand selection technique is a technique that selects virtual objects in a virtual world by having the user directly reach out to virtually touch an object and trigger a grab, conventionally using one hand.

C1935.name: grab
C1935.definition: Grab is part of a hand selection technique that selects virtual objects in a virtual world by having the user directly reach out to virtually touch the object.

C1936.name: go-go technique
C1936.definition: The go-go technique is a virtual hand selection technique for distant virtual objects that uses one-to-one mapping when the target is close, allows the user to change virtual arm and hand length interactively, and, as distance increases, maps smaller physical hand movements to larger and faster virtual hand movements, possibly exponentially, so distant objects can be reached quickly.

C1937.name: prism technique
C1937.definition: Prism technique is a travel technique for hand selection of virtual objects that applies scaled-down motion to the virtual hand when the user's physical hand moves below a specified speed, and keeps the virtual hand still when the hand velocity is below a minimum velocity.

C1938.name: intent-driven selection
C1938.definition: Intent-driven selection is a grabbing hand selection technique in which a user moves a virtual hand toward an object and either positions virtual fingers or uses their posture around it to indicate the confidence level in selecting it, typically using proximity spheres that encompass multiple objects and reduce in size to refine the selection to a specific object.

C1939.name: one-to-one mapping
C1939.definition: One-to-one mapping is a mapping of a physical hand's motion and orientation to a virtual hand, tying the virtual hand to the physical hand and allowing natural hand movements.

C1940.name: virtual arm length
C1940.definition: Virtual arm length is the length of the virtual hand.

C1941.name: hand velocity
C1941.definition: Hand velocity is the speed of the user's physical hand, used to decide when the virtual hand remains still in the prism technique.

C1942.name: proximity sphere
C1942.definition: A proximity sphere is a selection area used by intent-driven selection techniques that encompasses multiple objects at a larger distance and progressively reduces in size, depending on hand or finger postures, as the user moves closer, refining the selection to a specific object.

C1943.name: grabbing technique
C1943.definition: Grabbing technique is a hand selection technique such as intent-driven selection.

C1944.name: virtual ray
C1944.definition: Virtual ray is a short line segment or infinite line attached to a virtual hand, head, or eye that a user extends in pointing-based selection to point at objects and select the first intersected object.

C1945.name: hand pointing
C1945.definition: Hand pointing is a form of pointing for pointing-based selection that is done with a hand or a handheld input device, and it can trigger selection in methods that combine it with gaze pointing.

C1946.name: head pointing
C1946.definition: Head pointing is pointing for pointing-based selection in which a head-mounted display extends a ray from the head position and moves it with head movement without using the hand.

C1947.name: eye-gaze pointing
C1947.definition: Eye-gaze pointing is a pointing method for pointing-based selection that uses an eye tracker.

C1948.name: eye tracker
C1948.definition: An eye tracker is used for eye-gaze pointing for pointing-based selection.

C1949.name: ray casting
C1949.definition: Ray casting is the most basic pointing-based selection method in which the user points at objects with a virtual ray.

C1950.name: bend cast
C1950.definition: Bend cast is an improvement over basic ray casting in which the system bends the ray toward the closest selectable object, detected by calculating the point-line distance from each selectable object, so the user need not point precisely; a circular arc can provide visual feedback for the bending.

C1951.name: selectable object
C1951.definition: A selectable object is an object in bend cast whose point-line distance from a ray is calculated to detect the closest object.

C1952.name: point-line distance
C1952.definition: Point-line distance is a distance calculated from each selectable object to detect the closest selectable object in bend cast.

C1953.name: depth ray
