C1953.definition: Depth ray is an improved ray-casting technique that uses a user-controlled depth marker, positioned by moving the hand forward or backward, to disambiguate multiple intersected objects and select the object intersected by the pointing vector and closest to the marker.

C1954.name: depth marker
C1954.definition: A depth marker is a user-controlled marker, positioned by moving the hand forward or backward, that disambiguates multiple intersected objects and selects the object intersected by the pointing vector and closest to the marker.

C1955.name: two-dimensional
C1955.definition: Two-dimensional (2D) is used to describe selection techniques, image planes, and games or interactive content.

C1956.name: head crusher technique
C1956.definition: Head crusher technique is an image plane selection technique in which the user positions the thumb and forefinger so that they surround or enclose the desired object in the two-dimensional image plane.

C1957.name: image plane
C1957.definition: Image plane is a two-dimensional image in which a user positions fingers or hands to surround or enclose an object.

C1958.name: sticky finger technique
C1958.definition: Sticky finger technique is an image plane selection technique in which the object underneath the user's finger is selected.

C1959.name: lifting palm technique
C1959.definition: The lifting palm technique is an image plane selection technique in which a user selects an object by flattening an outstretched hand and positioning the palm below the object as if trying to lift it with the palm.

C1960.name: framing hands technique
C1960.definition: The framing hands technique is an image plane selection technique in which the user positions hands to form the two corners of a frame in a two-dimensional image surrounding an object.

C1961.name: box
C1961.definition: A box is a three-dimensional region in volumetric selection, usually a cube but possibly a rectangular parallelepiped, that a user positions, orients, and progressively reduces to select objects in virtual space.

C1962.name: cube
C1962.definition: A cube is a primitive object type that can be created directly in Unity and can be a three-dimensional region used in volumetric selection in virtual space.

C1963.name: sphere
C1963.definition: A sphere is one of the possible 3D regions for volumetric selection of objects and a primitive object type that can be created in Unity.

C1964.name: cone casting flashlight technique
C1964.definition: The cone casting flashlight technique is a volumetric selection technique that extends ray casting by casting a cone instead of a ray to a distance and selecting objects within the cone, so it can select multiple objects, though selecting smaller or tightly grouped objects may be difficult.

C1965.name: sphere casting flashlight technique
C1965.definition: The sphere casting flashlight technique is a volumetric selection technique that casts a sphere onto the nearest intersected surface and selects the objects found within that sphere.

C1966.name: two-handed box selection technique
C1966.definition: Two-handed box selection technique is a bimanual volumetric selection technique that uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box, usually a cube but possibly a rectangular parallelepiped, and progressively reduces it to select a specified region of 3D space.

C1967.name: bimanual
C1967.definition: Bimanual is a kind of volumetric selection technique in which the user uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box to select a region of three-dimensional space.

C1968.name: rectangular parallelepiped
C1968.definition: A rectangular parallelepiped is a possible shape of the box used in a two-handed box selection technique for selecting a region of three-dimensional space.

C1969.name: scale
C1969.definition: Scale is one of an object's properties; in a game object, its transform stores scale with position and rotation, and scale can be modified during object manipulation.

C1970.name: texture
C1970.definition: Texture is a stored bitmap image that is applied over a mesh surface to assign colors to pixels and that can represent other aspects of a material's surface, such as reflectivity and roughness.

C1971.name: behavior
C1971.definition: Behavior is one of the properties of an object that can be modified during object manipulation.

C1972.name: manipulation technique
C1972.definition: Manipulation technique is a technique that includes hand manipulation, indirect manipulation, bimanual manipulation, and integrated hybrid manipulation.

C1973.name: hand manipulation
C1973.definition: Hand manipulation is a manipulation technique that uses a virtual hand to manipulate objects and is implemented using smart gloves, gesture-based manipulation, or controller-based interaction; it is the most intuitive way of manipulating objects.

C1974.name: indirect manipulation
C1974.definition: Indirect manipulation is a manipulation technique sometimes used for virtual objects in which the user does not directly manipulate the virtual object with the physical hand, but manipulates other objects mapped to the virtual object, and the mapped objects manipulate the virtual object.

C1975.name: bimanual manipulation
C1975.definition: Bimanual manipulation is a manipulation technique.

C1976.name: integrated hybrid manipulation
C1976.definition: Integrated hybrid manipulation is one of the manipulation techniques.

C1977.name: hand selection
C1977.definition: Hand selection is what precedes hand manipulation.

C1978.name: gesture-based manipulation
C1978.definition: Gesture-based manipulation is a way of implementing hand manipulation, which follows hand selection and is used to manipulate objects.

C1979.name: computational power
C1979.definition: Computational power is required for hand manipulation, which needs somewhat more of it or specialized devices that may be relatively costly.

C1980.name: three-dimensional widget
C1980.definition: A three-dimensional widget is a simple indirect manipulation technique that places controls directly in a 3D scene with virtual objects, so manipulating a widget manipulates its associated object; each widget is typically responsible for only a small set of manipulation degrees of freedom.

C1981.name: indirect proxy
C1981.definition: Indirect proxy is an indirect manipulation technique that lets the user manipulate a local proxy, such as a physical proxy prop, so that moving it moves the linked virtual object in the virtual world.

C1982.name: local proxy
C1982.definition: A local proxy is a proxy that a user manipulates, such as a physical proxy prop linked to a neurological data set, so that moving the local proxy moves a linked virtual object in a virtual world.

C1983.name: physical proxy prop
C1983.definition: A physical proxy prop is a local proxy in an indirect manipulation technique, linked to a neurological data set, so moving it moves a linked virtual object in a virtual world.

C1984.name: neurological data set
C1984.definition: A neurological data set is a data set linked to a physical proxy prop that is used as a local proxy in an indirect manipulation technique.

C1985.name: world in miniature
C1985.definition: World in miniature (WIM) is an indirect proxy that provides a miniature handheld model of a virtual environment, representing all objects in the virtual world. Manipulating a model object manipulates the corresponding virtual object, even if it is outside the user's reach; moving certain model objects can also change the virtual viewpoint.

C1986.name: miniature model
C1986.definition: Miniature model is a handheld model of a virtual environment that represents all objects in the environment, so manipulating an object in the miniature model manipulates the corresponding object in the virtual environment.

C1987.name: bimanual manipulation technique
C1987.definition: A bimanual manipulation technique is a technique for manipulating objects with both hands, in which hand movement is synchronous, with both hands moving together, or asynchronous, where the hands do not need to move simultaneously.

C1988.name: synchronous
C1988.definition: Synchronous is a hand movement in a bimanual manipulation technique in which both hands move together.

C1989.name: asynchronous
C1989.definition: Asynchronous is a kind of hand movement in a bimanual manipulation technique in which both hands do not need to move simultaneously.

C1990.name: spindle technique
C1990.definition: Spindle technique is a symmetric synchronous bimanual manipulation technique that uses two handheld controllers with six degrees of freedom, placed symmetrically on both sides of an imaginary axis and moved simultaneously, to define a virtual spindle for moving or rotating a virtual world object.

C1991.name: imaginary axis
C1991.definition: An imaginary axis is an axis used in bimanual manipulation techniques, on both sides of which two handheld controllers may be placed symmetrically.

C1992.name: virtual spindle
C1992.definition: A virtual spindle is a virtual object defined by two handheld controllers with six degrees of freedom, placed symmetrically on both sides of an imaginary axis and moved simultaneously.

C1993.name: virtual world object
C1993.definition: Virtual world object is an object in a virtual world that, in the spindle technique, can be moved and rotated simultaneously by moving both hands in unison.

C1994.name: spindle plus wheel
C1994.definition: Spindle plus wheel is an asymmetric but synchronous technique that extends the spindle technique by moving both hands together without requiring them to be symmetrically placed around the sides of an imaginary axis.

C1995.name: integrated hybrid manipulation technique
C1995.definition: An integrated hybrid manipulation technique is a technique that automatically switches from selection to manipulation after selection, without an explicit user signal, and switches back to selection mode after manipulation, so selection and manipulation are not performed separately.

C1996.name: Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting
C1996.definition: Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER) is an integrated hybrid manipulation technique in which the user selects an object by ray casting, the virtual hand automatically moves to and attaches to the object instead of the ray attaching, and hand manipulation changes the object’s position and orientation until the user ends it with a trigger or gesture.

C1997.name: wayfinding
C1997.definition: Wayfinding is the component of navigation, other than locomotion or travel, that provides location awareness, ascertains a path to a destination, transfers spatial knowledge to the real world, and builds a mental model of the environment.

C1998.name: exploration
C1998.definition: Exploration is a kind of travel in navigation that has no explicit goal or target point, where the user moves around to see, learn, or explore.

C1999.name: search
C1999.definition: Search is a way of traveling in navigation that involves moving to a specified target location.

C2000.name: maneuvering
C2000.definition: Maneuvering is a type of travel in navigation that comprises short, precise movements that change the viewpoint or break a path into small segments to reach a destination.

C2001.name: walking-based locomotion
C2001.definition: Walking-based locomotion is a locomotion technique for traveling in a virtual environment in which physical walking or movement in the physical world is mapped to corresponding movement in the virtual environment, and it is broadly divided into three categories: full gait techniques, partial gait techniques, and gait negation techniques.

C2002.name: selection-based locomotion
C2002.definition: Selection-based locomotion is a category of locomotion technique in which the user selects where to go rather than continuously specifying how to move there by steering or looking. Its two types are target selection-based locomotion and route planning-based locomotion; route planning-based locomotion has the user select a route to the target rather than only the endpoint.

C2003.name: manipulation-based locomotion
C2003.definition: Manipulation-based locomotion is a type of locomotion technique in which the user's position, orientation, or scale is manipulated using gestures that control either the virtual viewpoint or the virtual world.

C2004.name: full gait technique
C2004.definition: Full gait technique is a walking-based locomotion technique that is the most natural way to travel and in which the user's actual real-world walking, restricted within a specified physical limit, is translated into any amount of virtual movement in a potentially infinite virtual space, creating a mismatch between physical and virtual movement.

C2005.name: partial gait technique
C2005.definition: A partial gait technique is a walking-based locomotion technique in which the user walks in place without changing position, requiring specialized devices to map the pattern of walking in a single place to different types of walking in the virtual space.

C2006.name: gait negation technique
C2006.definition: A gait negation technique is a walking-based virtual locomotion technique that requires a specialized setup to cancel the user's lateral movements and keep the user's physical position fixed before the movement is mapped to virtual navigation.

C2007.name: virtual navigation
C2007.definition: Virtual navigation is the movement in a virtual space produced by translating or mapping a user's physical movement.

C2008.name: immersive hardware
C2008.definition: Immersive hardware is hardware that is used with specialized devices to provide input in partial gait techniques.

C2009.name: active walking interface
C2009.definition: An active walking interface is a specialized input device that may be used in partial gait techniques that map a user's pattern of walking in a single place to different types of walking in virtual space.

C2010.name: pressure mat
C2010.definition: A pressure mat is an active walking interface that can be used in partial gait techniques to provide input.

C2011.name: pressure sensor
C2011.definition: A pressure sensor is one of the active walking interfaces that may be used in partial gait techniques, in addition to other immersive hardware, to provide input and map a user's pattern of walking in a single place to different types of walking in the virtual space.

C2012.name: linear treadmill
C2012.definition: A linear treadmill is a specialized setup used in gait negation techniques.

C2013.name: motorized floor tile
C2013.definition: Motorized floor tile is one of the specialized setups used in gait negation techniques.

C2014.name: human-sized hamster ball
C2014.definition: A human-sized hamster ball is one of the specialized setups used in gait negation techniques.

C2015.name: friction-free platform
C2015.definition: A friction-free platform is a specialized setup used in gait negation techniques.

C2016.name: steering-based navigation
C2016.definition: Steering-based navigation is a navigation category in which direction and speed are continuously controlled while the user moves from one point to another. Its two types are spatial steering-based navigation, controlled by the user's body parts, and physical steering-based navigation, controlled by vehicular props or additional hardware.

C2017.name: spatial steering-based navigation
C2017.definition: Spatial steering-based navigation is a type of steering-based navigation that is controlled using the user's body parts. It can be gaze-directed, hand-directed, or body-leaning directed.

C2018.name: physical steering-based navigation
C2018.definition: Physical steering-based navigation is a type of steering-based navigation that uses physical setups, vehicular props, or additional hardware, in which physically moving the steering controls causes travel in the virtual world.

C2019.name: gaze-directed
C2019.definition: Gaze-directed is a form of spatial steering-based navigation in which looking at a target location moves the user continuously in the direction of looking.

C2020.name: hand-directed
C2020.definition: Hand-directed is a form of spatial steering-based navigation in which hand gestures determine the direction of travel.

C2021.name: body-leaning directed
C2021.definition: Body-leaning directed is a kind of spatial steering-based navigation in which leaning the body toward a movement direction is mapped to corresponding travel.

C2022.name: bike locomotion platform
C2022.definition: Bike locomotion platform is a physical setup or separate hardware used in physical steering-based navigation.

C2023.name: virtual reality simulator
C2023.definition: A virtual reality simulator is separate hardware involved in physical steering-based navigation, in which physically moving the steering controls results in travel in the virtual world.

C2024.name: target selection-based locomotion
C2024.definition: Target selection-based locomotion is a type of selection-based locomotion in which the user selects a destination or target, and the virtual viewpoint changes so that the user feels moved to that target.

C2025.name: route planning-based locomotion
C2025.definition: Route planning-based locomotion is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the user selects a route to the target rather than only the endpoint, moving along that route through changing viewpoints.

C2026.name: map dragging
C2026.definition: Map dragging is a target selection-based locomotion technique in which the user fixes a location to move there instantly.

C2027.name: jumper technique
C2027.definition: The jumper technique is a target selection-based locomotion technique in cave-type systems.

C2028.name: cave-type systems
C2028.definition: Cave-type systems are systems in which the jumper technique is used for target selection-based locomotion.

C2029.name: homer technique
C2029.definition: The homer technique is a technique that can be used, in combination with the go-go technique and the world in miniature metaphor, to implement manipulation-based locomotion.

C2030.name: path
C2030.definition: Path is a sequence of vertices or points of interest in a virtual world or graph that is followed to reach destinations and optimized for travel time and importance.

C2031.name: destination
C2031.definition: A destination is a desired location that a wayfinding path leads to or that a selected route in virtual vehicle travel moves the user to.

C2032.name: spatial knowledge
C2032.definition: Spatial knowledge is the essential knowledge base of a wayfinding mental model, comprising landmark knowledge of the surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment.

C2033.name: environment design
C2033.definition: Environment design is the design of an environment whose objective is to make it easier for the user to build a mental map.

C2034.name: wayfinding mental model
C2034.definition: A wayfinding mental model is a mental model whose essential knowledge base is spatial knowledge, consisting of landmark knowledge of the surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment.

C2035.name: landmark knowledge
C2035.definition: Landmark knowledge is part of the spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model, covering the surroundings and other places.

C2036.name: procedural knowledge
C2036.definition: Procedural knowledge is knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path.

C2037.name: topological knowledge
C2037.definition: Topological knowledge is the spatial knowledge of the overall environment in a wayfinding mental model.

C2038.name: knowledge base
C2038.definition: A knowledge base is the essential collection of spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model, formed by landmark knowledge of surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment.

C2039.name: wayfinding support
C2039.definition: Wayfinding support is essential support in complex virtual environments that helps users find targets by using landmarks, maps, colored paths, breadcrumb trails, or direction indicators, so travel techniques can be used effectively.

C2040.name: locomotion or travel support
C2040.definition: Locomotion or travel support is support in a virtual environment that, by itself, is not sufficient for wayfinding.

C2041.name: landmark support
C2041.definition: Landmark support is wayfinding support that uses obvious, distinct, non-mobile objects positioned in a given place, and a good landmark should be clearly visible from several different locations or viewpoints.

C2042.name: landmark
C2042.definition: A landmark is an obvious, distinct, non-mobile object positioned in a given place that supports wayfinding, and a good landmark should be clearly visible from several different locations or viewpoints.

C2043.name: map support
C2043.definition: Map support is wayfinding support that can provide maps of the virtual space or place.

C2044.name: world in miniature display
C2044.definition: A world in miniature display is a display for wayfinding that can show the entire virtual world with objects at different points, the current position of the user, and different routes to different points.

C2045.name: path following support
C2045.definition: Path following support is a wayfinding support that can denote multiple paths through a single space by colors, so the user knows that there are different paths to reach a destination.

C2046.name: breadcrumb support
C2046.definition: Breadcrumb support is support for wayfinding that leaves a trail of markers along the path followed by predecessors, so users can recognize that a path has already been explored, avoid getting lost, and choose another path or destination to save time.

C2047.name: compass
C2047.definition: A compass is a direction indicator that can support wayfinding by specifying directions in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space.

C2048.name: direction indicator
C2048.definition: A direction indicator is used to support wayfinding by specifying directions in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space.

C2049.name: two-dimensional space
C2049.definition: Two-dimensional space is a space in which a compass or direction indicator can specify directions to support wayfinding.

C2050.name: command
C2050.definition: A command is a regular operation in software use that changes system state or mode, such as launching an application, changing system settings, or opening a file.

C2051.name: system mode
C2051.definition: System mode is a mode of a system that can be changed by commands issued through interaction for system control.

C2052.name: physical controller
C2052.definition: A physical controller is one of the interactive methods for system control, for example a button or switch.

C2053.name: switch
C2053.definition: A switch is a physical controller used in interactive methods for system control.

C2054.name: graphical menu
C2054.definition: A graphical menu is an adapted two-dimensional menu suitable for three-dimensional massive environments, used as an interactive method for system control.

C2055.name: two-dimensional menu
C2055.definition: A two-dimensional menu is one of the interactive methods for system control, adapted to be suitable for three-dimensional massive environments.

C2056.name: one degree of freedom menu
C2056.definition: One degree of freedom menu is an interactive method for system control.

C2057.name: gesture command
C2057.definition: Gesture command is one of the interactive methods for system control, with examples including mimic gestures, symbolic gestures, sweeping gestures, sign language, speech-corrected hand gestures, and whole-body interactions.

C2058.name: mimic gesture
C2058.definition: A mimic gesture is a gesture command that is used as an interactive method for system control.

C2059.name: symbolic gesture
C2059.definition: A symbolic gesture is a gesture command used as an interactive method for system control.

C2060.name: sweeping gesture
C2060.definition: Sweeping gesture is a gesture command used as an interactive method for system control.

C2061.name: sign language
C2061.definition: Sign language is one of the gesture commands used as an interactive method for system control.

C2062.name: speech-corrected hand gesture
C2062.definition: Speech-corrected hand gesture is a gesture command used as an interactive method for system control.

C2063.name: whole-body interaction
C2063.definition: Whole-body interaction is a gesture command, one of the interactive methods for system control.

C2064.name: tool
C2064.definition: A tool is one of the interactive methods for system control.

C2065.name: physical tool
C2065.definition: A physical tool is a tool that is an interactive method for system control.

C2066.name: virtual tool
C2066.definition: A virtual tool is a tool included among interactive methods for system control.

C2067.name: multimodal interaction technique
C2067.definition: A multimodal interaction technique is an interactive method for system control that combines multiple techniques.

C2068.name: user experience design
C2068.definition: User experience design is a design consideration for an experience, and its first stage is to identify the users so that the experience can be designed accordingly.

C2069.name: minimap
C2069.definition: A minimap is a local world-in-miniature map of a specific place, distinct from a global map, that shows the arrangement of 360-degree images as white dots, with the current image highlighted green, to support local orientation and wayfinding.

C2070.name: notification system
C2070.definition: A notification system is a design element incorporated into a virtual reality tour in response to user feedback and interaction.

C2071.name: user controls
C2071.definition: User controls are incorporated design elements for a virtual reality tour, added in response to user feedback and interaction with users.

C2072.name: information point
C2072.definition: An information point is a geographically spread place in a virtual tour that reveals related information for interactive exploration and contains many points of interest.

C2073.name: curved screen
C2073.definition: A curved screen is a screen used in an immersive setting at the start of a virtual tour to show introductory and tutorial videos.

C2074.name: introductory video
C2074.definition: An introductory video is a video shown at the starting point of a virtual tour.

C2075.name: tutorial video
C2075.definition: A tutorial video is a video that explains to users how to control and use a system.

C2076.name: boat ride experience
C2076.definition: Boat ride experience is the opening part of a virtual tour that uses a 360-degree boat ride video to give the user the feeling of being transported by boat from one river bank to the other.

C2077.name: 360-degree boat ride video
C2077.definition: A 360-degree boat ride video is a video used in a boat ride experience at the very start of a virtual tour to give the user the feeling of being transported by boat from one bank of a river to the other.

C2078.name: icon
C2078.definition: An icon is an interface object that can be used to indicate user categories or provide information.

C2079.name: preprocessing
C2079.definition: Preprocessing is a process for collected images and videos that improves their visual appearance and the user's quality of experience by using high-resolution content and removing unwanted elements.

C2080.name: quality of experience
C2080.definition: Quality of experience is an aspect of the user's experience that is improved by realistic visual appearance and properly assigned colors, but reduced by visual distortion.

C2081.name: high-resolution content
C2081.definition: High-resolution content is used in preprocessing collected images and videos to improve visual appearance and the user's quality of experience.

C2082.name: 360-degree camera
C2082.definition: A 360-degree camera is a camera whose tripod or shadow may be an unwanted element in collected images and videos.

C2083.name: image editing tool
C2083.definition: An image editing tool is a tool used to edit images and videos for uniform illumination.

C2084.name: ambient sound
C2084.definition: Ambient sound is a type of sound used in a virtual reality tour to enhance realism and create an authentic ambience depending on the place visited.

C2085.name: tablet interface
C2085.definition: Tablet interface is a virtual interface that serves as the main interface in a virtual tour system, providing navigation tools, a video player, and access to information content, with a design inspired by real-world tablet use.

C2086.name: navigation tool
C2086.definition: A navigation tool is a tool provided by a virtual tablet interface, such as a left-side island map presented as a world in miniature and buttons for opening a mini map.

C2087.name: video player
C2087.definition: A video player is a part of a virtual tablet interface in a virtual tour that lets users view cultural or ecological videos relevant to their current location, including 360-degree, drone, or 2D videos, with a volume controller and other controls.

C2088.name: information content
C2088.definition: Information content is content that users access through info elements on the virtual tablet interface.

C2089.name: island map
C2089.definition: An island map is a world-in-miniature map that shows the entire island or a specific place on it to provide location awareness, wayfinding, and orientation awareness.

C2090.name: volume controller
C2090.definition: A volume controller is one of the controls in a video player in a virtual tablet interface.

C2091.name: control
C2091.definition: Control is a part of a video player in a virtual tablet interface.

C2092.name: information element
C2092.definition: An information element is used by a virtual tablet interface to provide access to information content.

C2093.name: local orientation
C2093.definition: Local orientation is a sense of belonging to a specific place that a minimap can give a user.

C2094.name: navigation arrow
C2094.definition: A navigation arrow is an arrow shown to a user that indicates which way to move and, when selected, moves the user in that direction from one 360-degree image to another, guiding the user toward points of interest and preventing random movement.

C2095.name: notification
C2095.definition: Notification is an informative alert or textual description in a virtual tour that tells users whether a cultural video or activity is available at a location, shown through an information icon or tablet interface.

C2096.name: cultural video
C2096.definition: A cultural video is a video in a virtual reality tour that, when available at a location, is indicated by a tablet notification and can be played on the tablet interface.

C2097.name: information icon
C2097.definition: An information icon is an icon in a virtual tour that becomes active at a point of interest and, when selected, provides further details about that place, mostly as textual information, including whether a cultural video is available.

C2098.name: dual maps
C2098.definition: Dual maps are two maps used by a system for location awareness: a global world-in-miniature map of the entire island on a tablet interface and a local minimap on a local interface, reducing clutter and providing clear navigation support.

C2099.name: local interface
C2099.definition: A local interface is an interface on which a local minimap is shown for location awareness and clear navigation support.

C2100.name: orientation awareness
C2100.definition: Orientation awareness is the dynamic spatial awareness of which direction to move, helping users wayfind and create a mental map.

C2101.name: island tour
C2101.definition: An island tour is a tour in which each place is designed using a series of 360-degree images, so moving from one point to another is moving from one image to another.

C2102.name: view interpolation
C2102.definition: View interpolation is a method that blurs the boundaries between two 360-degree images to ensure a smooth visual transition and prevent sudden movement or jerks.

C2103.name: virtual vehicle metaphor
C2103.definition: A virtual vehicle metaphor is a three-dimensional (3D) model of a vehicle that facilitates long-distance travel within a tour.

C2104.name: walking-based technique
C2104.definition: Walking-based technique is a virtual locomotion technique that involves physical walking to move from one point to another in a virtual reality tour.

C2105.name: virtual vehicle travel technique
C2105.definition: The virtual vehicle travel technique is a selection-based locomotion technique in which a pre-planned route is chosen by selecting a destination, not by target selection or instantaneous movement; it gives the user a seated viewpoint inside a vehicle, changes surrounding scenes as the vehicle moves to create motion, and uses ray casting interactions for direction and destination.

C2106.name: seated viewpoint
C2106.definition: Seated viewpoint is a viewpoint inside a virtual vehicle that the virtual vehicle travel technique gives the user.

C2107.name: selection-based locomotion technique
C2107.definition: Selection-based locomotion technique is a type of locomotion technique.

C2108.name: route selection
C2108.definition: Route selection is a selection-based locomotion technique, not target selection or instantaneous movement, in which the user selects a destination to select a pre-planned route.

C2109.name: target selection
C2109.definition: Target selection is a selection-based locomotion technique distinct from route selection.

C2110.name: instantaneous movement
C2110.definition: Instantaneous movement is a selection-based locomotion technique other than route selection and target selection.

C2111.name: virtual tour system
C2111.definition: A virtual tour system is a virtual-world system that provides a tablet interface for location-relevant videos and spot-specific video lists, as well as textual place descriptions and point-of-interest guidance using directional arrows and information icons.

C2112.name: location
C2112.definition: Location is a place in a virtual world that can be the user's current point, can be selected on a map and moved to, and for which videos and descriptions are available.

C2113.name: user type
C2113.definition: User type is used to determine which relevant information is available for a given spot in the virtual tour system's tablet interface.

C2114.name: point-of-interest awareness
C2114.definition: Point-of-interest awareness is supported in a virtual tour system by directional arrows that guide users toward points of interest and by information icons that provide further details, so users do not overlook important elements.

C2115.name: controlled navigation technique
C2115.definition: Controlled navigation technique is a navigation technique in which users navigate or teleport using a joystick, so that controlled movement does not support abrupt movements that can cause cybersickness.

C2116.name: vehicular movement
C2116.definition: Vehicular movement is a movement in which the speed of change of viewpoint may cause cybersickness if it is not chosen carefully.

C2117.name: speed of change of viewpoint
C2117.definition: Speed of change of viewpoint is a speed in vehicular movement that may cause cybersickness if it is not chosen carefully.

C2118.name: visual cue
C2118.definition: Visual cue is used in system design, and consistent visual cues help maintain spatial orientation, give a better feeling and awareness of the place, reduce anxiety and sensory conflicts, and avoid severe cybersickness effects.

C2119.name: smooth transition
C2119.definition: Smooth transition is used in system design to help maintain spatial orientation, give the user a better feeling and awareness of the place, reduce anxiety and sensory conflicts, and in the long term avoid severe cybersickness effects.

C2120.name: spatial orientation
C2120.definition: Spatial orientation is the user's awareness of place that consistent visual cues and smooth transitions in system design help maintain.

C2121.name: analysis and specification
C2121.definition: Analysis and specification is a stage in the interactive system development lifecycle, following the feasibility study stage and preceding the design, prototyping, and quick evaluation cycle.

C2122.name: quick evaluation
C2122.definition: Quick evaluation is the stage of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle in the interactive system development lifecycle that evaluates a prototype, may use methods such as cognitive walkthrough or heuristic evaluation, and the results of the evaluation are used to refine the design until it stabilizes.

C2123.name: code evaluation
C2123.definition: Code evaluation is one of the standard software development lifecycle stages in interactive system development.

C2124.name: system evaluation
C2124.definition: System evaluation is one of the standard software development lifecycle stages in interactive system development, with nothing special or distinct for virtual reality or augmented reality systems.

C2125.name: cycle
C2125.definition: A cycle is a repeated loop of stages in an interactive system development lifecycle; the design-prototype-evaluate cycle refines a design based on evaluation results until the design stabilizes, and other cycles may connect code design, coding, implementation, code testing, usability evaluation, requirement gathering, or interface design.

C2126.name: experience design
C2126.definition: Experience design is an iterative design process whose design-prototype-evaluate cycle consists of designing, quickly prototyping, evaluating, finding problems, refining, and repeating with new prototypes and evaluations until the design stabilizes.

C2127.name: cost overrun
C2127.definition: Cost overrun is a result of increased turnaround time in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle when usability evaluation is not done quickly.

C2128.name: prototyping techniques
C2128.definition: Prototyping techniques are used for quick prototyping and quick evaluation of a prototype, typically to collect feedback on the usability of design ideas.

C2129.name: full implementation
C2129.definition: Full implementation is a complete implementation of a software idea that involves highly skilled programmers and many cost components, including setting up or procuring resources and engaging manpower.

C2130.name: final product
C2130.definition: A final product is the fully implemented result into which a prototype can evolve through incremental refinement and testing as development progresses.

C2131.name: horizontal prototype
C2131.definition: Horizontal prototype is a prototype that depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing its look, feel, and appearance without functionality or interaction, so it is used to discuss, brainstorm, and elicit feedback about whether the interface is understandable, intuitive, and usable.

C2132.name: vertical prototype
C2132.definition: A vertical prototype is a type of prototype that implements a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in depth, from the first screen to the last, to represent interactions rather than all system functionalities.

C2133.name: functionality
C2133.definition: Functionality is the interaction or feature aspect of an interface that enables real work, in contrast to its look, feel, and appearance.

C2134.name: system
C2134.definition: A system is a developed, executable thing whose usability is evaluated with end users in interactive system development.

C2135.name: low-fidelity prototype
C2135.definition: A low-fidelity prototype is a prototype of an interface made without technological intervention, programming, code, or a computer, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood, and to represent interaction it needs a series of interface sketches, often called a storyboard, rather than a single sketch.

C2136.name: low-fidelity prototyping
C2136.definition: Low-fidelity prototyping is a prototyping approach that provides a quick and cheap way to make and modify prototypes, does not rely on computers or digital media, and uses a series of interface sketches, a practice often called storyboarding, to brainstorm alternative designs and obtain user feedback on usability, primarily for horizontal prototypes but also for vertical prototypes.

C2137.name: horizontal prototyping
C2137.definition: Horizontal prototyping is a kind of prototyping that low-fidelity prototyping is intuitively primarily associated with, although low-fidelity prototyping can also implement vertical prototypes.

C2138.name: interface sketch
C2138.definition: An interface sketch is a simple drawing that can be made on paper and depicts an interface’s major components, appearance, and layout. It expresses an interface idea for comments and feedback. A single drawing gives a horizontal prototype, whereas a series can give a vertical prototype of interaction.

C2139.name: storyboard
C2139.definition: A storyboard is a low-fidelity prototype consisting of a series of interface sketches, each a keyframe, that captures the sequence of user actions and screen changes for a specific task from beginning to end.

C2140.name: keyframe
C2140.definition: A keyframe is a snapshot of an interaction at a particular point in time that, in a storyboard, visualizes the interaction for a specific task and its scenes.

C2141.name: medium-fidelity prototyping
C2141.definition: Medium-fidelity prototyping is a prototyping approach that uses a computer to create simple prototypes without coding, primarily for horizontal prototypes as static interface sketches without real functionality and for vertical prototypes as animations or slideshows that simulate interaction.

C2142.name: high-fidelity prototyping
C2142.definition: High-fidelity prototyping is a sophisticated prototyping approach that uses computer programs or programming, effectively reduced-scale software development requiring skilled programmers, and requires much more effort than low- or medium-fidelity prototyping and is primarily suited to vertical prototypes rather than horizontal ones.

C2143.name: computer program
C2143.definition: A computer program is used in high-fidelity prototyping to create a prototype.

C2144.name: programmer
C2144.definition: A programmer is a skilled person with programming expertise who is needed for high-fidelity prototyping.

C2145.name: programming expertise
C2145.definition: Programming expertise is a skill that skilled programmers have and that high-fidelity prototyping requires.

C2146.name: static interface sketch
C2146.definition: A static interface sketch is a medium-fidelity prototyping sketch that can be created on a computer, and using only such sketches produces a horizontal prototype because no real functionality is present.

C2147.name: Adobe Flash animation video
C2147.definition: An Adobe Flash animation video is an animated video used in medium-fidelity prototyping to simulate interaction and create a vertical prototype.

C2148.name: Microsoft PowerPoint slideshow
C2148.definition: A Microsoft PowerPoint slideshow is a slideshow used in medium-fidelity prototyping that can simulate interaction and create a vertical prototype with simple key presses or timers.

C2149.name: key press
C2149.definition: A key press is used in medium-fidelity prototyping to simulate interaction, as in an animation or slideshow that creates a vertical prototype.

C2150.name: timer
C2150.definition: A timer is a simple item in a PowerPoint slideshow in medium-fidelity prototyping that can be used to simulate interaction and create a vertical prototype.

C2151.name: wizard of oz approach
C2151.definition: The wizard of Oz approach is a prototype-creation technique in which a human subject believes they are interacting with an autonomous computer, but an unseen human operator called the wizard operates the computer and returns the requested response or result.

C2152.name: wizard
C2152.definition: A wizard is an unseen human operator in a Wizard of Oz prototype who operates the computer and returns the requested response to a subject who believes the computer is autonomous.

C2153.name: international business machines
C2153.definition: International Business Machines (IBM) is an organization that used the Wizard of Oz approach in a listening typewriter experiment to test a speech recognition idea before building a speech recognizer.

C2154.name: listening typewriter experiment
C2154.definition: The listening typewriter experiment is a Wizard of Oz test of a speech recognition idea in which a user spoke to a computer believed to be real, a hidden person typed what was heard, and text appeared on the user’s screen as if automatically recognized.

C2155.name: speech recognition system
C2155.definition: A speech recognition system is a technology that can be tested for acceptability before committing resources to build it.

C2156.name: throwaway prototype
C2156.definition: A throwaway prototype is a prototype that is easy and fast to create, is used for quick evaluation, and is then discarded.

C2157.name: incremental prototype
C2157.definition: An incremental prototype is a kind of prototype that is created by dividing a system into units or modules, separately prototyping and testing each module, and integrating the modules into the overall system.

C2158.name: evolutionary prototype
C2158.definition: An evolutionary prototype is a prototype created by prototyping and testing the whole system, starting with a simpler version, refining it, adding more functionalities, and altering it based on testing results until it becomes the final product, rather than by prototyping separate modules and combining them.

C2159.name: low-fidelity cardboard mockup
C2159.definition: A low-fidelity cardboard mockup is mainly suitable for throwaway prototypes because it is less costly and discarding it does not incur significant cost.

C2160.name: paper sketch
C2160.definition: A paper sketch is mainly suitable for throwaway prototypes because it is less costly and discarding it does not incur significant cost.

C2161.name: module
C2161.definition: A module is a part into which a system design divides a system for an incremental prototype, and each module is prototyped and tested separately before the modules are integrated into the overall system.

C2162.name: expert evaluation
C2162.definition: Expert evaluation is a quick, cheap usability test of a prototype at an early design stage, in which design-team members or domain experts independently report usability issues, and a few end users may be included optionally.

C2163.name: robust evaluation technique
C2163.definition: A robust evaluation technique is an evaluation technique that typically involves suitably skilled evaluators, resources, and an evaluation setup.

C2164.name: evaluator
C2164.definition: An evaluator is a skilled person who examines a prototype and reports usability issues or heuristic violations.

C2165.name: evaluation setup
C2165.definition: Evaluation setup is one of the things typically involved in a robust evaluation technique.

C2166.name: evaluation team
C2166.definition: An evaluation team is a group, mainly the design team or domain experts and optionally a few end users, used to assess a prototype in quick or expert evaluation, with expert evaluations using three to five members who assess independently.

C2167.name: design team
C2167.definition: A design team is a team that can serve as the evaluation team for quick or expert evaluation and that can combine evaluators' usability issue reports into a final list of usability issues.

C2168.name: skilled designer
C2168.definition: A skilled designer is a designer with knowledge and skill in the problem domain who may be part of an evaluation team for quick or expert evaluation.

C2169.name: problem domain
C2169.definition: Problem domain is the subject area in which skilled designers have knowledge and skill for quick or expert evaluation.

C2170.name: domain expert
C2170.definition: A domain expert is someone relied on for quick or expert evaluation instead of end users, because engaging them is less complicated, quicker, and cheaper than engaging a full evaluation team with end users.

C2171.name: usability issue
C2171.definition: Usability issue is a problem in the usability of an interface or prototype that evaluators identify during evaluations, and that users are likely to face while performing tasks.

C2172.name: cognitive walkthrough
C2172.definition: Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert usability inspection method in which evaluators identify problems by performing interface-level tasks converted from a scenario on at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype, guided by usability questions framed in advance.

C2173.name: usability inspection
C2173.definition: Usability inspection is a method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype.

C2174.name: low-fidelity vertical prototype
C2174.definition: A low-fidelity vertical prototype is a prototype that supports several tasks and is the minimum required for a cognitive walkthrough.

C2175.name: high-fidelity prototype
C2175.definition: A high-fidelity prototype is a prototype that is more welcome for a cognitive walkthrough but involves more time and cost.

C2176.name: paper prototype
C2176.definition: A paper prototype is a simple, low-fidelity prototype for a cognitive walkthrough, made as a storyboard: a series of sketches showing screen changes after each interaction.

C2177.name: scenario
C2177.definition: A scenario is a description of a task created for evaluators in a cognitive walkthrough, whose described task is converted into the actions that must be performed in a prototype.

C2178.name: interface-level task
C2178.definition: Interface-level task is an action that must be performed in a prototype to accomplish a task described in a scenario.

C2179.name: usability question
C2179.definition: A usability question is a question framed before a cognitive walkthrough to reflect usability issues; evaluators use it as a guideline to identify likely user problems and must answer it with a detailed report rather than a simple yes-or-no response.

C2180.name: report
C2180.definition: A report is a detailed answer that evaluators give for each usability question, rather than a simple yes or no answer, explaining where difficulty was felt in an interface or interaction and why, and it is collected, combined, and analyzed to identify broader usability issues.

C2181.name: evaluation session
C2181.definition: An evaluation session is a session at the end of which evaluators' reports are collected, combined, and analyzed to identify broader usability issues.

C2182.name: heuristic evaluation
C2182.definition: Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to identify usability problems across the whole system at an early design stage.

C2183.name: checklist
C2183.definition: A checklist is a list of heuristics used in heuristic evaluation to assess a prototype or interface by checking whether each heuristic is followed or violated. Checklists can be detailed and system-specific, or focused on broader usability principles, and broader checklists contain fewer heuristics.

C2184.name: heuristic
C2184.definition: A heuristic is a checklist item that is used in heuristic evaluation to assess a prototype and determine whether the heuristic is followed or violated.

C2185.name: task scenario
C2185.definition: A task scenario is something not used in heuristic evaluation, in which evaluators assess a presented prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics to perform a comprehensive evaluation of the whole system rather than a task-specific evaluation.

C2186.name: task performance
C2186.definition: Task performance is part of a task-specific evaluation, whereas heuristic evaluation assesses a whole system without a task scenario or task performance.

C2187.name: system-specific checklist
C2187.definition: A system-specific checklist is a detailed checklist for evaluating an interface.

C2188.name: usability principle
C2188.definition: A usability principle is one of the broader principles that checklists focus on when evaluating interfaces.

C2189.name: broader checklist
C2189.definition: A broader checklist is a checklist for evaluating interfaces that focuses on broader usability principles, contains fewer heuristics, and is not specific to any particular interface.

C2190.name: Nielsen's ten heuristics
C2190.definition: Nielsen's ten heuristics is a general set of usability heuristics, primarily for graphical user interfaces but applicable to most interactive systems. It consists of: visibility of system status, real-world match, user control, consistency, error prevention, recognition over recall, flexibility, minimal design, error recovery, and help and documentation. It is used to identify usability problems early from low-fidelity prototypes.

C2191.name: visibility of system status
C2191.definition: Visibility of system status is a heuristic that says the status of a system should be visible to the user.

C2192.name: match between system and the real world
C2192.definition: Match between system and the real world is a heuristic stating that what a user does on a system should closely match the user's real-world experience.

C2193.name: user control and freedom
C2193.definition: User control and freedom is a heuristic that concerns whether a user is given freedom and what kind of controls are provided.

C2194.name: consistency and standards
C2194.definition: Consistency and standards is a heuristic in which elements and layout should be consistent across different screens and standards should be followed.

C2195.name: recognition rather than recall
C2195.definition: Recognition rather than recall is a heuristic in which a user should not have to remember what to do, but should be able to recognize from elements what to do, because recollection is more difficult than recognition.

C2196.name: flexibility and efficiency of use
C2196.definition: Flexibility and efficiency of use is one of Nielsen's 10 heuristics.

C2197.name: aesthetic and minimalist design
C2197.definition: Aesthetic and minimalist design is a heuristic in which the design should have a minimum number of elements and should be aesthetically pleasing.

C2198.name: help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors
C2198.definition: Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors is one of Nielsen's 10 heuristics.

C2199.name: help and documentation
C2199.definition: Help and documentation is a heuristic in which a system should provide help and documentation support.

C2200.name: user evaluation
C2200.definition: User evaluation is a quick evaluation technique that obtains feedback by asking users directly using rating scales, and it requires user involvement.

C2201.name: subjective data
C2201.definition: Subjective data is user feedback data collected with rating scales in user evaluation.

C2202.name: questionnaire
C2202.definition: A questionnaire is a set of questions or statements provided to users to rate in user evaluation, although it need not contain questions.

C2203.name: post-task data collection
C2203.definition: Post-task data collection is the collection of user evaluation data after each task, using suitable questionnaires.

C2204.name: after scenario questionnaire
C2204.definition: After scenario questionnaire (ASQ) is a post-task questionnaire in which users rate three statements about satisfaction with ease of completing tasks, time taken to complete tasks, and support information on a seven-point scale.

C2205.name: expectation measure
C2205.definition: Expectation Measure (EM) is a well-known questionnaire available for post-task data collection.

C2206.name: post-session data collection
C2206.definition: Post-session data collection is user-evaluation data collection performed at the end of a session, using suitable questionnaires.

C2207.name: system usability scale
C2207.definition: System usability scale (SUS) is a post-session questionnaire containing ten statements, not questions, that users rate on a five-point agreement scale after completing all tasks, giving a quick percentage indication of whether a system has usability problems.

C2208.name: computer system usability questionnaire
C2208.definition: Computer system usability questionnaire (CSUQ) is one of the well-known questionnaires available for post-session data collection.

C2209.name: questionnaire for user interface satisfaction
C2209.definition: Questionnaire for user interface satisfaction (QUIS) is one of the well-known questionnaires available for post-session data collection.

C2210.name: usefulness satisfaction and ease of use questionnaire
C2210.definition: Usefulness satisfaction and ease of use questionnaire (USE) is one of the well-known questionnaires available for post-session data collection.

C2211.name: post-task questionnaire
C2211.definition: A post-task questionnaire is a kind of questionnaire, such as the After Scenario Questionnaire.

C2212.name: statement
C2212.definition: A statement is a questionnaire item, rather than a question, that users rate on an agreement scale.

C2213.name: seven-point rating scale
C2213.definition: A seven-point rating scale is a rating scale for statements that ranges from 1 to 7, with 1 indicating strong disagreement and 7 indicating strong agreement.

C2214.name: average rating
C2214.definition: Average rating is a way of summarising feedback by averaging ratings either for each statement across all participating users or for all statements together.

C2215.name: post-session questionnaire
C2215.definition: A post-session questionnaire is a questionnaire that contains statements rather than questions and is administered at the end of a session after users have completed all tasks.

C2216.name: five-point agreement scale
C2216.definition: A five-point agreement scale is a rating scale in which 1 indicates strongly disagree and 5 indicates strongly agree.

C2217.name: System Usability Scale score
C2217.definition: The System Usability Scale score (SUS score) is a usability score calculated from all ten statement ratings and interpreted directly as a percentage, with 70% or higher typically indicating an interface is usable or has only minimal problems.

C2218.name: statement rating
C2218.definition: A statement rating is a user's rating of one System Usability Scale statement on a 5-point agreement scale, used to calculate a System Usability Scale score.

C2219.name: quick prototype evaluation
C2219.definition: A quick prototype evaluation is a limited-scale early evaluation that uses a limited number of evaluators to evaluate prototypes, so it can quickly identify some major usability issues but cannot give a conclusive result about the overall usability of the end system.

C2220.name: design review
C2220.definition: Design review is a possible response to usability problems that a System Usability Scale score may indicate.

C2221.name: brainstorming
C2221.definition: Brainstorming is an activity used in interactive system development to identify usability problems, provide a basis for interface design, or produce code design.

C2222.name: aesthetic survey questionnaire
C2222.definition: Aesthetic survey questionnaire (ASQ) is a generic questionnaire applicable to any interactive system, not specifically meant for extended reality (XR) systems.

C2223.name: Majuli virtual reality system
C2223.definition: The Majuli virtual reality system is an immersive virtual reality experience that has a full version and a compressed mobile version.

C2224.name: Unity engine
C2224.definition: Unity engine is an engine used to develop a VR tour for the Oculus Quest 2 and Android smartphones.

C2225.name: Oculus Quest 2
C2225.definition: Oculus Quest 2 is a standalone computing device comprising a headset and handheld controllers, with its own processor and memory, that does not need to be tethered to a fixed computer.

C2226.name: extended reality toolkit
C2226.definition: An extended reality toolkit is a toolkit used for a virtual reality version.

C2227.name: Autodesk Maya
C2227.definition: Autodesk Maya is software used to create three-dimensional (3D) models.

C2228.name: application size
C2228.definition: Application size is the storage space an application requires on a device.

C2229.name: gigabyte
C2229.definition: Gigabyte (GB) is used to express the size of an application or system.

C2230.name: cloud
C2230.definition: Cloud is a service that stores videos and is used to load them when requested, reducing local storage, data-access, and computational requirements.

C2231.name: video thumbnail
C2231.definition: A video thumbnail is a selectable part of a video player used to load a video.

C2232.name: client device
C2232.definition: A client device is a device on which an application is deployed and on which videos can be stored, rather than in cloud services.

C2233.name: video playback
C2233.definition: Video playback is a feature of a virtual reality system that can be removed to reduce storage requirements and make the experience less realistic, or retained using cloud-based services.

C2234.name: 360-degree image tour
C2234.definition: A 360-degree image tour is an implementation of the Majuli virtual reality tour that uses 360-degree images, cultural videos, 360-degree videos, and ambient sound.

C2235.name: three-dimensional model tour
C2235.definition: The three-dimensional model tour is an implementation of the Majuli virtual reality tour that uses three-dimensional models textured from real images, rather than 360-degree images and videos, to create a realistic-looking appearance.

C2236.name: mobile-device tour
C2236.definition: Mobile-device tour is the Google Cardboard implementation of the Majuli VR tour, a reduced form of the full Oculus Quest experience that uses a smartphone to provide a 360-degree experience, with simpler controls and fewer features.

C2237.name: start screen
C2237.definition: Start screen is a screen in a 360-degree-image virtual reality tour implementation that uses a ray-casting-based selection method and plays introductory videos and a tutorial explaining how to control and use the system.

C2238.name: ray-casting-based selection method
C2238.definition: A ray-casting-based selection method is a selection method used on the start screen of a virtual reality tour.

C2239.name: user group selection
C2239.definition: User group selection is a step in a virtual reality implementation that occurs before the user begins the experience.

C2240.name: arrow key
C2240.definition: An arrow key is a key that a user can use to move forward and backward inside a 360-degree-image virtual reality location.

C2241.name: vehicle-metaphor route-planning method
C2241.definition: A vehicle-metaphor route-planning method is a route-planning method in which the road route is fixed and the user experiences motion as if riding a vehicle along the road.

C2242.name: fully implemented system
C2242.definition: Fully implemented system is the overall system, rather than a prototype, that is evaluated in a conclusive usability assessment.

C2243.name: user behavioral data
C2243.definition: User behavioral data is data that a controlled experiment collects and analyzes for a conclusive usability assessment of a fully implemented system.

C2244.name: research question
C2244.definition: A research question is a question formulated in the first stage of an empirical study, which the experiment is conducted to answer and on which data collection and analysis are based, and it should avoid generalized concepts that make it untestable.

C2245.name: variable
C2245.definition: A variable is an item in a testable research question that is identified after the research questions are formulated, without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed; its two most important types are independent variables, or factors, that can take levels or values, and dependent variables that depend on those factors and levels.

C2246.name: experiment
C2246.definition: An experiment is the designed and executed part of an empirical study that collects and compares objective data to answer a research question and measure the usability of an implemented interface.

C2247.name: data
C2247.definition: Data are collected in an experiment and analyzed to reach a reliable conclusion about a system's overall usability aspects.

C2248.name: empirical data
C2248.definition: Empirical data is data collected in an experiment or empirical study that answers a research question, and it is processed and tested for statistical significance before conclusions are drawn.

C2249.name: data analysis
C2249.definition: Data analysis is the fourth stage of the system implementation process in which empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before drawing conclusions about a design's efficacy.

C2250.name: text entry
C2250.definition: Text entry is a graphical user interface whose quality can be judged by users.

C2251.name: text input interface
C2251.definition: A text input interface is an interface that lets a user enter text.

C2252.name: Microsoft Word
C2252.definition: Microsoft Word (MS Word) is a text input interface compared with a new text input interface on quality and speed.

C2253.name: standalone evaluation
C2253.definition: Standalone evaluation is an evaluation that elicits feedback.

C2254.name: text input task
C2254.definition: A text input task is a task in which a user enters text, used to compare interfaces on speed.

C2255.name: subjective interpretation
C2255.definition: Subjective interpretation is a user's interpretation that non-testable research questions depend on, while testable research questions allow objective conclusions to be drawn independently of it.

C2256.name: text entry speed
C2256.definition: Text entry speed is objective data that is logged as characters per minute (CPM) and used to determine which text entry interface is faster.

C2257.name: subjective feedback
C2257.definition: Subjective feedback is feedback that is problematic to depend on, as responses can split and may not support a definitive conclusion.

C2258.name: objective data
C2258.definition: Objective data is data, such as text entry speed or task performance data, that can be collected and analyzed to draw objective conclusions independently of users' subjective interpretation.

C2259.name: characters per minute
C2259.definition: Characters per minute (CPM) is an objective measure of text entry speed that records users' input speed and allows CPM values to be compared to determine which interface is faster.

C2260.name: testable research question
C2260.definition: A testable research question is a research question that allows a study to collect objective data and draw reliable conclusions independent of users' subjective interpretation.

C2261.name: non-testable research question
C2261.definition: A non-testable research question is a broader, generalized research question that cannot be directly tested objectively because it depends on users' subjective interpretation and feedback, so a controlled experiment cannot collect objective data and a reliable scientific conclusion generally cannot be drawn.

C2262.name: scientific conclusion
C2262.definition: A scientific conclusion is a reliable, definite conclusion that testable research questions allow, because they support objective data collection rather than subjective user feedback.

C2263.name: generalized concept
C2263.definition: A generalized concept is a concept, such as whether something is good, that is ambiguous and can lead to untestable research questions.

C2264.name: testability
C2264.definition: Testability is one side of a trade-off with generalization in empirical study, balanced by framing testable research questions covering different aspects of a system.

C2265.name: generalization
C2265.definition: Generalization is the empirical-study aim of reaching a definitive conclusion about a broader untestable generalized question by combining conclusions from multiple testable research questions covering different aspects of a system.

C2266.name: independent variable
C2266.definition: An independent variable is a variable whose values are assigned and controlled; these values are called levels and are used to design an experiment.

C2267.name: level
C2267.definition: A level is a value assigned to an independent variable or factor in an experiment.

C2268.name: test condition
C2268.definition: A test condition is a combination of factor levels that is used to design an experiment.

C2269.name: dependent variable
C2269.definition: A dependent variable is a variable whose value depends on an independent variable or factor, specifically on its levels.

C2270.name: text entry rate
C2270.definition: Text entry rate (TER) is a dependent variable in research question 3 (RQ3), whose value depends on the levels of the interface.

C2271.name: research question framing
C2271.definition: Research question framing is the first stage of the empirical research process that addresses broader generalizable but untestable questions by framing multiple testable research questions, collecting objective data for each, reaching definite conclusions for each, and combining those conclusions to draw a conclusion about the untestable questions.

C2272.name: experiment design
C2272.definition: Experiment design is used to select a representative sample of potential users as participants, using a well-defined user profile.

C2273.name: sample
C2273.definition: Sample is a subset of all potential users chosen for an experiment or empirical study to represent the larger population, so conclusions about that population are valid.

C2274.name: homogeneous user group
C2274.definition: A homogeneous user group is a user group whose members have similarities such as the same age group and similar educational, socio-economic, and/or cultural backgrounds.

C2275.name: age group
C2275.definition: An age group is one of the similarities that members of a homogeneous user group can share.

C2276.name: educational background
C2276.definition: Educational background is one of the backgrounds that can be similar among members of a homogeneous user group.

C2277.name: socio-economic background
C2277.definition: Socio-economic background is one of the backgrounds that may be similar among members of a homogeneous user group.

C2278.name: cultural background
C2278.definition: Cultural background is one of the similarities that members of a homogeneous user group may share, along with age, educational, or socio-economic background.

C2279.name: homogeneous subset
C2279.definition: A homogeneous subset is a user group whose members have the same age group and similar educational, socio-economic, and/or cultural backgrounds.

C2280.name: heterogeneous user group
C2280.definition: A heterogeneous user group is a user group for which using a homogeneous subset is not reliable for drawing conclusions.

C2281.name: user profile
C2281.definition: A user profile is a set of well-defined user characteristics or entries that, in experiment design, defines a user and is the only basis for selecting experiment participants.

C2282.name: user profile characteristic
C2282.definition: A user profile characteristic is one of the well-defined elements of a user profile that, in experiment design, defines a user and is the only basis for selecting experiment participants.

C2283.name: typing behavior
C2283.definition: Typing behavior is a user characteristic that can vary with age and computer-use frequency, and it is considered when choosing experiment participants based on user profiles.

C2284.name: typing speed
C2284.definition: Typing speed is a user characteristic that can differ among users and must be considered when choosing experiment participants based on user profiles.

C2285.name: number of participants
C2285.definition: Number of participants is the count of participants in a controlled empirical experiment, generally assumed to be between 12 and 25 to draw reliable conclusions.

C2286.name: task performance data
C2286.definition: Task performance data are mostly objective data collected from users performing tasks in a controlled experiment evaluating an interface, and are analyzed to draw conclusions about the interface.

C2287.name: representative task set
C2287.definition: A representative task set is a small, well-defined subset of the tasks that potential users most frequently or commonly use when an interface is deployed in practice, from which empirical studies ideally choose one or more tasks so that collected data and drawn conclusions are reliable.

C2288.name: typing task
C2288.definition: A typing task is a task used to compare typing interfaces.

C2289.name: typing interface
C2289.definition: A typing interface is an interface compared using typing tasks.

C2290.name: random piece of text
C2290.definition: A random piece of text is a text used for a typing task to compare typing interfaces, but it is not a representative task.

C2291.name: text string
C2291.definition: A text string is a piece of text that can be used as a representative task in a typing task for comparing typing interfaces when chosen by certain metrics and measures.

C2292.name: metric
C2292.definition: A metric is used, along with measures, to choose representative typing tasks for comparing typing interfaces.

C2293.name: measure
C2293.definition: Measure is used, along with metrics, to choose representative text strings for typing tasks that compare typing interfaces.

C2294.name: typing skill
C2294.definition: Typing skill is a user skill indirectly encompassed by representative tasks used to compare typing interfaces.

C2295.name: experimental study
C2295.definition: An experimental study is a study in which tasks can be assigned using either a within-subject or a between-subjects design.

C2296.name: within-subject design
C2296.definition: Within-subject design is an experimental design in which every participant performs tasks corresponding to all test conditions; because repeated practice can confound the analysis, the task sequence may be randomized or systematically varied to reduce the practice effect.

C2297.name: between-subjects design
C2297.definition: Between-subjects design is an experimental design in which the tasks for all test conditions are divided and distributed among subsets of participants.

C2298.name: practice effect
C2298.definition: Practice effect is, in a within-subject design, an improvement in task performance from repeated practice that is a confounding variable and adds noise to the data, because performance gains may be due to practice rather than the interface.

C2299.name: confounding variable
C2299.definition: A confounding variable is, for example, a practice effect in a within-subject design that confounds the analysis by adding noise to the data, because performance gains may be due to practice rather than to the interface.

C2300.name: task sequence
C2300.definition: Task sequence is the sequence of tasks allocated to a participant, which can be randomized or systematically varied to reduce the practice effect in a within-subject design.

C2301.name: Latin square design
C2301.definition: A Latin square design is a design that systematically varies the task sequence allocated to each participant.

C2302.name: system implementation process
C2302.definition: The system implementation process is a process that includes its fourth stage, data analysis, in which empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before drawing conclusions about a design's efficacy.

C2303.name: statistical significance
C2303.definition: Statistical significance is a reported result of a statistical significance test of empirical data from an experiment, used before drawing conclusions about whether a difference, such as in group means, is statistically significant.

C2304.name: empirical interface study
C2304.definition: An empirical interface study is an interface study that obtains data from a sample of users rather than the actual population and draws conclusions about a larger population.

C2305.name: population
C2305.definition: Population is, in empirical interface studies, the larger actual population, such as any user and any text-entry interface, rather than the sample of users from which data are obtained, and the conclusions of interest are about it.

C2306.name: statistical significance test
C2306.definition: A statistical significance test is a test that indicates whether an observed data difference is reliable by showing whether the difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions.

C2307.name: observed data difference
C2307.definition: An observed data difference is a difference in observed data that a statistical significance test indicates is reliable by showing whether the difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions.

C2308.name: statistically significant difference
C2308.definition: A statistically significant difference is an observed difference in data that a statistical significance test indicates is not due to chance.

C2309.name: non-significant difference
C2309.definition: A non-significant difference is an observed data difference that is due to chance rather than to the tested conditions.

C2310.name: mean text-entry speed
C2310.definition: Mean text-entry speed is the value for each group used when comparing two text-entry interfaces.

C2311.name: relative difference
C2311.definition: Relative difference is used when comparing two text-entry interfaces to consider the difference between the groups' mean text-entry speeds rather than their absolute values.

C2312.name: absolute value
C2312.definition: Absolute value is a value that may be contrasted with the relative difference between mean text-entry speeds when comparing two text-entry interfaces.

C2313.name: experimental design
C2313.definition: Experimental design is one of the things on which the method for performing a statistical significance test depends, along with the nature of the input data.

C2314.name: absolute difference
C2314.definition: Absolute difference is a difference in group means that can be included in the result of a statistical significance test.

C2315.name: group mean
C2315.definition: Group mean is a mean whose absolute difference can be included in the result of a statistical significance test.

C2316.name: p-value
C2316.definition: P-value is a probability in a statistical significance test that the data were obtained by chance, with a lower value meaning the result is less likely to have been obtained by chance.

C2317.name: t value
C2317.definition: T value is a value that can be included in the result of a statistical significance test.

C2318.name: paired sample t-test
