C2318.definition: Paired sample t-test is a parametric statistical significance test used for a within-subject design with one factor and two levels to show whether differences between the levels are statistically significant.

C2319.name: parametric test
C2319.definition: A parametric test is a statistical significance test that belongs to one of two groups of such tests.

C2320.name: non-parametric test
C2320.definition: A non-parametric test is a statistical significance test that can be used in between-subject or within-subject experimental designs with one or more factors having two or more levels.

C2321.name: scale of measurement
C2321.definition: A scale of measurement is a scale in an experimental design, such as a nominal or categorical scale.

C2322.name: nominal scale
C2322.definition: A nominal scale is a scale of measurement in an experimental design.

C2323.name: chi-square test
C2323.definition: Chi-square test is a non-parametric test used for a between-subject experimental design with a nominal or categorical scale of measurement and one factor having two levels.

C2324.name: McNemar's test
C2324.definition: McNemar's test is a non-parametric test that is used for a within-subject design with a nominal or categorical scale of measurement and one factor having two levels.

C2325.name: independent samples t-test
C2325.definition: An independent samples t-test is a parametric test that can be used in a between-subject design with one factor having two levels and no other condition mentioned.

C2326.name: Mann-Whitney U test
C2326.definition: The Mann-Whitney U test is a non-parametric test that can be used for a between-subject design with one factor having two levels.

C2327.name: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
C2327.definition: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is a non-parametric statistical significance test that can be used in a within-subject design with one factor having two levels.

C2328.name: analysis of variance
C2328.definition: Analysis of variance (ANOVA) is a parametric test that is used for between-subject or within-subject designs with one factor having more than two levels, or with two or more factors each having two or more levels.

C2329.name: one-way analysis of variance
C2329.definition: One-way analysis of variance is a parametric test used in between-subject designs for one factor with more than two levels.

C2330.name: factorial analysis of variance
C2330.definition: Factorial analysis of variance is a parametric test used for between-subject designs with two or more factors, each having two or more levels.

C2331.name: Kruskal-Wallis test
C2331.definition: The Kruskal-Wallis test is a test that can be used for a between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels.

C2332.name: repeated measures analysis of variance
C2332.definition: Repeated measures analysis of variance is a parametric test that can be used for a within-subject design with one factor having three or more levels, or with two or more factors each having two or more levels.

C2333.name: Friedman test
C2333.definition: Friedman test is a non-parametric test that can be used for a within-subject design with one factor having three or more levels, or for a within-subject design with two or more factors each having two or more levels.

C2334.name: user engagement
C2334.definition: User engagement is a usability aspect of a virtual reality system that is measured during evaluation.

C2335.name: comfort
C2335.definition: Comfort is a usability aspect of a virtual environment that an evaluation study measures.

C2336.name: structured questionnaire
C2336.definition: A structured questionnaire is a questionnaire used to collect data from end users in an evaluation, related to the evaluation's research question, and capable of measuring objective or behavioral data or, sometimes, of collecting data through a rating scale.

C2337.name: behavioral data
C2337.definition: Behavioral data is a kind of data that a structured questionnaire can measure.

C2338.name: mean age
C2338.definition: Mean age is a value used to state the ages of the participants in the Majuli virtual reality tour empirical evaluation study.

C2339.name: standard deviation
C2339.definition: Standard deviation is a value reported with mean values for participant ages and presence ratings.

C2340.name: joystick-based controller
C2340.definition: A joystick-based controller is a type of controller used in a virtual reality or non-virtual reality context.

C2341.name: Meta Quest 2
C2341.definition: Meta Quest 2 is a head-mounted display (HMD).

C2342.name: Oculus Link
C2342.definition: Oculus Link is a standard setup used to connect a head-mounted display to a personal computer.

C2343.name: 64-bit
C2343.definition: 64-bit is a characteristic of a computer used to render stimuli in an empirical evaluation study of a virtual reality tour.

C2344.name: Windows 11 Professional
C2344.definition: Windows 11 Professional is an operating system that was run on a 64-bit computer used to render stimuli in an empirical evaluation study.

C2345.name: quad-core processor
C2345.definition: A quad-core processor is a processor in a 64-bit computer used to render stimuli in a virtual reality evaluation study.

C2346.name: GeForce GTX 1080
C2346.definition: A GeForce GTX 1080 is a graphics processing unit (GPU).

C2347.name: questionnaire for environmental presence
C2347.definition: The questionnaire for environmental presence (QEP) is a questionnaire used to measure presence. It is a revised version of the standard presence questionnaire and includes 19 core items and 3 optional sound-related items, answered on a 1-to-7 Likert scale.

C2348.name: Majuli virtual reality tour assessment
C2348.definition: Majuli virtual reality tour assessment is an assessment in which a QEP questionnaire was tailored and simulator sickness questionnaire scores were computed and compared before and after exposure.

C2349.name: total sickness
C2349.definition: Total sickness is one of the scores considered from the simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ), alongside nausea, disorientation, and oculomotor discomfort.

C2350.name: pre-experiment training session
C2350.definition: A pre-experiment training session is a brief session before a VR experiment that demonstrates the features and use of the system used in the experiment, bringing participants to the same level and reducing or nullifying familiarity or prior-experience bias.

C2351.name: prior-experience bias
C2351.definition: Prior-experience bias is a bias in a virtual reality experiment that may lead to incorrect conclusions when unfamiliar users produce results much different from familiar users.

C2352.name: pre-exposure assessment
C2352.definition: A pre-exposure assessment is an assessment completed before exposure to a system.

C2353.name: exploration time
C2353.definition: Exploration time is the amount of time given to users in a VR tour evaluation to explore the tour and obtain heritage information while minimizing cybersickness.

C2354.name: pilot study
C2354.definition: A pilot study is one of the sources used, together with trials and literature, to estimate an exploration time for users, helping to minimize the possibility of cybersickness.

C2355.name: involvement
C2355.definition: Involvement is one of the presence measures used to evaluate a virtual tour.

C2356.name: interface quality
C2356.definition: Interface quality is one of the presence measures used to evaluate a virtual tour.

C2357.name: adaptation or immersion
C2357.definition: Adaptation or immersion is one of the presence measures used to evaluate a virtual tour.

C2358.name: visual fidelity
C2358.definition: Visual fidelity is a presence measure used to evaluate a virtual tour.

C2359.name: tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity
C2359.definition: Tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity is a presence measure used to evaluate a virtual tour.

C2360.name: mean
C2360.definition: Mean is a numerical value reported for a rating measure.

C2361.name: coefficient of variation
C2361.definition: Coefficient of variation is a value reported with the mean and standard deviation for ratings.

C2362.name: prior exposure
C2362.definition: Prior exposure is the exposure of users to digital or virtual tours, and it always helps users gain a better experience.

C2363.name: Welch t-test
C2363.definition: A Welch t-test is a test used to reveal a statistically significant difference between two user groups.

C2364.name: Majuli virtual tour
C2364.definition: The Majuli virtual tour is a virtual tour that contains many geographically spread information points and uses walking within each point and teleportation or a vehicle metaphor between points to present rich multimodal content.

C2365.name: pre-exposure
C2365.definition: Pre-exposure is questionnaire data or outcomes collected before exposure in a cyber sickness evaluation and compared with post-exposure results.

C2366.name: post-exposure
C2366.definition: Post-exposure is the later SSQ data-collection stage in a cyber sickness evaluation, with its data or outcomes compared with pre-exposure values.

C2367.name: box plot
C2367.definition: A box plot is a plot of data or ratings that shows differences between conditions.

C2368.name: stable interface design
C2368.definition: Stable interface design is an interface design in interactive system development that is reached after repeating a design-prototype-evaluate cycle until further evaluation is unlikely to produce many new issues.

C2369.name: data flow diagram
C2369.definition: Data flow diagram (DFD) is one of the design languages or notations used to produce a code design in interactive system development.

C2370.name: entity relationship
C2370.definition: Entity relationship (ER) is one of the design languages or notations used in code design in interactive system development.

C2371.name: object-oriented approach
C2371.definition: Object-oriented approach is a design language or notation used in code design for interactive system development.

C2372.name: unified modeling language
C2372.definition: Unified modeling language (UML) is a design language or notation used in code design for interactive system development.

C2373.name: primary-level testing
C2373.definition: Primary-level testing is a form of code testing in implementation that may be review-based.

C2374.name: review-based testing
C2374.definition: Review-based testing is a form of code testing that may be used as primary-level testing in implementation of interactive system development.

C2375.name: secondary-level testing
C2375.definition: Secondary-level testing is a level of code testing that may be more systematic or structured than primary-level testing.

C2376.name: black box testing
C2376.definition: Black box testing is a type of secondary-level code testing used in interactive system implementation.

C2377.name: white box testing
C2377.definition: White box testing is one kind of systematic, structured, secondary-level code testing.

C2378.name: unit-level testing
C2378.definition: Unit-level testing is a level of code testing performed during interactive system implementation, before integration and system-level testing.

C2379.name: system-level testing
C2379.definition: System-level testing is a level of testing that is performed after unit and integration testing in interactive system development.

C2380.name: feasibility study report
C2380.definition: A feasibility study report is one of the documents required before deployment in the standard interactive system development lifecycle.

C2381.name: design document
C2381.definition: A design document is one of the documents required before deployment in the standard interactive system development lifecycle, for interface and interaction design, and for code.

C2382.name: code testing document
C2382.definition: A code testing document is one of the documents required before deployment in the standard interactive system development lifecycle.

C2383.name: usability study report
C2383.definition: A usability study report is a document required before deployment in the standard interactive system development lifecycle.

C2384.name: agile development
C2384.definition: Agile development is a development framework that starts small, avoids collecting all requirements initially, and adds features over successive iterations to deliver projects quickly that are acceptable to clients. Its process flow consists of conceptualization, inception, iteration or sprint, release, production, and retirement.

C2385.name: conceptualization
C2385.definition: Conceptualization is a part of the agile development process flow; together with inception, it roughly refers to physical feasibility study and requirement gathering.

C2386.name: inception
C2386.definition: Inception is a stage of the agile development process flow in which the team is created and funds and resources are arranged.

C2387.name: sprint
C2387.definition: Sprint is a stage in the agile development process that typically requires four to six weeks and includes requirements, development, testing, and delivery.

C2388.name: release
C2388.definition: Release is a stage in an agile development process in which testing, training, documentation, and deployment occur.

C2389.name: production
C2389.definition: Production is a stage of the agile development process that involves ongoing support and maintenance after delivery.

C2390.name: retirement
C2390.definition: Retirement is the stage of the agile development process flow that covers end-of-life activities.

C2391.name: physical feasibility study
C2391.definition: Physical feasibility study is a part of the agile development process that conceptualization and inception roughly refer to, together with requirement gathering.

C2392.name: development
C2392.definition: Development is a part of an agile sprint that occurs after requirements and before testing.

C2393.name: delivery
C2393.definition: Delivery is a part of an agile sprint in which the system is delivered to production, and agile development adds features over successive deliveries.

C2394.name: sprint backlog
C2394.definition: A sprint backlog is what the requirements in an agile sprint are based on, together with customer and stakeholder feedback.

C2395.name: daily meeting
C2395.definition: Daily meeting is a meeting that a development team holds to deliver within an agile sprint.

C2396.name: demonstration
C2396.definition: Demonstration is what a development team provides after each iteration within an agile sprint.

C2397.name: agile method
C2397.definition: Agile method is a method used to develop acceptable products for practical purposes.

C2398.name: scrum
C2398.definition: Scrum is a popular agile method or framework.

C2399.name: extreme programming
C2399.definition: Extreme Programming is a popular agile method or framework.

C2400.name: disciplined agile delivery
C2400.definition: Disciplined agile delivery (DAD) is one of the popular agile methods or frameworks.

C2401.name: dynamic system development method
C2401.definition: Dynamic system development method (DSDM) is one of the popular agile methods or frameworks.

C2402.name: prototype building
C2402.definition: Prototype building is one of the human-computer interaction concepts recommended for further study.

C2403.name: prototype evaluation
C2403.definition: Prototype evaluation is one of the concepts in the design and implementation of human-computer interfaces.

C2404.name: optimization
C2404.definition: Optimization is the balancing of psychophysiological experience and resource utilization in an extended reality system so that immersive experience is maximized while resource requirements and cybersickness are minimized.

C2405.name: psychophysiological experience optimization
C2405.definition: Psychophysiological experience optimization is a perspective of optimization in virtual reality that is roughly taken to mean designing the experience to minimize cyber sickness or the possibility of its induction.

C2406.name: resource optimization
C2406.definition: Resource optimization is the technological optimization of resource requirements in extended reality (XR), including virtual reality (VR), that minimizes those requirements while maximizing immersive experience without compromising it. It generally focuses on client-end hardware so users can have a good experience with affordable hardware.

C2407.name: resource requirement
C2407.definition: Resource requirement is the technological optimization concern of an XR system, which is generally resource-hungry and whose resource requirements are minimized without compromising the immersive experience.

C2408.name: susceptibility to motion sickness
C2408.definition: Susceptibility to motion sickness is an internal factor that can induce cybersickness.

C2409.name: type of display
C2409.definition: Type of display is one of the hardware factors that can induce cybersickness.

C2410.name: type of input
C2410.definition: Type of input is an external hardware factor that can induce cybersickness.

C2411.name: full gait
C2411.definition: Full gait is a walking-based virtual locomotion technique that involves physical walking to move from one point to another.

C2412.name: partial gait
C2412.definition: Partial gait is a walking-based virtual locomotion technique that involves physical walking.

C2413.name: steering-based technique
C2413.definition: Steering-based technique is one of the virtual locomotion techniques (VLTs) used to navigate or perform a virtual reality (VR) tour by moving from one point to another.

C2414.name: selection-based technique
C2414.definition: A selection-based technique is one of the virtual locomotion techniques used to navigate or perform a virtual reality tour by moving from one point to another.

C2415.name: manipulation-based technique
C2415.definition: Manipulation-based technique is one of the virtual locomotion techniques used to navigate or perform a virtual reality tour by moving from one point to another.

C2416.name: user-controlled virtual reality tour
C2416.definition: A user-controlled virtual reality tour is a virtual reality tour in which the user controls how and where to navigate using controllers or other input modalities.

C2417.name: system-controlled virtual reality tour
C2417.definition: A system-controlled virtual reality tour is a navigation mode in a virtual reality tour in which the system or application controls the user's movement, often along a predetermined path or sequence of movements.

C2418.name: navigation mode
C2418.definition: Navigation mode is a type of navigation in a virtual reality tour, such as a system-controlled tour in which the system forces the user to move from one place to another.

C2419.name: realistic walking experience
C2419.definition: A realistic walking experience is an experience in a system-controlled tour that helps the user feel present rather than controlled by the system and reduces awareness of the difference between realistic and unrealistic elements.

C2420.name: user input
C2420.definition: User input is what a system or scene can respond to or change with, and it may be continuous.

C2421.name: walking speed
C2421.definition: Walking speed is a speed in system-controlled tours that can be difficult to align with user input.

C2422.name: optic flow
C2422.definition: Optic flow is the rate at which the visual scene changes, producing the perception of movement as the view of the surroundings changes.

C2423.name: user movement
C2423.definition: User movement is movement in a virtual reality tour that appears as a constantly changing scene.

C2424.name: real-world walking speed
C2424.definition: Real-world walking speed is the actual or typical speed at which a user walks in the real world, used to match scene-change speed in a system-controlled virtual reality tour where walking is assumed.

C2425.name: virtual reality walking speed
C2425.definition: Virtual reality walking speed is a walking speed in virtual reality, contrasted with the user's real-world walking speed for scene-change speed.

C2426.name: instantaneous walking speed
C2426.definition: Instantaneous walking speed is the user's walking speed used by a system-controlled virtual reality tour to match its optic flow for a more realistic tour.

C2427.name: walking speed model
C2427.definition: A walking speed model is a model of a user's typical walking behavior that is used to match a system-controlled virtual reality tour's optic flow to the user's instantaneous walking speed.

C2428.name: constant optic flow
C2428.definition: Constant optic flow is an optic flow in a system-controlled virtual reality tour that is not very realistic because people rarely walk at a constant speed.

C2429.name: realistic walking behavior model
C2429.definition: A realistic walking behavior model is a model that can be used for system-controlled virtual reality (VR) navigation to address the need for a realistic walking experience.

C2430.name: natural walking behavior
C2430.definition: Natural walking behavior is a walking behavior that can be modeled for system-controlled virtual reality (VR) navigation to provide a realistic walking experience.

C2431.name: system-controlled virtual reality navigation
C2431.definition: System-controlled virtual reality navigation is a form of virtual reality navigation for which a model of natural walking behavior can be used as a realistic walking behavior model to address the need for a realistic walking experience.

C2432.name: empirical research
C2432.definition: Empirical research is a development step used to collect empirical data for building a realistic walking behavior model for system-controlled VR navigation.

C2433.name: creation
C2433.definition: Creation is a step in developing a realistic walking behavior model for system-controlled virtual reality (VR) navigation.

C2434.name: validation
C2434.definition: Validation is one of the steps in developing a realistic walking behavior model for system-controlled virtual reality navigation.

C2435.name: speed estimation model
C2435.definition: A speed estimation model is a model proposed by an empirical study that collected real-life data of a user moving from one point to another.

C2436.name: walking behavior
C2436.definition: Walking behavior is a behavior that is affected by height.

C2437.name: corridor experiment
C2437.definition: The corridor experiment is an experiment that used a corridor in a physical building in which seven paintings representing images of the seven wonders of the world were placed at distances from the start.

C2438.name: video recording
C2438.definition: Video recording is a recording of a user's footsteps made with a camera fixed on the user's back and focused on the user's legs.

C2439.name: data-analysis stage
C2439.definition: The data-analysis stage is a stage in which participants' instantaneous step frequency is computed from foot-strike timestamps and distances.

C2440.name: instantaneous step frequency
C2440.definition: Instantaneous step frequency is the number of steps per second, where a step is one foot strike to the next foot strike on the ground.

C2441.name: step
C2441.definition: A step is an interval that extends from one foot strike on the ground to the next foot strike on the ground.

C2442.name: foot strike
C2442.definition: Foot strike is a ground event whose timestamp is noted, and it marks one end of a step, the interval from one foot strike to the next.

C2443.name: timestamp
C2443.definition: Timestamp is a recorded foot-strike time used in data analysis to calculate step frequencies.

C2444.name: slow-in-slow-out pattern
C2444.definition: The slow-in-slow-out pattern is a pattern in step frequency plotted against distance in which step frequency starts low, increases to a maximum, plateaus, and then decreases to zero at a target where the user stops.

C2445.name: slow-in-slow-out walking pattern
C2445.definition: A slow-in-slow-out walking pattern is a walking pattern that starts, remains approximately constant, and returns to zero, like a square pulse wave, and is modeled by a Fourier-series expansion of harmonically related sinusoids with weights calculated from empirical data.

C2446.name: fourier series
C2446.definition: Fourier series is a weighted sum of harmonically related sinusoids that can approximate any continuous periodic function to arbitrary precision, with practical approximations using the first few terms.

C2447.name: square pulse wave
C2447.definition: A square pulse wave is a wave that has a Fourier-series approximation that starts, remains approximately constant, and then returns to zero.

C2448.name: continuous periodic function
C2448.definition: A continuous periodic function is a function that can be approximated to arbitrary precision by a Fourier series with appropriate weights.

C2449.name: sinusoid
C2449.definition: A sinusoid is used in a Fourier-series expansion to model a slow-in-slow-out walking pattern.

C2450.name: virtual walking
C2450.definition: Virtual walking is a movement in which the user's actual movement speed and perceived movement speed need not be the same, and the user generally perceives visual or optic flow more slowly than the actual movement.

C2451.name: actual movement speed
C2451.definition: Actual movement speed is the user's movement speed in virtual walking, which is related to instantaneous step frequency and may differ from perceived movement speed.

C2452.name: perceived movement speed
C2452.definition: Perceived movement speed is the perceived speed of scene change in virtual walking; it is not necessarily the same as actual movement speed, users generally perceive it more slowly than actual movement speed, and it is computed as a visual gain times that actual speed.

C2453.name: visual gain
C2453.definition: Visual gain is a factor in a natural walking speed model that multiplies actual instantaneous walking speed to compute the desired perceived scene-change speed.

C2454.name: initial frequency
C2454.definition: Initial frequency is the frequency f0, equal to 1/(2d), where d is the distance between source and destination.

C2455.name: natural walking speed model
C2455.definition: Natural walking speed model is a model for a system-controlled virtual reality tour that displays a visual speed, or optic flow, matching the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed by multiplying actual instantaneous walking speed by a visual gain factor, to provide a realistic walking experience.

C2456.name: computed natural walking behavior
C2456.definition: Computed natural walking behavior is the part of a natural walking speed model that is multiplied by a visual gain factor to let a user perceive natural walking.

C2457.name: constant speed
C2457.definition: Constant speed is a speed level used by system-controlled navigation to move a user through a virtual environment.

C2458.name: virtual art exhibition environment
C2458.definition: A virtual art exhibition environment is a virtual environment in which system-controlled navigation moves the user through pictures, stopping at each picture.

C2459.name: system-controlled navigation
C2459.definition: System-controlled navigation is a form of navigation used in an empirical study of a virtual art exhibition environment, in which the system moved the user through pictures at a constant speed or an instantaneous natural walking speed.

C2460.name: randomized order
C2460.definition: Randomized order is an order in which conditions are experienced, used to avoid practice effect and bias in subsequent data collection.

C2461.name: bias
C2461.definition: Bias is what randomized condition order and breaks are used to avoid in subsequent data collection.

C2462.name: user preference
C2462.definition: User preference is a dependent variable measured on a rating scale in a study comparing constant and instantaneous speed levels.

C2463.name: perceived instantaneous walking speed
C2463.definition: Perceived instantaneous walking speed is the visual speed a user perceives in the natural walking-speed model and equals the visual gain of 2.1 multiplied by the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed.

C2464.name: perception of movement
C2464.definition: Perception of movement is a perception that a virtual reality tour produces by displaying optic flow that matches the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed.

C2465.name: virtual reality navigation experience
C2465.definition: Virtual reality navigation experience is a navigation experience in virtual reality that an approach using the natural walking model optimizes to address cyber sickness by controlling the duration of exposure in the virtual world.

C2466.name: virtual world size
C2466.definition: Virtual world size is the geographical area of a virtual environment that a user needs to cover while traveling and exploring.

C2467.name: virtual travel speed
C2467.definition: Virtual travel speed is the speed of movement through a virtual world, a higher speed reduces exposure duration, and it cannot be set arbitrarily for a realistic walking experience.

C2468.name: travel time
C2468.definition: Travel time is the duration that moving between vertices in a virtual world takes, calculated from their distance and a natural walking-speed model; for a path, it is the sum of the times between consecutive vertices.

C2469.name: interaction time
C2469.definition: Interaction time is the time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects in virtual reality.

C2470.name: distance between points of interest
C2470.definition: Distance between points of interest is a virtual-world distance that can be adjusted to reduce travel time and exposure time.

C2471.name: system-controlled virtual reality tool
C2471.definition: A system-controlled virtual reality tool is a virtual reality tool in which users do not interact with virtual objects.

C2472.name: semi-interactive tour
C2472.definition: A semi-interactive tour is a system-controlled virtual reality navigation scenario in which travel is automatic, users may interact only with a small set of objects at points of interest after a navigation task, and cannot interact with other objects.

C2473.name: system-controlled navigation scenario
C2473.definition: A system-controlled navigation scenario is a virtual reality navigation scenario in which travel is automatic and users may interact only with a limited set of objects at points of interest after a navigation task is complete.

C2474.name: semi-interactive virtual tour
C2474.definition: A semi-interactive virtual tour is a virtual tour in which interaction time at each point of interest can be limited in advance, after which the system automatically forces the user to move to another point of interest.

C2475.name: optimum path
C2475.definition: An optimum path is a navigation path in virtual reality that, under a limit on interaction time, either minimizes total navigation and interaction time to experience all points of interest or maximizes the number of points of interest experienced within a fixed time limit.

C2476.name: original graph
C2476.definition: Original graph is the weighted graph input to an optimal-path algorithm that represents a virtual world, with vertices as points of interest, directly connected edges weighted by Euclidean distance, connected but not necessarily complete, and importance and waiting time specified for each node.

C2477.name: vertex set
C2477.definition: Vertex set is the set of all points of interest, represented as vertices, in a weighted graph that represents a virtual world.

C2478.name: weighted edge
C2478.definition: A weighted edge is an edge between points of interest in a weighted graph that represents a top view of a virtual world.

C2479.name: edge weight
C2479.definition: Edge weight is a number assigned to a graph edge that represents the Euclidean distance for directly connected vertices, a very large number for non-directly connected vertices initially, the shortest path length after modification, or travel time in the final time-weighted graph.

C2480.name: euclidean distance
C2480.definition: Euclidean distance is the edge weight assigned to a directly connected pair of vertices or points of interest in a graph for travel-time minimisation.

C2481.name: infinity symbol
C2481.definition: The infinity symbol is a symbol used to represent a very large number as an edge weight for two vertices that are not directly connected.

C2482.name: optimum travel path problem
C2482.definition: The optimum travel path problem is the problem of finding a path in a given graph that covers all vertices, the points of interest, in the least possible time while maintaining a realistic speed throughout so the user gets a realistic feeling.

C2483.name: travel-time algorithm
C2483.definition: The travel-time algorithm is an algorithm whose first stage computes the time to travel between two directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model.

C2484.name: directly connected node pair
C2484.definition: A directly connected node pair is a pair of nodes for which the first stage of the travel-time algorithm computes a travel-time estimate using the natural walking-speed model.

C2485.name: actual instantaneous realistic walking speed
C2485.definition: Actual instantaneous realistic walking speed is the realistic walking speed in the natural walking-speed model, used to calculate perceived instantaneous walking speed and travel time.

C2486.name: distance element
C2486.definition: A distance element is an element of the distance between directly connected nodes used to calculate instantaneous time for travel.

C2487.name: instantaneous time
C2487.definition: Instantaneous time is the time for a distance element, calculated as that element divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed, and integrated over a distance to give total travel time.

C2488.name: integral
C2488.definition: An integral is solved to estimate travel time over a distance between directly connected nodes.

C2489.name: travel-time estimate
C2489.definition: Travel-time estimate is the estimated travel time for a directly connected vertex pair under the natural walking model, computed using a Fourier-series expansion.

C2490.name: V naught
C2490.definition: V naught is a constant for a given user height, used in the travel-time estimate for a directly connected vertex pair under the natural walking model.

C2491.name: travel-time minimisation problem
C2491.definition: Travel-time minimisation problem is a graph problem, a variation of the travelling salesman problem, whose objective is to find a path containing all vertices with the minimum total travel time. The graph is connected and not assumed to be a complete graph; for vertices not directly connected, a hypothetical edge is weighted by the shortest path length.

C2492.name: travelling salesman problem
C2492.definition: Travelling salesman problem (TSP) is a problem that, given a complete graph, asks for the shortest path that visits each node exactly once and returns to the starting node, where the shortest path is defined by the total weight of the edges in the path.

C2493.name: complete graph
C2493.definition: A complete graph is a graph in which every pair of vertices is connected by an edge; where a direct edge is absent, a hypothetical edge representing the shortest path between the vertices is used.

C2494.name: shortest path
C2494.definition: Shortest path is a path between two vertices in a graph that has the least total weight of its edges.

C2495.name: hamiltonian path
C2495.definition: A hamiltonian path is a path that covers all nodes and visits each node exactly once.

C2496.name: hypothetical edge
C2496.definition: A hypothetical edge is an edge introduced between two vertices not directly connected in a graph used for travel-time minimisation, representing the shortest path between them for travel-time computation.

C2497.name: modified edge weight
C2497.definition: Modified edge weight is a computed weight for a direct or hypothetical edge between two vertices in a graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem, equal to the Euclidean distance for direct edges and to the shortest path length for hypothetical edges.

C2498.name: shortest path length
C2498.definition: Shortest path length is the sum of the edge weights in the shortest path between two vertices in a connected graph.

C2499.name: connected
C2499.definition: Connected is a property of a graph that makes the shortest path lengths for hypothetical edges well-defined in a travel-time minimisation problem.

C2500.name: edge set
C2500.definition: An edge set is a set that is part of the original graph G, which is given with the vertex set V as input to an optimal-path algorithm.

C2501.name: optimal time
C2501.definition: Optimal time is the amount of time taken by the path that covers all vertices of a graph in the least time.

C2502.name: optimal path
C2502.definition: Optimal path is a path through points of interest that maximizes the total importance of the points visited and the number of the most important points covered while keeping total traveling and waiting time below a time threshold beyond which cybersickness may occur.

C2503.name: complete time-weighted graph
C2503.definition: A complete time-weighted graph is a complete graph whose edge weights are travel times between vertex pairs rather than Euclidean distances, and it can be solved to obtain an optimal path.

C2504.name: travelling salesman problem solver
C2504.definition: A travelling salesman problem solver is a standard solver that takes a complete time-weighted graph as input and outputs the optimum time and optimal path; its optimal path may contain hypothetical edges that are replaced by shortest paths in the original graph.

C2505.name: time threshold
C2505.definition: Time threshold (TTH) is the maximum duration of user movement, experience, or virtual reality exposure in a virtual tour, beyond which cybersickness may occur; it is the upper time limit used when optimizing a tour path.

C2506.name: minimum-time approach
C2506.definition: Minimum-time approach is a cybersickness-minimizing approach that models a virtual world as a graph of points of interest, completes it with shortest-path travel times from the natural walking-speed model, and solves a TSP to find the minimum-time path covering all points of interest.

C2507.name: optimum time
C2507.definition: Optimum time is the travel time that a travelling salesman problem solver outputs, along with an optimal path, in the minimum-time approach.

C2508.name: final solution path
C2508.definition: Final solution path is the path produced after removing hypothetical edges from the optimal path produced by a travelling salesman problem solver.

C2509.name: alternative path optimization approach
C2509.definition: Alternative path optimization approach is an approach in which a time limit is used, motivated by the possibility that a minimum-time approach covering all points of interest may still produce a travel time beyond the threshold beyond which cybersickness may occur.

C2510.name: time-constrained virtual tour optimization approach
C2510.definition: A time-constrained virtual tour optimization approach is an optimization approach that seeks an optimal path covering the maximum number of points of interest (POIs) while completing within a time threshold (TTH).

C2511.name: movement time
C2511.definition: Movement time is the duration of a user's movement in a virtual reality tour, and it should be kept within the time threshold for cybersickness.

C2512.name: experience time
C2512.definition: Experience time is the duration of a virtual reality tour that should be kept within the time threshold for cybersickness.

C2513.name: virtual world graph
C2513.definition: A virtual world graph is a graph all of whose vertices can be covered by a virtual tour optimized for minimum time.

C2514.name: traversal time
C2514.definition: Traversal time is the duration of a virtual tour, and traversal time can exceed a threshold above which cybersickness occurs.

C2515.name: movement speed
C2515.definition: Movement speed is a factor that recommended time thresholds may depend on, along with content.

C2516.name: tour
C2516.definition: A tour is a planned visit to points of interest to be completed within a given time threshold, and visiting every point of interest is neither mandatory nor always possible.

C2517.name: importance
C2517.definition: Importance is a positive real number assigned to each node, vertex, or point of interest, and larger values indicate higher importance for determining which nodes to cover within a time threshold.

C2518.name: importance function
C2518.definition: An importance function is a function that maps every node, vertex, or point of interest to a positive real number, with a larger number indicating higher importance.

C2519.name: total importance
C2519.definition: Total importance is the sum of the individual importances of the nodes in a path.

C2520.name: virtual reality path optimization model
C2520.definition: Virtual reality path optimization model is a model in which each node, a point of interest, has an importance and a waiting time, the maximum time a user requires to inspect or interact with the object at that node, and a path's total importance is maximized subject to total completion time plus waiting time not exceeding a time threshold.

C2521.name: waiting time
C2521.definition: Waiting time is the maximum time, represented by a positive real number, that a user requires to inspect or interact with the object at a node in a virtual reality path optimization model; total waiting time for a path is the sum of the nodes' waiting times.

C2522.name: waiting time function
C2522.definition: The waiting time function is a function in a virtual reality path optimization formulation that maps each node, a point of interest, to the positive real number representing the maximum time a user requires to inspect or interact with the object at that node.

C2523.name: total waiting time
C2523.definition: Total waiting time is the sum of the individual waiting times of the vertices of a path in the revised virtual reality path optimization problem.

C2524.name: total completion time
C2524.definition: Total completion time is the time T(P) + W(P) for a path P in a virtual reality path optimization problem.

C2525.name: vehicle routing problem with profit
C2525.definition: Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem, an operations research problem, in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit, the importance of the nodes, within a time constraint.

C2526.name: vehicle routing problem
C2526.definition: Vehicle routing problem (VRP) is an operations research problem.

C2527.name: operations research problem
C2527.definition: An operations research problem is a problem, such as the vehicle routing problem.

C2528.name: profit
C2528.definition: Profit is the importance of nodes in the vehicle routing problem with profit; a route maximizes it within a time constraint when not all nodes must be visited.

C2529.name: vehicle routing problem with profit solver
C2529.definition: A vehicle routing problem with profit solver is a solver that, given a graph and the importance and waiting time of each node, finds an optimal path within a chosen time threshold that maximizes the importance of the nodes covered while accounting for their maximum wait times.

C2530.name: optimal-path algorithm
C2530.definition: Optimal-path algorithm is an algorithm for a virtual environment that finds a path covering the most important points of interest while keeping total travel and waiting time below a threshold; it completes the input graph with shortest paths, replaces Euclidean edge weights with natural walking-model travel times, and expands the chosen path into original-graph paths.

C2531.name: fully connected graph
C2531.definition: A fully connected graph is a graph, not necessarily a complete graph, that serves as the input to an optimal-path algorithm for a virtual environment.

C2532.name: total exposure time
C2532.definition: Total exposure time is the traveling time plus the waiting time for a path.

C2533.name: modified optimal path
C2533.definition: A modified optimal path is the path an algorithm returns after modifying the optimal path from a solver by replacing each hypothetical edge between two vertices with the shortest path between those vertices in the original graph.

C2534.name: optimal path approach
C2534.definition: Optimal path approach is a virtual reality navigation optimization approach that identifies a path letting a user explore all points of interest in minimum time, and it can be used to propose optimized navigation paths to maximize user experience.

C2535.name: navigation optimization
C2535.definition: Navigation optimization is a VR navigation approach: its first approach identifies a path for exploring all points of interest in minimum time, and its second approach assigns relative importance and maximum wait times to point-of-interest nodes when that time exceeds a threshold.

C2536.name: Majuli River Island virtual tour
C2536.definition: The Majuli River Island virtual tour is a very large virtual world in which a path that lets a user explore all points of interest in minimum time may still take longer than a user's expected exposure duration.

C2537.name: walking-based exploration
C2537.definition: Walking-based exploration is a virtual reality exploration that a system-controlled virtual reality tour uses with a natural walking speed model to provide a realistic experience.

C2538.name: optimal path under a time constraint approach
C2538.definition: Optimal path under a time constraint approach is an approach for walking-based virtual reality exploration that sets an upper time limit, called the time threshold, and within that duration identifies an optimized navigation path covering the maximum number of most important points of interest, including interacting with or inspecting them and navigating between them, to maximize user experience.

C2539.name: covering
C2539.definition: Covering is the process in a virtual tour that involves interacting with or inspecting points of interest and navigating from one to another.

C2540.name: Auniati Satra
C2540.definition: Auniati Satra is a Satra on Majuli explored in a virtual reality tour.

C2541.name: relative importance
C2541.definition: Relative importance is the importance assigned to each point of interest node in a navigation optimization approach, from discussions with people.

C2542.name: maximum wait time
C2542.definition: Maximum wait time is the time a user needs to stop at a point of interest, inspect it, interact with it if possible, and resume navigation.

C2543.name: resource
C2543.definition: Resource is any hardware, software, manpower, or supporting infrastructure required for extended reality (XR), particularly virtual reality (VR).

C2544.name: manpower
C2544.definition: Manpower is one of the resources in extended reality, especially virtual reality, and can include staff for development, deployment, maintenance, and marketing.

C2545.name: supporting infrastructure
C2545.definition: Supporting infrastructure is a resource in extended reality, particularly virtual reality, and in virtual reality it includes rooms to store hardware setup, electricity supply, furniture, and network infrastructure.

C2546.name: development tool
C2546.definition: A development tool is one kind of software resource in extended reality and virtual reality.

C2547.name: software package
C2547.definition: A software package is a type of software resource that can be included in extended reality, and particularly virtual reality.

C2548.name: application package
C2548.definition: An application package is a software resource in extended reality, particularly virtual reality.

C2549.name: network infrastructure
C2549.definition: Network infrastructure is a type of supporting infrastructure in virtual reality, with examples such as network gear, switches, routers, wires, and servers.

C2550.name: network gear
C2550.definition: Network gear is an example of the network infrastructure included in the supporting infrastructure for virtual reality (VR) systems.

C2551.name: router
C2551.definition: A router is part of the network infrastructure included among supporting infrastructure in virtual reality.

C2552.name: wire
C2552.definition: A wire is an example of network infrastructure included in the supporting infrastructure for VR.

C2553.name: server
C2553.definition: A server is part of the network infrastructure included in the supporting infrastructure for extended reality (XR) and virtual reality (VR).

C2554.name: resource type
C2554.definition: Resource type is a kind of resource in extended reality (XR) that can be optimized separately.

C2555.name: client end
C2555.definition: The client end is the end used by the end user in VR, and its hardware requirements are the focus of resource optimization for the end user to have a good experience with affordable hardware resources.

C2556.name: hardware requirement
C2556.definition: Hardware requirement is the client-end hardware resource that virtual reality resource optimization generally focuses on so that end users can have a good experience with affordable hardware.

C2557.name: client-end hardware
C2557.definition: Client-end hardware is hardware needed to support rendering and computer graphics requirements and to manage related issues for a good virtual reality immersive experience.

C2558.name: interface object
C2558.definition: An interface object is one of the geometric objects, such as menus and icons, in the image of the whole interface displayed on a computer screen.

C2559.name: menu
C2559.definition: A menu is an interface object that is part of the image displayed on a computer screen.

C2560.name: binary representation
C2560.definition: Binary representation is a representation of zeros and ones that computers understand, unlike realistic representations perceived by humans.

C2561.name: representation
C2561.definition: Representation is used in computer graphics to represent objects or parts of an image, either as zeros and ones understood by computers or as realistic imagery perceived by humans.

C2562.name: synthesis
C2562.definition: Synthesis is one of the basic issues of computer graphics, in which objects are synthesized into a scene or parts of an image are synthesized to form complete realistic imagery.

C2563.name: generic graphics system
C2563.definition: A generic graphics system is a system with a host computer and a display, with a display controller, video memory, and a video controller between them; the CPU sends display commands to and may receive interaction data from the display controller, and the CPU passes rendering tasks to the display controller for execution in its GPU.

C2564.name: host computer
C2564.definition: A host computer is a part of a generic graphics system that communicates with the display controller by sending display commands and possibly receiving interaction data.

C2565.name: video memory
C2565.definition: Video memory is the dedicated part of a computer's overall memory hierarchy, typically part of a separate graphics unit, that stores a digital image generated by a display controller for a video controller to render on a screen.

C2566.name: video controller
C2566.definition: A video controller is a component of a generic graphics system that uses data stored in video memory to render an image on the display by converting the digital image into analog voltages that activate the pixels.

C2567.name: display command
C2567.definition: Display command is a command sent by the CPU of a generic graphics system to a display controller.

C2568.name: interaction data
C2568.definition: Interaction data is data that a host computer may receive from a display controller in a generic graphics system.

C2569.name: analog voltage
C2569.definition: Analog voltage is a voltage required to activate pixels on a screen when a video controller converts a digital image.

C2570.name: graphic device
C2570.definition: A graphic device is a device that is broadly of two types, determined by the method used for excitation of pixels: vector scan and raster scan devices.

C2571.name: vector scan device
C2571.definition: A vector scan device is a graphic device that views an image as continuous geometric primitives, such as lines and curves, and renders it by exciting only selected pixels, requiring high precision and making it costly and typically used in specialized settings.

C2572.name: geometric primitive
C2572.definition: A geometric primitive is a continuous part, such as a line or curve, that vector scan devices view an image as composed of.

C2573.name: line
C2573.definition: A line is a continuous geometric primitive, a geometric shape, that is rendered by coloring specific pixels.

C2574.name: curve
C2574.definition: A curve is a continuous geometric primitive that can be represented by a higher-degree polynomial or by smoothly joined lower-degree polynomial pieces in spline representation.

C2575.name: precision
C2575.definition: Precision is the level required by vector scan devices to target and excite specific pixels, and raster scan rendering requires less precision.

C2576.name: raster scan device
C2576.definition: A raster scan device is a graphic device that views an image as a whole pixel grid and activates all its pixels in sequence, typically left to right and top to bottom, using a frame buffer that stores each pixel's intensity.

C2577.name: pixel grid
C2577.definition: Pixel grid is a discrete coordinate system of pixels that a display device uses to render an image, and its points can only have integer coordinates.

C2578.name: scanning
C2578.definition: Scanning is the sequential activation of all pixels in a pixel grid, typically left to right and top to bottom, with inputs that make the pixels emit light at appropriate intensities.

C2579.name: raster scan rendering
C2579.definition: Raster scan rendering is a type of rendering in which pixels are excited in a left-to-right, top-to-bottom order.

C2580.name: vector scan rendering
C2580.definition: Vector scan rendering is a type of scan rendering that requires more precision and is much more expensive than raster scan rendering.

C2581.name: television
C2581.definition: Television is a commercial product that typically comprises a raster scan display.

C2582.name: frame buffer
C2582.definition: Frame buffer is a video memory component of a raster scan system that contains one memory location for each pixel, stores the pixel's intensity as a bit string, and has a size equal to the screen resolution.

C2583.name: memory location
C2583.definition: A memory location is a part of a frame buffer that stores the intensity value for one pixel as a bit string of 0s and 1s.

C2584.name: bit string
C2584.definition: A bit string is a string of 0s and 1s used by a frame buffer in a raster scan system to store a pixel's intensity.

C2585.name: screen resolution
C2585.definition: Screen resolution is the size of a screen in a raster scan device.

C2586.name: light-emitting element
C2586.definition: A light-emitting element is a part of a display pixel that emits light; in color displays, each pixel typically contains three such elements that emit red, green, and blue primary colors at different intensities.

C2587.name: screen refreshing
C2587.definition: Screen refreshing is the periodic re-excitation of pixels on a raster scan device, done to avoid fading and distortion and to keep the rendered image uniform even when the image is not changing.

C2588.name: refresh rate
C2588.definition: Refresh rate is the number of times a scene is refreshed per second on a screen, represented in hertz.

C2589.name: virtual reality screen
C2589.definition: Virtual reality screen is a screen in a virtual reality experience that is much closer to the eyes than a screen in typical computer usage.

C2590.name: color display
C2590.definition: Color display is a display in which each pixel contains multiple light-emitting elements, typically three that emit red, green, and blue primary colors at different intensities, sometimes four, and the eye perceives color from their mixed light.

C2591.name: red
C2591.definition: Red is one of the three primary colors whose light intensity, with green and blue, combines to produce the observed color in color displays and colored light-source models.

C2592.name: green
C2592.definition: Green is one of the red, green, and blue components of light intensity in a colored light source model and one of the primary colors emitted by a color display.

C2593.name: blue
C2593.definition: Blue is one of the red, green, and blue primary color components in a color display or colored light source model, whose intensity combines with the red and green components to form a perceived color.

C2594.name: primary color
C2594.definition: A primary color is one of the red, green, and blue colors emitted by color display pixels, and in a colored light source model each has a corresponding intensity component whose combination gives the perception of any color.

C2595.name: object representation
C2595.definition: Object representation is the first stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that defines the objects that form the rendered image in each object's local coordinate system.

C2596.name: color value
C2596.definition: Color value is a value stored in the frame buffer and computed by the display processor.

C2597.name: display processor
C2597.definition: A display processor is part of the display controller that computes the color values stored in the frame buffer in distinct stages.

C2598.name: graphics pipeline
C2598.definition: Graphics pipeline is the set of distinct stages in which the color values stored in the frame buffer are computed.

C2599.name: display mechanism
C2599.definition: A display mechanism is a mechanism driven through a video controller by the pixel intensity values that the 3D graphics pipeline stores in the frame buffer.

C2600.name: local coordinate system
C2600.definition: A local coordinate system is an object's own coordinate system in the 3D graphics pipeline, in which objects are defined before modeling transformation transforms them to the world coordinate system.

C2601.name: modeling transformation
C2601.definition: Modeling transformation is the second stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that transforms an object’s local coordinate description into the common world coordinate system so that objects can be assembled into a scene.

C2602.name: world coordinate system
C2602.definition: The world coordinate system is the common reference frame in which all scene points are defined and to which objects are transformed from local coordinate systems to construct the scene.

C2603.name: device coordinate system
C2603.definition: The device coordinate system is a continuous two-dimensional coordinate system used to define the viewport, equivalent to but not the same as the screen, into which window-to-viewport transformation maps the two-dimensional view coordinate system, and whose real-number coordinates are converted by scan conversion into a discrete pixel-grid description.

C2604.name: viewing pipeline
C2604.definition: The viewing pipeline is the fourth stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that selects a portion of a 3D scene and transforms it from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system through viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

C2605.name: viewing transformation
C2605.definition: Viewing transformation is a sub-stage of the viewing pipeline in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that defines the view coordinate system and maps a scene from the world coordinate system to the three-dimensional view coordinate system.

C2606.name: hidden surface removal
C2606.definition: Hidden surface removal is a GPU pixel-processing activity that identifies and removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are not visible from the viewer because they are occluded, using a depth buffer algorithm before rendering, to reduce computational complexity and support realistic image generation.

C2607.name: projection transformation
C2607.definition: Projection transformation is a sub-stage of the viewing pipeline in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that maps objects from a three-dimensional view coordinate system to a two-dimensional view plane or coordinate system.

C2608.name: window-to-viewport transformation
C2608.definition: Window-to-viewport transformation is a transformation in the viewing pipeline that maps a point from an abstract window representation to a device-specific viewport representation, transforming the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

C2609.name: three-dimensional view coordinate system
C2609.definition: Three-dimensional view coordinate system is a coordinate system that is defined from camera position, view-up point, and center of interest by three mutually orthogonal unit basis vectors and represents a scene after viewing transformation for clipping, hidden surface removal, and projection.

C2610.name: two-dimensional view coordinate system
C2610.definition: Two-dimensional view coordinate system is a coordinate system in the 3D graphics pipeline that projection transformation maps the 3D view coordinate system to and that window-to-viewport transformation maps to the device coordinate system.

C2611.name: screen coordinate system
C2611.definition: A screen coordinate system is one of the coordinate systems in a 3D graphics pipeline, the discrete pixel-grid coordinate system produced by scan conversion, in which each pixel coordinate is an integer.

C2612.name: three-dimensional object representation
C2612.definition: Three-dimensional object representation is a representation of objects in a synthesized environment that balances realistic rendering of their shape, size, and intricate detail with the space and time efficiency of the subsequent stages of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline.

C2613.name: pixel intensity
C2613.definition: Pixel intensity is the value between 0 and 1 that a lighting model computes for a pixel, which is mapped to a device-supported intensity whose bit pattern is stored in a frame buffer.

C2614.name: three-dimensional object representation technique
C2614.definition: A three-dimensional object representation technique is one of the different object representation techniques available; broad categories are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation, and the appropriate technique must be chosen for a particular problem.

C2615.name: point sample rendering
C2615.definition: Point sample rendering is the simplest broad category of three-dimensional object representation techniques, in which scene information is captured from the real world as raw data points on the scene, each carrying attributes, and the points are processed or mapped to pixels to generate a synthetic image, relying on real-world information rather than synthetically defining objects.

C2616.name: boundary representation
C2616.definition: Boundary representation is a broad category of three-dimensional object representation techniques in which objects are represented by the surfaces that define their boundary, with those surfaces being polygonal or curved. It comprises mesh, parametric, and implicit forms, with mesh as the most basic form.

C2617.name: space partitioning based representation
C2617.definition: Space partitioning based representation is a broad category of 3D object representation in which the space occupied by an object is divided into disjoint, non-overlapping regions, so any point inside the object lies in exactly one region and the object is represented by the occupied regions.

C2618.name: mesh
C2618.definition: Mesh is a basic boundary representation technique in computer graphics that represents a three-dimensional object's surface as connected polygons, usually triangles, and stores the vertices and connections needed to reconstruct it.

C2619.name: parametric representation
C2619.definition: Parametric representation is a form of boundary representation; higher-level boundary representations use it, and spline representation for curved surfaces or curves falls under it.

C2620.name: implicit representation
C2620.definition: Implicit representation is a boundary representation technique for three-dimensional objects, used in higher-level boundary representations.

C2621.name: octree method
C2621.definition: The octree method is a space partitioning based representation technique for 3D objects.

C2622.name: binary space partitioning method
C2622.definition: Binary space partitioning method is one of the space partitioning based representation techniques for three-dimensional objects.

C2623.name: constructive solid geometry method
C2623.definition: Constructive solid geometry method is a space partitioning based representation technique for three-dimensional objects.

C2624.name: data point
C2624.definition: A data point is a raw point in a scene that carries captured scene information as attributes in point sample rendering.

C2625.name: attribute
C2625.definition: An attribute is the captured scene information carried by a raw data point in point sample rendering.

C2626.name: three-dimensional range scanner
C2626.definition: A three-dimensional range scanner is an input sensor that captures real-world scene information as points in point sample rendering.

C2627.name: range finder
C2627.definition: A range finder is one of the input sensors used in point sample rendering to capture scene information from the real world as points.

C2628.name: synthetic image
C2628.definition: A synthetic image is an image generated in point sample rendering by processing or mapping captured points to pixels.

C2629.name: polygon
C2629.definition: A polygon is a geometric shape used in a polygonal mesh to approximate an object's boundary.

C2630.name: vertex list
C2630.definition: A vertex list is a list in mesh representation that stores all vertices and their connections.

C2631.name: edge list
C2631.definition: An edge list is a list in a mesh representation that stores all edges and their connections, allowing the object to be reconstructed.

C2632.name: triangle
C2632.definition: A triangle is a polygon that most graphics systems use to form meshes approximating object surfaces in rendered scenes.

C2633.name: simple convex polygon
C2633.definition: Simple convex polygon is a polygon that may be used, besides triangles, to approximate non-polygonal surfaces in mesh representation.

C2634.name: pipeline
C2634.definition: A pipeline is part of computer graphics, and all other representations are converted to a mesh representation at its end before objects are rendered.

C2635.name: spline representation
C2635.definition: Spline representation is a higher-level boundary representation for curves and curved surfaces, falling under parametric representation, that represents complex shapes that simple polygons or simple polynomial equations cannot represent by several smoothly joined lower-degree polynomial pieces, each a basis or blending function, instead of one complex polynomial.

C2636.name: curved surface
C2636.definition: A curved surface is a surface for which spline representation is a higher-level boundary representation that falls under parametric representation.

C2637.name: simple polygon
C2637.definition: A simple polygon is a surface representation that cannot represent complex surfaces with complex properties.

C2638.name: polynomial equation
C2638.definition: A polynomial equation is a simple representation that cannot represent complex surfaces with complex properties.

C2639.name: polynomial representation
C2639.definition: Polynomial representation is a representation of a curve by a polynomial, in which more complex curves are represented by higher-degree polynomials.

C2640.name: polynomial
C2640.definition: A polynomial is used to represent curves, with higher-degree polynomials for more complex curves, and in spline representations lower-degree polynomial pieces, most commonly third-order, compute points on curve segments.

C2641.name: polynomial piece
C2641.definition: A polynomial piece is one of several lower-degree polynomials that make up a complete curve in spline representation; it computes points on the curve segment it represents, and the pieces must join smoothly and satisfy certain geometric and other properties.

C2642.name: curve segment
C2642.definition: A curve segment is a portion of a complete curve in spline representation that is represented by one lower-degree polynomial piece, called a blending or basis function.

C2643.name: third-order polynomial
C2643.definition: A third-order polynomial is a form of polynomial most commonly used to construct spline curves.

C2644.name: spline curve
C2644.definition: A spline curve is a curve commonly constructed using third-order polynomials.

C2645.name: space partitioning tree
C2645.definition: A space partitioning tree is a hierarchical, tree-like structure that represents the space occupied by an object and is used to create a space partitioning representation.

C2646.name: fractal representation
C2646.definition: Fractal representation is a specialized representation method for self-repeating structures.

C2647.name: particle system representation
C2647.definition: Particle system representation is a specialized representation method for objects such as a waterfall that relies on the simulation of physical properties.

C2648.name: skeletal model
C2648.definition: A skeletal model is a specialized representation method for complex characters that captures their overall appearance and motion behavior, typically used in animation or computer animation to represent objects or complex characters.

C2649.name: computer animation
C2649.definition: Computer animation is a context in which skeletal models are typically used to represent objects or complex characters.

C2650.name: pipeline stage
C2650.definition: A pipeline stage is a part of a 3D graphics or render pipeline.

C2651.name: sub-stage
C2651.definition: A sub-stage is part of a 3D graphics pipeline implementation, and the order of sub-stages may differ from the stage-wise sequence used to show how computations occur.

C2652.name: intensity calculation
C2652.definition: Intensity calculation is a computation, although there is no computation as such related to it in the object representation stage of the 3D graphics pipeline.

C2653.name: object coordinate system
C2653.definition: An object coordinate system is an individual coordinate system local to an object in which that object's position and dimension are defined, and from which a modeling transformation places it in a common scene or world coordinate system.

C2654.name: dimension
C2654.definition: Dimension is part of an object's local or object coordinate system description and is defined in the object's own coordinate reference frame.

C2655.name: translation
C2655.definition: Translation is a basic transformation in modeling transformation, and in 2D it moves an object by translation amounts Tx and Ty along the x and y directions and is represented by a 3 by 3 matrix in the homogeneous coordinate system.

C2656.name: angle
C2656.definition: An angle is used in rotation in modeling transformation, where an object is rotated clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis.

C2657.name: axis
C2657.definition: Axis is used in a modeling transformation for rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around it.

C2658.name: scaling
C2658.definition: Scaling is a basic geometric transformation that increases or reduces an object's size using scaling factors along coordinate directions, and can be combined with other basic transformations to construct a scene.

C2659.name: shearing
C2659.definition: Shearing is a basic modeling transformation that changes an object's shape. In 2D homogeneous coordinates, it can be represented by a 3 by 3 matrix using shearing factors along the x and y directions.

C2660.name: matrix
C2660.definition: A matrix is typically used to represent a transformation in a homogeneous coordinate system, where one extra dimension is added, and 2D and 3D transformations can be represented by 3 by 3 and 4 by 4 matrices.

C2661.name: homogeneous coordinate system
C2661.definition: A homogeneous coordinate system is a coordinate system in which one extra dimension is added so that a two-dimensional transformation can be represented by a 3 by 3 matrix and a three-dimensional transformation by a 4 by 4 matrix.

C2662.name: two-dimensional transformation
C2662.definition: Two-dimensional transformation is a transformation that can be represented by a 3 by 3 matrix in a homogeneous coordinate system.

C2663.name: three-dimensional transformation
C2663.definition: A three-dimensional transformation is a transformation that can be represented by a 4 by 4 matrix in a homogeneous coordinate system, where one extra dimension is added.

C2664.name: translation amount
C2664.definition: Translation amount is an amount along the x or y direction that is used to represent two-dimensional translation in the homogeneous coordinate system by a 3 by 3 matrix.

C2665.name: rotation angle
C2665.definition: Rotation angle is an angle used with 3 by 3 matrices to represent two-dimensional rotation in a homogeneous coordinate system.

C2666.name: scaling factor
C2666.definition: A scaling factor is a factor along the x or y direction that is used in a 3 by 3 matrix to represent two-dimensional scaling in a homogeneous coordinate system.

C2667.name: shearing factor
C2667.definition: A shearing factor is one of the factors used in 3 by 3 matrices representing two-dimensional shearing along the x and y directions in a homogeneous coordinate system.

C2668.name: column vector
C2668.definition: A column vector is a representation of a point in an object's local coordinate system that is multiplied by a transformation matrix to transform the point to the world coordinate system.

C2669.name: transformation matrix
C2669.definition: A transformation matrix is a matrix that, when multiplied by a point vector, transforms the point from one coordinate system to another and is multiplied into a composite transformation matrix in right-to-left order of application.

C2670.name: matrix multiplication
C2670.definition: Matrix multiplication is used to transform a point in an object's local coordinate system into a new point in the world coordinate system by multiplying a column vector for the point by a transformation matrix, and it is not commutative.

C2671.name: composite transformation matrix
C2671.definition: A composite transformation matrix is a transformation matrix formed by multiplying individual transformation matrices, arranged right to left in the order the transformations are applied, to transform vertices or points when multiple basic transformations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, or shearing, are required.

C2672.name: world coordinate scene
C2672.definition: A world coordinate scene is a scene in which transformed vertices are obtained by multiplying vertices in a local coordinate system by a transformation matrix, using a composite matrix when multiple basic transformations are required.

C2673.name: basic transformation
C2673.definition: Basic transformation is a geometric or modeling transformation, such as translation, rotation, scaling, or shearing, for constructing a world coordinate scene.

C2674.name: scaling matrix
C2674.definition: A scaling matrix is a matrix that has Sx, the scaling factor along the x direction, and Sy, the scaling factor along the y direction.

C2675.name: x-direction scaling factor
C2675.definition: The x-direction scaling factor is the scaling factor along the x direction in a scaling matrix.

C2676.name: y-direction scaling factor
C2676.definition: Y-direction scaling factor is the scaling factor along the y direction in a scaling matrix.

C2677.name: translation matrix
C2677.definition: A translation matrix is a matrix with Tx and Ty, the translations along the x-axis and y-axis, and, when translation is applied after scaling, it is placed to the left of the scaling matrix and multiplied to obtain the composite transformation matrix.

C2678.name: translation along the x-axis
C2678.definition: Translation along the x-axis is the value in a translation matrix used to move an object along the x-axis.

C2679.name: translation along the y-axis
C2679.definition: Translation along the y-axis is a value in a translation matrix that gives the movement of a vertex along the y-axis.

C2680.name: order of application
C2680.definition: The order of application is the sequence in which individual transformations are applied, determining the placement of the transformation matrices in a composite transformation matrix: the first-applied matrix is rightmost and each later matrix is placed to the left. Because matrix multiplication is not commutative, an incorrect sequence may produce an incorrect transformed result.

C2681.name: transformed vertex
C2681.definition: A transformed vertex is a vertex in a world coordinate scene that is obtained by multiplying a current vertex by a transformation matrix.

C2682.name: computer graphics pipeline
C2682.definition: The computer graphics pipeline is a staged process that includes object definition, scene construction, color computation using lighting or shading models, view transformation, and scan conversion or rendering.

C2683.name: color computation
C2683.definition: Color computation is the third stage of the computer graphics pipeline that uses lighting or shading models to assign colors to objects in a scene.

C2684.name: shading model
C2684.definition: A shading model is an approximation of the color-assignment methods used by lighting models, which it relies on to assign colors to objects in the computer graphics pipeline while reducing computation without compromising the quality of experience.

C2685.name: depth
C2685.definition: Depth is the viewer's distance with respect to each pixel in a two-dimensional projection of a three-dimensional scene.

C2686.name: continuous intensity value
C2686.definition: A continuous intensity value is essentially a real number, typically within the range 0 to 1 and typically normalized, that lighting models use to compute colors and that is mapped to a discrete value.

C2687.name: discrete value
C2687.definition: A discrete value is a computer-supported value to which continuous intensity values in lighting models are mapped.

C2688.name: surface point
C2688.definition: A surface point is a point on a surface in computer graphics at which light falls directly or, in some cases, after reflection and is reflected to a viewer's eye, the reflected intensity determining the perceived color.

C2689.name: reflected light
C2689.definition: Reflected light is light incident on a surface point and reflected to a viewer's eye, with its intensity determining the surface point's perceived color.
