C2690.name: simple lighting model
C2690.definition: Simple lighting model is a lighting model that models the light intensity reaching the viewer from a surface point as the sum of ambient light intensity and the diffuse and specular reflection intensities of direct light.

C2691.name: ambient light intensity
C2691.definition: Ambient light intensity is a light intensity falling on a surface point, and in a simple lighting model it is one of the three intensities summed to give the light intensity reaching a viewer.

C2692.name: diffuse reflection intensity
C2692.definition: Diffuse reflection intensity is one of the three light intensities in a simple lighting model, whose sum is the light intensity reaching a viewer from a surface point.

C2693.name: specular reflection intensity
C2693.definition: Specular reflection intensity is one of the three intensities in the simple lighting model that are summed to give the light intensity reaching the viewer from a surface point, specifically the specular reflection intensity of direct light.

C2694.name: direct light
C2694.definition: Direct light is the light in a simple lighting model whose diffuse and specular reflection intensities are summed with ambient light intensity to give the intensity reaching a viewer from a surface point.

C2695.name: diffuse reflection component
C2695.definition: Diffuse reflection component is direct light reflected in a diffuse manner from a surface in a simple lighting model, computed from the diffuse coefficient, source intensity, and the dot product of surface normal and light source direction, or zero when that dot product is not positive.

C2696.name: specular reflection component
C2696.definition: Specular reflection component is light in a simple lighting model that comes from a light source and is reflected with a specular effect, producing a shiny bright spot.

C2697.name: reflected light intensity
C2697.definition: Reflected light intensity is the intensity of light reflected from a surface and reaching the viewer's eye, a fraction of the incident light intensity determined by the surface's reflection coefficient.

C2698.name: incident light intensity
C2698.definition: Incident light intensity is the light intensity that, together with a surface's reflectivity, determines the intensity of light reflected from the surface and reaching the viewer's eye.

C2699.name: reflection coefficient
C2699.definition: A reflection coefficient is a surface property that determines the fraction of incident light intensity reflected from a surface and reaching the viewer's eye. In the simple lighting model, the ambient, diffuse, and specular coefficients range from 0.0 to 1.0, where values near 0.0 are dull and values near 1.0 are shiny.

C2700.name: specular component
C2700.definition: The specular component is the part of a simple lighting model that is computed for direct light with the Phong approximate model as Ks Is (V·r)^Ns, or 0 when V·r is not greater than 0.

C2701.name: ambient reflection coefficient
C2701.definition: Ambient reflection coefficient (Ka) is a reflection coefficient in a simple lighting model for ambient light, used to compute the ambient component of reflected light intensity by multiplying the ambient light intensity falling on a surface point by Ka.

C2702.name: diffuse reflection coefficient
C2702.definition: Diffuse reflection coefficient is a reflection coefficient in a simple lighting model for diffuse reflection of direct light, used to compute the diffuse reflection component.

C2703.name: specular reflection coefficient
C2703.definition: Specular reflection coefficient is a reflection coefficient in a simple lighting model that is used for specular reflection of direct light.

C2704.name: ambient component
C2704.definition: The ambient component is the component of reflected light intensity computed by multiplying the ambient light intensity falling on a surface point by the reflection coefficient for ambient light.

C2705.name: source light intensity
C2705.definition: Source light intensity is a factor used in computing the diffuse and specular reflection components of direct light.

C2706.name: dot product
C2706.definition: The dot product is a vector computation used in the simple lighting model and by the GPU to compute vertex color.

C2707.name: surface normal vector
C2707.definition: The surface normal vector is a vector at a surface point from which light is reflected, used in computing diffuse reflection and the ideal specular reflection direction.

C2708.name: light source direction vector
C2708.definition: A light source direction vector is a vector used with a surface normal vector to compute a diffuse reflection component and an ideal specular reflection direction vector.

C2709.name: Phong model
C2709.definition: The Phong model is an approximate model used to compute the specular component.

C2710.name: specular angle
C2710.definition: Specular angle is the angle in the specular calculation between the viewer direction vector and the ideal specular reflection direction vector, the direction a mirror would reflect the light, and its cosine is the dot product of the two vectors.

C2711.name: viewer direction vector
C2711.definition: Viewer direction vector is a direction vector used in specular calculation, where it and the ideal specular reflection direction vector form the angle phi.

C2712.name: ideal specular reflection direction vector
C2712.definition: The ideal specular reflection direction vector is the direction a mirror would reflect light, equal to twice the dot product of the light source direction vector and the surface normal vector times the surface normal vector, minus the light source direction vector.

C2713.name: radial intensity attenuation factor
C2713.definition: Radial intensity attenuation factor is a lighting factor that accounts for the decrease in light intensity with distance from a light source to a surface point, typically computed as an inverse quadratic function of that distance using coefficients a0, a1, and a2, that can be varied for a more realistic effect.

C2714.name: inverse quadratic function
C2714.definition: An inverse quadratic function is a function of the distance between a light source and a surface point, used to compute the radial intensity attenuation factor, with coefficients that can be varied for a more realistic effect.

C2715.name: coefficient
C2715.definition: Coefficient is an adjustable value used in the radial intensity attenuation factor to make the diminishing of light intensity with distance more realistic.

C2716.name: angular intensity attenuation
C2716.definition: Angular intensity attenuation is an attenuation factor in a simple lighting model, used primarily to generate spotlight effects by making elements outside the spotlight region darker and by multiplying the sum of the diffuse and specular reflection components, together with radial attenuation, while leaving the I_M intensity component unchanged.

C2717.name: spotlight effect
C2717.definition: A spotlight effect is an effect in which elements inside the spotlight region are visible or brightly visible and elements outside the spotlight zone are darker.

C2718.name: spotlight region
C2718.definition: Spotlight region is the angular range in a spotlight effect, defined by theta, in which elements are visible or brightly visible and outside which they are darker.

C2719.name: angular intensity attenuation factor
C2719.definition: An angular intensity attenuation factor is a factor in a lighting model that, in its commonly used form, multiplies the sum of the diffuse and specular reflection components by zero for a surface point outside the angular limit of a spotlight cone and by the cosine of phi to a positive angular attenuation exponent inside it.

C2720.name: angular limit
C2720.definition: Angular limit is the range of the spotlight cone, outside of which a surface point's angular intensity attenuation factor is zero.

C2721.name: angular attenuation exponent
C2721.definition: An angular attenuation exponent (A1) is a positive exponent used in a spotlight's angular intensity attenuation factor, specifically the power to which the cosine of phi is raised for a surface point within the spotlight cone's angular limit.

C2722.name: intensity component
C2722.definition: Intensity component is the I_M component of the simple lighting model modified for radial and angular intensity attenuation, and it is left unchanged.

C2723.name: colored light source model
C2723.definition: A colored light source model is a model in which emitted light intensity is a three-element red, green, and blue vector rather than a single component, and its components are computed individually and combined to give the perception of any color.

C2724.name: source intensity
C2724.definition: Source intensity is a three-element vector in a colored light source model, with individual red, green, and blue components whose combination gives the perception of any color.

C2725.name: vector
C2725.definition: A vector is used to represent three components or coordinates, such as the red, green, and blue components of light intensity or the position of a 3D point.

C2726.name: single-light-source lighting model
C2726.definition: A single-light-source lighting model is a lighting model that, for n light sources, gives the light at a point as ambient light plus each light source's contribution, calculated separately and added, with red, green, and blue components computed separately for colored light sources.

C2727.name: colored light source
C2727.definition: A colored light source is a light source whose contribution in a lighting model is computed separately for the red, green, and blue components.

C2728.name: intensity mapping
C2728.definition: Intensity mapping is the mapping in which a lighting-model pixel intensity, which can be any value in an infinite range between 0 and 1, is mapped to the nearest finite device-supported table intensity, so the corresponding bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer.

C2729.name: 8-bit display
C2729.definition: An 8-bit display is a display that supports 256 intensity values per pixel.

C2730.name: device-supported intensity value
C2730.definition: Device-supported intensity value is one of the finite intensity levels supported by a display, determined from minimum and maximum values by successive multiplication by a factor r, because humans perceive relative changes, and used to map lighting-model pixel intensities to frame-buffer bit patterns.

C2731.name: minimum device-supported intensity value
C2731.definition: Minimum device-supported intensity value is the minimum of the device-supported intensity values, measured with a photometer and used to determine the successive device-supported intensity values.

C2732.name: photometer
C2732.definition: A photometer is used to measure the minimum device-supported intensity value.

C2733.name: maximum intensity value
C2733.definition: The maximum intensity value is the known intensity value, 1, used in the determination of device-supported intensity values.

C2734.name: multiplicative factor
C2734.definition: Multiplicative factor is a factor used to calculate successive device-supported intensity values from an initial intensity, based on human perception of relative rather than absolute intensity changes.

C2735.name: psychophysiological property
C2735.definition: Psychophysiological property is a property that humans perceive relative changes between two intensity values rather than absolute changes in intensity values.

C2736.name: relative change
C2736.definition: Relative change is a change between two intensity values, rather than an absolute change in intensity values, that humans perceive.

C2737.name: absolute change
C2737.definition: Absolute change is a change in intensity values, rather than a relative change between two intensity values.

C2738.name: table
C2738.definition: A table is a store that holds calculated device-supported intensity values and their assigned bit patterns, used to map a lighting-model pixel intensity to the nearest stored intensity and the corresponding bit pattern.

C2739.name: bit pattern
C2739.definition: A bit pattern is an assigned pattern for a device-supported intensity value that is stored in the frame buffer at a pixel location.

C2740.name: two-dimensional display
C2740.definition: A two-dimensional display is a view plane onto which a selected portion of a three-dimensional scene is projected.

C2741.name: three-dimensional viewing transformation
C2741.definition: Three-dimensional viewing transformation is a transformation from 3D world coordinates to 3D view coordinates that simulates looking at a scene with a camera. After a view coordinate system is defined from camera parameters, it is performed by translation and rotation using a composite transformation matrix.

C2742.name: camera viewing mechanism
C2742.definition: A camera viewing mechanism is a mechanism used in a 3D viewing transformation to simulate looking at a scene.

C2743.name: camera parameters
C2743.definition: Camera parameters are the camera position, view-up point, and center of interest, also called the look-at point, used to set up the view coordinate system for a 3D viewing transformation.

C2744.name: origin vector
C2744.definition: Origin vector is a vector representing the camera position in the world coordinate system and one of the camera parameters used to set up the view coordinate system.

C2745.name: view-up point
C2745.definition: View-up point is a camera parameter, represented as a vector, whose vector from the camera origin gives the view-up direction used to set up a view coordinate system.

C2746.name: center of interest
C2746.definition: Center of interest is a camera parameter that, with the camera position, determines the looking direction used to set up the view coordinate system.

C2747.name: unit basis vector
C2747.definition: A unit basis vector is one of three mutually orthogonal vectors that define a view coordinate system.

C2748.name: looking direction
C2748.definition: Looking direction is a direction in a view coordinate system that is opposite the unit basis vector N, which is obtained from the camera origin vector and the look-at point.

C2749.name: view-up direction
C2749.definition: View-up direction is the direction of the unit basis vector V in the view coordinate system, and V is obtained from the vector from the origin point to the view-up point.

C2750.name: origin point
C2750.definition: An origin point is a point used to define a view coordinate system, from which the vector to the view-up point is obtained for the view-up basis vector V.

C2751.name: cross product
C2751.definition: The cross product is used to obtain U, the unit basis vector of a view coordinate system, from the unit basis vectors V and N.

C2752.name: view-coordinate axis vector
C2752.definition: A view-coordinate axis vector is a vector used with its scalar components to form the transformation matrices that translate and rotate world-coordinate points into view coordinates.

C2753.name: scalar component
C2753.definition: A scalar component is a component of a view-coordinate axis vector used to form matrices that transform world coordinates into view coordinates.

C2754.name: view volume
C2754.definition: A view volume is a three-dimensional region in the scene that defines the portion of the scene projected onto the view plane; objects inside it are projected, and objects outside it are discarded. For parallel projection it is a rectangular parallelepiped, and for perspective projection a frustum, with one face or side serving as the clipping window.

C2755.name: perspective projection
C2755.definition: Perspective projection is a projection type in which projectors from an object in a three-dimensional view coordinate system to the view plane are not parallel but converge at a center of projection; the view volume is a frustum, and realistic rendering is produced for realistic scenes.

C2756.name: center of projection
C2756.definition: A center of projection is the point where projectors from an object in the 3D view coordinate system to the view plane converge in perspective projection, or the point at infinity in parallel projection.

C2757.name: parallel projection
C2757.definition: Parallel projection is a projection type in which the projectors from an object to the view plane are parallel to each other, so their center of projection is at infinity and they never meet.

C2758.name: frustum
C2758.definition: A frustum is the view volume for perspective projection, with one face or side serving as the clipping window on which objects inside it are projected.

C2759.name: naive clipping method
C2759.definition: The naive clipping method is a method that computes the intersection of view volume boundaries with object boundaries, a calculation that is computationally intensive for arbitrarily shaped view volumes such as frustums.

C2760.name: canonical view volume
C2760.definition: Canonical view volume is a normalized cube into which any arbitrarily defined view volume for parallel or perspective projection is converted to simplify pipeline computations.

C2761.name: point vector
C2761.definition: A point vector is a vector in a three-dimensional view coordinate system that is multiplied by a projection matrix when computing a parallel or perspective projection.

C2762.name: parallel projection matrix
C2762.definition: A parallel projection matrix is a four-by-four matrix, in which D is the distance of the clipping window from the origin, that is used to compute a parallel projection by multiplying a point vector in the 3D view coordinate system and dividing the obtained homogeneous coordinate values by w, typically not 1, to obtain Cartesian x, y, and z values.

C2763.name: origin
C2763.definition: The origin is a point in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system that is used for the distance of the clipping window and is typically assumed to be the center of projection.

C2764.name: homogeneous coordinate value
C2764.definition: A homogeneous coordinate value is a coordinate value obtained when a 3D point vector is multiplied by a parallel projection matrix or a perspective projection matrix, and it is divided by the homogeneous factor w to obtain Cartesian coordinates.

C2765.name: homogeneous factor
C2765.definition: The homogeneous factor is a factor, typically not equal to 1, by which obtained homogeneous coordinate values are divided to obtain Cartesian coordinates in parallel and perspective projection.

C2766.name: cartesian coordinate
C2766.definition: A cartesian coordinate is one of the x, y, or z values obtained by dividing homogeneous coordinate values by the homogeneous factor w when computing a projection of a point vector in a three-dimensional view coordinate system.

C2767.name: perspective projection matrix
C2767.definition: A perspective projection matrix is a matrix used to compute a perspective projection by multiplying a point vector in the 3D view coordinate system, where D is the distance from the clipping window to the center of projection, typically assumed at the origin; the obtained homogeneous coordinate values are then divided by the homogeneous factor w.

C2768.name: viewport
C2768.definition: A viewport is a portion of the final screen in device space, not on the view plane, where a scene is rendered, defined relative to the display origin and dimensions in a continuous coordinate system.

C2769.name: device space
C2769.definition: Device space is the final screen or display coordinate space in which viewports are defined and triangles are represented before mapping to discrete space.

C2770.name: window point
C2770.definition: A window point is a point in the abstract window representation, given as (Wx, Wy), that is mapped by the window-to-viewport transformation to a viewport point.

C2771.name: viewport point
C2771.definition: Viewport point is a point in a device-specific viewport representation, mapped from an abstract window point by the window-to-viewport transformation.

C2772.name: window-to-viewport transformation matrix
C2772.definition: The window-to-viewport transformation matrix is a three-by-three matrix whose Sx and Sy are defined in terms of window and viewport dimensions, and whose Tx and Ty are computed from Sx, Sy, and those dimensions. Multiplying a window point vector by the matrix yields a homogeneous coordinate representation, whose Cartesian point is obtained by dividing by the homogeneous factor W.

C2773.name: homogeneous coordinate representation
C2773.definition: Homogeneous coordinate representation is a point representation with a homogeneous factor W, in which a Cartesian point is obtained by dividing the represented point by W.

C2774.name: cartesian point
C2774.definition: A cartesian point is a point obtained by dividing a point in homogeneous coordinate representation by the homogeneous factor W.

C2775.name: computational complexity
C2775.definition: Computational complexity is a rendering characteristic that clipping and hidden surface removal reduce and that rich, realistic, interactive virtual reality content increases.

C2776.name: viewer position
C2776.definition: Viewer position is a particular position from which hidden surface removal identifies objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are not visible because they are occluded before rendering.

C2777.name: occlusion
C2777.definition: Occlusion is objects, surfaces, or surface points not being visible from a particular viewer position.

C2778.name: view pipeline
C2778.definition: View pipeline is the part of the 3D graphics pipeline after the viewing transformation that includes clipping and hidden surface removal in the 3D view coordinate system, projection transformation from the 3D view coordinate system to the 2D view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the 2D view coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

C2779.name: continuous coordinate system
C2779.definition: A continuous coordinate system is a coordinate system whose coordinate values can be any real number.

C2780.name: mapping algorithm
C2780.definition: A mapping algorithm is an algorithm used in scan conversion that transforms continuous two-dimensional viewport coordinates into a discrete pixel-grid coordinate system by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels.

C2781.name: viewport coordinates
C2781.definition: Viewport coordinates are the continuous two-dimensional coordinate values in the device coordinate system used to define a viewport, mapped to discrete pixel-grid coordinates by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels during scan conversion.

C2782.name: pixel-grid coordinate system
C2782.definition: Pixel-grid coordinate system is a discrete coordinate system into which scan conversion transforms continuous two-dimensional viewport coordinates by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels, so a line is rendered by coloring specific pixels.

C2783.name: point rendering
C2783.definition: Point rendering is a rounding method that maps a point with real-number coordinates in device space to the nearest integer coordinate values in discrete space, suitable for points but not for other geometric shapes such as lines or circles.

C2784.name: real-number coordinate
C2784.definition: A real-number coordinate is a coordinate used to represent a point in point rendering before the point is mapped to the nearest integer coordinate values.

C2785.name: integer coordinate value
C2785.definition: An integer coordinate value is a coordinate value in discrete space to which a point's real-number coordinate is mapped in point rendering by taking the nearest integer.

C2786.name: discrete space
C2786.definition: Discrete space is the integer-coordinate space in point rendering into which real-number point coordinates are rounded from device space.

C2787.name: rounding
C2787.definition: Rounding is a method in point rendering that maps real-number coordinates to the nearest integer coordinate values, moving a point from device space to discrete space, and is suitable for points, not for other geometric shapes.

C2788.name: circle
C2788.definition: A circle is one of the geometric shapes for which efficient rendering algorithms exist.

C2789.name: line rendering
C2789.definition: Line rendering is a method for drawing a line by identifying the pixels that approximately represent it, and efficient methods use integer arithmetic to avoid floating-point operations.

C2790.name: floating-point operation
C2790.definition: A floating-point operation is a computer operation, such as rounding, division, and sometimes floating-point multiplication, that slows down a computer and is avoided in efficient line rendering.

C2791.name: line-rendering algorithm
C2791.definition: A line-rendering algorithm is an algorithm that identifies the pixels that approximately represent a line, and efficient versions aim to avoid floating-point operations.

C2792.name: Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm
C2792.definition: Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is a line-rendering algorithm that identifies the pixels approximating a line segment from its endpoints while using integer arithmetic and avoiding floating-point operations.

C2793.name: line slope
C2793.definition: Line slope is a value of a line segment used by the Bresenham line-drawing algorithm, for line slopes between -1 and +1, with a minor modification needed for other slopes.

C2794.name: line endpoint
C2794.definition: A line endpoint is one of the two x and y coordinate inputs that a line-drawing algorithm uses to approximate a line segment.

C2795.name: line segment
C2795.definition: A line segment is a line specified by two endpoints and rendered as a set of pixels that approximate it.

C2796.name: x coordinate
C2796.definition: An x coordinate is a coordinate of an endpoint in a line-drawing algorithm, used to compute delta x and initialize x.

C2797.name: y coordinate
C2797.definition: A y coordinate is one of the coordinates of an endpoint or pixel used in a line-drawing algorithm.

C2798.name: delta x
C2798.definition: Delta x is the difference between the x coordinates of two line endpoints, computed in Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm.

C2799.name: delta y
C2799.definition: Delta y is the difference between the y coordinates of the two endpoints in Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm.

C2800.name: decision parameter
C2800.definition: Decision parameter is a value in a line-drawing algorithm for line slopes between -1 and +1 that is computed as twice delta y minus delta x and used to decide whether the next pixel increments x only or both x and y.

C2801.name: integer arithmetic
C2801.definition: Integer arithmetic is a type of simple arithmetic, involving operations such as addition and multiplication, that is used in a line-drawing algorithm and can be performed by GPU cores.

C2802.name: division
C2802.definition: Division is a floating-point operation avoided in line rendering.

C2803.name: floating-point multiplication
C2803.definition: Floating-point multiplication is a floating-point operation that Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm avoids in favor of integer arithmetic.

C2804.name: interactive graphics
C2804.definition: Interactive graphics is a kind of graphics in which each user input can change the scene and require redrawing a large number of line segments.

C2805.name: ellipse
C2805.definition: An ellipse is one of the geometric shapes for which efficient rendering algorithms exist.

C2806.name: filled area
C2806.definition: A filled area is a geometric shape for which efficient rendering algorithms exist, and those algorithms are more complex than line rendering.

C2807.name: distortion
C2807.definition: Distortion is a perceptible effect, such as aliasing, that may occur in an original shape after scan conversion when pixels are close to, rather than exactly at, points on the original shape, and it may become visible with a change in resolution, reducing the quality of experience.

C2808.name: anti-aliasing
C2808.definition: Anti-aliasing is the additional operations that use complex algorithms to remove or reduce the distortion caused by aliasing so that the end effect is better. It adds further computation to the overall computation of pixel intensities along with other rendering stages.

C2809.name: rendering stage
C2809.definition: A rendering stage is one of the stages in the overall computation of pixel intensities.

C2810.name: dynamic scene
C2810.definition: A dynamic scene is a scene that changes with user input.

C2811.name: graphics library
C2811.definition: A graphics library is a library that provides application programming interfaces (APIs) to deal with lower-level tasks, eliminating the need to know every detail of the underlying system or platform, such as processor, memory, or operating system detail, to build a graphics application.

C2812.name: argument
C2812.definition: An argument is an appropriate item used to invoke a graphics library function to perform a specific task.

C2813.name: graphics application
C2813.definition: A graphics application is an application that can be built using APIs provided by graphics libraries, which eliminate the need to know underlying system or platform details.

C2814.name: layered virtual reality software architecture
C2814.definition: Layered virtual reality software architecture is a VR software architecture arranged from top to bottom as an application layer, SDK layer, VR engine or game engine layer, native rendering library layer, operating system layer, and hardware layer, with each upper layer calling or sitting on the layer below.

C2815.name: operating system layer
C2815.definition: An operating system layer is a layer in a layered virtual reality software architecture that sits on top of the hardware layer and beneath the native rendering library layer.

C2816.name: hardware layer
C2816.definition: The hardware layer is a layer of a layered virtual reality software architecture that is at the bottom, below the operating system layer, and includes the graphics processing unit (GPU).

C2817.name: layered virtual reality system
C2817.definition: A layered virtual reality system is a virtual reality system in which a software development kit (SDK) layer gives a developer access to a virtual reality engine that lets the developer deal with graphics through application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by native rendering libraries without directly accessing the native rendering libraries.

C2818.name: memory element
C2818.definition: Memory element is a memory part of a separate graphics card.

C2819.name: graphics operation
C2819.definition: A graphics operation is a highly parallel operation whose inherent parallelism a graphics processing unit exploits in computer graphics and virtual reality.

C2820.name: multicore system
C2820.definition: A multicore system is a system in which many cores, each capable only of simple integer and floating-point arithmetic, work simultaneously on a single instruction and produce data simultaneously.

C2821.name: core
C2821.definition: A core is one of the many parts of a typically multicore GPU that is capable only of simple integer and floating-point arithmetic and works simultaneously on one instruction.

C2822.name: floating-point arithmetic
C2822.definition: Floating-point arithmetic is one of the simple arithmetic operations, alongside integer arithmetic, that GPU cores can perform.

C2823.name: instruction
C2823.definition: An instruction is what many GPU cores work on simultaneously and produce data simultaneously.

C2824.name: streaming multiprocessor
C2824.definition: A streaming multiprocessor is a unit in a GPU made of several cores, each capable of simple integer and floating-point arithmetic, that work simultaneously on one single instruction, with a parallel data cache.

C2825.name: host
C2825.definition: A host is one of the components of a GPU, along with input assemblers and a thread execution manager.

C2826.name: input assembler
C2826.definition: Input assembler is a part of the broad organization of a GPU.

C2827.name: thread execution manager
C2827.definition: A thread execution manager is a part of a GPU that allocates work to many streaming multiprocessors.

C2828.name: parallel data cache
C2828.definition: A parallel data cache is a part of a streaming multiprocessor in a GPU.

C2829.name: texture storage
C2829.definition: Texture storage is high-speed storage on a graphics card that holds texture images, or predefined surface colors, which pixel calculations access to replace computed pixel colors with texture colors.

C2830.name: global memory
C2830.definition: Global memory is a memory with which elements of a GPU exchange data through load and store information.

C2831.name: vertex vector
C2831.definition: A vertex vector is a per-vertex vector that a GPU multiplies by a transformation matrix to produce transformed triangles from local coordinates to world coordinates in real-time rendering.

C2832.name: local coordinates
C2832.definition: Local coordinates are the coordinates from which objects or vertices are transformed or transferred to world coordinates in rendering and scene creation.

C2833.name: real-time rendering
C2833.definition: Real-time rendering is a process that requires millions of vertices to be processed per second, and even more for a realistic immersive experience.

C2834.name: vertex color
C2834.definition: Vertex color is a color computed by a GPU simultaneously for multiple vertices by performing vector dot products.

C2835.name: projection stage
C2835.definition: Projection stage is a GPU stage that combines viewing, projection, and viewport transformations in a composite matrix multiplied with vertices, producing a stream of triangles in screen or device coordinates ready to be converted to pixels.

C2836.name: viewport transformation
C2836.definition: Viewport transformation is a transformation in the GPU projection stage that is combined with viewing and projection transformations in a composite matrix multiplied with vertices.

C2837.name: composite matrix
C2837.definition: A composite matrix is a matrix that combines viewing, projection, and viewport transformations in the GPU projection stage and is multiplied with vertices to produce triangles in screen or device coordinates.

C2838.name: coordinate space
C2838.definition: Coordinate space is a continuous space of screen or device coordinates in which a stream of triangles is ready to be converted to pixels.

C2839.name: pixel processing stage
C2839.definition: Pixel processing stage is a GPU stage that performs surface texturing and hidden surface removal.

C2840.name: surface texturing
C2840.definition: Surface texturing is an activity in the GPU pixel processing stage that, in its simplest method, applies stored texture images to the geometry being rendered by replacing the computed pixel color with the texture color at the corresponding texture point.

C2841.name: texture color
C2841.definition: Texture color is the color at the corresponding texture point in a stored texture image, used to replace the computed pixel color in the simplest surface texturing method.

C2842.name: texture point
C2842.definition: A texture point is a corresponding point in a stored texture image whose texture color replaces a rendered pixel's computed color in the simplest surface texturing method.

C2843.name: memory cache
C2843.definition: Memory cache is used in pixel processing to reduce access time to texture storage on a graphics card, because nearby pixels tend to access nearby texture image locations.

C2844.name: depth buffer algorithm
C2844.definition: A depth buffer algorithm is an algorithm used in hidden surface removal that uses a dedicated depth buffer to store the depth information for points in a three-dimensional scene before projection onto a two-dimensional plane, where depth is the viewer's distance with respect to each pixel.

C2845.name: depth buffer
C2845.definition: A depth buffer is a dedicated buffer used in hidden surface removal that stores the depth information for points in a three-dimensional scene before projection onto a two-dimensional plane, where depth is the viewer's distance with respect to each pixel.

C2846.name: two-dimensional plane
C2846.definition: A two-dimensional plane is a plane onto which points in a three-dimensional scene are projected in the pixel processing stage of hidden surface removal.

C2847.name: walking
C2847.definition: Walking is a navigation technique used within an information point.

C2848.name: Majuli multimodal archive
C2848.definition: The Majuli multimodal archive is a multimodal archive that consists of regular images, 360-degree images, and videos for indigenous architectural heritage of satras (Vaishnavite monasteries) and village life, 3D models for landscape and architecture, 2D drone shots for landscape, flora, and fauna, 2D videos for intangible cultural heritage, and textual descriptions.

C2849.name: regular image
C2849.definition: A regular image is one of the image types in a multimodal archive.

C2850.name: multimodal content
C2850.definition: Multimodal content is content in an application that includes several different media types.

C2851.name: static image
C2851.definition: A static image is a simple image whose rendering involves lower computational requirements than rendering rich interactive multimodal content.

C2852.name: storage and retrieval support
C2852.definition: Storage and retrieval support is fast support required for real-time realistic interactive rendering of rich, interactively changeable multimodal content.

C2853.name: real-time interactive rendering
C2853.definition: Real-time interactive rendering is the rendering of rich multimodal content that can be interactively changed, including videos and animations, and it requires fast storage and retrieval support and has a high computational requirement.

C2854.name: standalone computing device
C2854.definition: A standalone computing device is a computing device comprising a headset and handheld controllers, with its own processor and memory, and that does not need to be tethered to a fixed computer.

C2855.name: tethered
C2855.definition: Tethered is a connection to a fixed computer that a standalone computing device does not need.

C2856.name: fixed computer
C2856.definition: A fixed computer is a computer that a standalone computing device does not need to be tethered to.

C2857.name: high-end graphics workstation
C2857.definition: A high-end graphics workstation is a high-end platform with good graphics processing unit (GPU) support that is typically used for render pipelines requiring a good amount of resources.

C2858.name: computing power
C2858.definition: Computing power is a quantity that a device has, and when it is lower, an application may require optimization to reduce computations and memory access.

C2859.name: storage
C2859.definition: Storage is the space in an XR system required to store data, and it can be reduced by storing data in the cloud rather than locally.

C2860.name: application
C2860.definition: An application is the top layer in a Unity layered architecture.

C2861.name: computation
C2861.definition: Computation is an application-related activity, including memory access, that can be reduced by reducing the application's size.

C2862.name: memory access
C2862.definition: Memory access is an associated computation of an application that is reduced when the application's size and rendering requirements are reduced.

C2863.name: rendering requirement
C2863.definition: A rendering requirement is a requirement that is reduced, along with associated memory access, when the size of an application is reduced.

C2864.name: cloud computing
C2864.definition: Cloud computing is a computing concept used in scalable and affordable extended reality systems for resource optimization, with videos stored in the cloud and loaded from the cloud rather than stored locally.

C2865.name: cloud-based video loading optimization
C2865.definition: Cloud-based video loading optimization is an optimization that stores videos in the cloud and loads them when selected, rather than storing them locally, reducing storage and data-access requirements. It requires high bandwidth support, network coverage, and minimal latency to load high-quality videos in real time.

C2866.name: data-access requirement
C2866.definition: A data-access requirement is a requirement that can be reduced by loading data from the cloud rather than storing it locally.

C2867.name: computational reduction
C2867.definition: Computational reduction is a reduction in computation that corresponds to a reduced application size on a client device.

C2868.name: cloud server
C2868.definition: A cloud server is a server that a cloud-based video-loading optimization relies on to load high-quality videos in real time.

C2869.name: bandwidth
C2869.definition: Bandwidth is a requirement, together with network coverage and minimal latency, for cloud-based video-loading optimization to load high-quality videos in real time.

C2870.name: network coverage
C2870.definition: Network coverage is a network connectivity requirement, together with high bandwidth and minimal latency, for cloud-based video-loading optimization to load high-quality videos in real time.

C2871.name: network connectivity
C2871.definition: Network connectivity is a requirement for cloud-based video-loading optimization, involving high bandwidth support, network coverage, and minimal latency to load high-quality videos in real time.

C2872.name: cardboard virtual reality headset
C2872.definition: A cardboard virtual reality headset is a low-cost cardboard housing for a smartphone that, when the smartphone displays stereoscopic views and the housing is worn as a headset, provides an immersive environment without an expensive headset.

C2873.name: optimization strategy
C2873.definition: An optimization strategy is used to adapt a virtual reality system deployment when the full system's size and associated computation exceed what average smartphones typically support, for example by compressing images and removing video playback support.

C2874.name: image compression
C2874.definition: Image compression is an optimization technique used to reduce the storage requirements of images and address computational issues in immersive experiences.

C2875.name: storage requirement
C2875.definition: Storage requirement is a virtual-reality system requirement that can be reduced by compressing images and removing video playback support.

C2876.name: cloud-based service
C2876.definition: A cloud-based service is one of the approaches to address computational issues associated with rendering immersive experiences, and it could allow video playback to be retained.

C2877.name: compression technique
C2877.definition: Compression technique is one of the approaches to address computational issues associated with rendering immersive experiences.

C2878.name: device
C2878.definition: A device is used to run and deploy immersive virtual reality and marker-based AR applications, receive builds over USB, and perform rendering.

C2879.name: unity editor interface
C2879.definition: The unity editor interface is essentially an integrated development environment whose menu options provide developers the features required to build and deploy a system, and it allows developers to build and deploy realistic immersive environments without having to master and implement the computer graphics pipeline.

C2880.name: object definition
C2880.definition: Object definition is a part of the computer graphics pipeline.

C2881.name: lighting effects
C2881.definition: Lighting effects are part of the computer graphics pipeline.

C2882.name: cross-platform
C2882.definition: Cross-platform is used to describe a game engine.

C2883.name: Unity Technologies
C2883.definition: Unity Technologies is the entity that initially released Unity.

C2884.name: mobile
C2884.definition: Mobile is one of the platforms supported by Unity.

C2885.name: Android-based mobile
C2885.definition: Android-based mobile is one of the platforms that Unity supports for two-dimensional and three-dimensional games or interactive content.

C2886.name: Apple's iOS mobile platform
C2886.definition: Apple's iOS mobile platform is one of the platforms that Unity supports for two-dimensional and three-dimensional games or interactive content.

C2887.name: Unity Game Engine
C2887.definition: Unity Game Engine is middleware and an interface that allows developers to build extended reality experiences or systems and deploy them on a specific platform.

C2888.name: integrated development environment
C2888.definition: An integrated development environment (IDE) is a menu-based environment that provides developers with the features required to build and deploy systems and is used to develop and compile scripts for customized experiences.

C2889.name: preference tab
C2889.definition: The preference tab is a tab in an editor interface that lets a developer select extended reality settings for virtual reality, mixed reality, and augmented reality.

C2890.name: scene view
C2890.definition: Scene view is the developer's interactive view that shows the scene being created in the Unity editor interface and lets the developer select, manipulate, and modify the game objects that together comprise the scene.

C2891.name: game view
C2891.definition: Game view is the final view in the Unity editor interface used to preview a developed scene, rendering the scene from the camera set by the developer to represent the final published or deployed application.

C2892.name: hierarchy window
C2892.definition: Hierarchy window is a part of the Unity editor interface.

C2893.name: inspector
C2893.definition: The inspector is a window in the Unity editor interface that is used to check variable values and scale a 3D model.

C2894.name: toolbar
C2894.definition: Toolbar is part of the Unity editor interface.

C2895.name: status bar
C2895.definition: A status bar is a part of the Unity editor interface.

C2896.name: project window
C2896.definition: The project window is a part of the Unity editor interface from which a prefab is dragged into a script component's My Prefab field.

C2897.name: console window
C2897.definition: Console window is part of the Unity editor interface.

C2898.name: game object
C2898.definition: Game object is a fundamental object in Unity that represents characters, props, or a scenario and acts as a container for components that implement its functionality, so its properties are given by adding components.

C2899.name: Unity asset
C2899.definition: A Unity asset is any item used in a Unity project to create an application. It can represent visual or audio elements and can be imported from outside Unity as a file or created inside Unity.

C2900.name: Unity project
C2900.definition: A Unity project is a project that can contain any number of Unity scenes, in which Unity assets are used to create an application.

C2901.name: unity script
C2901.definition: A unity script is a C# script that can be attached as a component to a game object to control its behavior, letting it trigger events, modify component properties over time, and respond to user input when the game runs.

C2902.name: Unity prefab
C2902.definition: A Unity prefab is a template created by configuring and storing a Unity game object, allowing a user to make instances of that game object in a Unity scene.

C2903.name: audio file
C2903.definition: An audio file is a file that can be imported from outside Unity as a Unity asset.

C2904.name: component
C2904.definition: A component is a Unity asset that can be added to a game object to implement part of the object's functionality or properties, and can be a built-in component type or a custom component created by scripting.

C2905.name: layer
C2905.definition: A layer is a part of a Unity project, and the number of layers can affect how many scenes the project contains.

C2906.name: scene interface
C2906.definition: A scene interface is a Unity interface used to create, edit, or modify a scene.

C2907.name: built-in component type
C2907.definition: A built-in component type is a component type that can be assigned to Unity game objects through the Unity editor interface.

C2908.name: custom component
C2908.definition: A custom component is a component that can be created using scripting application programming interfaces (APIs).

C2909.name: capsule
C2909.definition: A capsule is a primitive object type that can be created directly within Unity as a Unity game object.

C2910.name: cylinder
C2910.definition: Cylinder is a primitive object type that can be created directly within Unity as a Unity game object.

C2911.name: plane
C2911.definition: A plane is one of the primitive object types that can be created directly in Unity as a game object.

C2912.name: primitive object type
C2912.definition: A primitive object type is an object type that can be created directly within Unity as a Unity game object.

C2913.name: instance
C2913.definition: An instance is a Unity game object that a user can make in a Unity scene from a Unity prefab.

C2914.name: render pipeline support
C2914.definition: Render pipeline support is a graphics support offered by Unity that supports implementation of the entire render pipeline and lets users have customized control over individual pipeline stages.

C2915.name: render pipeline
C2915.definition: A render pipeline is a graphics pipeline that implements camera and view transform, lighting, meshes, materials, textures, shaders, and environment creation, and can be pre-built or custom.

C2916.name: view transform
C2916.definition: View transform is a part of the render pipeline that render pipeline support helps implement.

C2917.name: shader
C2917.definition: A shader is one of the elements of a render pipeline.

C2918.name: environment creation
C2918.definition: Environment creation is a part of render pipeline support that creates world scenes or world-coordinate-system scenes, special environments such as skies, and different visual effects.

C2919.name: world scene
C2919.definition: World scene is a form of environment creation in a render pipeline, specifically world-coordinate-system scene creation.

C2920.name: world-coordinate-system scene creation
C2920.definition: World-coordinate-system scene creation is a type of environment creation included in the render pipeline.

C2921.name: sky
C2921.definition: Sky is a special environment that is part of environment creation in a render pipeline.

C2922.name: visual effect
C2922.definition: Visual effect is a part of render pipeline support and can be applied to the camera, game objects, light sources, and other elements of a game.

C2923.name: pre-built render pipeline
C2923.definition: A pre-built render pipeline is a render pipeline provided by Unity, rather than a custom render pipeline created using Unity's scriptable render pipeline APIs.

C2924.name: built-in render pipeline
C2924.definition: Built-in render pipeline is one of Unity's pre-built render pipelines, with limited customization options.

C2925.name: Universal Render Pipeline
C2925.definition: The Universal Render Pipeline (URP) is a pre-built Unity render pipeline that provides a quick and easy way to customize graphics and create optimized graphics across a wide range of platforms, while the pipeline implementation takes care of pipeline-implementation optimization to some extent so resource requirements are minimized.

C2926.name: High Definition Render Pipeline
C2926.definition: High Definition Render Pipeline (HDRP) is a pre-built, customizable Unity render pipeline that is intended to create high-fidelity, photorealistic graphics, but typically requires substantial resources and is meant for high-end platforms.

C2927.name: custom render pipeline
C2927.definition: A custom render pipeline is a render pipeline that can be created by a developer using Unity's scriptable render pipeline APIs.

C2928.name: scriptable render pipeline application programming interface
C2928.definition: Scriptable render pipeline application programming interface is an application programming interface that a developer can use to create a custom render pipeline.

C2929.name: high-end platform
C2929.definition: A high-end platform is, for example, a high-end graphics workstation with good graphics processing unit (GPU) support, for which a high-definition render pipeline is typically meant.

C2930.name: model file
C2930.definition: A model file is a file that represents a three-dimensional object by containing data on its shape and appearance, and may contain mesh, material, and texture data, as well as animation-related data if the object is an animated character.

C2931.name: animation data
C2931.definition: Animation data is data in a model file that is included when the object represented by the file is an animated character.

C2932.name: model file format
C2932.definition: Model file format is a standard or proprietary format for models that can be imported into Unity and made to work.

C2933.name: fbx file format
C2933.definition: Fbx file format is one of the model file formats supported by Unity for importing models.

C2934.name: dae file format
C2934.definition: Dae file format is one of the model file formats that Unity supports for importing models.

C2935.name: dxf file format
C2935.definition: The dxf file format is a model file format.

C2936.name: obj file format
C2936.definition: The obj file format is a model file format that can be imported into Unity.

C2937.name: graphics primitive
C2937.definition: A graphics primitive is, in Unity, mainly a three-dimensional mesh, with triangulated or quadrangulated polygonal meshes supported.

C2938.name: quadrangle
C2938.definition: Quadrangle is a polygon used in quadrangulated polygonal meshes.

C2939.name: mesh rendering workflow
C2939.definition: Mesh rendering workflow is a Unity workflow in which a mesh renderer takes geometry from a mesh filter and renders it at the position defined by a game object's transform component.

C2940.name: mesh renderer
C2940.definition: Mesh renderer is a renderer that takes geometry from the mesh filter and renders it at the position defined by the game object's transform component.

C2941.name: mesh filter
C2941.definition: A mesh filter is a part of a mesh rendering workflow from which the mesh renderer takes geometry.

C2942.name: transform component
C2942.definition: Transform component is a component of a game object that defines the position used by a mesh renderer to render geometry.

C2943.name: tiling information
C2943.definition: Tiling information is information included in a material's description of how an object's surface should be rendered.

C2944.name: color tint
C2944.definition: A color tint is a piece of information included in a material to specify how an object's surface should be rendered.

C2945.name: bitmap image
C2945.definition: A bitmap image is an image applied over a mesh surface as a texture to assign basic color and many other aspects of a material's surface, such as reflectivity and roughness.

C2946.name: roughness
C2946.definition: Roughness is one of the aspects of a material's surface that textures can represent.

C2947.name: scene creation
C2947.definition: Scene creation is a process that involves transferring objects from local coordinates to world coordinates and using tools to create or modify environmental features.

C2948.name: terrain tools preview package
C2948.definition: The terrain tools preview package is a package that provides additional functionality on top of the built-in terrain features in the Unity editor.

C2949.name: terrain features
C2949.definition: Terrain features are built-in features in the Unity editor.

C2950.name: tree editor
C2950.definition: The tree editor is a Unity editor tool that lets developers design trees directly in the editor.

C2951.name: speedtree toolkit
C2951.definition: Speedtree toolkit is a toolkit supported by the latest Unity version in place of the Tree Editor.

C2952.name: skybox
C2952.definition: A skybox is a sky background that a camera draws before rendering a frame, made as a cube with different textures on its faces to create the feel of a 360-degree environment and rendered at the back.

C2953.name: light direction
C2953.definition: Light direction is the direction of light that developers can specify for realistic lighting on game objects.

C2954.name: light color
C2954.definition: Light color is the color of a light that developers can specify for realistic lighting on game objects.

C2955.name: real-time shadow
C2955.definition: A real-time shadow is a shadow that can be rendered using shadow mapping to support realistic lighting on game objects.

C2956.name: shadow mapping
C2956.definition: Shadow mapping is used to render real-time shadows for realistic lighting on game objects.

C2957.name: halo effect
C2957.definition: The halo effect is a visual effect that creates light areas around light sources, typically to give the impression of small dust particles in the air.

C2958.name: lens flare effect
C2958.definition: Lens flare effect is a visual effect that simulates the way lights refract inside a camera lens.

C2959.name: line renderer effect
C2959.definition: Line renderer effect is a visual effect that takes an array of two or more points in 3D space and draws a straight line between those points, allowing anything from a simple straight line to a complex spiral to be drawn.

C2960.name: camera component
C2960.definition: A camera component is a component that is added to a game object to create a camera.

C2961.name: directx
C2961.definition: DirectX is a major native graphics library supported by Unity, primarily in the Windows environment.

C2962.name: windows environment
C2962.definition: The windows environment is the environment in which DirectX is primarily used.

C2963.name: metal
C2963.definition: Metal is a major native graphics library supported by Unity for Apple systems.

C2964.name: apple systems
C2964.definition: Apple systems are the systems for which Unity supports the Metal native graphics library.

C2965.name: graphics application programming interface
C2965.definition: A graphics application programming interface is an application programming interface that accesses native graphics library application programming interfaces.

C2966.name: default graphics application programming interface
C2966.definition: A default graphics application programming interface is a Unity graphics application programming interface that accesses native graphics library application programming interfaces.

C2967.name: player settings editor interface
C2967.definition: The player settings editor interface is an editor interface opened through Edit Project Settings and used to select the Player category, navigate to Other Settings, and check the AutoGraphics API option.

C2968.name: edit project settings
C2968.definition: Edit project settings is used by a developer to open the Player Settings editor interface.

C2969.name: player category
C2969.definition: The player category is a category in Unity's Player Settings editor interface that is selected to navigate to Other Settings, where the AutoGraphics API option is checked.

C2970.name: other settings
C2970.definition: Other settings is a part of the Player Settings editor interface used to check the AutoGraphics application programming interface (API) option.

C2971.name: autographics application programming interface
C2971.definition: Autographics application programming interface is an option in Unity Player Settings that, when checked for a platform, makes a player build include a set of built-in graphics application programming interfaces and use the appropriate one at runtime; when unchecked, Unity's editor selects the first supported graphics application programming interface in the list of graphics application programming interfaces.

C2972.name: unity player build
C2972.definition: A unity player build is a build that, when the AutoGraphics API option is checked, includes built-in graphics APIs and uses the appropriate one at runtime.

C2973.name: built-in graphics application programming interface
C2973.definition: A built-in graphics application programming interface is one of a set of graphics application programming interfaces included in a Unity player build when the AutoGraphics application programming interface option is checked, with the appropriate one used at runtime to produce the best-case scenario for a platform.

C2974.name: Unity physics engine
C2974.definition: The Unity physics engine is a physics engine that simulates physical laws in a project so that objects correctly accelerate and respond to collisions, using rigid bodies, colliders, joints, physics articulation, and character controllers to give a realistic feeling.

C2975.name: rigid body
C2975.definition: A rigid body is a physics component that, when attached to a game object, allows the object to respond to gravity, so falling or bouncing from a surface appears realistic.

C2976.name: collider
C2976.definition: A collider is a component in a physics engine that defines a game object's shape for physical collisions. It can be static, use primitive or mesh shapes, or be a trigger that other colliders pass through.

C2977.name: physics articulation
C2977.definition: Physics articulation is a Unity component that represents the overall movement of a structure or object comprising joints, with its articulation body representing the joints as a constrained tree and automatically implementing joint constraints for realistic physics behavior.

C2978.name: character controller
C2978.definition: Character controller is one of the essential components included in the Unity physics engine to give a realistic feeling.

C2979.name: isKinematic property
C2979.definition: The isKinematic property is a property used with a Unity rigid body that can remove an object from physics engine control, allowing a script to move it kinematically and letting the developer choose whether it follows gravity.

C2980.name: primitive collider
C2980.definition: A primitive collider is a type of collider in Unity, such as a box, sphere, or capsule collider, that defines the shape of a game object for physical collisions.

C2981.name: box collider
C2981.definition: A box collider is a primitive collider in Unity that defines the shape of a game object for physical collisions.

C2982.name: sphere collider
C2982.definition: Sphere collider is one of the primitive collider types in Unity, used to define the shape of a game object for physical collisions.

C2983.name: capsule collider
C2983.definition: Capsule collider is one of the primitive collider types in Unity that define the shape of a game object for physical collisions.

C2984.name: mesh collider
C2984.definition: A mesh collider is a type of collider in Unity that is more processor-intensive but accurate.

C2985.name: static collider
C2985.definition: A static collider is a thing that can be added to a game object without a rigid body component to create motionless elements of a scene.

C2986.name: physics material
C2986.definition: A physics material is a Unity material that is used to configure the friction and bounce of a surface.

C2987.name: friction
C2987.definition: Friction is one of the things configured by physics materials in Unity for a surface.

C2988.name: bounce
C2988.definition: Bounce is one of the things that physics materials in Unity are used to configure for a surface, along with friction.

C2989.name: isTrigger property
C2989.definition: The isTrigger property is used in Unity to configure a collider as a trigger, so that the collider does not behave as a solid object and allows other colliders to pass through.

C2990.name: ball and socket joint
C2990.definition: A ball and socket joint is a kind of joint used to model the realistic movement of specific objects or characters, such as hips or shoulders.

C2991.name: skeletal joint
C2991.definition: A skeletal joint is an example of a joint that can be used to model the realistic movement of objects or characters.

C2992.name: articulation body
C2992.definition: An articulation body is a class or component that represents an articulation as a logical tree of joints, whose parent-child relationships reflect mutually constrained relative motion, and automatically implements joint constraints so a complex figure can move realistically without controlling each joint.

C2993.name: joint constraint
C2993.definition: A joint constraint is what the inbuilt support in an articulation body automatically implements, so a developer does not need to control each individual joint to make a complex figure move realistically.

C2994.name: logical tree
C2994.definition: A logical tree is a representation of an articulation body in which each node is a joint and each parent-child relationship reflects mutually constrained relative motion, so the relations and relative movements of the joints define the overall articulation.

C2995.name: parent-child relationship
C2995.definition: A parent-child relationship is a relationship in a logical tree of joints that reflects mutually constrained relative motion.

C2996.name: relative motion
C2996.definition: Relative motion is the mutually constrained motion between parent and child joints in an articulation body.

C2997.name: animation system
C2997.definition: An animation system is a system that supports importing, aligning, and previewing animation clips, retargeting humanoid animations, transitions and interactions between animations, and animating different body parts with different logics.

C2998.name: animation clip
C2998.definition: An animation clip is an animation in an animation system that can be imported, aligned, previewed, and used in transitions and interactions with other animations.

C2999.name: humanoid animation retargeting
C2999.definition: Humanoid animation retargeting is the ability to apply animations from one character model onto another.

C3000.name: character model
C3000.definition: A character model is a model used in humanoid animation retargeting, where animations are applied from one model to another.

C3001.name: audio sense
C3001.definition: Audio sense is supported in immersive experiences through dedicated components for audio perception and playback.

C3002.name: audio perception
C3002.definition: Audio perception is part of the support for the audio sense in immersive experiences, provided through dedicated components such as audio source, audio listener, and audio filters.

C3003.name: playback
C3003.definition: Playback is part of the audio sense in immersive experiences for which dedicated components are provided, including an audio source that lets an audio clip be played back when triggered.

C3004.name: audio source
C3004.definition: Audio source is the primary Unity component attached to a game object to make it play a sound, allowing an audio clip to be played back when triggered through a mixer, code, or by default.

C3005.name: audio listener
C3005.definition: Audio listener is a Unity component that listens to all audio playing in the scene and transfers it to computer speakers; all heard audio is with respect to its positioning, and by default only one should be in the scene, attached to the camera.

C3006.name: audio filter
C3006.definition: An audio filter is a Unity component that modifies the output of an audio source or the intake of an audio listener to generate various sound effects.

C3007.name: audio clip
C3007.definition: Audio clip is a standard audio file that can be played back by a Unity audio source when triggered.

C3008.name: mixer
C3008.definition: A mixer is one way a Unity audio source can be triggered to play back an audio clip.

C3009.name: scripting environment
C3009.definition: A scripting environment is the part of Unity that is used to develop and compile scripts.

C3010.name: package
C3010.definition: A package is software in Unity whose APIs are used, either as part of the installed Unity environment or imported to access platform-specific functions not included in Unity's built-in support.

C3011.name: Visual Studio
C3011.definition: Visual Studio is one of the integrated development environments that can be used to develop and compile scripts in Unity.

C3012.name: Visual Studio Code
C3012.definition: Visual Studio Code is one of the integrated development environments that Unity supports.

C3013.name: JetBrains Rider
C3013.definition: JetBrains Rider is one of the integrated development environments (IDEs) that Unity supports.

C3014.name: compile
C3014.definition: Compile is a step in Unity development, performed with an integrated development environment, in which scripts are compiled after using Unity and SDK functions and before building and deploying.

C3015.name: c-sharp
C3015.definition: C-sharp is an object-oriented programming language that Unity supports as its scripting language.

C3016.name: object-oriented programming language
C3016.definition: An object-oriented programming language is a kind of programming language, such as C#.

C3017.name: game event
C3017.definition: A game event is an event that a developer can trigger with a C# script attached as a component to a game object.

C3018.name: component property
C3018.definition: A component property is a property of a component that can be modified over time by a C# script attached to a game object in Unity.

C3019.name: project panel
C3019.definition: The project panel is a Unity panel in which the selected folder is where new C# scripts are created.

C3020.name: namespace component
C3020.definition: A namespace component is a component that a Unity C# script file begins with.

C3021.name: using statement
C3021.definition: A using statement is a part of a Unity C-sharp (C#) script file.

C3022.name: system.collections
C3022.definition: System.collections is a using statement in a Unity C# script file.

C3023.name: public class
C3023.definition: A public class is a class that a Unity C# script file defines, typically inheriting from MonoBehaviour and named the same as the file.

C3024.name: monobehaviour
C3024.definition: Monobehaviour is a class from which a public class in a Unity C-sharp script file is typically inherited.

C3025.name: start function
C3025.definition: A start function is an initialization event function in a Unity script that is called as the starting point whenever the script is called.

C3026.name: update function
C3026.definition: An update function is a Unity script function that is called in each frame.

C3027.name: frame
C3027.definition: A frame is a successive point in a sequence of execution and rendering, at which update functions are called and coroutines can continue.

C3028.name: vector3
C3028.definition: Vector3 is a data type that represents the position of a three-dimensional point by storing three coordinates as three elements of a vector.

C3029.name: data type
C3029.definition: Data type is used in Unity scripts, for example Vector3, which represents a 3D point position, and homogeneous data types can be used in for each loops over arrays or collections.

C3030.name: three-dimensional point
C3030.definition: A three-dimensional point is a position represented by three coordinates stored as the three elements of a vector.

C3031.name: coordinates
C3031.definition: Coordinates are stored as three elements of a vector to represent the position of a three-dimensional point.

C3032.name: unity hub editor
C3032.definition: Unity hub editor is an editor in Unity on which a developer can check variable values in the Inspector interface.

C3033.name: variable value
C3033.definition: A variable value is a value that a developer can check in the Inspector interface on the Unity Hub editor.

C3034.name: debug.log function
C3034.definition: The debug.log function is a function in a Unity script that prints a message to console output, which can be seen after running the game or application or after the script has been executed.

C3035.name: console output
C3035.definition: Console output is where a message printed by a script can be seen after a game or application is run or the script is executed.

C3036.name: Destroy function
C3036.definition: Destroy function is a function in Unity's MonoBehaviour class that destroys a game object from the scene after a specified delay, typically in seconds.

C3037.name: MonoBehaviour class
C3037.definition: The MonoBehaviour class is a class in Unity's scripting environment under which the Destroy function comes.

C3038.name: prebuilt function
C3038.definition: A prebuilt function is a function used in Unity scripts that is critical for making a script work.

C3039.name: user-defined function
C3039.definition: A user-defined function is a function that is defined by the user, rather than prebuilt, and is typically part of a good script.

C3040.name: event function
C3040.definition: An event function is a Unity function that Unity activates in response to an event during gameplay, passing control to it so its body executes and then returning control to Unity.

C3041.name: gameplay event
C3041.definition: A gameplay event is an event in Unity that has an event function, commonly a regular update, initialization, graphical user interface (GUI), physics contact, or trigger-related event.

C3042.name: regular update event
C3042.definition: A regular update event is one of the common gameplay events.

C3043.name: FixedUpdate function
C3043.definition: The FixedUpdate function is one of Unity's regular update event functions.

C3044.name: LateUpdate function
C3044.definition: The LateUpdate function is one of the regular update event functions in Unity.

C3045.name: initialization event
C3045.definition: An initialization event is one of the common Unity gameplay events.

C3046.name: Awake function
C3046.definition: The Awake function is an initialization event function in common Unity gameplay events.

C3047.name: graphical user interface event
C3047.definition: A graphical user interface event is a Unity gameplay event whose event functions can be used to impose interactive behavior.

C3048.name: OnGUI function
C3048.definition: An OnGUI function is a graphical user interface (GUI) event function included among common Unity gameplay events.

C3049.name: OnMouseOver function
C3049.definition: The OnMouseOver function is one of the graphical user interface (GUI) event functions.

C3050.name: OnMouseDown function
C3050.definition: The OnMouseDown function is one of the graphical user interface event functions in Unity gameplay events.

C3051.name: physics event
C3051.definition: Physics event is a Unity gameplay event function that relates to contact being made or broken.

C3052.name: OnCollisionEnter function
C3052.definition: The OnCollisionEnter function is one of the Unity physics event functions that relate to contact being made or broken.

C3053.name: OnCollisionStay function
C3053.definition: The OnCollisionStay function is one of the common Unity physics event functions that relate to contact being made or broken.

C3054.name: OnCollisionExit function
C3054.definition: The OnCollisionExit function is one of the Unity physics event functions that relate to contact being made or broken.

C3055.name: physics-related event
C3055.definition: A physics-related event is a Unity gameplay event function that is called when a collider is configured as a trigger.

C3056.name: OnTriggerEnter function
C3056.definition: The OnTriggerEnter function is a Unity physics-related event function that is called when a collider is configured as a trigger.

C3057.name: OnTriggerStay function
C3057.definition: The OnTriggerStay function is one of the other physics-related Unity gameplay event functions that are called when a collider is configured as a trigger.

C3058.name: OnTriggerExit function
C3058.definition: The OnTriggerExit function is a Unity physics-related event function that is called when a collider is configured as a trigger.

C3059.name: realistic behavior
C3059.definition: Realistic behavior is behavior that can be imposed by event functions, such as physical behavior in physics-event functions and interactive behavior in graphical user interface event functions.

C3060.name: physical behavior
C3060.definition: Physical behavior is a kind of realistic behavior that can be imposed in Unity's physics-event functions.

C3061.name: physics-event function
C3061.definition: A physics-event function is a Unity event function that can be used to impose physical behavior.

C3062.name: graphical user interface event function
C3062.definition: A graphical user interface event function is an event function that can be used to impose interactive behavior.

C3063.name: instantiation
C3063.definition: Instantiation is used at runtime with a prefab, where the script needs a reference to that prefab and the prefab is attached to a script component in the editor.

C3064.name: reference
C3064.definition: A reference is what a script needs to instantiate a prefab at runtime.

C3065.name: if-else statement
C3065.definition: An if-else statement is a standard conditional statement supported by a scripting environment.

C3066.name: loop
C3066.definition: A loop is a scripting-environment construct that executes a loop body under a loop condition, with entry-controlled loops checking the condition before the body and exit-controlled loops checking the condition after at least one execution.

C3067.name: entry-controlled loop
C3067.definition: An entry-controlled loop is a type of loop in a scripting environment in which the loop condition is checked before the loop body executes.

C3068.name: exit-controlled loop
C3068.definition: An exit-controlled loop is a loop in a scripting environment whose body executes at least once and whose condition is checked after the loop body executes.

C3069.name: for loop
C3069.definition: A for loop is an entry-controlled loop in a scripting environment that checks the loop condition before the loop body executes.

C3070.name: while loop
C3070.definition: A while loop is an entry-controlled loop in a scripting environment whose loop condition is checked before the loop body executes.

C3071.name: loop condition
C3071.definition: A loop condition is the condition in a loop that is checked either before the loop body executes, in entry-controlled loops, or after the loop body executes, in exit-controlled loops.

C3072.name: loop body
C3072.definition: The loop body is the part of a loop that executes; in for and while loops the loop condition is checked before it executes, and in do-while loops it executes at least once before the condition is checked.

C3073.name: do-while loop
C3073.definition: A do-while loop is an exit-controlled loop in a scripting environment, in which the loop body executes at least once and the loop condition is checked after the loop body executes.

C3074.name: for each loop
C3074.definition: A for each loop is a loop that can be used for arrays or collections of homogeneous data types, allowing the programmer to work with the collection directly instead of dealing with individual data types.

C3075.name: array
